I love every aspect of this game. The gameplay, most importantly, is top-notch. It's easy to learn and hard to master, and there's a ton of tactical choices that give it depth. I can't say much more about that; if you are a fan of classic turn based shooting games like Scorched Earth, Tank Wars or Worms, this is definitely going to be up your alley.
The animation is quirky and the graphics are colorful, which helps to make the unique setting feel upbeat and fun despite it being basically a post apocalyptic dystopia, which could've very easily been presented as bleak and desperate. This helps the game feel lighthearted and enjoyable even when you're getting your rusty metal♥♥♥♥♥kicked.
That brings me to the challenge level; it can be as hardcore as you want it to be or nice and easy if you're not too serious of a gamer. However regardless of what mode you choose, the game is generally pretty fair. Enemies can sometimes spawn near you but only at doors, so you know where they'll be coming from. Also they can't attack on the first turn they appear. This prevents the game from cheap-shotting you; you've always got time to adjust your strategy when something new comes up.
Overall I think this is really worth a try and is definitely one of the best indie games I've played in a while.

The description of "Mad Max meets FTL" is accurate - this game felt very much like the awesome FTL but with more freedom to choose my path as my convoy trundled along the desert wastes. There are a bazillion pop-culture references which add a sense of humour but also detract slightly from the consistency of the world, and the randomness can work both for and against you - I died very quickly on my first attempt but on my second I managed to win a drone in a "guess what's behind the door" puzzle which allowed me to destroy everything I met for the rest of the game... but I doubt I'll be so lucky if I have a third attempt. For now, I'm going to move onto the other zillion games in my Steam library and if I feel the urge for a sci-fi tactical rogue-like... then I'll play FTL instead. Also, some of the language and scenes in the game made it very unsuitable for small children (which wasn't immediately obvious) - shame, because if those weren't in it the playing audience would be much bigger.

God Mode překvapil. God Mode je poměrně lehká střílečka (co se týče pochopení), běžíte, střílíte, sbíráte bonusy. To je asi tak vše co v této hře děláte. God Mode je poměrně repetetivní, ale pokud máte kamarády s kterými hrát, na několik hodin zabaví, protože jeho zajímavý systém "test of faiths" zaručí, že každá hra bude mírně jinačí a ze začátku bude překvapovat.
Systém spočívá v tom, že každý "maze" je rozdělen na pár částí a v každé části aktivujete "test of faith" který vyvolá náhodný event. Nemusí být vžd na vaší straně, jsou tu pozitivní eventy i negativní eventy. A to zapříčiňuje tomu že každý maze se bude vyvíjet trochu jinak.
Škoda avšak je že ve hře je málo map. Až každou projedete (jedno na jakou obítžnost) tak už v podstatě nebudete mít co dělat. Žádný komunitní obsah, nové mapy nebudou. Slyšel jsem že devs zbankrotovali a tak je tato hra oficiálně mrtvá.
Jde vidět že devs chtěli do hry dát mnohem víc, protože je tam až nechutně hodně upgradů a skillů na odemčení a přitom jen pouhých pět map, kdy jednu dohrajete cca za 30 min (Bronze difficulty). Takže to je škoda.
Dalším obrovským problémem je matchmaking, pokud nemáte kamaráda/y co by s vámi hráli, musíte se smířit s faktem, že budete hrát jen solo. Matchmaking systém je naprosto neschopný a nenajde nic.
A ještě jednou k pozitivním věcem. Líbí se mi ten humor a zvláštní nápad. Vojáčci co pobíhají po mytologickém prostředí a přitom brutálními zbraněmi drtí mytologické příšery. Líbí se mi variace, nepřátel je několik druhů. Bossové jsou avšak docela nezajímavý. Ve hře je také bestiář, takže si můžete každou stvůru prohlédnout, přečíst si  o ní jednu-dvě věty a pak se s ní utkat v praxi. Zbraní je taky dost a každá se ještě dá upgradovat. Máme tu také abilities, ovšem upgradovatelné. A aby se to ještě dokořenilo, máme tu i kosmetické předměty. Kloboučky, helmičky, brejličky a tvářičky. Vše odemknutelné skrz herní gold takže žádné mikro-transakce nejsou nutné.
Co se týče ceny, je jen 6,99€ momentálně. Což je obsahu docela odpovídající.

Closure is a solid little puzzle game with unique mechanics, excellent atmosphere, and some truly challenging puzzles. It can be unforgiving, small missteps making a level un-winnable, and the physics occasionally uncooperative, but a quick reset button and generally short levels curb the frustration.
The unique light mechanics make for some wonderful puzzles, and the art design complements them well. Certainly though, the music in the game caught me by surprise. It works perfectly for the puzzles. With its wide variety of ambiance, Closure's soundtrack has become one of my favorites.
The dev commentary is also a nice little addition that I wish I saw more often in games.
In any case, I definitely recommend this game for anyone who enjoys a good puzzle.

Opinion after six hours EA from OpenTTD addict:
I really like the potencial this game has to be the "next openttd". I like the rail grid system and general theme feeling. Also multiple currecies and economy model with station/industry upgrades are interesting.
It's reasonable stable -- I got only one crash in six hours during alt-tab.  But it's still somewhat empty during this stage of development. Also reasonable performance even with moderate number of trains (around 100).
What do I miss the most are any macro management features as duplicate train, any sort of train group management as mass replacing vehicles, mass change of orders and automatic placement of signals with some interval. But I think taht developers will add these in the future. It gets really tedious micromanagement exercise pretty soon.
I would really appreciate better support for separate drop & pickup stations, because atm I did not discover any way of disabling product buildup on drop station. Ability to disable what products are flowing to which station would be great - one way would be through station ui, other is ttd way don't put anything on station till first train with appropriate vagons comes.
Also advanced signaling would be nice -- at least entry&exit (&combo) which should be relatively easy to implement on top of current block signals (compared to implementing PBS).
Overall this game gives reasonable amount of fun at current state for current price but as an openttd addict I feel like playing with my hands tied because of mentioned missing tools.

Lovin' it!  Works OK so far, had a crash when changing graphics and a few in-game.  The transition from the planning/building map to a beautiful 3D map is seamless.  Remember you'll likely need to select your main video card as it started as default on my onboard one.

Gameplay is intuitive (the signals are a bit clunky though) and station detail icons need some work, especially the passenger one where they all look like male lab-coated physicians.
Biggest missing piece is that there are no people, not birds, no animals.  It's a beautiful but dead world.
I am excited to see how this grows and improves - it's clearly a labor of love, so lets hope it's not bought out by a big name company, renamed, re-sold, and fixed, for twice the price.   If you enyoy train games, just get it.

This is a fun train game that stands on it's own - it's not OTTD2, it's not RRT4, it's not RailRoads 2 or Train Fever 3. If you approach it as a new game with new systems to learn, you'll really enjoy it.
The economy is absract, so you won't be making $10M dollars a year, instead you'll make cash, wood, coal, and steel tokens to spend on buildings, trains, maintenance, and track. It's a really interesting and fun dynamic.
The scale and signals can be a little confusing at first, but once you grasp the unique concepts of the game it becomes a lot easier and very fun.
The game in the current state (launch day) does limit you to two of the seven eras. The additional eras are yet to come in EA development, along with Multiplayer and many other improvements. This was the most disappointing aspect of the game for me. This does not stop you from playing - you can go on indefinitely - but it does stop the advancement of technology and missions. There's still a lot of fun in running your trains and expanding your network.
If you played Transport Fever and managed to get over the fact that the economy in that game is unique, you'll love Mashinky. If not... well you'll still probably love Mashinky but you'll have to give it some time.
It's like a TTD blast from the Past, It's a tad buggy but so far quite enjoyable..  Can't wait to see what else is in store for this game in the future!

I saw this on a top ten scariest games list so I decided to give it a go.
Condemned: CO does have atmosphere that is immersive and mildly creepy (complemented by a gloomy soundtrack). This is the strongest aspect of the game and it is this, along with the semi-engaging story (with the hope for a satisfying ending or something that could conjure an interesting idea), that compelled to me play through to the end.
After it was all over, I was ultimately dissapointed with this as a survival horror title. For one, there were no puzzles (which are a staple of the genre). Instead, you have fetch quests (i.e. find sledgehammer to break lock on door or find valve someplace to turn off steam). The fetch quests are not even difficult because the levels are fairly linear and you are not given the option to interact with many objects outside anything that can be used as a melee weapon.
The enemies (maybe with the exception of the mannequins in the department store), were not disturbing at all. And this is a major complaint for a survival horror game because it, unfortantely, bogged down the dread/scare factor quite a bit. Most of the time, you'll encounter hobos running at or away from you with x melee weapon. To the game's credit, there are well executed jump-scares at times, but for the most part you see it coming (even when they are hiding behind a wall with one arm clearly hanging out).
Combat system is clunky, as it should be in this type of game, but becomes repetitious after awhile. Thus, it doesn't feel clunky anymore and engagments with enemies felt more like busywork instead of terrifying encounters. The melee weapons do vary in damage and speed but the technique (block, hit, hit, repeat) remained the same. Occasionally you can find a firearm to spice things up a bit but primarily you will be using a melee weapon.
When the story wrapped up, I was underwhelmed which was a shame because the set up was decent and had potential. This would've been forgivable if there were in-depth character examinations. Yes, you do learn about the characters but it's nothing extensive that makes you either connect with them or intrigues the mind. Thus, I had no desire to replay the game for the story/characters at all.
If you're a fan of atmospheric games and on the fence, then I would recommend getting it on discount because, for all its faults, it does have redeeming qualties that made me (somewhat) glad I played it. It's possible that you might find the experience more terrifying than I did because, after all, horror is subjective. However, if you are looking for a game on par with something like Amnesia in terms of horror, then I'd pass this one up.

This game is really good, the controls take a bit of getting used to, but then the game is a blast. It offers so much variety with the combos of classes and abilities, and really grabs the style of an old JRPG like Final Fantasy.

TL;DR: The game has a lot of features older games it pays homage to didn't have, it's very customizable for beginners or experts and if you like JRPGs and have needed a fix here on Steam, this game fits the bill perfectly. (If it's on sale there's no reason not to get this, if it's not  $10 is still a steal)
[Length - very good]: I'm 30 hours in and only 16% done with it. There's tons of sidequests, puzzles, monster hunting, treasure hunting, achievements, crafting and other challenge modes you can take on so there is a ton of more time to put into the game. I forgot to add they've got an expansion and full-on sequel in the works.
[Soundtrack - bad]: My only negative is that the music can be a little grating because certain notes are too high or off key. I don't hate it by any means but I can see it being really annoying to people who are sound sensitive. (You can turn off the music at least)
[Characters - good]: You get to pick from 8 classes, multiple of the same class can be chosen, and each one has a unique purpose as well as being able to upgrade to a more advanced form. There's custom stat placement, skill trees and of course equipment to choose from.
[Story - good]: I can't give a real score for this yet since I'm not too far in, but it's keeping me interested to find out more so that's a plus. As a side note- Depending on your party choices, the results of events in the story change.
[Combat - good]: It's exactly like any other turn-based JRPG of old except for the macro option which makes killing trash while traveling somewhere go much faster.
[Difficulty - good]: It's entirely up to you how hard or easy you want the game to be and you can change the difficulty at any time from the in-game options.
[Graphics - average]: It is what it is, RPG Maker for one thing, but the content and execution is what makes RPGs so charming and the fact this game is trying to be a homage to old school games makes it justifiable.

The Good:
Tons of content, with more to come (devs are currently producing an expansion).  Scratches that ol' SNES Final Fantasy itch.  Non linear to a degree, if that's your thing.  Great stat allocation.
The Not-So-Good:
The map is monumentally awful.  Balance could be better, as if you're a grinder you can quite easily become so powerful that nothing but the Superbosses (and navigating the ludicrous map) present any real challenge.  Ending left me wanting, but that's likely down to taste.
Worth the purchase if you dig JRPGs, though, for sure.  I've spent almost a hundred hours interacting with this thing, and only now am I finding myself bored.  Looking forward to the new expansion.

After starting you are greeted with the same old 'Unity Personal Edition' splash screen that we all know and love. Within the first second of playing the game you can tell it's just another Unity Asset flip. The people who make these type of games shouldn't even call themselves "Developers". Typically Unity Asset flip games are just built using no effort whatsoever, they just pay 20 bucks to use premade models and code available on the unity store for use in the unity engine. It takes zero effort to plug and play these games into existence. They usually have no decent control schemes, absent developers, and very low prices. These prices may not sound like much, but a lot of people on steam just love spending money on cheap things to play, no matter how bad they are. The thing that sucks about that though is that due to the low low price of the game, and the mass amounts of people who have 99 cents to burn, these people actually make a crapton of money. For doing absolutely nothing.
If you were to play it I guarantee you too would be asking yourself "how the hell did this get on steam". Well, the answer is the steam community groups that offer similar games like this one for free and ask for greenlight votes in return. To better explain that, these 'developers' work alongside groups like Cubic Bundle and other no-effort steam groups to offer free copies of the games and in return ask for greenlight votes and whatnot for their next 'game'. It's all a big sham on both ends of the spectrum, they get to pump out more games, make more money, pay off the groups, while we get stuck with absolute garbage flooding steam, and people buying it up. It sucks that steam is allowing this kind of behavior, but sadly I don't think any of this will fix itself unless steam enforces and patrols greenlight themselves.
The game itself is horrible as well, just read the other reviews. There is no combat, or anything really implemented in it. You can jump and lift your arm up. No controls are listed in-game, the developers literally only made an announcement with them in it. There's no responses from the developers in the games discussion forums, and I'm glad that I got it for free just to write about it. It's literally just an empty shell of a game, and anyone interested in buying it should really look somewhere else. We shouldn't support this type of behavior on steam. Start going on greenlight and downing the garbage before all of the upvotes from people looking to get 'free games' makes it all seep up through the sewer grates and makes it into our store.

Let's get one thing straight: I'm a sucker for a novel premise. If a game brings forth something that I haven't seen, I've gonna play the game a lot. That's the biggest drawing point of this game - it takes the generic puzzle platformer and changes the mechanics of the game.
That being said, it has a lot of virtually soul-crushing moments, whether it's doing something blatantly wrong or 99% right with the 1% throwing you off the edge of a cliff. But that's what you buy a puzzle platformer like this for. You buy it for the mental and physical test, with willpower on top of it. This isn't Mario (farm 99 lives and blaze through most levels) and this isn't just a puzzle game.
It's a great package of art, music (startling moments of sound in game), and gameplay. It's short, but I'd definitely rank it pretty high on my list of games.

I was very curious about Convoy when I first found out about it, since I enjoy roguelikes, and the strategic vehicle combat seemed like a nice touch. I was lucky enough to get a review key for it, and after spending a bit more than 10 hours in the game, here are my thoughts:
The story is simple enough. Your spaceship has crashed, and you need parts for repairs, so you set out on an unknown planet to find the parts and get the spaceship operational again.
From the map view, you plan on where to go next, either to your quest markers, camps (for shopping, upgrading and resupplies), or random encounters marked at the map. The locations of all of these are random each time you start a game (although the map structure: roads/mountains etc is always the same), and what happens at each place will also differ.
Sooner or later, you'll get into combat, and this is where you'll spend most of the time in Convoy. You have a main vehicle to protect, and you use smaller escort vehicles that you can command and attack the enemies with. The strategy you have to use differs, depending on what weapons and special items/abilities you manage to find during each run. If you find lots of weapons and extra escort vehicles, it's easier going full out, while a run where you're not so lucky will make you take a more cautious approach.
The combat is show from an aerial view, and most of the time you're best off pausing the game, issuing commands, selecting and aiming special attacks/abilities, then unpause to see the chaos unfold. Battles normally last between 30 seconds and two minutes, depending on how well equipped you are, and how many enemies you encounter, so it's quite fast-paced, and you'll see many battles when playing the game.
Roaming the map, doing both main missions and sidequests, upgrading your vehicles and finding new ones can be a lot of fun. The upgrades are very basic, but together with the equippable weapons/abilities you can go for a certain approach, but towards the end of each game, chances are you've maxed many of the upgradeable skills for each vehicle, and swapped weapons/abilities for the best ones you could find during your run.
The random aspect of everything means you can't play the game the same time each run, you won't find the same things. One game I found no shields at all, and had to adjust how I engaged in battle according to that. This can sometimes be a bit frustrating, but as in all roguelikes, success isn't a guarantee.
One thing I enjoyed is all the pop culture references in the game. When you find different random encounters from the map, you will get a text conversation (no voice acting), where you'll often find something you might recognise from films, other games, books or TV shows. A nice touch that keeps you entertained.
I had lots of good fun with the game, but after a while, I got the feeling I've seen most of it. You get some persistent "upgrades" (choice of starting vehicles) after completing certain goals, and that makes you come back for more, to a certain extent. I would love to see more content, with even more options for returning players. A shop allowing you to tailor your starting convoy with exactly the vehicles and loadouts you wanted, where you would afford a more expensive convoy the more times you've played the game (with modifiers for difficulty, achievements etc) would have been very nice.
Still, it was a very enjoyable game, so if you know (or think!) roguelikes and strategic combat is your thing, you would probably enjoy your time with Convoy!

This free RPG punches above its weight with hilarious dialogue, standout music, and innovative combat.
This game satirizes early JRPGs. Occasionally those games would lampshade their own quirks, and I want to be clear that this game goes way beyond that. Basically every line of dialogue (from main characters to random townspeople) is story-relevant, funny, or both. The dialogue is the essential distinguishing element of the game.
The music is uniformly excellent- much better than should realistically be expected of a free game.
The combat system dispenses with common character-levelling mechanics and adopts a puzzle-like system in which success and failure rest on the player's skill alone. There's no XP or treasure to grind for, but you may need to practice combat to get past some challenging boss fights.
It's actually a really fun game to go around and talk to each NPC, the dialogue is really funny and well written.

If you enjoy playing RPG's, especially the ones of old, then as a random, wandering adventurer, I implore you to play this.
It's not the longest game, but that is more IN it's favor than not, as it does a great job of making you laugh, while keeping you entertained with it's mix of references, jokes, and (stratetgic) battles. I say stratetgic battles as this:
1. In your attack phase, connect as many foes in your 5 slide movement as you can, while keeping a similar combo, such as RED to RED or MAGE to MAGE. Each attack that follows this suit adds to your combo meter, causing the last foes in the chain to take quite a beating if your chain is 3 (2 damage) or at 6 (4 damage). Chaining is the only way to damage bosses. If you wipe out ALL the enemies in a single sweep (in that wave), the next wave appears, but does not get to attack.
2. In your Defense phase, all your enemies gang up on you, and you die. Unless you "casually cheat" and quickly memorize where they're about to hit, and dodge out of the way by hitting the correct "DODGE" panel(s). They attack in turn, with two moves being shown one after the other. So long as you pay attention (and have preschooler-level mouse moving skills), you'll have little issue with your evades. Every foe of a given type (grunt, heavy, mage, ect.) uses the same attack patterns, making it all the more of a "DOH" when you mess up a simple dodge, or forget what panels the archer is about to hit.
Outside of bosses, the most hp something can have is 4 (like you, for example). With a bit of quick thinking, a good 90% of the battles can be dealt with, without taking any risk of being hurt.
For the LOW, LOW PRICE OF FREE....

I originally played this on the XBox 360 when it was first released and decided to see how much better the PC version was, and I also wanted to play it again.
PC version is a solid 60 FPS even when I was streaming with almost no slowdown. Other than that, the graphics didn't seem any better than the 360 version. Keep in mind, this game is VERY old, and what I consider a classic. In its time, the graphics were pretty good, but it certainly has not aged well, so bare this in mind. The story for its time was very interesting and easy to follow with a satisfying ending.
Mouse and Keyboard controls are more effective than using a Controller, as FPS games tend to be. You rely more on melee weapons but guns are still useful, just limited in ammunition and you can't reload them, but you can use them as blunt weapons once you've run out of ammo until you find something better.
The game can be brutal and even on Normal you'll get hit hard at times, so it might be a bit of a challenge. On what is now my 3rd playthrough of this game total (1st two being on the 360), I beat it in 7 hours without going out of my way for the collectibles. It might take you 10 hours on your first playthrough, more if you intend to get as many collectibles as possible.
It's a satisfying experience and if you're not new to video games and just happened to miss this gem, or you enjoy Horror games and aged graphics don't bother you, I highly recommend this game. If you're new to games, don't really care for story, and/or Graphics mean a lot to you, eh, maybe look elsewhere.

Ok, so from what I've seen from screen shots and old gameplay videos CONDEMNED: CRIMINAL ORIGINS has pretty decent graphics even for today. However, I installed it on a laptop with an i7 4700 HQ and GTX 860 4GB and the result was a choppy slur. This game was created around 2000 so my only thought is that maybe my hardware may be too new and that the game wasn't optimized to use it. After dialing back the lighting effects I was able to get it to a playable level at the sacrifice of some precious eye candy.
Level design is on par with similar heavy hitting titles of the time such as fear and should sport graphics good enough to put up a decent fight with them. The story on the otherhand is... well lackluster. The game centers around a detective investigating a series of serial murders. That alone makes sense, but behind this the game is constantly putting emphasis on an occult background causing all of the madness. Don't hold your breath though, the game continually sends you on erands to advance and finish the serial killer plot but will never stop to explain the so called "event" behind it all. The closest you will get to understanding it will be in a final boss battle which... to be honest... doesn't get your heart pumping like any good fight should.
The mechanics of the game were pretty good and the AI did a fantastic job. Enemies would fight you, run away, then wait behind a wall for you to walk into just like a player would have done to the game. The game also has its fair share of jump scares aswell as an incredibly tension filled final location on par with that of DOOM 3 (You'll understand if you get there).
CONDEMNED: CRIMINAL ORIGINS took me exactly the length that will show up at the top of this review for my gameplay hours due to the fact that there is nill a reason to replay the game. Sure there are hidden objects in each level that unlock achievments, but those achievments don't unlock secrets nor do they link to actual achievments on steam.
Overall the game wasn't bad for a boring night with nothing to do. If you see it on sale for 2 or 3 dollars it is definitely something to look into.
My Final Score:
[Mehh...Good, but better for time travelers from 2001 that want to get this game cheaper than when it first came out.]

SteamWorld Heist accomplished everything a tactical platformer could do.
Your teammates are varied, as are the weapons and items. There's a very well
done sliding difficulty scale coupled with gradually increasing skills and powers
for your team. While I did feel a bit overwhelmed at first managing all the different
teammates, I eventually figured out each member's unique skill set. The soundtrack
was high-quality and delivered that steampunk vibe. The art and animation was both
nostalgic and beautiful (especially considering how small the development team was).
If you've got a few bucks, or if you picked this up in the last Humble Bundle like I did,
grab and copy or install the copy that's been sitting in your Steam library for the past few
weeks. I had a blast.
I finished the game in a bit over 20 hours, but if you don't repeat any of the missions I imagine
it could be done in half that time or quicker.
Pros:
Fun, tactical game with a Steampunk theme and soundtrack
Progressive experience (meaning you start weak and end strong,
as do the enemies).
Varied items and weapons, and HATS!
Cons:

Under Zero is supposed to be an Early Access survival game in arctic conditions. You're supposed to find a way to escape by activating the beacon. No surprise there, the achievement tells you that. However, getting anything done in the game is kind of a joke.
You walk around in the snow, with the ever present crunch crucnh of your boots as you plod along, hoping that the below zero temperatures will end your suffering. Unfortunately, they don't. While other people have obviously died, you are invincible. However, don't get stuck in a pit, because though you can survive long falls, and look inside wolves brains, you cannot jump or climb to save your life. Not that your life is in any danger, only one wolf seems able to kill you.
Story: Non-existent.
Sounds: Crunch crunch is what you'll hear most of the time. Unless the random wanna be creepy music kicks in suddenly... and then you'll still hear the crunch crunch but at a subdued volume. Wolves are totally silent. Walking up one set of wooden stairs, reveals that you're half a thief. One foot makes no noise and the other makes tons of noise. Mom always said, not to replace your limbs with stranger's body parts. Storms instantly kick in and instantly cease. There is no rise or fall in volume level.
Graphics: I have no idea what is going on here. While you're walking around, your arm sticks out.... The game is made up of square shapes for the most part, that sometimes overlap causing weird issues as the devs didn't bother to shorten them so they wouldn't stick through each other. While the SNOW is okay.... pretty much just really bad for everything else.
Gameplay: What gameplay? Try putting something heavy on your up arrow or w key and walking away then come back in a bit, you might have found a building. You cannot jump, though the config tool clearly shows a jump setting. You cannot crouch, so some items are impossible to retrieve. You have no cross hair option, so you have no idea if you're pointing at what you want and it just doesn't respond, or if you just can't interact with it. The controls themsevles are just a joke. There is nothing to tell you what they are, except the config tool at the beginning and even then, it doesn't cover everything. I have no idea how to make a fire either, though apparently T is the key for that. I'm not sure how I managed to fire my gun off, because I seemed to press buttons that didn't do antyhing before, but then suddenly I could shoot once I'd pressed H to get my rifle out. I have zero ideas how to select any other item in the inventory.
I've met 3 wolves. Only one apparently has teeth. Though the others jump at me, obviously they just want to lick my face while smiling very big because they are so adorable. You can see through their heads if you get close enough and face them. There is no map or anything. I could go on and on and on, but what's the point? In this case, it's just a really bad game and nothing works.
Oh, one other thing, if you go to settings in the menu, you can essentially choose graphic quality. Your choices are Standard, something else that sounds appropriate and Height.... wtf? I know they mean, High, but seriously?
Overall: 2/10 - At least it runs? Seriously, stay the hell away from this game. Don't even get it for free. Though it's advertised as Early Access, this is not even ready to be in that stage of development. This game needs a lot of work, and the dev is basically silent on the forums. Congratulations, people paid for your game and you stopped talking to them... that or you're just sitting there counting funds.
Do Not Get This Game.

What an entertaining little game! It's basically Settlers crossed with one of those casual strategy games Like the Rescue Team games (good games, get them!). You'll build your Greek empire and will unlock new buildings by accomplishing small tasks; some being easy like exploring a distant place or more complex like building temples and whatnot.
And the city simulation, even if 'casualized', is very detailed and developed for a small game. It will start really easy and will eventually end up close to Settlers - all simplified of course - with the food production buildings (wheat fields, cabbage farms, dairies, fishers, etc), storage buildings, schools, temples, dwellings, banks... And there’s even research to do! There are real production lines: wheat is transformed into flour and later into bread of it for example.
The gameplay (exploring new lands while constantly developing your city) will often be interrupted by random small events like lightning strikes, fires (you'll see all your people passing on water buckets to extinguish the flames!), workers strike (yup!), etc. There’s a small story with a lot of scripted events, all very lighthearted. You play a God noobie and are confronted to others, some friendly and others not. The game will become a bit challenging on the end, constantly rushing you to do a couple of things at the same time but there’s absolutely no time limit at all, you could be well play it all at the speed of a snail if you want, you won’t be penalized.
I was afraid of the game being old and thus becoming unstable but nope, no problem – except one thing: don’t alt-tab! The game froze when I did it. The bad: no choices to make or strategy to choose, the gameplay is pretty simple, straightforward and fully scripted: it is a casual strategy game, but instead of having 50 small levels, it’s one main huge level. Which brings us to no sandbox either, even though the game looks like one, you’ll always be guided (even forced) into making this or that. Also a consequence: no replayability. There’s a lot of achievements to make but sadly they’re not on Steam, which does removes the incentive of unlocking them (some even involve destroying your town!). The game lasts 5-6 hours.
But still, this game is terribly fun! I have already played this game eons ago outside of Steam and it was a blast to play it again. Yes, it’s amusing to play a God, use God powers, forget the time passing by and suddenly realize that it's morning already! :)

The game looks like an RTS, but it's not. You build your city, but there's no real challenge or losing conditions. Running out of food will make people protest. Enemies will wreak havoc, stopping a building's production. Aside from an in-game acievement for playing for x amount of hours without upsetting your people, there's no real repercussions for messing up.
The game consists of a single level which plays out linearly until the endgame grind for very expensive decorative buildings. It's fairly balanced, and playing normally the game will unlock new buildings as you need them. You can still completely break the tutorial by predicting tasks, though.
Is it a good game? Maybe not. But it is colorful, playable without sound, and easy to follow. If you've got a couple of bucks to spare and need something colorful and easy to follow while listening to a three hour podcast, this game serves perfectly well.

A nice little strategy/simulation where you take the role of a would-be Roman God. Your mission is to build a tribe from scratch and gain the favor of the other Gods by doing various (building / resource collecting / exploration) tasks for them, all the while protecting your tribe from Mars.
The game "forces" you to plan the construction of all buildings carefully, as you get limited space. Earning money is also fairly difficult at first. But as soon as you start expanding your territory, everything becomes much easier and more enjoyable. Even though collecting resources, trading, and investing in science (new buildings and abilities) is as basic as it can be, it still encourages you to keep playing and see what comes next.
Once you finish the game, there's literally nothing extra you can do, so the replayability factor is nonexistent. Still, All My Gods is a surprisingly relaxing and addictive experience that can provide you with several hours of pure, simple fun.

From this base, there is enough variation not to be bored along the way.
Please note that the atmosphere is very strange and gloomy in this game, which you may or may not like.
If you want a demo, I advise you to try the Flash prototype the devs published a long time ago at Newsground. The final game is slightly better and more refined iirc, but it should give you a taste.
The mechanic of "if it's not lit it doesn't exist" IS new and interesting, but not engaging enough for me to play for more than a few minutes.

Closure is a solid puzzle-platformer, hampered only slightly by its limited scope but aided by gorgeously stark visuals and moody score.
You play as a weird little spider thing that puts on masks of people's faces and traverses their memories (I assume, as there's no spoken dialogue). Platforms are only solid when a light source is illuminating them, and you manipulate a variety of these to create or remove terrain so you can reach the exit door in each stage. The mechanic is consistent, buta llittle finnicky -- terrain partially lit by orbs tends to create sloped edges or free-floating pixels of floor, which combined with slippery controls will kill you a few times. The most frustrating moments come from falling through a floor or wall after painstakingly setting up platforms in a 1-2 minute stage, because you weren't quite precise enough. But engine quirks come with the territory in indie platformers, so it's easily overlooked.
What makes Closure really work is the way the level chains are paced. It has over 100 levels, but cerebral puzzle-solving is broken up by stages that serve only to (literally) illuminate the backstory of the characters whose lives you're navigating. You only realize this as you're moving through it, and realize there's no puzzle beyond carrying the light to the exit and seeing the environment unfold ahead of you. It's a neat trick that made me want to keep playing in a way that an unbroken string of puzzles wouldn't have.
The game has some rough edges, but it's a very enjoyable playthrough if you like puzzle-platformers. Definitely recommend.

Last Dream is just...generic. If it had anything that stood out positively or negatively, this review would be much longer. You know that younger sibling or cousin of yours who tries to imitate a celebrity, only to get the most basic aspects of them down and nothing else, and then when you tell them their impression is inaccurate, they say, "It's totally spot on!" or something similar? This game is that younger sibling or cousin, and the celebrity it's trying so desperately to imitate is Final Fantasy. Just get a classic Final Fantasy game instead. There's like 6 to choose from.

Yes, this is clearly a game made in RPGMaker, which other titles have given a poor reputation, for good reason.
Despite that, there are so many things Last Dream gets right, that I would advocate it being worth $5-10.
1) The character selection is a clear callout to FF1, with designing a party of 4 from 8 very distinct classes. This makes for some thoughtful character development decisions as well a major contribution to improving the replayability of the game.
2) Character development... You have full control over how your level ups improve each individual stat. This does kinda encourage min-maxing, but in a very good way. Even your damage dealers gotta have something to provide defense.
3) The game is not afraid of hiding lots of valuable treasures away for people who want to look for them, in the form of side quests and a very open world map that encourages you to find these locations. This is kinda a double edged sword on balance/difficulty, but the main quest can only be made very easy by beating side quests that likely were much more difficult than the main quest to begin with.
4) The soundtrack is very full of variety and a whole bunch of excellent tracks... Many of which are recognizable by people who have snagged these tracks that are commonly freely available on the internet before. It's cheap, but it really is a solid implementation of doing with minimal resources.
5) Puzzles! In just about every dungeon in the game, there's at least 1 room with a different kind of puzzle that needs to be solved. This puzzle room is free of monster-spawning, and is completely optional, for the sake of getting more loot. For me, they struck a perfect balance between challenging and solveable.
6) Replayability: Learning all the tricks to the all the above ultimately leads to a major design decision the developer made. Lots of support/achievements for speed-running, accomplishing 100% of the side quests (there are a LOT), etc.
Some potential negatives that exist:
1) The game almost encourages you to go ahead and try and break the balance. To some, this is a system that works really well, and to others, well, that's understandable.
2) Pretty obvious reuse of a lot of RPGMaker graphical assets. Given the market for the game, I don't forsee this being much of an issue.
3) At one point of the main quest, you'll probably find yourself doing something that you don't want to do in order for the quest to proceed. (being ambiguous to avoid spoiler alert).

I especially hated the world map, and often I wouldn't know where to go. All in all, there's better RPG Maker games out there. Avoid this one.

- overall: recommended if you like party RPGs (or JRPGs)
- playtime: around 40 hours for a single playthrough on "normal", not finishing every single questline (but most of them). high replayability.
- story: at first it seems like an excuse for a hack'n'slash, but then it gets actually interesting, especially mid game. the final cutscene can be VERY annoying if it's late and you just want to finish the game and go to sleep. (it's a ~15 min cutscene).
- gameplay/combat: overall good, though some things are a bit unbalanced (thief's throwing stars, I'm looking at you). once you get the powerful abilities it gets a bit repetitive, since you just spam them and one-hit almost every non-boss. but I have to admit I was a bit overleveled by the endgame. other than that, bosses are (usually) a real challenge.
- gameplay/character progression: fantastic, you build them the way you want. LOTS of options, and not just "flavour" ones, every decission matters.
- level design: overall good. I didn't noticed anything annoying regarding it, so, that's a good signal. on the other hand, I'm not sure I liked the "flavoured" dungeons, e.g. the dread woods (was that one?), where it seems to be a perpetual storm. sure, it added immersion, but it was kinda difficult to see where you were going....
- puzzles: some of them are actually intelligent ones, but some of them are just a matter of skill (eg. run following a pattern). overall good. also, you can skip them if you want.
- graphics: they fit the game. but obviously, if you are looking for fancy 3D graphics (like skyrim's), then looks elsewhere. this game is not about graphics.
- bottom thoughts: maybe I haven't played anough JRPGs to make a better comparison, but it kinda reminded me of pokemon. It has that kind of replayability, sadly, my backlog is too huge to starti it again now. It will have to wait a bit. also, be sure to take a look at the manual/guide. I'm not saying you need to follow the walkthrough, but in some points, it's well worth it to take a look at where you are supposed to go next. else you could keep wandering around for some time.... or finish a dungeon before you were supposed to start it. (say, I got to the end of the marsh before getting the crystals... and the medallion wasn't there, lol. it was a difficult dungeon, so I ended up overleveled. but it was FUN to take such a high-level dungeon a few levels under the recommendation. maybe I need to try a higher difficulty on my next playthrough)

Another thing that seemed strange to me was the reload system, there is none. If you press the button R it just shows you how much ammo is left in the gun. Options 10/10
The game offers plenty of options to change the sound, graphics, difficulty. Unfortunately you can't change the fov ingame, you have to manualy go into the folder and change settings.

The gameplay is one of the most important parts of the game and this game got it perfectly, I didn't find a moment while playing where I was bored. As I stated earlier you are a detective so that means you get to do some detective work right? YEAH! Every time you find a clue you take out a different machine or device to catch fingerprints or dna samples which you send to your partner in crime, Rosa. Following up all the clues you start to wonder who the serial killer X really as. (It tells you at the end of the game.) This game took me 15 hours to complete without rushing and dying over and over xD
Final Verdict 8/10
This game is something else, a game not many people realize has potential. If you ever get the chance you should play it. I had a lot of fun and many raging moments in the game, but that's just me being a noob xD

Condemned is a first-person brawler with horror-ish setting and a hint of criminal investigation mechanics. Seeing the positive reviews and the fact it was developed by the same team that created one of my favorite games of all time: FEAR, I decided to give this game a try. Unfortunately Condemned turned out to be a quite disappointing and mostly dull experience.
Most of your time playing C:CO will be spent being engaged in a melee combat, so you would think developers would put extra thought into this part to make sure it is actually fun, yet it is not the case. The combat in Condemned it sluggish and clunky, to a point were it gets boring and annoying pretty fast, luckily it also doesn't require any special thought on normal difficulty. The biggest problem here is how little control you have over your swings and how slow they are - with bigger weapons you might start your attack on a completely open enemy, but then notice he takes a swing at you so much faster, so it would be better to block it - but you can't! Once the attack is in motion you have no choice but to observe it being played out, which is rather unfair considering your enemies are perfectly fine canceling their attacks (faking). Speaking of blocking, at first you might want to try and be clever about how you approach your enemies, by anticipating their attacks and blocking them (or "parrying" actually, since you can't hold the button down, you have to tap it), but you will soon find out it a very unreliable method - press the button too early or too late and your block will whiff; press at the right time, but your enemy has a bigger weapon and you will be damaged anyway. Also, your block becomes even more useless once you start encountering enemies in 2vs1 and 3vs1 situations. Add to that the fact that med-kits are quite common and it will quickly become apparent that the fastest and most reliable method is to just keep swinging till everything dies, while ignoring any damage dealt to you in the mean time. On the plus side, there are some occasional firearms here and there to make things more interesting - saving those 5 bullets (more or less) for head-shots is quite fun.
If instead of fighting you are more interested in Condemned's horror setting, then you need to know it is almost exclusively based on jump-scares and doesn't really try build any kind of tension. Maybe in one or two instances the developers tried to do something original, but most of the time it comes down to something jumping in your face. It also doesn't help that everything looks so blend, so rather than being scared, you will feel turned off by the low quality of the environments and, especially, the character models. Not to mention, for some reason, few significant cut scenes have their sound effects missing.
Finally, forget about doing any kind of real "investigation" - gathering evidence just comes down to pressing "X" when the game tells you to. Afterward you can't really even go anywhere, as you listen to the analysis results, so in the end the whole thing is nothing more than a nuisance.
Condemned: Criminal Origins might have been a decent game when it first came out, but by today's standards it unfortunately looks and feels like a budget game with almost nothing that would make it stand out of the crowd.

Let Monolith take you through a joyride with creepy atmosphere, scary visual effects that keep you on edge, a great story, and satisfying gameplay. Condemned Criminal Origins is a game where you play as FBI Detective Ethan Thomas who is framed by a serial killer for the deaths of his fellow officers. The only thing he can do is prove his innocence by tracking down the killer. But it's not a simple walk in the park, along the way you will fight violent civilians whose number has been growing in the city recently.
The enemies themselves are so scary because they seem like regular people from far away but every time you get close to take a swing you see their messed up demonic faces. It's really cool. The enemies kind of behave how I imagine crack heads would. They usually have a melee weapon with them but they can, if forced to, grab a weapon from the map. Combat is really satisfying as you can swing, block (which causes a stun if done successfully), and kick. It's kind of like Kirby games because you can get different weapons mid-level that you choose depending on your mood (except for the scary crack heads). There are also guns in the game. Both you and the enemy can use it. The guns are more like a Get out of jail free card because it usually kills an enemy with one shot. There's also a taser but it's similar to the gun because it makes things too easy (except for one situation).
The investigation scenes are also better than the ones in F.E.A.R. In F.E.A.R you are given more pieces to the puzzle of what is going on by pushing E on a computer and letting your friend talk about what you found. In this game you have to use forensic tools to find the clues rather than hit a simple button. For me it’s more satisfying to use the tools because you actually see the evidence and hear the results of its analysis.
Only con of the game is that your character walks SO SLOW. His sprint is as fast as a normal walking speed but it only lasts 5 seconds. This is bad for two reasons. One there are collectable birds and metal pieces that you can find in the level. How do you expect me to explore when I am so slow. I go to a place where I think there will be a bird, there isn't, I try to run back to the path but I run out of sprint, I cry from frustration. The second reason why the running speed is bad is because some enemies (only a few each level) have guns. So you have to run towards them and take them out but you can't do that because you are so slow. The only way around it is to use a gun or the taser.
Nonetheless this is a great horror game that gets under your skin rather than relies on jump scares. Definitely get it if you like F.E.A.R.

Trust your initial reaction to this review's headline. I expect you'll either be excited for another fairly well made entry into one of your favorite genres or you'll bemoan that the indie scene is oversaturated with these types of games. I find myself starting to lean toward the latter.
Generally Closure's puzzles are cleverly designed with an adequate amount of variation. There are some that were too easy as well as some that, for me, crossed into frustration territory. These aggravating stages were always the longer stages where if you made even one mistake you'd have to start over and redo numerous steps that quickly become tedious. Where the game faltered most for me is that I'd estimate a third of my a little over 7 hours playing the game was spent on these infuriating levels.
Adding to the challenge are 30 collectable moths hidden throughout the game that you'll need to gather all of to get any kind of ending. I got 17 of them during my playthrough then elected to watch the ending on Youtube rather than go back for the remaining 13. I'd suggest skipping the moths unless you are really enjoying the game.
Taking a look at global Steam achievements suggests that the game isn't as widely appealing as its positive reviews would make you believe. Currently, 48.2% of game owners have completed the tutorial stages. Only 8.4% have completed the first 24 levels called "the Factory." In other words, only 17.4% of players who completed the tutorial felt compelled to keep playing to the end of the first of 4 acts. To be fair, you can play the first 3 acts in any order but the way they are laid out in the hub and the general difficulty curve steers you toward playing them in a specific order. 5.1% of players completed "the Hospital," 5.0% of players completed "the Circus" and 3.5% completed the main game. Looking at a few similar games, Braid and LIMBO are much better in these numbers and FEZ is modestly better.
From an artistic standpoint Closure does well at creating a creepy, dark ambiance. The visual style is like moving scratchboard art and is quite striking. Unfortunately, due to the light/dark gimmick much of the screen will always be black, making it difficult to get a big picture view of the environments you are in. What story there is is told purely through visuals that can be similarly tough to uncover. Most of the joy you can get out of the story will come from treating it like another puzzle where you try to piece together some meaning. It's hard to praise this aspect of the game as it really doesn't have much discernible depth, but it does dance along the line of being just vague enough to get your imagination going to fill in the details. The music is solid and adds to the atmosphere, even if it gets a bit repetitive at times.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Under Zero
Update Version: Initial
Disclosure: The game copy was bought by the reviewer through a bundle.
I have been examining the Early Access program for about a year now and can easily locate the tell tale signs of certain categories the games released end up falling into. It is a known fact there are plenty of older titles still wasting away on the store page with no activity while others try tooth and nail to prolong their stay in the status despite no real progress. It is a terrible realization when you think of all the potential developers that could be helped with the aid of Early Access that are stained with the stigma the last couple of years have built with abandoned products. One reason this happens is due to a title being released into Early Access too soon and Under Zero is a clear example of it.
Unity has become a dangerous warning light when  Early Access come to mind and it seemed to be an accurate one. Visually the game is nothing special with the snowy landscape populated by rectangular shapes and some none boxy trees. You spawn next to a lighthouse that is somewhat difficult to climb due to the boxy shapes of the stairs overlapping each other. A few squarish buildings exist outside as well with some items, but they are also poorly designed with the potential of getting stuck. Invisible walls outline the boundary of the region which is inhabited by some decent looking wolves, but they clip into themselves, constantly chase you without hurting you or just stand there looking at you. One of the wolves followed me and managed to trap me inside a building (I could not walk through or past it). The design choices and layout feel as if it was all done in a afternoon without any fine rendering.
Music was non-existent for the first half of my initial and secondary play through with the load clumping of your footsteps making up the entirety of the soundtrack. There is a flashlight and a gun, but the gun lacks a basic design. Other items exist, but have no purpose (cherry soda for example). Settings for the game also seem off putting and confusing with the graphical setting for high spelled Height (at least I think high is what it is suppose to represent). The cursor disappears when you open the menu in-game unless you hit the ESC key while the character model still has the ability to look around. To even say this game lacks content is being overly generous: there is no content. It might have achievements (almost all are bugged) and trading cards, but these are not selling points.
For a game with no content and very low tier graphics, it sure has some performance issues. The game managed to crash on me a couple of times and the loading screen froze when I tried entering the game from the main menu. I already mentioned the fact you can be trapped by a wolf in the buildings, but the glitchy nature of the wolf needs addressing,again. The AI is non-existent as well, just endless chasing or standing. This really is the bare-basic concept of a game I have seen on Early Access, which is the worst thing you could say.
Any program can be founded on good intentions, but it doesn't mean those intentions will protect it from games that slip through the cracks. I am told often you cannot judge a game by what it is, but instead from what it will become. It is that mindset that creates the problems Early Access has right now and those issues will not stop unless people start taking responsibility. I am not saying the developer for Under Zero is in the wrong here by releasing the game in this state, but it is up to the developer to reflect on how the game functions at the moment and act on it. It takes a great person to know when something is not worth the price of admission and work toward making something that is before selling it. Under Zero shouldn't be in Early Access in the state it is in, especially at the price it is asking. I really hope it can prove me wrong in my assumptions of what category it will end up in down the line, but very few games have so far.
Pros
- None
Cons
- No Content
- Crashes and Loading Screen Freezes
- Graphical glitches
- Game breaking errors (wolf and floor boards trapping in building)
- Music and sound issues
- Settings
- No Gameplay
- No Purpose

So, it's a good kind of fun. It's got a lot of similarities with FTL, but the combat's a bit more fast-paced. It's also just a touch less interactive, in my opinion. Although, I did lose an escort vehicle my very first combat, and didn't manage to keep its replacement in one piece for very long at all, so someone with better luck might find the extra vehicles change things significantly.
I did Quite A Lot of ramming my vehicles into other vehicles, which was unpleasant, but effective. I didn't much care for losing health with every hit, but it did a significant amount of damage, allowed me to control the positioning of my enemies, and make them run into walls. That was the main method I used for eliminating targets.
The parts of the soundtrack I heard were alternately nice and unremarkable. Not very intrusive, but enjoyable when I had attention to spare for them.
Traversing the main map is boring. The icon that represents your convoy moves really slowly, and slower over higher elevations. It doesn't make it clear how this affects "scenario" rates (the games term for encounters), and is just ... well, they could double the speed without losing much.
The writing is a bit of a clashing mix between bizarre pop culture references, slapstick comedy, and serious wasteland survival drama. Not really a selling point, but I didn't find it frustrating enough to be a turn-off, either.
My final recommendation: buy it on sale.

This is basically
's weirdo, slightly disabled cousin-in-law. It's certainly got excellent atmosphere, and the soundtrack is great, but it has too many issues for me to really like. Which is a shame, because I was kind of looking forward to it when I heard about it before release. I played mainly with a non-Steam copy, so bear with my low playtime here.
I'll say right off that the combat is a mixed bag, but not an entirely bad one. It certainly
awesome to shoot and smash your enemies in what amounts to a top down Mad Max car chase - the developers nailed the aesthetic here. While this game likes to compare itself to FTL, and I'll certainly indulge it there, this isn't exactly FTL On Wheels. In practice it feels more like a tactical JRPG.
Hitpoint/shielding totals make some encounters less a question of tactical skill and more of focusing fire on each enemy in turn & grinding them into dust...unless of course you stumbled into high-level enemies while unprepared. It doesn't help that avoiding obstacles that smash your valuable vehicles to bits is a learned skill, and that's if they don't run into any bugs (in the game, not on the road). It's just not as deep as FTL's combat, overall.
I don't particularly mind not being able to move my main convoy vehicle (MCV), because the focus is on the smaller vehicles protecting it. It's annoying that enemies like to shoot your MCV instead of said vehicles, but it makes sense that they'd usually want to aim for the big valuable target, and it means you can move in for the kill if your MCV can hold up. There's a large downside here though: this means that if all your other vehicles die, and if your MCV has no damage-dealing capability, you're pretty much dead in the water without even the courtesy of an automatic game over. I also wish you could position your vehicles when not in combat without learning not to automatically bring the map up every time you win a fight - there's no way to position them once you go back to the map until you enter combat again.
Long-term strategy is less predicated on being randomly handed shops and items like in FTL, and more on not running into enemies that will absolutely destroy you before you make it to a shop to repair and restock. This is also kind of luck-based, but since you can see where faction influence is strong on the map, you have a shot at trying to avoid stronger enemies if you're weak. At least crushing weaker enemies in turn can be pretty fun.
The game map is fixed, although the placement of factions and objectives is randomized each time. It's pretty big, although of course you will be traveling from one end to another anyway.
On a more positive note, Convoy's final boss is easily fairer and generally more pleasant to fight than FTL's. It doesn't violate the established meta (as much) and doesn't crush you outright like the Rebel flagship, although on harder difficulties and without adequate preparations I imagine it's more capable of doing so. On that note, easy difficulty in Convoy is actually
, and the other difficulties are also self-descriptive. Contrast to FTL, where easy is normal, normal is hard, and hard is almost impossible.
I also appreciate that Convoy has a robust unlock system to match FTL's, and Steam achievements/Workshop support/included Unity modding tools where FTL had none. The fact that Convoy's soundtrack isn't a separate DLC item in the Steam store is a bit odd, though.
Now. The writing.
The main story is fine, pretty interesting even. Your frigate breaks down, so you make an emergency landing on the nearby planet of Omek Prime and lead a convoy into the wasteland to find needed replacement parts. This entails dealing with three factions that control the portion of the planet you landed on, and while they're rather generic with annoying and repetitive combat initiation soundbytes, at least they fill their role decently. Again, the atmosphere overall is good. Too bad the events are more often than not frigging
.
To borrow a comparison from
, comparing the handful of pop culture reference-ridden, poorly thought-out scenarios on display here to Chris Avellone's work in FTL Advanced Edition is like comparing a toilet of spoiled meat with a bottle of fine wine. I don't expect all my games to be literary masterpieces, but I
expect more than ham-fisted
encounters (only a couple of months after he passed away, even) and other non sequiturs. The only improvement over FTL is that the choice outcomes are randomized for each playthrough, so there's always an element of risk, albeit one that could outright end a playthrough that's already on the ropes.
That's not to say that every event is terrible, but too many of them are either bad or mediocre. If the writers wanted to have fun with what is essentially Mad Max: JRPG On Wheels, that would have been fine, but they
went overboard with the references.
wasn't this bad, and that was more than 15 years ago; you know, back when the standard video game aesthetic was Big Hunkman and/or Big Sexyboob starring in some quality of ridiculously edgy, generic fantasy or both.
It's my hope Convoy's writing will become more and more of an outlier in a medium that increasingly recognizes the value of actual worldbuilding. I would have absolutely loved finding out what exactly happened to Omek Prime to turn it into such a blasted hellhole, much less learning what makes the factions tick. You're told to go meet the T.O.R.V.A.K. organization, one of the three factions, to find one of the ship parts you need, but you're not given any indication that your crew even knows what T.O.R.V.A.K. are or how they know about their existence! The devs could even have split plot information over multiple playthroughs and kept a log of collected information for the player to read between runs. There was
here, damn it.
If you're not as picky as me, you'll probably like this, and I'd probably recommend it to you if you had enough disposable income to justify it. It's not terrible, and it's different enough from FTL to make it an interesting experience (perhaps a fairer one overall when you factor in FTL's RNG), but it doesn't quite add up for yours truly. Not for 15 bucks.

An enjoyable survivalist romp with some rogue-like elements.   Think FTL in a Max Max setting.    A very satisfying value while on 50% sale, but not at the full asking price. Several missed opportunities prevent this title from being an all-star, most notably the lack of content.
Pluses:
+ Intriguing real-time tactical convoy-based combat.    You must maneuver your vehicles to protect your transport while giving them an optimal firing angle.
+ Good battle pacing.  You *almost* have enough time to pay attention to everything, which brings to each fight just the right amount of harried eye-hand flicking.     (But see UX minus below)
+ Varied vehicle builds.  You can build ramming tanks, light DPS machines, mine layers, and other configurations.
+ Charming retro soundtrack.
+ Witty writing and flavor text.   Some "choose your own adventure" gameplay that doesn't involve convoy combat.   Lots of geek references.
Minuses (more of missed opportunities):
+ Desperately needs more content.    There's only one base map which never changes, just the quest markers on top of it.   The 'randomized' quest comes from a small pool that will repeat often.
+ UX and grpahics go a little too far into being retro, so that they don't provide the player with needed information.
+ What's with the default resolution being boxed?  Yes, you can stretch to fullscreen, but then the retro graphics get really ugly.   Perhaps done for a future tablet port, which makes sense, but this choice cheapens the PC experience.
+ RNG a bit too random, denying opportunities of player choice.   (You may never get a 3rd or 4th vehicle for your convoy due to chance, severely limiting your play.)   Some form of  crafting/salvage system would solve the random problem, and be very in-theme.

Going back to the slightly simple graphics of classic games such as Wolfenstein 3D does not mean the quality of the game will drop. On the contrary, a lesser priority on graphics allows for more focus on gameplay. Eldritch gets the gameplay right, and even the simplified graphics suit the game, instead of looking dated.
Eldritch is a difficult game, forcing you, the player, to maintain a constant vigil against anything that could deprive you of your meager health (3 hits, and you're down). Then you've got such difficult decisions to make such as do I take the gun, or the knife? Knife is melee, gun is ranged. Gun runs out of ammo, where the knife lasts forever. Now add in shrines to the forgotten Old Gods which grant you powers when you pray at them, angry penguins, fish people, and soul munching shoggoths, and you have Eldritch.
I've not seen too much of the game, having repeatedly died in the first book (it'll make sense when you play the game, but think, level), but that's the nature of rogue-like games, and it does nothing to detract from the fun.
Is it Steamified?
Yes. Yes it is. Eldritch has both Steam achievements, and Steam trading cards. I have no idea how you'll get some of the achievements though, to my limited skills at least, they are all but impossible. Fun trying though.

Quaint city builder where you are trying to win the approval of all the Roman gods in order to become a god yourself.  I completed the game in about 5 hours.  The game gives you quests that first act as a tutorial and then as general guidance.  As part of the story, you keep courting Venus, which pisses Mars off and gets his mommy Hera involved.  This has the effect of making the game become a bit tedious towards the end.  You have to keep putting out fires from Mars tantrums and repair buildings from Hera's thunder fits.
The problem is that you end up having a lot of buildings all crammed together since space is somewhat precious, especially in the beginning.   Trying to spot which building needs to have a fire put out or be repaired gets to be a somewhat trying after a few hours of Mars and Hera attacks.  The sooner you can get the Trojan horse at the East most point of the map, the better, since that finally quiets Mars down.  Then Hera can be calmed down with a large enough bribe.
This means you need to have at least the trading post and lot of the production buildings going so you can have a constant export of trade.  Once you have this in place, and later get the port, you have pretty much an endless source of gold.  I highly recommend to build as many shrines and temples, fully upgraded, as soon as you can.  Nothing beats being able to scoop whatever resources you happen to need whenever you want.  Having enough little devoted followers means your divine mana replenishes very quickly.   Towards the end I was pretty much spamming the divine hand whenever I need it.  This was very unlike the beginning where you have to be very conservative with how you use it since initially it takes forever to refill.
Overall, this game was fairly enjoyable.  It doesn't really have any replay value once you finish it, since it really doesn't have much depth in terms of strategy.  Once you understand what you need to do, there really isn't much of a challenge.  The fun aspect to playing this game in this discovery of what each of the buildings do, and then the final challenge in building each of the seven wonders.

Easily one of the best multiplayer shooters ever made. The gunplay, movement, progression and variety all make for an incredibly satisfying game that plays out that Battlefield pace in spectacular fashion. The one thing that hampers it is it's netcode and the fact that it's port isn't necessarily the best like the later entries, but it's more than playable at least and doesn't get in the way at all; just simply doesn't do the game complete justice. Still runs at above 100fps at all times on maxed out 1440p on my 1060 and R5 1600 and looks great. Servers and players are always present and generally speaking the pings tend to not be too bad.
Oh and btw, there's no need to get Vietnam which is one of the most awesome DLCs that I've seen in a game of this kind (even if it plays really exactly the same it's atmosphere and asthetic just totally gets you into it, it's great) since there are servers that boot you into Vietnam even without owning it. Oh, and speaking of servers there are many of them and they tend to run pretty alright. And there are many with a lot of different kinds of mods to spice things up, such as making all weapon stats and equipment be 2 or 10 times so hey 20 grenades and burst fire RPGs okay why not and doing the same for XP so you can level up to 50 by like just spotting someone and someone else killing them + removing some of the map boundaries so you can glitch out really easily. It's totally broken and I love it. Though vanilla servers exist too so nobody is left out.
Basically: Get this and enjoy the days when EA were actually alright and allowed developers like DICE to fully realize their visions and really just make experiences for their fans to love and enjoy. To play and not just to pay. To innovate and make real good games such as this.

Okay, so you've probably heard of this game before. It was developed by Monolith Studios alongside F.E.A.R., so yeah, there's good things to expect here. You play as Ethan Thomas, an FBI agent stationed in NYC who's framed for the murder of two fellow police officers and is being chased by the Bureau while he attempts to find clues and follow the trail of the real criminal behind it all. The atmosphere is superb and full of creepy noises and heart-pumping suspense to go with the eerie locales including (but not limited to) an abandoned subway, an abandoned department store (WITH CREEPY AS ♥♥♥♥ TELEPORTING MANNEQUINS), an abandoned school... yeah a lot of abandoned areas, hence "Condemned". Complete with these areas are enemies galore, all of which are pretty much mentally screwed up drug addicts, both minor and major. The combat is satisfyingly brutal, crunchy, and has a great weight to it with every hit. It requires precision timing when blocking too, and takes a bit of practice to get it right. You can pretty much pick up anything layed about to use as a weapon (really, even a friggin' desk drawer) and firearms come into play later on. Weapons are plentiful, and health pill cabinets are found pretty easily throughout the game. It took about 8-9 hours to complete for me, so it's certainly every bit worth the price you pay, even if you don't get it on sale. Really, if you're a horror fan, this is a MUST BUY!

The plot for the whole thing is pretty simple, you're framed by a killer of two cops and you're on a journey to find him. Throughout that journey you experience weird shtuff that can mess your trousers quite a bit. The story itself is actually a bit interesting to say the least however I don't feel that it was told all that well whatwith it just being a bit slow on the telling despite how somewhat short the game itself is (like 6-8 hours).
As for the actual gameplay it's an extremely simple first person, mostly melee based combat; they attack, you time your block right, you get a chance to attack some more until they're down. If you're good enough you can have them start fighting each other. There
guns in the game but they're very limited and restraint; you can't collect ammunition and you can't reload them though you can turn them into very fragile melee weapons. The entire game itself is pretty linear and it has a habit of having you backtrace (ie. acquire item X from this location to open door Y that you passed through a little earlier) though I didn't find it to be unbearably strenous. Because you're a Serial Crimes Unit agent you'll also be using investigation tools to partake in some CSI stuff by finding evidence that the person who framed you left behind which what you find that advances the plot further can be interesting.
The real selling point of this game however is the survival horror part; you start to hallucinate spooky shtuff, most of where you go gets extremely claustrophobic & obviously dark, and the game can be downright freaky to move around in. For the most part I found it very uneasy to even go where I was supposed to and more uneasy whatwith me being a bit bad with the subject of horror in general. That's how I prefer my horror anyway, making you
terrified as opposed to using petty jump scares (though I tend to be bad with those as well and plus there aren't too many in this game I found).
Get it for when it's cheap.
