A lot of people say that this game is like XCOM, but in 2D. It's not at all like XCOM. About the only similarities are turn-based squad combat with cover, but there are a lot of games that fit that description. For example, in XCOM your choices matter (if you aren't savescumming). In this game, your choices don't matter. The worst that happens if you botch a mission is that you lose some easily replaced money.
With that out of the way, I can say that this game is a lot of fun! The combat mechanics are simple but solid, and the enemy design is devious enough to present a challenge without being obnoxious. The three enemy races you fight are fairly similar, but different enough to prevent the game from getting repetitive. There are ten characters to recruit, each with their own abilities, and a whole lot of different items to find, which are mostly well-balanced. The sound and music were better than I expected, and the graphics are stylish.
The story is simple but well-delivered, and a playthrough where you try to recruit and level up everyone should take about 25 hours, maybe more if you go for maximum reputation. If you really want a challenge, the game keeps track of the total number of turns and losses, and your reputation, and scores you at the end of the game. Getting a top score requires beating every map with max reputation and no losses, and doing so in a minimum of turns (preventing you from grinding to overlevel). There's also a hat-collecting mechanic, where you can shoot hats off of enemies' heads and collect them for your crew to wear.
Overall, there's a lot to do and the game is both good and good value for the money.

This game is basically a series of platforming precision challenge levels with save rooms containing an achievement-granting diamond every few levels. You have a jetpack that acts as infinite double jumps, a gun that's rarely used, as there's very few enemies throughout the game, and infinite lives. Your goal is to collect every square item to move to the next level, while navigating corridors with most of the time static and sometimes moving obstacles that kill you when touched. There's also a timer that kills you when it reaches 0, and it can be increased by collecting round items. As the game progresses the time constraints increase significantly, requiring you to play close to perfectly on some of the levels. There are only two bosses, one at the halfway point and one at the end.
I found that the game offers very little. It takes less than an hour to beat if you're half-decent at platformers. There's no extra challenges or side missions, you can get 100% achievements as you go. While some of the later levels can offer a good challenge, they mostly take just a few tries to beat. The bosses are easy, taking just mindless shooting and dodging. The last boss was particularly a huge disappointment, because you can just sit there and shoot at him and you will kill him in seconds. There's no story, no ending and no replay value. As such, I wouldn't recommend getting this game unless you buy it at a low price.

Every level has a timer, this time can be extended by picking up things that arent explained to you what they're supposed to do.
there is no reason why you are jumping around collecting things on a timer just that that's how it is.
The level design in 69 (that rhymes), is rather basic. one of the selling points according to the developer is
though to me this is more of a weakness then a plus because though most concepts are good they are executed very poorly. According to the developer the soundtrack is exceptional yet i see very little of this in the game, besides that the sounds of picking up objects and jumping is much louder then the music, and there is no way to change that either, i also thought that it was very basic and i dindt really like it. it has a very simple soundtrack that isnt catchy and sounds like the soundtrack of any generic indie platformer. all in all the soundtrack was very dissapointing

The jetpack sounds is a simple sound that although not amazing was good enough for the many hundreds of times i had to spam the jump button. The idea of difficulty to the developer is a bit strange, "if the level is nearly unplayable then it's hard" difficulty is not based on how bad you are at making a level but at the actual challenge it brings. and i think the developer hasnt quite got that idea.

TLDR: A fun sandbox WWII naval battle, "sim" lite/arcade game. Enjoyable gameplay with graphics that are pretty crisp, and the interface is easy to get the hang of. Sandbox campaign and a number or challenging historical battles.

Pros:
-The price:
Cannot beat it, everyone harping about this and that needs to adjust accordingly.
-Gameplay:
I really enjoyed the naval battles, they were at times intense with some really fun combinations of ships to play with. -----Gameplay II:
The "sim" lite / arcade gameplay is great, because you can jump right into the gameplay and focus on blowing up stuff.
-Manual control:
Very satisfying to take manual control of a battleship and rip through the enemy.
-Real time:
I enjoy that this is "real time" vs. turn based, you can adjust the speed of the action to your liking and pause to issue orders to your fleet.
-Ship detail:
The ships are rendered well, with some great detail...I wish there was a smidge more to dive into and really zoom in on...but meh.
-Campaign mode:
Three massive sandbox theatres to mess around within, and you can choose a number of different sides to play as...so adds to replayability. (note the campaign is also a con)
AI:
-The AI doesn't derp out. Not a resounding Pro, but it works well and I can issue broad orders and micro segments and the AI can handle itself and remembers to continue breathing on its on.
Cons:
-Campaign mode:
As the thumbs down have noted, the missions are kind of meh...and once you assembly a pretty big fleet there isn't much to stop you. ON THE FLIP SIDE...I just take my massive unbeatable, uber armada and deploy peices of it to match my opponent. (ex: they have a battle ship, cruisers, and destoyers?....I drop my battleship, crusiers and destoyers....and I hold back all my crazy aircraft carriers).
-RPG
Hard to say this is a con, but you have your character and your subsequent captains in your fleet and they rank up...but thats it. It would be amazing if there were some character building elements, and specialization + unlock proficiencies in your ships as they progress (al la warthunder et al.)
-"sim" lite / arcade
Mind you this is also a pro for me...that being said I wish there was a tad more sim aspect to this game. Watch the vid on the store page, you will see how combat unfolds...its great!...but in the same regard I wish there was just a touch more simulation'ishness in the game, just a hair more.
-Sandbox
Yes you can prowl around the seas helping your allied (or axis) homies...but there isn't a terrible amount of cohesion to the theatre. I mean you can rampage around and not really think twice about anything...honestly I dont know what would improve this..but there is a vague niggling sense in the back of my head that wants more to this. And now I am being critical of a game I love. It is a touch too arcadie, and as above I don't know how to improve upon this without ruining the fun...its like when homer simpson designer the perfect car with everything everyone wanted...but I wish there was just a touch more to the gameplay.

Victory At Sea is a fun little wargame that suffers from a few front-loaded annoyances.  Like many games in this genre, the campaign has a strategic map in which you sail from port to port, and a tactical map for in-game combat.  The tactical gameplay is quite strong, whether you elect to pay it RTS-style by letting the AI control your armada, or if you use the quite versatile pause-any-time engine to control most of your ships manually.
The biggest gripe with this game is the mission engine.  At ports, you can request a mission from HQ, but these these missions are often wildly unbalanced or outright mechanically impossible.  The Mediterrean campaign seems to be the worst in this regard; sailing from base to base frequently takes longer than you're given to complete a mission.  That said, there's no penalty for failing, and you don't need to take missions to complete the game.
Like many World War II naval games, Victory at Sea heavily emphasizes naval aviation.  Aircraft carriers are far and away the dominant class of ships in the mid-to-late game.  Besides their historical advantages, aircraft carriers in Victory At Sea enjoy operating at night just as well as they do during the day, and continuing landing and launching aircraft even while under direct fire from enemy forces.  As a result, much of the late game can be turn into great flock of aircraft carriers sailing from port to port, destroying defenders and capturing harbors for your team.
Overall, the game plays rather well, and I'd definitely suggest it for any fans of theater-scale naval warfare in the 1940's.  It keeps the subject matter interesting without sacrificing entertainment value in the name of historical accuracy.  Each campaign takes about six hours to play, and if you're like me, you'll get at least 5 campaigns out the game.

The second game in the SteamWorld series is, just like the first one, a ridiculous amount of fun.  SteamWorld Heist is a 2D strategy tactics game (Think X-COM, Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem, etc.).  You manage a group of characters, each with distinct abilities, in turn-based battles against a group of enemies, each with their own strenghts and weaknesses.  Manage your inventory and earn experience in order to customize your characters better to give them and edge on the battlefield.
Unlike the previously mentioned games, though, in which battles depend quite a bit on luck (look for the infamous picture of a soldier in X-COM having a shotgun pointed right at an alien's face with a 98% chance of hitting and still missing), battles here depend purely on skill.  Realistically, your characters hand don't stay completely still while aiming (though perhaps less realistically, considering they're robots), so it's up to you if they hit the target or not.  Also, some characters attack better from afar, others do more damage from the back, others can't attack after moving, and so on.  There's a lot of characters, abilities and weapons to juggle, and you can set your team as you like it, according to your preferred playstyle.  You're never forced to use a character you're not comfortable with if you have others at your disposal.
At times the game might infuriate you.  Most stages are randomly created through a procedural algorithm, and that means sometimes they'll be easier to handle (for instance, sometimes you might find a couple of small rooms with one or two enemies each and sometimes it'll be a large room where all congregate).  Losing or aborting a battle at most difficulties will make you lose half of your hard-earned cash.  On the plus side, re-entering the same stage might turn out to have it reconfigured on an easier way.  You might get angry and rage-quit the game at some point (I know I have), but a few minutes later you'll be drawn to the game again, because it IS that much fun.
The game includes a New Game+ option, which is always a nice thing.  Make no mistake, you will get lost in this game for days.

This review is based on Zoom v12 which was released earlier on June 2016.
Pros:
1. Extended customization functions. This is more aimed for power user, so people who want to just play their media might not find any of it useful. Required documentation before tweaking things, though. Online and offline helps are available fortunately.
2. Interface is clean and easy to use once YOU are familiar with it. It takes a bit learning curve, however.
3. Internal install center so it's easy to keep components updated. You don't need to download things outside the program e.g decoders.
4. Although it's packed with features, the software overall is pretty efficient, I'm trying to compare this directly with MPC and playing same file, it has quite comparable CPU and RAM usage (1080p file, 2.5 hours long movie). Both are using around 15% CPU (of my i5 5200u) and 160 MB RAM (of my 8 GB on Windows 10 x64). Program start up is instantaneous as well on my old SATA drive.
5. DRM free. It wasn't, but it is now when Developer realized it's only upsetting Steam customers for a product like this.
6. Continually updated. This player has undergone some major revisions over years and Steam users are getting those updates for free.
Cons:
1. Expensive. Unlike other freeware like FLV and/or Media Player Classic, this doesn't come cheap.... or free. If you're aiming to get it and think the features or 'pros' I listed above is enough for you, by all means get this software. But for me, this entry barrier (pricing) is enough to hold me off if I still didn't have the software. For information, I got this from Groupees bundles
so there's a chance that this will be bundled again in the future.  Or well, Steam might offer discount during major sales, so keep an eye.
2. No internal subtitle search function. Media Player Classic has it, and I love that feature. It often saves me time from searching through Google myself. This Zoom, sadly, doesn't have it. Hopefully they'll add it in the future.
3. As an audio player, leave this alone. When it's compared head to head against the likes of Foobar, it's not even a fair match. Foobar has much more functions e.g multi playlist that a modern audio player needs and we really don't need fancy video player features JUST for playing audio files.
Overall, if you want more than a basic functionality (but it works) of freeware video players out there, you can try this one. Otherwise, you can stick with what you're using.

Nifty piece of software with a range of weird and wonderful features including transparency modes and the ability to play animated GIFs, as well as standard features such as AB repeat and variable playback speed.
I still use WMP for audio playlists and VLC for 4k or 60FPS videos, but consider the Zoom Player an invaluable addition to my desktop software collection.
The version downloaded through Steam can be run without Steam (hence my recorded usage time is 7 mins, whereas in reality it has been used for many hours).

For transparency, I've used Zoom via the Steam interface for 2 hours before using the DRM free shortcut provided by the software. In total, I've used the program for 7 hours as of this review.
The Pros:
- A slick interface with easy shortcuts on command such as right clicking to find where the track is located on a hard drive, memorizing what folder a song came from to quickly add another track from that same folder, and a more responsive time tracker than VLC media player for me.
- Intuitive control panel to adjust settings with commonly desired information displayed first. For example, the Playback options are the second item in the Options Menu and displays 3 trees for video codecs to use for playing files, associating file types to specific codecs, and DVD playback instructions. Exactly what I want to see for ease of use.
- An auto update for audio and video codecs
- DRM Free! Requires a one time activation on Steam, then can be used without going through Steam. Makes it very useful due to some games using the exact Steam App being played first to determine if you are able to join another player's game. I have quite a few in my Library that do that, so this feature makes it a lifesaver on wanting to use this program while playing online without going through the hassle of starting a game up before launching Zoom
- Comparing the default Windows Media Player, Zoom is slightly louder when at the same audio levels. Mostly the bass sounds louder.
The Cons:
- Uses about 60mb when playing audio files. VLC used 20mb on the same mp3 file. Expect about twice the ram used for videos as well compared to some lightweight media players.
- The default video codec used is a little darker, but crisp compared to other players like WMPlayer. This is a potential problem since you might need to switch the default codec or adjust brightness settings.
- Fairly expensive, but not too bad for the price range of what it is capable of doing
OVERALL: I have tried other media players such MHC+, VLC, WMP and this pretty much does everything I want while sounding and looking better than what I've used. If you have the extra RAM on your system to use it, I recommend this easily. It feels like a modern day WinAmp for video and sound. Smooth perfection.

What a nice refreshing attempt to grab the 'player who does everything' -title that has been floating around for quite some time. It doesn't achieve this objective but it sure tries and gets very close.
My needs for a generic media player are not exactly heavy but diverse: living room pc. game rig. workshop pc. several laptops. preferably some type of dj/kiosk mode or settings that allow it to be used effectively during parties.
This far no setup does a 10/10 job but this one appears to be a good replacement candidate for Winamp on windows machines. This far Winamp+VLC combo has been the best tools i have used since they 'just work' (good enough/always available/rarely fail or start crashing). Yes i have tried other players too but always return back to this ol' workhorse duo sooner or later.
I especially liked the nice base interface and the fact that just about anything can be changed and settings can be exported to other machines. Gamepad can also be used for control which is good in living room.
edit: forgot one thing. some reviews mention bad video support but after doing 'Advanced interface' -> 'Help' -> 'Check update' and installing some plugins i can play just about anything i have on my rig and all works. So this means VLC is under the loop now too. This one has a better interface though only time will tell if it's better since crashing is what i hate mosly about VLC. If this one works better then it will beat VLC.

Used the Freeware version of this program for just about as long as it was first available. I've tried every major freeware video player on the market, all of which are useable, none of which are as customizable or feature rich as Zoom Player. I have a lot of old and new video I play using this program, so I have a lot of hours on record on Steam but probably 10x the amount of hours on the freeware, so I figured it was about time I help support the developers and buy the full version here on steam.
It's worth every penny at the current full price they charge here, getting it on special just makes it that much of a better deal.  Don't bother with the reviews with 0.1hrs.  If those people could actually read the feature list properly, they would understand that this player does not play back copy protected Blu-ray discs because that requires expensive licensing that would probably at least double the cost of this program.  Also do not listen to thor32123's review, because this program plays every major format available as long as you have the proper filters and codecs installed on your computer. I have played back: mpg, mp4, avi, ogm, mkv, rm, rmv, rmvb, asf, wmv, qt, etc.  Plays them all fine.  I don't use this for audio, but every audio file I have accidently played on this program has played fine: mp3, wav, ogg, flac, etc.
Pros:
Cons:
Overall: 9/10
While no copy protected Blu-ray playback support is a con, the program does not claim it does so you cannot fault the program for that.  The problematic updates through Steam are a hastle, but more of a nitpick than a real con. Most programs tell you to disable your AV prior to installation as a precaution anyway, but this was the first time I have had a problem with installing an update or any program for many years now that were caused by an Anti-virus program.
If you're a casual media playback user, you'll be fine with any of the freeware players out there, VLC being the best 'Video player for Dummies' out there.  If you absolutely have to have copy protected Blu-ray playback, look elsewhere. I have a set top player for my Blu-rays as well as a software player that came with my BD-R Writer so I did not need nor care about Blu-ray playback.  I've used the software player that came with my burner once, and that was just to test if it was actually a fully useable version or just a trial (it's a full version). Any time I play a Blu-ray, I do it with my set top player.
If you're a power user, or not afraid of learning how to work with this program (not that difficult), there's no better video player out there available at this price point or cheaper.

This game is by far one of the best 4x RTS Space games out there. You can defend planets with ground tanks, and soliders to increase your control.
You can take over Native or enemy planets with Native or enemy races on it and seize control. Absorbing their race into your faction.
As a Tinker robotic race you even borg them and take over the playable races and they appear later as Robotic creatures of their race. It's epic.
You can build spacde stations for increased production of a planet, or just to defend or simply to have a science bay and civiliation there.
You can post Outpost bases around planets that you can't colonize early in game and they become "outposts of yours".
You are able to edit and design new ships and bases. (Learn to do this or you won't last long)
You are able to mass armies all over the galaxy, but watch your taxes for them.
You are able to make Transport ships and convert them to Trade, when this happens they disappear from your control and you are no longer taxed for having them but now they produce +5 or more money in Trade.
You are able to Bombard enemy planets with ground defenses. Or planetary defense massive guns.
You are able to make semi friends with pirate race (the serpent race) and actually buy SHips from them with gold to add to your army.
There's a race of deep space beings that offer you a trade for your metal for their technology and they are expensive but always have the good stuff.
You are able to win this game by trading and diplomacy.  You are also able to win by killing everyone and genociding them or absorbing them into your Faction.

IMHO, this is the best successor to MOO2, and I mean that in every sense. That is, the game is simple (yet complex) and the graphics take you straight back to MOO2. If you enjoyed MOO2 and have been disappointed by the many, many attemps to reinvent then MOO2, then Stars in Shadow is for you (me). When you first boot it up, the retro-graphics are a bit of a surprise, after we're used to so many slick games (and failutres) in recent years. But once you warm up to the game, you start to like the graphics. Combat plays like MOO2, which I like. Moving population around planets plays like MOO2, which I like. And so on. BUT BUT BUT, although this game seems simple at first, it actually has a great deal of depth to it, more than MOO2 had, in terms of techs, strategies, races, and planets. So I am having fun. The only point that I could mention is that I have played 5 games and won all of them, playing on normal for first 3 games and hard for last two games. I think the AI needs help. But it's still a fun game if you have been waiting for that MOO2 all these years.

My one gripe is that I wish there were broader diplomatic options—you have the ability to offer a planet you have for sale, so why can't we make an offer for a planet that someone else owns? Or, if I'm allied with two factions that are at war with each other, why can't I broker peace between them? They aren't major things at least, and I've got my fingers crossed that it's the kind of stuff that may still be added.

I think this is one is the best of the MOO/MOO2 clones (before you get the pithfork out, that does not mean it is better than games that did not try to copy MOO2!). It is between MOO and MOO2 when it comes to streamlining, which is a good thing for me :you don't have to go through the same building queue for every planet, you just have a few slots dedicated to tech/production/money/farming, and that's it, so it is pretty close from Master of Orion 1 in this regard. The combat and ship designs are closer from MOO2, but with some streamlining here too: You have dedicated hardpoints for light/medium/heavy weapons, or fighter bays, and some othr for systems.
The game lacks some features of MOO2 (ship experience, leaders, unique Antaran techs...) to truely shine, and would nice some more work on AI and balancing (but which 4X wouldn't?), but the current package is quite fun. Most games are decided pretty early, and then, you need to mop up for a while, but that is usually the case in the genre, and here, you can at least win if all the factions left are allied to you, so it can speed things up a bit in the end.
It also looks like a MMO game and not some heartless 3D monster (but I still love you, Space Empires 4!).
It might not outclass its predecessors, but unlike most other space 4X, it feels like the devs understood what made MOO1/2 great.

The free to play game Emily is Away is a story rich singleplayer game, developed and published by Kyle Seeley.
In 2002 you start up your computer and log onto your local profile on a Windows XP operating system for the first time in this game. After that you sign up on a chat messenger and start texting to a good friend of yours.
The graphics in this game are kept very basic, in order to focus on the story. Also the graphic user interface is too simple in my opinion. The sounds seem not seem very realistic because, not even very old computers from 2002 sound like that. While texting you have to type yourself, but it does not matter what you are typing since any button you press on your keyboard will type in the next letter of the word which are already prepared. The heart-touching storyline itsself is made in a realistic way, therefore you could see yourself in such a situation in real life.
I think this game could need a graphic and sound update but since this is a free to play game you should not expect too much. The story might reflect some of your real life experiences. Therefore I would not recommend this game if you recently lost a friend of you broke up with your partner. This game also might not be your type if you did not enjoy any emotional story rich singleplayer games in your past. However I recommend this game to anyone else since it is a free to play and does not take much time.

I've never played any Battlefield campaign sooo this review will focus around the multiplayer portion. I have around 700 hours in this game and own around 4 different copies of it on the PC. I recently caved in and bought the steam version, mostly to get the dlc costume packs.
Multiplayer is what Battlefield is all about and Bad Company 2 does it better an all Battlefields. Even better than
which I also own. There's 4 modes of multiplayer in Bad Company 2:
- Conquest
- Rush
- Squad Deathmatch
- Squad Rush
Multiplayer is class-based and there's four classes: Assault (ARs with Noob Tubes and ammo boxes), Medic (Light Machine Guns, Medkits and Defibrillators), Engineer (Submachine Guns, Rocket Launchers [guided and free aim] and a Repair tool or Mines) and Recon (Sniper Rifle, C4 or Mortar Strike, Motion Mine). Most weapons are unlocked when reaching a designated amount of points with the class of your choice, but some are unlocked based on your overall rank (level). These weapons can then be used by every class and are mostly shotguns, with some Assault Rifles (like the M14, Thompson or G3).
The Map design in this game is definetly one of Bad Company 2's best features. It features some of the best maps and they're very diverse. All of them are varied and don't endorse camping. From huge open Battlefields (Heavy Metal or Harvest Day), Jungle Maps (Laguna Presa), Choke Point Maps (Port Valdez, Oasis & Isla Inocentes), Desert Maps (Arica Harbour or Atacama Desert) and snowy maps (White Pass).
Weapons are varied and include many the traditional FPS favorites : AUG, GOL, M95, M416, M16, UZI, SPAS-12, ETC - there should be something there to fill your itchy trigger finger. The guns feel different and mostly also shoot different (fully automatic, semi-automatic, burst2X and 3X are all there). Recoil is present, but not too insanley high to interfere with gameplay or too low to make targeting on full auto easy. Except for one gun which I only prefer to use, the G3. It probably has the highest recoil of all assault rifles and also maybe the worse hit-reg hehe, but I love that gun. I'm approaching
with it and IMO it's the best gun in the game despite my two previous cons.
Bullet drop in Bad Company 2 is different from all Battlefield games. This can be good or bad depending on the player. In the pistols (secondary) department, Bad Company 2 is well served, with a variety of pistols (including the Tracer dart) available to all classes.
PROS:
-It's Still Graphically Beautiful. The game is 7 years old and it still looks awesome. It still has some of the best weather effects like the sand and snow blowing everywhere and making it difficult to see anything.
-The sound in this game is just WOW.
-Fully destructible environments
-Vehicular combat works well and balanced
-Varied and large map design
-Awesome Community. Being a 7 year old game, the community has mostly veteran players with the occasional new player showing up whom eventually turns into a veteran player. The community is small, but dedicated to this game as I am.  There's still many servers to choose and play.
CONS:
-No Jets or Planes.. Only helis in this game ( I can't fly, never could in any battlefield game, so it really isn't a con for me hehe)
-You can't go prone. So find something to hide behind
That being said I love this game and I will for sure be playing until either DICE pulls the plug on this game or gives us Bad Company 3.. Lets hope for the latter.

It's time to openly recognize that 1C Maddox isn't a very good game developer. All of their games have had to be saved by independent developers who improved and stabilized their code after they shove half-finished products into the market.

Zoom Player has a ton of features, while making it easy to find the basic settings. The Advanced menu is huge, and it also has a search function to easily find the settings you want which is a huge bonus.
The intergrated Install Center allows you to download all the codecs you need to play 99% of all video out there: LAV Filter, FFDShow, MadVR, AC3filter and so on. There's no need to download those huge and confusing "codec-packs" that in my experience just mess up your playback.
There's a free version as well, available on the developer site, and it does basically everything the Steam version does, but you get some extra features here, and you are supporting a quality product (which IMO is important as well).
The most lacking feature might be the network streaming, like VLC has. But then again VLC was built from the ground up to be a networked media player.
I've been using Zoom for years now, and it outclasses all the other media players I've tried.
Personally I'd rather get it from the developers themselves, but having it in Steam is a nice addition.

Does not play normal Blu Ray movies.  That is to say, you can't buy a Blu Ray movie, put it in your Blu Ray drive, and play it with this media player.  A complete waste of money, as it just uses the FFMPEG codecs.  VLC is an easy replacement for this.

Between Steamworld Heist and Steamworld Dig the question remains, what can’t these Steambots do?
Take some Firefly, throw in some XCOM, and heaping helping of steampunk whimsy and you have got yourself Steamworld Heist. All ya need is a bot with a hammer for a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and you got Captain Malcolm Reynolds. Pop culture references aside, Heist is a homage to westerns, just substitute horses with spaceships.
While the game does have an amazing opening sequence that sets the scene for you, I will do my best to explain the story. After the Earth exploded, bots began to mine moisture for survival. You play a rag tag group of outlaw steambots on the fringes of space. Dealing with gangs, Royalists and all sorts of seedy characters. The setting is simple but eloquent. You play the captain of one these outlaw gangs and some bots begin to muscle in on your territory. Thus the Firefly-esque adventure begins with you taking up the mantle of the common people and making off with some decent loot as a benefit.
If you’re unfamiliar with the universe of Steamworld, I highly recommend playing Steamworld Dig as that is a fantastic title all on its own. Aside from being an awesome action/platformer it also gives insights into why Earth explodes.
Steamworld Heist on the other hand does a dramatic pivot from its predecessor. Where you controlled a single bot and primarily worried about mining, this time you steal, shoot, and control a whole squad. It was definitely one of the things that impressed me with the developer Image & Form. Instead of sticking with what they knew and had already learned they decided to take the series in a whole other direction and genre. It takes some moxie for that kind of thing and hats off to them for pulling it off.
At its most simple, Heist is a turn based strategy game that puts you behind the gun.
Aiming is by far Heists defining feature and what makes it fun. Trick shots, bouncing grenades, and shooting your enemies hat off is the bread and butter of this game. It’s satisfying every time when you bounce your sniper round off five walls and hit a bot in the back of the head.
The way the mission structure works equates to a train robbery. You crew boards the enemy vessel with a given set of objectives, steal, plunder, kill, deactivate, the usual stuff. You go through compartments, collecting loot and dealing with the ships inhabitants. Usually you have to make a speedy exit via escape pod at the end of missions. Difficulty antes up with giving the enemy better guns, turrets and improving aim. The XCOM mechanic kicks in with tactical placements of your crew and a cover  mechanic. While flanking enemies is possible, it tends to be difficult as all levels are procedurally generated. Additionally there are also classes and abilities that are reminiscent of XCOM.
While there are not many buttons to worry, about the game does feature full controller support and comes recommended. Reason being is that the aiming mechanic can be a bit tricky especially if you don’t have a scope. Otherwise there isn’t too much to fuss with, you move your troops, fire, and use special abilities. Every character you have/recruit has their own unique class and weapon set. As you complete missions they gain experience which unlocks new abilities. Guns range from light pistols, shotguns, to heavy weapons like rocket launchers.
This mixing of classes and abilities makes every mission unique as most characters have their own way of approaching things.
Thankfully, all missions are repeatable and there are several different kinds of difficulty depending on your skill level. These raise the stakes when it comes to loot/XP but also increases the punishment for failure. Unlike XCOM though, you don’t lose your Steambots permanently but just lose water, the games currency.
Between heists you have the galaxy map that you use to fly around. Steamworld Heists limits content you can access either through the story or by a reputation system that is given in stars. It comes off feeling a little bit like a mobile game as certain missions cannot be done until you achieve a certain star count. As you unlock more areas you gain access to bars/shops that let you recruit new Steambots and buy weapons/accessories. All of these mechanics flow into each other very smoothly but the game isn’t spotless.
The only issue I found lies in inventory management. This can become quite a headache. Despite having a huge ship, you only are allowed to carry a limited number of items. Your storage can be expanded upon later in the game but I always felt like I was running behind on space. While all bots can share accessories/guns, you end up having quite a few unique weapons/items or double up cause you might want two of the same class on a mission. Thankfully you can sell items at any point in space but I just would’ve enjoyed a bit more freedom in this area. This is magnified and very frustrating at the end of missions constantly deciding what I wanted to keep and sell. Preventing progression in the game.
While I enjoyed Heist’s gameplay quite a bit it does become a bit repetitive eventually. Even though the game breaks things up with different objectives and a boss fight occasionally, you eventually end up in a slog of just upgrading guns/accessories. I wouldn’t say the game failed to my hold my attention but it didn’t sweep me off my feet. Unlike Steamworld Dig that I played obsessively until I beat it. I think Heist is best enjoyed causally and slowly.
What drew my attention and love about this game series is its style.
This is something that matches its predecessors and improves upon significantly. I am constantly surprised how well Robots and Western themes just blend together. Every Steambot has an incredible amount of personality to them. From the charming Piper, whose more heart then metal to background characters like bartenders and merchants. When I docked with the Saloon and found a steambot band playing some really awesome tunes, I couldn’t stop smiling. It’s little moments like these that enhances Steamworld. Enemies, allies alike all have their own unique style of ships, weapons, and detail abounds.
Obviously there aren’t rendered clouds to gawk at or 60FPS Cup o’ noodle but that doesn’t stop Steamworld from feeling like a thriving and fun universe. Things are the same when it comes to combat and more action oriented scenes. Lasers sizzle, bullets zing, and bots crunch or scatter into pieces when they die.
I have no fault with the visuals or sound department of Steamworld Heist. The music is great and I never got tired of it. There were plenty of times the music actually surprised with me a jaunty tune. It isn’t all that surprising that you can purchase the soundtrack as well. The sound effects all had their proper amount of gravitas to them and made the actions more visceral.
There is plenty to give the game quite a bit of replay value. Like I mentioned earlier there are many difficulty settings that keep things fresh if you find it too easy. The game does feature Steam Achievements and cards. There is also some additional DLC that adds more weapons, missions, and a new crew member. Depending on your skill level the game could take anywhere from ten to twenty hours of gameplay.
From a game development standpoint, It takes balls to try something completely new.
Most of the time you improve upon a formula and do the best at it to make more money. This was something completely unexpected and I appreciated Steamworld Heist for what it is. It’s fun, smooth, and well made. I hope this isn’t the last we see of the Steamworld universe and I can’t wait to see what the developer cooks up next. As for Heist, if you enjoy strategy games with a bit of a casual nature I recommend this title easily. Coming in at the indie standard of $14.99/£10.99 this is a safe bet, and downright steal during a sale.

Pros:
-Simple graphics, tutorial, and interface help beginner tower defense players learn quickly.
-Fun, simple gameplay, with some strategic depth.
-Great difficulty curve that forces change of strategy on later levels.
-Many units are generally well-balanced and useful in their own way.
-Decent value game if you spend $6 or less.
-Family-friendly.
Cons:
-Low replay value; game is beatable in a few hours, nothing else really to do other than survival mode and minimal achievements.
-Suicide bomber enemies are OP. I would understand if all units die from bombers in one hit except for tanks, but even low-level tank units get killed by them in one hit. Only max-upgraded tanks can survive one blast, but with almost no HP left. Enemy suicide bomber damage should be reduced a bit so that level 1, 2, and 3 tank units can take more than one bomber hit, but no more than two, before death.
-Basic archer units should do a bit more damage.
-No way to see specific enemy stats, or how your unit buffs are affecting unit stats.
-When building units, no name indicators are given when choosing what unit to place. There needs to be names shown when mousing over the units, so that you can distinguish between each unit without incorrectly selecting the wrong unit to build.
-General bugs ruin gameplay: enemy units go right through defences when they shouldn't in certain levels, sometimes certain areas that you should be able to place units on become unbuildable during gameplay, bad melee AI makes them move to areas that you don't want them to move and attack units that you don't want them to.
-Limited music variety becomes tiresome to listen to.
-Unit placement voices are annoying.
-Barebones storyline and graphics.
Overall, 6/10. There are many better tower defense games out there (Dungeon Defence, Plants vs. Zombies, etc), but I would recommend this for family gamers, if you're looking for a budget TD game, if you're a huge TD game enthusist or if you're a TD beginner. Otherwise, look elsewhere.

Far too basic and unpolished...
Selknam defence is a basic tower defence game made by Bad Games (no Pun intended).
There isn't much story in the game. Basically, you play as the 'Selknam', a tribe, who has to defend their homeland from the invaders.
Gameplay is basic tower defence. The objective in the campaign is to protect your village from attack. Your village has four health and each enemy unit that reaches your village will decrease it's health by one. When your vilage's health gets reduced to zero the you lose and the game ends. Instead of towers you have infantry, who act like towers (ie. don't move around much). There a variety of units available which fall into one of four classes: archer, slinger, melee, wizard. Each class has three types of units such as mage healer and a mage that damages foes. You can buy new units from spending coins, which can be earned periodicly after each wave or by defeating enemies. At the end of each level you will earn stars (based on how  well your defence was) which you can spend upgrading units. You can only upgrade your units after each level (not during gameplay), which I didn't find appealing as it reduces your activities during gameplay.  A variety of foes will attempt to get to your town including knights, musketeers, pirates etc which all have unique stats and health. What I found was that there wasn't enough coin to spend at the start (or during gameplay) and that made building defences really difficult. Another problem is that unlike  in other tower defence games, there is no 'building time' in between each wave, with enemies constantly battling against the defences, it was difficult to repair and rebuild units. Units also don't show the range that they can attack ( a problem mainly for archers), which makes it difficult to place your units in ideal positions. Finally, although the game is 'tower defence' genre, gameplay mainly focuses on blocking enemy via mass unit walls as enemies will easily defeat your units one by one if they spread out.
Audio isn't good. Besides the poor combat sounds from units, the same background music is played over and over again which is quite annoying. There is no voice acting in the game, with characters speaking through text.
Graphics are another downer. Unit models lack detail as well as the enrironment, which barely has anything e.g. bushes, trees, etc and is therefore quite barren.
Level design is quite repetitive. Areas look too similar to each other, with some terrain moved to different locations and a new paint job.
If you want a really basic tower defence game with clunky mechanics, then this game might entertain you. Else, stay clear.

Warm, comforting, and a little moist.
You might expect, just like I did, from looking at this game, with its strange-looking clown protagonist and psychedelic atmosphere, to contain some subversive narrative, or that it's secretly a horror game. I thought there at least might be some predictable twist that Dropsy is a serial murderer, or a monster, or god knows what else. But it defied my expectations. While there are many dark themes running throughout this game, and a number of twists, Dropsy himself is pure-hearted.
It'd also be easy to pass this game off as just being too simple, sappy and over-sentimental, teaching you the same old things you learned in Sunday school; Don't judge a book by its cover, be nice to others, and so on. The game is about those things, yes, but it does it in a way that, at least to me, felt genuine.
Dropsy does a lot of things that fans of point and click adventures should enjoy. While there is a plotline to follow, the main thrust of the game is wandering around the world, meeting its inhabitants, and getting them to let you hug them. However, almost everyone you meet has some kind of problem, and one way or another are in a non-hugging mood. You solve their problem, then get to huggin'. All the dialogue they give you is done by representative pictures and symbols, which both help demonstrate Dropsy's loose grasp on language, and also make the thankfully simple puzzles a little more challenging, since you might not fully understand them at first. Many of these puzzles can only be solved once you have an item or a companion from doing the main story, but the rest you can solve at your own pace, and aren't required to finish the game. It's rare to see a game, especially a point and click adventure one, where you genuinely just help people out. It's a nice feeling, wandering back over familiar areas, and seeing a character you helped earlier in better spirits. Hell, you can even hug them again if you'd like.
What mainly will determine if you'll enjoy Dropsy is its presentation. Personally I found the artstyle quite charming, and each character is animated quite well. The soundtrack also really appeals to me, having a good variety between upbeat, bouncy tunes and softer, more atmospheric melodies. In The Court of the Junkyard King is a particular favorite of mine. The soundtrack is what seals the deal on this game for me, so keep in mind it's also available separately if you're interested.
Overall, it's a simple, charming experience with a unique personality and style. In a world that could always use more love, Dropsy has plenty to share.

The flight models in this sim are amazing. Hands down the best imho. I have flown planes in real life and can honestly say that this sim mimics real flight better than most. Especially the feeling of "being on rails".
This sim in my opinion is the true successor to IL-2 1946. NOT Battle of Stalingrad. While BoS is more worried about getting into your pockets with graphical gimmicks on an incredibly old and outdated engine and revised history with incorrect flight models that clearly were created to favor one side, this sim however, is about as true and accurate as you can get. Yes there will always be compromise in terms of accuracy because we are playing on a PC mind you. But it doesn't break away from the "sim" feel.
Team Fusion is incredible. These guys took a game completely broken game and fixed most of it. When this game initially released it was so broken it was a disgrace. But the developers of Team Fusion are just members of the Flight Sim community like you and I. They wouldn't let the game go to waste and fixed it themselves.
THE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF THE REVIEW..
Team Fusion is a great development team. And I think the biggest reason for it is because they are NOT some big corporation or company. They are guys just like us who enjoy flight sims and want an accurate and true experience. For that reason and that reason alone you can ALWAYS trust this development team over a team thats only drive is money. **Cough cough** Battle of Stalingrad **Cough cough**.
If you want to fly an accurate, fair, and true to its roots sim. Buy Cliffs of Dover and support the devs. If your an oldschool IL-2 1946 player I can almost promise you that you will hate battle of stalingrad and stay far away from it as possible as that has been the scenario with myself and countless other virtual pilots that have been around for over a decade.
MAKE SURE AFTER YOU DOWNLOAD THE INITIAL GAME TO GET THE TEAM FUSION BETA PATCH THROUGH STEAM. DO A GOOGLE SEARCH OF HOW TO DO THAT OR ELSE THIS GAME WILL BE COMPLETELY BROKEN AND POINTLESS!

My first real experience of being in awe of a flight computer game came as an 9yr old kid around 1990.
My more oppulent and older next-door-neighbour used to politely put up with me as I watched him play games on his  Amiga 500. That piece of hardware seemed to have a heavenly aura around it. I wanted it so much, but I knew i would unlikely ever have my own.

I would  peer over his shoulder and ask him a million questions about whatever game he played.
When i think on it, my neighbour really did have the patience of a saint, he never once kicked me out for being the pest I surely was.
I remember when he bought the game " Wings". I must have been around at his house everyday for near a month to watch him play.
A soon as the Red Baron would  appear on screen to enter the dog fight, i would be screaming in his ear to let him know that ♥♥♥♥ just got real...
And that "game over" music..., it affected my 9yr old mind, it seemed to explain the finality of death more clear than any textbook did at the time...at least until the next turn loaded up.
I rarely got to play the game, only what seemed liked seconds or maybe minutes. When my neighbour got called for an errand or took a quick break i would take the controls and invariably crash and solemnly watch on as my funeral party congregated around my grave.
As luck would have it, my neighbour and his family travelled to Goa, India, for a 3 week holiday that summer.
I was tasked with feeding their cats while they were away... I binged played Wings for three weeks solid, and fed the cats sometimes too. Those 3 weeks are amongst the most memorable of my gaming life.
So what has all of this got to do with il-2 Sturmovik Cliffs of Dover?????
Well in the 27 or so years following "Wings", i was never captivated by a flight game to the same extent.
Having been mostly preoccupied with a mix of strategy,  FPS, RPG style games, i guess flight sims seemed to fall between the cracks for me.
That is until recently.  I dipped my toe back in with Rise Of Flight United. This was a nice transition as it featured WW1 bi-planes featured in Wings but also introduced some actual sim elements as apposed to arcade Wings action!
I soon went out and bought a HOTAS and have been enjoying ROF ever since.
I decided to take a chance on Il-2 CLOD after stumbling onto some YT videos. The gameplay footage sold me straight away.
Il-2 Sturmovik Cliffs of Dover (Team Fusion Patch) is the most fun and addictive flight game i have played since Wings on the Amiga 500.
The game is simply fantasitic. I since bought Il-2 Battle Of Stalingrad (which graphically is an improvement and seems a great game),  but i just keep going back to CLOD.
There is a learning curve and i did pull my hair out trying to setup my HOTAS the way i want (it's still a WIP), but when you get flying in this game and turn on full realisim, well, i have few words to descibe what it feels like to take off, intercept an enemy and then land safely in this game. The game is pure bliss at times.
I dont know the full story of CLOD and it's orignal development, only that it was hurried to market and suffered as a result. The "Team Fusion Mod group" now seem to be updating this title and are doing their best to ensure it takes it place in WWII hall of fame for vidya games.
They say good wine gets better with age, well perhaps this applies to certain video games when the right group of modders can get their hands on it.

Highly recommended *
* You really need a  HOTAS to enjoy this game IMO.
Also, I've yet to try MP - So I dont know what server traffic is like - I'm happy with Campaign and SP for now.
No idea what the stock game is like - I have used the Team Fusion patch from purchase. Apply patch from game properties -Beta - Team Fusion Patch - Enjoy!

I'll start my review by saying I wanted to give it a so-so recommendation but because there is only a Yes or No option, I reluctantly opted for Yes.
The game is fun, colonizing planets, moving your citizens to different planets, developing those planets, negotiating peacefully or aggressively (through space combat and hostile elimination/takeover of their planets) with other alien races, obtaining new scientific discoveries and using them to develop more powerful ships.  The problems with the game is what leads me to give it a reluctant Yes on recommendation, the bugs.
I played the game on an older laptop, which does handle the game all right but with issues.  I was not able to play a space battle because the message DBGHELP.DLL too old would come up and crash the game when I clicked on any of my ships.  I've been playing Autocombat to get around this.
After playing for hours, it now comes up with the same message when I attempt to load my game, making it so I am unable to play my saved game.  I'm now hoping that a patch will come out soon which will help with the issue and let me go back to playing again.
Second issue I have is with the minor pirate factions.  They have the ability to produce multiple ships from one planet.  I'm aware they are there to purchase a ship to use (mercenary) but if you are at war with them, this strongly feels like a cheat tactic.  I knocked one pirate faction down to about two million people and one factory on a single planet.  They come back shortly later with a huge ship (they have no Ship Yard to produce this).  About five turns later they have about five smaller ships (produced in one turn) attacking one of my planets.  I managed to defeat them but if I had known they had that ability to make ships out of no where, I would have guarded my planet better.
I did enjoy discovering new native alien races which can be used to help you develop your planet and maybe used to go to other planets.  The ability to use transport ships to either move your people around or to become a part of your trading function to move food to different planets is helpful.
Its not a bad game but I would recommend purchasing the game when it is on a good sale.  And hopefully game issues will be cleared up by then.

I will start by saying that this game is very blue.
now my opinion of the game.
I wont write a long or complex review of this game, at the time of writing this i have sunk just over 6 hours of game play into it, Some may argue that this is not enough time to develope a good idea of what the game has to offer, but i disagree.
Ive played 4X Space empire strategy games for decades, they are my favourite strategy genre. If i was to compare this game to any that i have played before it would be Master of Orion 2. The art style and game mechanics are generally the same. With MOO2 i could build an empire and finish a game in a matter of hours and this game is much the same, It is a lite 4x game. The options are very limited in game apart from the different races having slightly different (locked) traits which can alter the evolution of the game slightly i find that every game i play generally plays out the same every time with predicable results. Which has rendered the replayability of this title for me at least somewhat limited. I am already finding my self uninterested in playing it much more.
The game is solid and runs fine, except that i got a glitch when i was hours into a game and doing well, That a unit was not accounted for in a turn and that this shouldnt happen in this version of the game... a big red box popped up inviting me to send a bug report to the devs.... the game crashed and my progress was ended as the game was essencially corrupted.
Which has kinda made me think twice about investing more time into this game... why bother if your efforts are blown away by a bug hours into play.
i like the art systle, which although are cartoony are actually well designed.
The mechanics are simple, although nothing is explained, but i feel their simplicity makes them more of a chore than an aspect of the game to be enjoyed during play. The research screen for example if anoying.. You simply stack research  from a list with one of two buttons and wait. The order in which you research is the same every game (because you beeline for certain technologies) and it just becomes redundant. Everytime i see the icon to restack my new research selections appear.... i sigh.
So much of this games interface and game play is rince and repeat and is very shallow.
However the combat is the games one saving grace. The building of custom ships (once you have an expanded tech tree) is interesting with the ability to build ships that are fit to task and sent into fleet combat which is acted out as a top down turn based strategy arena (exactly the same as Master of Orion 2) So many 4x Space empire games get the combat wrong, defaulting to a boring watch and see RNG - Rock paper sissors system, This game at least gets the combat right....although its not original.
My problem with this title is that its not flexlable or original in its execution and the game has already started to feel dry to me after only 6 hours of play.
This game needs options!
In summary, This is a lite 4x game designed i feel to be a homage to Master of Orion which is fine, Although that game is 20+ years old and while it was fresh and new then, its feels dated now.
I got this game in a sale for £10. It feels more like a 4x you would find on a modbile device than PC and for that reason i feel the £10 might be a little over priced. I certainly dont think its worth the full asking price because im bored at 6 hours.
I want to give this game a Maybe score... but im forced to chose between Thumbs up and thumbs down and as much as i appreciate the game which i honestly feels is well made (despite the bug which killed my game) at the moment i dont feel that its a very fleshed out or original experiance and other games are out there which are better and for the same price. So im going to have to say thumbs down.
If you want a quick 4x lite experiance which isnt taxing on your PC's hardware then maybe this is for you.

Between Steamworld Heist and Steamworld Dig the question remains, what can’t these Steambots do?
Take some Firefly, throw in some XCOM, and heaping helping of steampunk whimsy and you have got yourself Steamworld Heist. All ya need is a bot with a hammer for a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and you got Captain Malcolm Reynolds. Pop culture references aside, Heist is a homage to westerns, just substitute horses with spaceships.
While the game does have an amazing opening sequence that sets the scene for you, I will do my best to explain the story. After the Earth exploded, bots began to mine moisture for survival. You play a rag tag group of outlaw steambots on the fringes of space. Dealing with gangs, Royalists and all sorts of seedy characters. The setting is simple but eloquent. You play the captain of one these outlaw gangs and some bots begin to muscle in on your territory. Thus the Firefly-esque adventure begins with you taking up the mantle of the common people and making off with some decent loot as a benefit.
If you’re unfamiliar with the universe of Steamworld, I highly recommend playing Steamworld Dig as that is a fantastic title all on its own. Aside from being an awesome action/platformer it also gives insights into why Earth explodes.
Steamworld Heist on the other hand does a dramatic pivot from its predecessor. Where you controlled a single bot and primarily worried about mining, this time you steal, shoot, and control a whole squad. It was definitely one of the things that impressed me with the developer Image & Form. Instead of sticking with what they knew and had already learned they decided to take the series in a whole other direction and genre. It takes some moxie for that kind of thing and hats off to them for pulling it off.
At its most simple, Heist is a turn based strategy game that puts you behind the gun.
Aiming is by far Heists defining feature and what makes it fun. Trick shots, bouncing grenades, and shooting your enemies hat off is the bread and butter of this game. It’s satisfying every time when you bounce your sniper round off five walls and hit a bot in the back of the head.
The way the mission structure works equates to a train robbery. You crew boards the enemy vessel with a given set of objectives, steal, plunder, kill, deactivate, the usual stuff. You go through compartments, collecting loot and dealing with the ships inhabitants. Usually you have to make a speedy exit via escape pod at the end of missions. Difficulty antes up with giving the enemy better guns, turrets and improving aim. The XCOM mechanic kicks in with tactical placements of your crew and a cover  mechanic. While flanking enemies is possible, it tends to be difficult as all levels are procedurally generated. Additionally there are also classes and abilities that are reminiscent of XCOM.
While there are not many buttons to worry, about the game does feature full controller support and comes recommended. Reason being is that the aiming mechanic can be a bit tricky especially if you don’t have a scope. Otherwise there isn’t too much to fuss with, you move your troops, fire, and use special abilities. Every character you have/recruit has their own unique class and weapon set. As you complete missions they gain experience which unlocks new abilities. Guns range from light pistols, shotguns, to heavy weapons like rocket launchers.
This mixing of classes and abilities makes every mission unique as most characters have their own way of approaching things.
Thankfully, all missions are repeatable and there are several different kinds of difficulty depending on your skill level. These raise the stakes when it comes to loot/XP but also increases the punishment for failure. Unlike XCOM though, you don’t lose your Steambots permanently but just lose water, the games currency.
Between heists you have the galaxy map that you use to fly around. Steamworld Heists limits content you can access either through the story or by a reputation system that is given in stars. It comes off feeling a little bit like a mobile game as certain missions cannot be done until you achieve a certain star count. As you unlock more areas you gain access to bars/shops that let you recruit new Steambots and buy weapons/accessories. All of these mechanics flow into each other very smoothly but the game isn’t spotless.
The only issue I found lies in inventory management. This can become quite a headache. Despite having a huge ship, you only are allowed to carry a limited number of items. Your storage can be expanded upon later in the game but I always felt like I was running behind on space. While all bots can share accessories/guns, you end up having quite a few unique weapons/items or double up cause you might want two of the same class on a mission. Thankfully you can sell items at any point in space but I just would’ve enjoyed a bit more freedom in this area. This is magnified and very frustrating at the end of missions constantly deciding what I wanted to keep and sell. Preventing progression in the game.
While I enjoyed Heist’s gameplay quite a bit it does become a bit repetitive eventually. Even though the game breaks things up with different objectives and a boss fight occasionally, you eventually end up in a slog of just upgrading guns/accessories. I wouldn’t say the game failed to my hold my attention but it didn’t sweep me off my feet. Unlike Steamworld Dig that I played obsessively until I beat it. I think Heist is best enjoyed causally and slowly.
What drew my attention and love about this game series is its style.
This is something that matches its predecessors and improves upon significantly. I am constantly surprised how well Robots and Western themes just blend together. Every Steambot has an incredible amount of personality to them. From the charming Piper, whose more heart then metal to background characters like bartenders and merchants. When I docked with the Saloon and found a steambot band playing some really awesome tunes, I couldn’t stop smiling. It’s little moments like these that enhances Steamworld. Enemies, allies alike all have their own unique style of ships, weapons, and detail abounds.
Obviously there aren’t rendered clouds to gawk at or 60FPS Cup o’ noodle but that doesn’t stop Steamworld from feeling like a thriving and fun universe. Things are the same when it comes to combat and more action oriented scenes. Lasers sizzle, bullets zing, and bots crunch or scatter into pieces when they die.
I have no fault with the visuals or sound department of Steamworld Heist. The music is great and I never got tired of it. There were plenty of times the music actually surprised with me a jaunty tune. It isn’t all that surprising that you can purchase the soundtrack as well. The sound effects all had their proper amount of gravitas to them and made the actions more visceral.
There is plenty to give the game quite a bit of replay value. Like I mentioned earlier there are many difficulty settings that keep things fresh if you find it too easy. The game does feature Steam Achievements and cards. There is also some additional DLC that adds more weapons, missions, and a new crew member. Depending on your skill level the game could take anywhere from ten to twenty hours of gameplay.
From a game development standpoint, It takes balls to try something completely new.
Most of the time you improve upon a formula and do the best at it to make more money. This was something completely unexpected and I appreciated Steamworld Heist for what it is. It’s fun, smooth, and well made. I hope this isn’t the last we see of the Steamworld universe and I can’t wait to see what the developer cooks up next. As for Heist, if you enjoy strategy games with a bit of a casual nature I recommend this title easily. Coming in at the indie standard of $14.99/£10.99 this is a safe bet, and downright steal during a sale.

Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver is an old game with a very cool name.
Five hundred years after the events of Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain. Kain is  deified, having built a great vampiric Empire across the entirety of Nosgoth. Which is bad for us because we're people and filled with that red stuff they like to drink.
They bite me and I go “Ouch.”
Raziel, firstborn of Kain's lieutenants, and commander of the Razielim, one of the clans of Kain's empire. One fateful day, after Raziel reveals that he has surpassed his master in evolution by growing some neat wings. Kain tears his wings from his body and casts Raziel into the abyss, a whirlpool that burns the flesh from Raziel's bones.
But Raziel is resurrected by a strange entity known as the Elder God. The Elder God tells Raziel of the wheel of fate and that he has been resurrected as a “Soul Reaver”, a creature that consumes souls under the command of the Elder God.
Now, Raziel returns to Nosgoth centuries later and finds out its all gone down the toilet. Kain's empire is rotting, all of the vampires are all goopy looking, and there are those human guys walking around and shooting at the goopy vampires with crossbows and other cool stuff. Raziel must now hunt down Kain, avenge himself and his clan, and bring balance to Nosgoth.
All while not even being bothered by the fact that he's naked from the chest down.
Legacy of Kain is one of those classics people don't seem to talk about anymore, though it kind of makes sense, since the series had pretty much run it's course. That being said, the game still holds up to this day.
Soul Reaver is basically a marvel for it's time in both story telling and game play. It mixed platforming, puzzle solving, and combat in such a way that it fit the universe it took place in. You don't just fight and kill vampires, you straight up have to slay them, and use methods that other people have to use in universe to keep the bitey little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s down.
If you impale a vampire, it goes down and stays down, as long as it remains impaled. So what happens if you pull the weapon out of the corpse? The vampire gets back up. So how do you keep the smelly idiot down for good? Well you dump it in water or force it into sunlight.
Fortunately, Raziel can simply consume their souls after he has defeated them, giving them no chance of waking back up and giving Raziel a distinct advantage against some human who has to go toe to toe with a vampire. But it's just so cool that they took the time to just make combat lore-friendly to their own universe.
Puzzles in Soul Reaver seem daunting at first, but you soon realize that they're a lot easier than they look. I've heard of people actually having to buy the Prima strategy guide for this back in the day, or go on Gamefaqs, but I didn't have a problem solving any of them. They're mostly block puzzles or some sort of jumping puzzle, luckily they're never so complicated that they wear out their welcome.
Many of the areas you're in later on are basically one giant puzzle, with a plethora of smaller little brain teasers in between that all add up to a singular goal. Its rewarding to mess around with a bunch of puzzles that all end up making something cool happen in the end.
Like a Rubik's cube or throwing a badger into a school bus.
The voice acting is pretty astounding. Both Simon Templeman as Kain and Michael Bell as Raziel bring it home with their almost Shakespearean line delivery, their dialogue, monologues, and quips are something writers today wish they had thought of. Even the Elder God, played by the late Tony Jay, chews up every scene their in. There isn't a bad bad or out of place voice in the game, though it helps that basically everybody is played by either Templeman, Bell, or Jay, save for a few exceptions.
Also, get your hands on the soundtrack, seriously, that's the good♥♥♥♥♥♥
“Wow, Dirk!” You say. “You sure like this game! So what's wrong with it?”
Well, I'm glad you asked, person I just made up.
Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver came out in 1999, and there hasn't been anything done with it since that day. There was no modern updates that I can think of, and fan patches can only go so far.
As it stands on a fresh install, the game kind of looks like puke, it's pretty bumpy and blurry, and squirmy looking. Luckily, there is a resolution patch that makes the game look much better on a modern monitor.
What cant be fixed is the controls. I don't usually have problems with older games, but I couldn't get around just how wonky the keyboard controls were. I ended up trying to use a controller, but the game basically only seems to work with old logitech controllers from the 90s. I ended up having to get a third party program just so I could basically jury-rig the game to work with a modern controller, but even then it was janky and barely worked.
Luckily! Luckily. There is like, a million different ways to play this game.
You absolutely cannot go wrong with the PS1 version of the game, which is both easy to find physically as well as available digitally on the PS3. There's also the third option, you know what I'm talking about, wink wink nudge nudge.
The other option is the Dreamcast version, which is apparently the best version you can get. I myself can attest that this version is actually really good, it plays well and doesn't have the same problems as the PS1 version's slowdowns or the PCs weird control schemes.
Whichever way you play it is up to you, this is more of a review of the game as a whole than a specific version. I don't care how you play it, but you should probably play it if you somehow haven't already.

CLOSURE is a black and white alienish platform puzzle game where the world exists because of light. Without light, there is only nothing and I mean nothing, if you try to jump onto a platform that doesn't have light near it, you will fall through the world. If you are swimming and your light floats away, you will drop out of the world without it. Solid walls become jumps when there is no light on them. The object of each of the almost 100 levels is basically to make it to the door at the end. You can pick up lit orbs, you can put lit orbs into carriers that will carry them. This leads to some really interesting platform mechanics, such as moving lights turn into elevators when normally they'd be solid walls. You can put orbs into transporters that will make 2 areas lit instead of 1. There are push boxes, push rollers that will of course roll, lit push boxes, lamps that you can adjust to cast light onto different areas and so on. This is a unique, enjoyable, atmospheric, immerse game, but I have a feeling that once you're done, you're done. They made a really alien world here and the music is awesome and belongs in a suspense drama. After the tutorial levels when the game opens up, the music eases up so its not as intense. Very worth a play through, I own it a few different ways, Steam, GOG, did I mention its free for Playstation Plus members?

Have you ever played
?  If not, it's basically a game where you press a button and all adjacent buttons switch polarity from on to off and vice-versa.  The goal in that game was to make sure all of the lights went out...hence the name.  This time, you're given 3 colors: Green, Blue, and Cyan.  Your goal this time is to make sure all of the stars are the same color to pass the level...doesn't matter which it is, so long as all stars are the same matching color.  Also, it's not just adjacent stars...it's all stars in the whole line adjacent to the star you've selected.
In
, you're given various modes including a classic mode (all set maps for you to complete), a randomized and infuriating time trial (which has a bug to give you more time...and a new bug discovered where you can reach level 30 if you simply have a controller), an infinite play mode (for if you just want a casual experience), and a workshop where you can make your own maps.  This kind of thing's good if you're obsessed with
-type puzzles.
Personally, this experience is rather hit/miss with me.  It's basically the same game I've seen repeated in games like
,
,
, and various other games.  After enough time, you get the gist of what kind of solution the puzzle is expecting.  I wasn't pleased when I found out that this game was bugged.   It also has balance issues in its classic mode where the puzzles will seem easy, but will quickly ramp up to be difficult trials.
That said, I guess I could recommend
, but it still requires more polishing.  The asking price is $3, but you should get this for a far lower price such as $0.25-$1.00 given that it's a Unity product that recycles an old idea without much that's new.  Play if you really have nothing better to do, avoid if you're tired of the same kind of puzzles.  I could really take or leave it...just have a bit of a "middle of the road" view about this sort of game.
