There are 12 characters. Of the 12, only 3 can deal damage. The rest of the characters are specialized roles unable to deal damage. And all characters can be attacked, there's no hiding support characters off the main road to keep them out of harm's way. For example, within the cleric family, each character can cast only one type of buff (haste, heal, or strengthen) and cannot attack. Same with archers: the main archer can deal damage, but the slowing archer and poison archer can only add their effect. Since characters can only perform their one narrow role, buffs/support eat up more resources than they're worth.
Each character can be upgraded twice and twice only. And upgrades are done between levels. So in the beginning of each level, the characters overwhelm each wave easily, but by the third or fourth wave (of five), tables are turned and its the level three heroes who are easily overpowered.
For each role-character, there is an enemy counter. For example, within the warrior family there is a tank that can absorb but not damage. You can out a tank right on the path, but enemies can leave the path to go around the tank, and some enemies can go through the tank, and there are suicide bombers who can blow up multiple tanks in one hit. And even regular enemies can wear down tanks if the tanks aren't complimented with archers or warriors, because the tanks don't deal damage.
And all this wouldn't be so bad if the charaters could be instructed. For example, archers, focus on suicide bombers, or something like that. But everyone just focus on the most forward enemy.
This would be n uninspired flash game on kongregate or armor games or something. But on Steam? For five dollars?!? Pass, my friends. Pass.

I bought Stars in Shadow for half price, as I am a big 4x fan.
Stars in Shadow is a great concept: take a space 4x and simplify it for quick, fun play.  A game takes maybe 6 hours.  But the gameplay is limited too much as a result.  I have to downvote.  The game is unidimensional (essentially one victory condition) and needs hot keys.
Details follow.
The interface is streamlined and impressive for the most part, because by design you don't need many different displays.
There are many convenient ways to get information fast.  Stars in Shadow has a tablet interface.  You only need to left click.  For a touch screen, it would be ideal, because there is no cost/annoyance of moving the mouse across the screen.
Thankfully, the right click adds some functionality, especially if you turn on the option to right click close windows (escape works, too).
The game adds cool features, not seen in 4x often or at all.  It has tactical combat, which is exciting and also allows you to use tactics instead of watchning individual units from a stack pound each other.  The game also allows you to take back moves to go back and fix some sort of error.  This makes it painless to ask the question "Will this enemy fleet crush me?"  Without a save/load hassle.
Stars in Shadow would be a great 4x game for children (they could remote to a PC on their tablet) or 4x introductory game for adult players.
The game has some replay value, because each race has a big advantage, and figuring out how to exploit these is interesting.  I got 50 hours, not bad for $13.
The gameplay suffers, however, because of the victory condition, no hotkeys, and some bugs.
* No manual or tips to explain game content.  They made a manual, which you find in a hidden link, which tells you the overiew of the interface only.
* No hotkeys.  So there are no hotkeys.  Cuz it's a tablet interface.  So I have to keep moving my mouse across the screen to click stuff.  This all takes more time.  Also 4x without hotkeys?   Did I mention there are no hot keys? /ragequit
* Victory condition: you can either win the galactic council through diplomacy or use military to conquer the galaxy.
* Game flow:
* Conquering the galaxy could be fun, but gets monotonous because travel time is punitive.  I mean, do it once, but not every game.
* To achieve the diplomatic victory, all you need to do is (1) have a big enough armada that no one wants to take advantage of you (2) befirend other civilizations (don't declare war) and (3) ultimately make an alliance with multiple players, so they vote for you for diplomatic council.  All you need to do this is to contact civilizations, wait to accrue diplomacy points, and spend them.  This makes the game one dimensional and you basically just have to colonize planets and build ships/buy mercenaries while you wait to win.  Having said this, I think most 4x games typically have issues with victory condition.  An unfortunate side effect is you can always win half way through the tech tree.  No death spheres for you!
* An alliance (needed to win) does not force you to declare war to defend your opponents.  You can stop a war by spending diplomacy points immediately.
* Bugs are rare.  Trying to make an open border agreement with humans crashes about half the time.  You typically can recover when you learn what keys to hit  (F1 - not documented anywhere).  Another time, I tried to split my fleet to attack a planet with only some ships.  Fatal error.

This is how my first game went down:
1) Set every single setting on default, normal difficulty.
2) Explore the two closest systems to my starting position, colonize them.
3) Build farms and mines on the appropriate planets within the systems to benefit from various bonuses.
4) Scrap my only ship I had left (a scout) to save on maintenance costs.
5) Spam the "End Turn" button until something finishes building, then do it again.
6) Finally, a faction approaches me, I make an alliance with them using the "Social Currency" (think gold, but used to buy services like open borders, alliances, collaborative research, etc...)
7) Others soon contact me, do the same.
8) The more alliances you make, the more of that "Social Currency" you have per turn.
9) Become ally with all but one faction that hasn't made contact with me yet.
10) Everybody is fighting at least one of my allies, they periodically ask me "We are at war with [another ally of mine], would you help us fight them?" To which I say "not right now", and they respond, this is a direct quote: "Maybe another time then."
11) I'm farming ridiculous quantities of every currency, still haven't built a single combat ship, still haven't left my three starter systems.
12) After an hour or so, I finally get to contact the last faction, make an alliance, and then I'm greeted with a "The galaxy is ours, we have won." message, in my standard activity feed. Not even a victory screen.
tl;dr I was able to win the game by sitting at my starting position, making friends with everybody extremely easily, and ending turns more than actually playing. I didn't have to play a single fight.
Easily exploitable AI, not much to do. And the cherry on top, not even a victory screen, in a 4X game.
Bonus: You cannot rebind any of your keys.
This is a joke of a game. If you're a fan of 4X games, keep your money, and buy Age of Wonders, Civilization, or any other game within well established franchises.

I played through this on PS3. It's an interesting game, copying the black/white artstyle of Limbo.
Where this game differs, though, is in the gameplay mechanics. In this game, light is paramount. The only parts of the level that you can interact with (stand on, run into, etc) are the parts that light is shining on. It's an interesting puzzle mechanic, and it really adds an entirely new dimension to how we think things work.
Unfortunately, though, sometimes the puzzles feel like "hmm, I have no idea what to do, so let's try THIS." The beginning puzzles are certainly simpler, but some of the later puzzles descend into perceived randomness.
There's actually a pretty dark story to the game, too, if you really think about it. I enjoyed it.
Unfortunately, taken as a whole, I wasn't really a fan of the game. It could be because I plowed through this whole game in one night, but I was ready for it to be over long before it actually was. I wasn't a fan of Limbo either, so I must just not value the artsy-factor as much as other people do. Gameplay is far more important to me, and this game is middling in that regard.

In Energy Cycle, you turn a field of colored orbs into the same color. Clicking a particular orb on the field changes the color of every vertical and horizontal adjacent orb with it.
The background of every Energy Cycle puzzle is a hypnotizing spiral that distracted me.
Puzzle mode consists of 28 preset levels that get more difficult the further along you go. Some puzzles I had to defeat twice
It's possible to master Energy Cycle's gameplay and have no problem at all completing these levels in a few hours. The predetermined setup makes it possible for someone to film their run as a guide and allow people to cheat. But Energy Cycle addresses this problem with the other modes included.
Time Attack and Infinite Play modes are like each other, with the difference being that Infinite Play doesn't have the countdown on every puzzle that Time Attack does.
Level Editor mode gives control to the player to make an Energy Cycle puzzle of their own. You're given a blueprint grid in which you can place orbs or remove them at any particular unit of space on the map. After putting the orbs where desired, a second phase to the map maker allows you to change their color. When you finish creating your Energy Cycle brain teaser, the editor generates a level code that you can share with your friends. It's definitely a bold choice on the developer's part to include this. They put the power in the community's hands to see if they can do a better job at making puzzles than the developers.
Rating: 7.6/10

A functional but rather mediocre tower defense game. The units are all pretty standard: warriors, archers, healers, etc. They can be leveled up in between battles, but this simply improves their stats; they gain no new abilities. You can also unlock new types of units with slightly different abilities. You level up and unlock units with stars. After each battle, you get 1-3 stars, depending on how well you did. However, you only get these stars once for each battle. So once you've gotten three stars, there's no reason to ever replay earlier battles. The gameplay is disappointingly simplistic. You cannot level up units during a battle or use "spells" to directly damage or slowdown enemies, etc.; you simply place your units and hope for the best.  Moreover, the terrain has very little influence on battles, and you cannot create mazes to delay the enemies. In addition, some enemies are frustratingly unfair, such as bombers who can take out all of your units in one hit, leaving you without any way to defend yourself. There are also some annoying flaws in the units' AI. For example, healers will heal other units rather than themselves, even when they themselves are close to death, so they often end up dead when you need them the most. And sometimes they'll just stop healing units all together for no apparent reason.  All in all, while there is some simple fun to be had here, it's a lackluster game overall, and there are far better similar games, such as Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten, Kingdom Rush, or Prime World: Defenders.

Quite a fun original platforming puzzle game that uses light mechanics as the basis for the puzzle. The level goals are simple. Get to the door! But getting there is going to be one hell of a tricky ride most of the time, as you have to think WAY outside of the box.
You see, when an object is not lit up, it is as if it ceases to exist. A wall that you can not see because of no light is no longer a wall. It is instead, nothing.
So picture this. You hold up a lighted orb, and use it to light up the ground beneath you. You drop the orb, walk into the darkness, and bam, you fall to your death. Got it? Now get this. You pick up a lighted orb, and light up a wall with it. You can not get past this wall. On the other side, there is a lamp illuminating the ground beneath. So what do you do? You back up a little bit, just enough to make the wall disappear into the darkness. Drop the orb. Now jump OVER the darkness, onto the next platform. But wait, what happened to the wall? Where did it go?
That is the whole point of Closure. Wonderfully brilliant gameplay mechanic that makes for a very challenging puzzle mechanic, especially later in the game. Definitely recommend this to anyone who likes entirely original types of indie games that make you actually think before you react.

An excellent 2D turn-based strategy game.
The store description covers it: Steamworld Heist is a Worms and XCOM hybrid. Characters move and act much like XCOM soldiers, but on a 2D plane with a messload of steampunk robots. There's no base building or anything like that, however. There are various levels of difficulty, and it can be changed mid-game, so it's not quite as unforgiving as XCOM can be.
There's some RPG lite mechanics intertwined through this, with loot and experience driving the progression of your crew. Missions take place on ships with (more often than not) randomized layouts, and each mission has various objectives and enemy assortments. Usually you'll be taking two or three robots on a mission, but occasionally you will limited to one or be allowed to bring four. Unlike XCOM, when your characters die, they only forfeit any earned experience for the level.
Normal gameplay revolves around your crew's turn alternating with the enemy. Enemy ranks are usually dolled out slowly by opening ship doors or setting off alarms. Combat is straight forward: you aim your gun at the enemy and fire. Neither you or your enemies can dodge attacks normally, so taking cover is the only defense (aside from HP increasing items, anyway). Weapons don't tend to have laser sights unless they are "marksmen" style weapons, but lining up a shot isn't difficult at short or medium ranges. Most bullets and projectiles bounce, allowing you to make trick shots that bounce around cover or around corners.
All the different crew members have a different assortment of abilities, with some crossover skills between some characters, leaving a rather well-rounded group. None of the characters are useless, though some are better suited for mobility or taking hits. Each crew member can be utilize a weapon (most characters are proficient with one or two types of guns), two accessories and a hat, which is cosmetic. Weapons, accessories and currency are found by picking up loot items in the levels that are placed at the start. Hats are either purchased from some shops, or stolen from enemies by grazing their heads with a projectile. Enemies do not drop loot, nor do they give experience when killed, so farming kills is only useful for farming rare hats.
In between the combat, players use a map to pick missions or go to hubs/shops. It's sort of like Super Mario World, where you have to complete levels in order to progress down paths on the map. These hubs are mostly for story, hiring crew members and buying hats and equipment.
The game offers a new game plus mode that allows you to use any characters at the start of the game at the cost of all your equipment and experience. There's DLC that adds a new character, some missions and some hats, and those are peppered throughout the game (and are equally excellent). You can easily spend as little as 10 hours but as many as 30 on a playthrough, depending on how thorough you are.
The game's got a really snazzy art style that looks beautiful at high frame rates, and there's a subtle parallax effect on all the environments that's really neat to look at. The writing is pretty funny at times and not particularly verbose. For reference: there is no voice acting in the game, but it's not really needed anyway.
I kind of felt bad for getting this in a bundle, because $15 for a game like this is way more than fair.

This is an outstanding little puzzle game that lets you take your time going from map to map in a Worms-style shoot-out with a variety of bad-guy robots.  There's a great deal of flexibility in how you outfit your team, and you can repeat maps until you get all three stars -- the only penalty is that you lose (about) half of your water, which is the in-game currency, when you lose a map.  It's honestly not a huge penalty, since (a)you're usually spending as much water as you can between maps, to get all those nifty upgrades, and (b)if you hit a very-hard map, the penalty decreases with each failure to complete.
There's a funny obsession with hats in this game, which has nothing to do with game mechanics but does affect your achievements.  You can have your hat shot off, or you can shoot your enemies' off their heads...there is no tactical significance to it, but it adds flavor to this game that is charmingly fully fleshed out.
If you can get this as part of your Humble Bundle (I did), or if you can get it on sale, by all means, get this game.  You can play for 5 minutes, or for 2 hours at a time...you can play one map over and over again, to build up resources, or you can zip through them to unravel the story...I love puzzle games (like chess puzzles), I love tactical games (like X-Com's ground combat) and this one just fits right in.  It surprised me how engaging it is.  Try it, you won't be sorry!

This is a typical browser/tablet/mobile flash game ported for PC.You play as a monster that fights in the 1v1 arena vs another monster (AI controlled). Fights are turn-based,meaning you can use 1 skill  from the hand of randomly selected skills from your skill pool, and the pass the turn to enemy. When you kill your opponent,you are awarded a small amount of cash,exp and mutagens.Cash is used to buy consumables in shop during or outside of arena,mutagens are used to unlock various mutations,which give new skills and bonuses to your attributes. New levels unlock new tiers of mutations.
Doesn't sound too bad?Yes,the idea is good enough for a small indie game to pass some time.
However,the game suffers from typical browser/mobile ports problems,namely - bugs (a few skills simply don't work,game occasionally crashes,etc.), unclear descriptions (you wont find out how exactly your attack stat correlates with actual damage,why 10% evade stat often allows to evade up to 80% of attack damage and so on).
I do not expect to find grand strategy level of complexity in indie flash game,but since the game mentions "turn-based strategy battles",there has to be at least a couple of viable strategies to progress further. But alas, only a couple of skills have any practical use in this game,and winning depends heavily on RNG rather than on player's tactical schemes.
If you draw enough stuns in battle,you can stunlock mob and win ANY fight without any trouble at all.But if the enemy manages to stun you several times during battle,you are most likely going down (unless you eat a lot of consumables from the shop ofc).
This game has a multiplayer mode,but i didnt manage to test it - after half an hour in queue i havent found a single soul willing to PvP,so i cant really say anything about it.
I've played the game for ~3h and completed about 20% of the content,but all the fights are going according to one and the same scenario,so it gets boring really quick.
TL:DR  Typical flash game with interesting idea,but quickly gets boring due to bland and monotonous gameplay. Also a handful of bugs.

Despite Ampersand's overall negative reviews (and being a fan of futuristic racing titles) I thought I would give it the benefit of the doubt and pick it up to see how it is. Unfortunately, while its visuals, ship, and sound designs aren't atrocious, its complete lack of gamepad support of any kind and its clunky keyboard controls are enough to warrant not enjoying the game very much. The game is also quite difficult -more as a result of the controls being shoddy than anything else- but to unlock the next race in a series, you need to get first place in all of the preceding events to accumulate enough points (i.e. Track 4 is unlocked after getting 9 points total, 3 in each preceding track.)
While this is standard in other racing games as well, due to Ampersand's garbage keyboard control feedback you'll often be boosting during a race only to go crashing / bouncing off of walls clumsily toward the finish line. Whereas analog stick controller support might lead the player to be able to breeze into sharp corners, narrowly avoiding the wall and gracefully navigating the track, instead with the keyboard you're left to hope that you've let off the gas pedal (mapped to X...) just enough or have frantically pressed the left or right keys to somehow not bounce off of the wall. Whereas other racing games are rewarding when you do figure out "how fast to go into turn 6" Ampersand just feels like you're doomed to failure, or that the controls aren't responsive enough to do what you're intending.
Ampersand has some potential, but unfortunately it is squandered via the poor controls and feels like more of a waste of time than anything else.

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

Ultimately, the question is this: Are you a big classic Master of Orion fan? Because to me, this feels like Master of Orion 1.5, and that's not a bad thing. But if those two games specifically didn't interest you, you won't find much here. It's a great entry into the turn-based space 4X genre (which doesn't get much new these days), and I really enjoy the flavor of the game.
THE GOOD:
Visuals are clean, and the art style is simplistic but enjoyable.
Multiple planets per system and the ability to colonize to your heart's content.
Lots of tech to research, and you get to choose which to tackle.
THE BAD:
The art style may turn off some, given the cartoonish feel.
The diplomacy has no nuance. Have a lot of ciplomacy points? That's all you need to dictate terms to another race.
The largest map still feels too small.
No Steam Workshop!
THE REST:
A suggestion. Allow us to select our own color, symbol, and faction name. Maybe even pictures for advisors and leaders.

If you love turn-based tactical starship combat of MOO2, then this is the game you've long waited for.
Complaints it is like MOO2 miss the point entirely. The sequels, Starcraft 2 and Diablo 3, didn't reinvent the wheel, and neither has Stars in Shadows. Yet it is not a carbon copy.
Streamlined: planetary management offers fewer but far more decisive choices.
Improved: added minor races, more meaningful differences between factions, graphics and interface, no tech trading, etc.
Research is one area that has been changed, where the merits of those changes are a matter of opinion. The current tried and true system lets you research whatever you wish, but gone are the tense and tough decisions that M002 forced you to make. Admittedly though, some people really disliked this aspect of M002.
To put it simply, Stars in Shadows lives or dies by its turn-based tactical combat. Play it with that being your focus, and you'll probably love it.

Astervoid 2000 reminded me of the good old days when I used to play Asteroids on either the super old computer we had at the time or at the arcade. Astervoid 2000 is kind of like that. However, everything is pixel art instead of being old school, white wired frame-like. On top of that, you don’t have to leave the comfort of your own home to play it.
Astervoid 2000 has two options of how to play. Either you can play single player or vs up to four people. From there, you try to shoot the enemy ships before they shoot you. Along the way, you have to dodge obstacles like flying asteroids that will push you off of the screen. If you’re off the screen too long, you blow up. Also, there’s no screen wrapping in this game.
I really like the art in this game, and how some of the ships looked like a squid or a crab. That’s the only reason why I chose those ships to use. Plus, after you get the hang of it, it becomes a tad bit addicting. I made it to #36 on the leader boards.
It’s a modern spin to a classic, and reminds me of the good old days. It’s great for parties!

Fast, snappy dual joystick control and clean mechanics. Feels similar to TowerFall or Smash Bros., where it's not so much variety of moves or abilities, but how you can use the simple tools made available to you in Astervoid 2000 that make it a fun pick up and play game for a group of friends.
The Single player wave mode is very entertaining for a few minutes at a time, and it's the sort of thing I can see myself coming back to in fits and starts for a long while to come.
Everything included, music, graphics, mechanics, is polished to a high shine, but there might not be enough there to keep anything less than a group of 3 or 4 engaged for a long time. An incredibly polished, original turn-based tactics game. Given that it's played from a side perspective, it plays a bit like a mix of XCOM and Worms, but with a big focus on bullet ricochets, and absolutely no random chance to miss. Instead, skill is prime, and your success is decided entirely by your creativeness and ability to aim. The crew of 9 (10 with DLC) all with different passives, abilities, and weapon choices offers you a wide range of potential strategies given that most missions only allow you to bring along 3 of your crew (1 being the lowest, 4 the highest).
Probably some of the most fun I've had with a strategy game in years.
Gamepad highly recommended.

Well this one came at me totally by surprise. I got it bundled in the most recent Humble Monthly, which I had picked up pretty much for X-COM 2 alone. But once I poked at this one curiously, I kept at it until I had completely finished.
Speaking of X-COM, a comparison is fitting. With a lot of similar rules, you can apply some of the very same strategies here as you do there. Shooting or sprinting ends your turn, but you can move once then shoot. Full cover is better than half cover. Enemies get a free turn to move once they see you. And so on.
Unlike the X-COM games though, numbers will never make you miss. With manual aiming for all shots you take, you only miss through your own bad aim or positioning. A lot of weapons can ricochet off walls and cover to pull off some fancy trick shots if you line it up right, too. Which feels pretty awesome to get right. For the most part, when enemies can hit you they will, though their aim seems to have a bit of randomness to it, meaning you can get lucky misses or unlucky hits from afar.
Also unlike X-COM, there's no overarching doom timer pressuring you to beat the game fast enough. Nor are there save slots - it autosaves every few turns, so mistakes stick with you. Thankfully, the only penalty for party member loss is lost XP, or lost money if you lose them all in one mission. You're also allowed to grind completed missions for money and XP if you're having trouble, but it's not necessary to win.
There are numerous party members to recruit, each with their own class, skills, and preferred weapon types. You don't get to make your own characters, but there's customization in the form of gear. And hats. Piper and her crew are a likeable enough bunch of robotic rogues to push me through to the end, though the plot's fairly straightforward 'fight the bad guys' kind of stuff. It lacks voice acting, but that's fine in my book.
It was a good challenge at the middle difficulty, called "experienced", but rarely frustrating. Bosses can seem like huge difficulty spikes at first, but didn't usually take me more than two tries to get right without any losses.
The soundtrack is also enjoyable, especially since bosses get their own "boss defeated!" victory song thanks to nerdy band Steam Powered Giraffe. Who I've only recently discovered and I love the dorks. Combat music on the other hand can get repetitive, but that's a minor flaw.
I can't think of much to complain about here. It's a charming game with style. It has a good idea to add to the turn-based strategy formula. It feels and sounds good. There's plenty of content, but it doesn't overstay its welcome or require you to grind. It's challenging, but not unfair. And it gets +1 over X-COM if you hate RNG-based games, given it's more about skill and timing than numbers.
Great stuff that deserves your attention all on its own. Not just another bundle game. I might even play through it again sometime.

I admit that I played this game briefly (refund=playtime <2h), and I did find it a very old formula to the genre as it copies heavily from MoO. Now, this is not a bad thing per se, but since so many games have done so recently, it has become a very tired formula to see again and again.
Beyond the intersting cartoon graphics (which I do like), it doesn't seem to offer anything new, nor it is particularly interesting and I had a hard time reading the badly pixellated fonts (EDIT: Now fixed with the latest patch?).
The planet management is really minimal (you can build a very limited number of buildings on each planet, and with very limited I mean about 3-7, depending on the planet size), the research tree lacks a proper presentation and feels really underwhelming, and in general the UI could use a rework on how things are accessed.
Space combat is turn-based but, for space 4x games, I feel it's a mistake since tactical combat would be better suited for games like X-COM where the tactical aspects actually matters, so you spend most of your turns issuing orders to go forward, stand in front of your enemy and shoot, which becomes tedious fast and could have been handled much better with real-time pausable combat.
Also, forget about changing resolution (no option there whatsoever).
If you want to actually play a good 4x space game you'd be better off with Stellaris (continually expanded, but a bit pricey), Endless Space 2 (each race offers an almost completely different gameplay style, giving you great replay value), and even StarDrive 2 Sector Zero (fantastic space combat & ship design).

To write a review for 4x game after only an hour of playing is really strange, but in this case totally justified.
From the start you understand - it is a MOO2 clone. The good thing - you are correct, new graphics can't hide MOO2 core system. The bad thing is - it is yet another BAD clone. Interface reminds me of a phone/tablet game, science is generic with lacking tech description, ship designer relies on hull types that have preset slots (and that limits your ability to build various ships heavily as there are only a few good ways to arm each ship), combat is MOO2 minus balancing, planet economy feels illogical.
Long story short: it took me only an hour to start a game and get totally disappointed in it. Maybe in a few years, if devs don't drop it, the game will become the thing I was looking for, but right now it looks more like a beta.

'Stars in Shadow' is an interesting take on classic 4x games. While not as powerful or flexible as 'Stellaris' it remixes the classic MOO2 look and feel with some very interesting new elements - such as starting the Human faction off with a 'Battlestar Galactica'-esque fleet of refugees, and having two of the playable factions belonging to the same species. It also brings in the epic backstory a la 'Distant Worlds', but mixes it up by having only 3 factions (inc Humanity) as fallen empires, while the rest are newly emergant starfarers. It also beats Distant Worlds's setup by allowing for lots and lots of "aboriginal" species, although the scope of the game's map is more akin to MOO2 rather than the vast expansiveness of 'Stellaris' or 'Distant Worlds'. On the other hand, it IS entirely turn based! >_>
Additionally, the art style is fabulous, with pleasing ship and character designs, and the interface is smartly crafted, pretty in a functional way, with plenty of tool-tips and explanation to be found on every screen (although there are a few missing references here and there...)
All in all, a great MOO2-style 4x game!

The makers of this game have been playing Master of Orion 2. The look is nearly identical and the tech tree, game play, and even tactical combat are carbon copies. It was a great game to be inspired by. Let's see how they did...
The good: The graphics are an upgrade. It's more challenging than MoO2 was once you figured things out. There are more indigenous races and they're quirky and interesting. The ships can be auto-upgraded. Every race can get every technology (which always annoyed a completionist like me in MoO2). You don't have to build so many things to get a colony functioning, which speeds up the game. The "go back" button is simply genius, in that I don't have to save my game every turn to avoid stupid and avoidable mistakes.
The bad: The music is forgettable. The races' back-stories mean they can't be customized. The MoO2 antagonists (the Antarens) are space pirates here, but don't seem dangerous and almost never happen (encountered once in three games). Diplomacy is missing a large number of actions (threatening them to get out of your territory, asking them to surrender, asking them to surrender a planet or system, surrendering a planet or system to them (possibly for peace or reputation), and the trade doesn't seem to work with anybody but the mercenaries and slavers...in which case, why offer it for normal races?). This game, slowed down and on a large galaxy, could take days or weeks on normal...nevermind hard or very hard. The weapons for auto-upgrading ships can be very paper-rock-scissors and you can get pwned without seeing it coming. It's the strategic equivalent of putting platforms off the screen on a platformer game and requiring a leap of faith...and hoping you won't die. I guess you need that "go back" button after all...
The ugly: This game simply doesn't pop. It's not bad, but neither is it great. In 50 years or longer, I'll never forget MoO2. I own a CD and now use a DOS emulator when I get nostalgic. I once saw a computer running MoO2 in a video game museum. My wife even asked if this was that old-fashioned space game that I used to play when she saw it. This game is a worthy effort, and kept me up for a few nights, but in the end this game seems like exactly what it is: a copy of a great game using current graphics and systems to seem better. Super Mario 2 may have had better graphics, but it wasn't the massive improvement over Super Mario Bros. that SMB was over, say, Atari.
My final word: They gave it a shot. This game is worth the try. But it won't stand the test of time. If someone asks me about in in a year, I won't know what they're talking about. That being said, if you never played MoO2, and don't want to pirate an emulator copy or buy a CD so you own a license, then this game is worth trying. It is a decent space game and carries the best of MoO2 over, with some new innovations. There are better games, but also many, many worse. I give it 3.8 out of 5.

Stars in Shadow is a nice little indie 4X space game. It has unique combat and empire mechanics that set the game apart from most other 4X titles. Stars in Shadow has several massive flaws, but is updated regularly, so this game is at least one to keep an eye on. It has an asking price well below the space 4X juggernauts of Endless Space 2/Stellaris, and as a consequence it's also significantly lighter in features and polish. Despite its flaws, it is a game that I can recommend when on sale.
The biggest strike against this game is that, as of this review, it lacks multiplayer. A strong multiplayer community is critical to the longevity of a 4X game, and the lack of one will strongly reduce the game's replayability. If you're not interested in multiplayer, then carry on. But if you're looking for multiplayer, then you should hold off on this game for now.
Starting with the bad, Stars in Shadow has the absolute worst snowballing that I have ever seen in a 4X game. There's almost no gate to how quickly you can expand. A single technology will unlock colonization on ANY type of planet in the game. Your population growth rate increases if you expand. Colonizing a new planet increases your strategic range, which increases the number of planets that you can expand to. The only limit is the number of planets in the game and how quickly you can pump out ships. Of course it feels bad when your empire is limited by an arbitrary number that most 4X games impose on you. However rampant snowballing is toxic to 4X games, making luck during map generation more important than actual strategic decisions.
The snowballing isn't a big issue if you're a casual 4X player, but anyone with experience in the genre will probably feel it. The game is almost always decided in the early game, and the rest of the game is just a chore until you hit one of the quick-and-easy diplomatic victory types, or grind out a military one.
The UI is rather clunky, but it's functional. Ship management is an absolute nightmare to deal with, and definitely feels like the older games that Stars in Shadow pays homage to. Population management is actually extremely compelling and rewarding (sometimes doubling the amount of population a planet can hold if you have the right people in your empire). However, it also becomes a painful chore in the mid-late game, because there's no single screen that unifies all the required information. Tool tips and ingame documentation are poor, but you should be able to pick up all the mechanics after about an hours of play. I have yet to come across gamebreaking bugs, and the most recent patch fixed a lot of the crashes. The game gets extremely laggy late game on a big map, but it's usually decided well before then.
If you can look past those flaws, then there's a decent game underneath all of it.
There are standard 4X resources: money, production, food, and science. Metal is acquired exclusively from mines and gates how quickly you can build ships. Influence is gained from treaties with AI (or your capital if you're playing the Phidi) and gates your diplomatic interactions. Every unit of population yields some amount the standard money, food, production, and science. You'll stumble across native population that typically has worse yield than your primary race, but hopefully inhabits different biomes. Sometimes you will encounter native population that exists solely to hinder a colony, which motivates the relocation of your own species onto said planet to take up land. Basically like Space Palestine.
The combat is instanced, turn-based, and grid-based. It's pretty unique and satisfying, but unfortunately inconsequential. Like many space games, alpha strike is absolutely important and often decides the combat if it's not already decided beforehand. After the novelty of the combat system wears off, you'll almost always use either autoretreat or autocombat. If your combat involves more than 10 ships, you will hate yourself if you try to do it manually. The ship designer is barebones, and your new weapon unlocks are almost always direct upgrades over your older ones. Carriers are extremely strong for most of the game, and you will always want point defenses on every ship after midgame due to the sheer amount of damage that bombers/strike fighters can put out. However, all other weapon systems become pointless as soon as you get the endgame weapon Stellar Surge Beam. It's the longest range, highest damage weapon in the game, and the only meaningful decision at that point is how many of them you want in your fleet.
The AI is decent. It declares war on you when you're weak, and is will ally with you when you're strong. Allied victories are surprisingly easy to come across, mostly because the AI doesn't care about who your other allies are (you can easily enter an alliance with two empires that are at war with each other). It's only weakness is that it is incapable of min-maxing and specializing planets, which the game heavily rewards. If you feel lazy, you can leave your production to the AI and you won't really fall behind.
Ultimately, Stars in Shadow is a game that pays homage to the older titles of the 4X space genre. It has a charming aesthetic that grows on you, and doesn't take itself too seriously. Sadly, the UI shows my hedonistic seahorse traders using coins that are stamped with the faces of space dinosaurs, but that's only a minor hiccup in immersion. There are significant differences between each faction which makes each one feel unique, but not so much that it increases the learning curve. It's solidly between the Civilization series and Endless series in that regard.
Stars in Shadow is not a game to pick up if you want difficult and compelling strategy gameplay. To be honest, I can't quite explain why I liked Stars in Shadow as much as I did. There are major flaws, but the combination of aesthetics and atmosphere made something that I could definitely enjoy.

The game's visuals, camera controls, a bit of clunkiness inherent of the era the game came out in, etc...numerous things are making the game a big cringey today, even though I played and enjoyed it when it was new enough, completing the game and liking it pretty well at the time. These aspects of the game could be a little divisive for players, since it's hard
to notice how hard it is to look up or manage the camera at times, and how Raziel's jumps can be a little tough to anticipate at times, combat's a little clunky, etc.
I'm not prepared to say that Soul Reaver should just go away, though. What we have here is a bunch of great premises: a vampire turned into something else that consumes souls instead of blood, out to get revenge on the sire who wounded him, stealing powers from his brothers he destroys along the way, each of whom have mutated into freaking-cool-looking monstrosities, all while serving some mysterious cool-voiced underworld entity with fantastic voice acting and a cool setting. It has a good story and premise, great voice acting, and I
using vampires' weaknesses to destroy them, such as chunking them into direct sunlight, impaling them, tossing them in water, lighting them on fire, etc.
Nosgoth seems like a
cool setting that technical limitations and budgetary concerns have been hampering its exposure to the world. We see a couple of humans in very brief about-to-die moments, which would have been fun to see expanded out a little into something more, to better feel the impact of the vampire scourge on Nosgoth. Older tech also meant less foliage, wall decorations, knick-knacks/details in indoor areas, and just such a bare-bones approach.
I guess what I'm getting at is that people who think the original game is perfect as is have that perfect experience they enjoy, while I would love to see a remake along the lines of the GameCube Resident Evil, in that virtually everything is improved while keeping the spirit and story of the original and all of the memorable stuff that was great. I would buy and play the living hell out of a remake of this game done with that level of improvement and modification to modernize, innovate, and yet still maintain the integrity of what matters most in the game.

An incredibly polished, original turn-based tactics game. Given that it's played from a side perspective, it plays a bit like a mix of XCOM and Worms, but with a big focus on bullet ricochets, and absolutely no random chance to miss. Instead, skill is prime, and your success is decided entirely by your creativeness and ability to aim. The crew of 9 (10 with DLC) all with different passives, abilities, and weapon choices offers you a wide range of potential strategies given that most missions only allow you to bring along 3 of your crew (1 being the lowest, 4 the highest).
Probably some of the most fun I've had with a strategy game in years.
Gamepad highly recommended.

Well this one came at me totally by surprise. I got it bundled in the most recent Humble Monthly, which I had picked up pretty much for X-COM 2 alone. But once I poked at this one curiously, I kept at it until I had completely finished.
Speaking of X-COM, a comparison is fitting. With a lot of similar rules, you can apply some of the very same strategies here as you do there. Shooting or sprinting ends your turn, but you can move once then shoot. Full cover is better than half cover. Enemies get a free turn to move once they see you. And so on.
Unlike the X-COM games though, numbers will never make you miss. With manual aiming for all shots you take, you only miss through your own bad aim or positioning. A lot of weapons can ricochet off walls and cover to pull off some fancy trick shots if you line it up right, too. Which feels pretty awesome to get right. For the most part, when enemies can hit you they will, though their aim seems to have a bit of randomness to it, meaning you can get lucky misses or unlucky hits from afar.
Also unlike X-COM, there's no overarching doom timer pressuring you to beat the game fast enough. Nor are there save slots - it autosaves every few turns, so mistakes stick with you. Thankfully, the only penalty for party member loss is lost XP, or lost money if you lose them all in one mission. You're also allowed to grind completed missions for money and XP if you're having trouble, but it's not necessary to win.
There are numerous party members to recruit, each with their own class, skills, and preferred weapon types. You don't get to make your own characters, but there's customization in the form of gear. And hats. Piper and her crew are a likeable enough bunch of robotic rogues to push me through to the end, though the plot's fairly straightforward 'fight the bad guys' kind of stuff. It lacks voice acting, but that's fine in my book.
It was a good challenge at the middle difficulty, called "experienced", but rarely frustrating. Bosses can seem like huge difficulty spikes at first, but didn't usually take me more than two tries to get right without any losses.
The soundtrack is also enjoyable, especially since bosses get their own "boss defeated!" victory song thanks to nerdy band Steam Powered Giraffe. Who I've only recently discovered and I love the dorks. Combat music on the other hand can get repetitive, but that's a minor flaw.
I can't think of much to complain about here. It's a charming game with style. It has a good idea to add to the turn-based strategy formula. It feels and sounds good. There's plenty of content, but it doesn't overstay its welcome or require you to grind. It's challenging, but not unfair. And it gets +1 over X-COM if you hate RNG-based games, given it's more about skill and timing than numbers.
Great stuff that deserves your attention all on its own. Not just another bundle game. I might even play through it again sometime.

SodaCity is a small indie game that offers old-school gamers a familiar (yet distant) experience; one of the retro shoot-'em-ups, in classic 2D side-scrolling perspective with countless hours of fun distpaching enemies left and right and dying over and over again .
This game is pretty straightforward, very what-you-see-if-what-you-get.
The gameplay, as I described, is old-school cool that us adult gamers (at the time of my review anyway) will feel at home with, but it's also worth noting that once you've played a few hours, it's easily discernible that it's also deeper than it seems at first glance. Truly, each type of weapon offers very distinct possibilities, for example.
The graphics and visuals are retro with their peculiar aesthetic which I found charming and no doubt not everyone will necessarily like, but it's pretty neat and effective.
The audio is good too; there's clear cues for everything, distinct sounds and a simply superb soundtrack/score with music not only greatly done but also varied and fitting for each scenario and atmosphere.
Although the game might at first seem to rely on repetition of a number of goals or objectives, after a little replay each area and each evidently has its own thing going on, its own flavor, and it's easy to recall them and formulate strategies for them. That should occur naturally after being beaten many times over the course of a level. That leads me to the point that this game is challenging, but I never found it to be excessively so or otherwise unfair.
It's also worth noting that the game does offer a fair amount of replayability, especially for those who don't mind grinding/farming a little bit to enjoy the benefits of fully upgraded weapons. That also begs the distinction that grinding in this game doesn't become much of a chore, it hardly forces the player to do so and those who choose so will have more fun than dull repetition in seeking to gain more currency for upgrades or better weapons.
SodaCity, all in all, offers more than I initially thought and it will be a game to go back to every once in a while for sure. The fun is there, the appeal of a great game in a genre that seems long-forgotten in  the industry is there, the replay value of the game itself without the nostalgia attached is there.
Last, but not least, I simply want to go over some of the details other reviews are criticizing which I found unfair, especially given how at the time of my review, those reviews have hardly two hours or less game time, and thus, in my opinion, extremely limited play to accurately judge the game as a whole. Here's what I think:
-Some reviws call SodaCity out on the graphics... to this I ask, what is one to expect from an indie game from a small team? Super Meat Boy, The Binding of Isaac, Terraria, Monaco and even better, Hotline Miami hardly offer much more in that department. None of them are AAA games, even if some did achieve similar sales, and that doesn't keep them from being awesome games.
-Quick deaths/dying a lot... Let us remember that this game, by its very genre if nothing else, can easily be seen as an ode to old-time games, from consoles such as the NES, SNES, Genesis, etc... I never beat many of those games. Videogames back then used to be hard and you used to die a lot trying. Some modern games have even appealed to that principle, such as the illustrious Souls series. I find this more of a taste-type-thing than a fault within the game.
-The aesthetic or lack of a deeper-developed story. As I mentioned previously, shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off soda cans may not be for everybody, but dammit if it isn't fresh and indeed silly! It's good stuff for those can don't need every game to be serious and have an encyclopedia worth of lore.
Summary:
SodaCity isn't a game for everyone, the genre certainly isn't trending the way near-future FPS or medieval-fantasy RPGs are. But for adult-aged gamers, there is a ton of appeal to be found here, and to anyone willing to give a fair shot, tons of fun to be had as well. I found the first few levels to be among the slower parts, but if you can play a little bit beyond that, I'm betting it can easily draw most people in and have them hooked for days.
This is a solid and promising start for a young development studio. Imagine a sequel with full miltuplayer integration on console... Personally, I'd buy that with no second thoughts! Very much a recommendable game. Hopefully one of indie game's next big titles.

Closure is an amazing gothic/black metal looking art stylized game. It plays like a side scroller with light based puzzles. The music is awesome and very dark, extremely fitting for this game. If you have a lap top there may be issues with older gfx cards. Great game, great music and art and plenty of interesting puzzles to figure out.    Between this, limbo and binding of isaac you will have a nice set of games with great music and dark humor/imagery.

Part of me wasn't looking forward to playing Closure, and that was because it was a puzzle-platformer, a type of game that I haven't had many positive experiences with.  Luckily, the other parts of me, namely the parts that like graphic design and music, told the first part what a bozo it was and I picked up Closure.  Man, am I glad I did.
Two things surprised me about Closure.  The first was the difficulty.  Now, I may not be the sharpest knife in the drawer, but I haven't been faced with such difficult puzzles in a long time.  The main mechanic of "light solidifying reality" is absolutely genius, and it often took me quite the sit-down-and-think to wrap my head around some of these puzzles.  I did, sometimes, become quite frustrated at the difficulty, but I never gave in because of the other thing that surprised me.
Closure is one of the most unnerving games I've ever played.  The musical score oozes melancholy, the puzzles are sadistically crafted, and the graphic design perfectly conveys the enormous rift that can stand between hope and despair.  Every aspect of the game adds to this terrifyingly bleak atmosphere that kept me in just the right mood to sit quietly and stew through the brain-benders that the game provides.  It may have been a cheap purchase, but the experiences that Closure has given me will torture me for a long time.  And I love it.

As a game reviewer, Energy Cycle makes me want to tear my hair out... But in a joyous way. To understand why this is, understand that it's a cheap, well designed logic puzzle, with an aesthetic that I can safely say is fairly unique, that it supports colourblind folks very well (Often a problem in the games industry), and so, in a sense, there is nothing to talk about. Because it *works*, and it's cohesively designed.
How, pray tell, are you going to write between 500 and 1000 words about that, eh?
It works.
It's got a neat aesthetic that I think should be experienced at least once.
It costs less than a takeaway, and lasts you longer.
It has digital cats.
What the hell else do you want? Oh, cons? Yeah, one, and I expect it'll be obsolete before too long: The menu button in the top right isn't quite as visible as it could be. That's, er... It. This game reminded me of what was probably my first handheld video game… Merlin in 1978, and brings back a lot of happy memories. Yeah, video games have come a long way, but only recently have we begun to see a variety of fresh new expansions beyond the traditional shooter and racing genres. Sometimes You is already becoming well known for bringing out games with a novel approach to gaming, such as Retention and Energy Balance. Where those focused on photography and Math, Energy Cycle focuses on the Math of patterns and arrays… color synchronization.
Energy Cycle consists of patterns of lights that when pressed, toggle on or off adjacent lights. It’s a definite mind-bender, and the ambient electronic themes add to the “mind music” effect. When I first saw the trailer it reminded me of my old Merlin. But, where Merlin only had a limited field of about 9 lights to work with, Energy Cycle expands on the idea by presenting a variety of arrays and multiple colors. Each puzzle becomes increasingly complex, forcing you to use a part of your brain that doesn’t really get a lot of gaming time. Forgive me for lapsing into the old “right-brain/left-brain” ideas, but yeah it’s difficult to analyze a visual pattern that uses no words (like with the 1st game Retention.) If you love puzzle and thinking games, then you will definitely want to give this a try.
The Deluxe Collector’s Edition includes wallpapers, a "process" art book and a photo album of art that features nostalgic moments... especially of cats. It also includes the soundtrack with a mix of high energy, at times melancholic techno-funk sound effects. These were interesting to me because I enjoy getting some background on what goes into a game. It adds something a little extra to see how the creative process took off. And, that’s what makes Steam a great platform for gamers, because no matter how many gaming magazines you read, you can’t get all that in a magazine.
There is a level editor as well, where you can make your own patterns, and you are given a level code. But, I haven’t gotten far enough yet to figure out whether or how you share that code with friends to play each other’s designs. I will explore that more when I solve level 10, which I got stuck on.
I grabbed a couple of extra copies, which I will be giving away over on Steam Gifts just as soon as they add the game to their giveaways list. The giveaways will show up on this link, probably in the next day or so...

This is a fine X4 space strategy game. It has many similarities to Master of Orion II (the gold standard for X4 space strategy games). You develop planets, research technologies, design and build ships, and of course fight and invade other empires.
The game's economy is a little more complex than MOO II. All planets have production, science research, money, and food production. The new feature is minerals -- building any ship will consume a certain amount of these, and you will always be short of minerals in the mid-late game. Some ships are more mineral effficient, less production efficient, and vise versa.
The first few games were surprisingly difficult, and I got crushed on normal difficulty until I figured out the optimal economics involved in empire management. You can also get crushed by fleets whose tech matches up badly against you (e.g., if you don't have much point defense, and go up against a fleet heavy on fighters or missiles). There are lots of tech interactions as you progress through the tech levels.
The game is a little rough on the edges. Diplomacy isn't fully implemented (or as functional as in MOO II), and there are some odd ways to exploit the point-based system it uses (diplomatic ability is a resource, like food or resources). As in MOO II, the AI for fleet management isn't that good (although planetary production management is done well).
Despite a few minor criticisms, the game is well done, and still improving. I have enjoyed play of this more than the new Master of Orion, and at least as much as Stellaris.

Also the concept of 4 shield sectors is absolutely irrelevant. Ships are so veeeery slow that you never shoot at something else than the front shield. Also weapons can shoot over a very long distance compared to the speed of ships. I never saw a midrange weapon fire a single shot because the combat was over before any ship got into that range.
There are some nice ideas on the planetary economy like the slavetrading business. Right now the slaves are more nuisance than help because they riot to much (and the game does tell you about the upcoming problem ONLY when you directly selecti the system!) but the basic idea is nice.
Summa:
If this game sees further development and drastic adjustments in balancing it may become realy nice.

I don't understand why Steam still doesn't have a "maybe" option - this is a game that would deserve it (in its current state). It's a nice little 4X based on the legendary Master of Orion 2 (MOO2). It has a solid (if flawed) gameplay and is a lot of fun most of the time.
However, there are some questionable design decisions, simplification of some aspects of the game, and technical problems that drag the overall experience down.
The Good:
- Planet building has been simplified. You no longer build dozens of structures on each of your planets. You have simply 6 base buildings (factory, mine, research lab, market, farm, and defense) which get upgraded for free once you discover relevant technologies. This is great, in my opinion, as it eliminates the tedious micro-management when you have a lot of colonies (there is still some, but nowhere near the "late game MOO" level).
- Every race not only has its own splash screens, but also ship models, leader banter, and some techs. It's a nice touch and increases immersion.
- The game has that "just one more turn" feel to it.
- AI is actually quite capable strategically - it researches and builds fast, expands very fast (perhaps too fast - see below) even on lower difficulties.
- Unlike the recent official "remake" of MOO, this one has tactical turn-based combat. You can win even if you are outnumbered and outgunned, if you play your cards right.
The Bad:
- This is one of those fake "full releases" - despite posing as a full release, it's still very much early access quality. LUA script errors are everywhere (this was partially eliminated in the latest patch but still, the game was released in this state and I cannot overlook it), CTDs to desktop are a thing on huge maps in late game, game balance is a mess.
- Ship design has been simplified, being slot-based instead of weight-based. Meaning that you can never fit more weapons on a ship that the devs intended. On one hand, this is good, because you cannot cheese by building a warship from hell (but you can cheese in other ways), on the other hand, it greatly reduces variability.
- It's unbalanced. Railguns rule the mid/late game. Strike craft and missiles rule the end game. Railguns are simply OP here, having highest range, no range dissipation, shield piercing, AND top damage of all of their counterparts. Rails put even some higher tier weapons to shame. AI, no matter the faction, always spams heavy cruisers and battleships with railguns and PD cannons, simply because it's the most effective way to design ships with direct-fire weapons. Weapon range is everything in combat because bigger ships are painfully slow. This makes above-mentioned weapons stupidly powerful and short range weapons almost useless. It also invalidates alternative tactics (boarding, disabling, etc.) once you get far enough in the game.
- AI is crazy about expansion and if you ally yourself with an AI player he will instantly send swarms of colony ships into your space and colonize all unclaimed worlds in your sphere of influence. For this reason, you can never go into an alliance until you've secured every single planet you want. This is insane and should be removed - your ally shouldn't steal worlds from you just because he can (manners?).
- AI is strong in some regards but is dumb as a rock in combat.
- Late game battles aren't epic but tedious - this is mainly because of slow combat animations. It seems like a small thing but it really adds up when you have a fight with dozens of large ships. Such battles can take over 10 minutes, 9 mins 40 seconds of which is waiting for animations to finish. Now imagine that when war breaks out in the late game you fight 2-3 such battles every turn... "Faster animations" option in settings doesn't seem to do much, if anything (again, I smell rushed release here). Autocombat is even more useless than it usually is in this type of games because it always makes you lose about 3x more ships compared to what you'd lose if you fought manually.
I am giving this a thumps-up because its core gameplay is pure old-school goodness. If you love MOO and don't mind flaws that SiS has, get it, it's worth it. It will be even more worth it once devs squash the bugs and balance things out.

I'm conflicted in my review.  The game is every bit as you remember it, be that good or bad.  You have 2 speeds: run and sprint, which often means falling off of small platforms.  The camera controls are some of the worst (no free control, only a quick snap to behind your character).  The story is as great as ever and the game does look better than it did in 1999 and the voice acting is still top notch.
The problem, and the reason I can't recommend this game, is the problems getting it to even load.  The first time I got it to load, it took me 3 hours of trial and error.  The solution?  It loads perfectly once out of about 50 attempts.  No compatibility mode, no running as admin.  Just load, crash, load, crash, fiddle with settings, load, crash, load crash, default settings, load, crash, load, crash....(10 minutes later)..... load, works fine.  Seriously.  I managed to play it enough in 2 days to finish it but getting it to even start became a chore.
Then there's the controller issues.  I used a wireless Xbox 360 controller (with the wireless receiver) and Pinnacle Game Profiler.  I recommend it.  Download the existing profile, then edit it.  The downloaded scheme is terrible.  Right trigger for attack, 2 buttons to devour souls, you get the idea.  I had one sound issue which forced me to restart the game (complete with several dozen crashes again), but otherwise it worked fine..... if you want to call it that.  If you're really jonesing for some nostalgia, watch a let's play on YouTube.  You'll save yourself a lot of frustration.
The Good:
+ Voice acting is still great
+ Story holds up
The Bad:
- Camera controls are still a mess
The Ugly:
-- Constant crashes at launch.
Bottom line: this game performs like an abusive significant other.  It's crash, after crash, after crash, and just when you're ready to give up, it loads and works perfectly making you remember all the wonderful times you had when you first played it; making you think it's worked out its issues.  Then you try to start it again another time and it's right back to crashing and the cycle repeats.  Thankfully, it's a relatively short game.

Completely unexpected and completely charming. I think a lot of people will probably look at Dropsy and wonder when the other shoe is going to drop... you keep expecting it to turn gross and creepy and "edgy". But the simple fact that makes the game so pleasantly surprising is that Dropsy is simply a very positive, very engaging point-and-click adventure with a wholly earnest and lovable protagonist. He may look king of scary and act weird, but Dropsy's whole point is what an honestly good person he is despite how unfairly he's judged and often treated, and I think that's kind of wonderful.
From a gameplay point, I would call Dropsy fairly standard for the genre. There's a lot of backtracking and some questionable puzzle logic, but exploring the world (and thankfully eventually finding quicker ways to travel around it) feels very organic and rewarding. Unlike a lot of point-and-click adventures, Dropsy doesn't lock you into rails, so it can be easy to feel overwhelmed when you discover so many places and people and puzzles, all at once, and trying to figure out when and how to tackle them can be daunting as a result. If you follow the main story, however, you'll usually come across items as you need them, and anyone looking for classic adventure with a lot of charm and heart should absolutely check it out.

A game that lacks punch, and the bigger issue is the game design complementing the genre in question. There are reasons that several basic game design rules are in place for side scrolling shooters, it's there to complement the action in question. Here, the game is somewhere between boring and frustrating. Very quick times to die from a barrage of bullets, in particular with bosses, will frustrate players as it overly punishes simple mistakes that can easily be made. Developers need to be careful of making comparisons or indicating influences of past games, as using TMNT: Turtles in Time and Battletoads & Double Dragon as strong influences for the game set up expectations of quality that the game's staff and resources may not be able to reach, even with the most skilled programmers in the world. SodaCity has core problems that makes me not able to recommend it, and the game lacks impact for the price point that it's being offered for.

Stars in Shadow pretty much hits the sweet spot for a space 4x game. it doesn't really add anything new to the table, but it focuses pretty tightly on the core gameplay.
For instance, planets only have 4 buildings - one for money, one to mine metal, one for research, one for growing food. These things improve as you go down the tech tree, but the game upgrades them automatically.
Similarly, there's a fairly limited number of ships and weapons. Missile, Carriers, or Beam ships, then they all basically converge into one type that does everything.  There's some choice, but the tech tree is fairly short and manageable.
It has turn based tactical combat like the original two Master of Orions (and one of Iceberg's other title, Horizon), but it's somewhat on a cramped map. There is some tactics, but not a lot. Still, it's better than watching pictures of the computer fight itself as in most space 4x games these days.
It's fairly quickly paced. I've now played 40 hours and completed 4 games: 2 on regular galaxies, 2 huge ones (90 stars). The latter bogged down my computer somewhat near endgame, with everything getting a bit sluggish. I have a pretty old PC though.
It's not a Moo2 killer by any means, but it's a good solid game. Will you be playing it a year from now? Maybe. 10 years? Probably not.

My vote is a delighted "thumbs up" for Stars in Shadow.  Below some early impressions and my take on some other dissatisfied reviews.
Typical sci fi game:  "This race is thought to be distantly related to a species of sauroids possibly descended from those present during the jurassic age of the legendary planet Terra"
Stars in Shadow (paraphrasing):  "This is a race of space dinosaurs."
In other words, SiS cuts out a great deal of hype and pretentious language and imagery to deliver an entirely playable, enjoyable, sensible, fun 4x game.  At the same time there are a few things I don't like:
I see no screen to tell me about myself.  What I mean is, my race, its bonuses, and a very general summary of my empire (number of colonies or whatever).  There doesn't seem to be a mirror on the wall, so to speak.   Haven't found it yet, if it does exist.
Also, there is no kind of tutorial.  Granted, the game really is intuitive and I am learning it just fine by playing it, but there was an initial discomfort I could have been spared with a little intro spiel.  The argument that "let's play" segments exist on youtube is no excuse for leaving a customer without any guidance.
It turns out the reason for that discomfort was my assumption that there would be tons of distraction and mechanical hype that would confuse me, which there aren't.  An example of what I mean is the way Civ 5, for example, urges the player to be involved in city-state affairs long before his empire is really able to do so (Civ 4 BTS, before it, would throw quests like to build rediculous numbers of troops.  The naive player listened and lost the game trying).  You can actually lose games chasing after features that the game, itself, thinks are very cool but which, in fact,  are gameplay red herrings.  This sort of overdone, self-admiring feature is absent in SiS.  The game sticks to what you need to do.  Causes and effects, as they become revealed, tend to explain themselves.
Another irritant:  I colonized a planet that already had an indigenous race living there.  This added 3 bonus pop to my single colonist pop.  Sounds like a deal!  Nope.  Because the moment you colonize, the natives immediately become completely dependent on your empire's food supply.  So there was immediate mass starvation, because the plankton or chickens or coconuts the natives feasted on suddenly vanished when my ship landed.  Now, perhaps this is as-intended for purposes of some game balance equation, but it simply makes no sense at all and should be changed.
There are a few other irritants, but none of them seriously damages a marvelous, creative, engaging game of galactic conquest with space dinosaurs (or whatever you prefer).  Multiple reviews have cited the apparent tribute to Master of Orion 2 in this game's design, and I concur.  But it is not a clone nor living under the shadow of MOO2.  It is its own game, beautiful and new.  The music and graphics lend a lightness to the atmosphere.  It is family-friendly, errr, if mass starvation due to poor colony planning can be any kind of friendly thing.  Cough.
My hunch is that disappointed players are those who expected a torrent of new mechanics and concepts and, in general, a game that takes itself entirely too seriously and favors esoteric and obtuse mechanics.  I can't say exactly how hard the game is, not having played far enough into it.  But I will really enjoy getting to that point and recommend Stars in Shadow heartily if you're looking for a good 4x time.

I really wanted to enjoy this game, put a good number of hours into it hoping to find a gem. Sadly there are just too many elements that dont work well here. In no particular order:
- Managing your empire is tedious. There is a ton of micro management here, very much like Gal Civ 3. Every time you unlock a new tech that affects your worlds you need to go visit them one by one. You will spend more time managing than fighting/strategizing
- Combat is just weak. The game tries to duplicate Master of Orion 2 and fails at it. Ship movement much too slow for any strategic depth. You just move forward. Weapons are too powerful resulting in many one shot kills. Troop transports like to hang out in the middle front of your forces instead of at the rear.
- Ship designer doesnt work well. There arent enough ways you can meaningfully tweak your ships and there is a clear one or two "best" loadouts
- Diplomacy feels like a place holder and is just for the AI to ask you for stuff which you can use to appease them and keep them from going hostile with you.
- Exploration is pointless beyond the initial few turns. The AI however loves to build endless amounts of exploration ships, even hundreds of turns into a game.
- The independant/pirate forces are terribly unbalanced. They get battleships seemingly before anyone else and put up a bigger fight than the regular AI races as a result. Since when do pirates get top of the line tech?
- It is better to bombard an enemy colony out of existance and then settle it yourself than it is to conquer it and have to deal with stacking lots of ground forces to prevent it from going into rebellion.
- The UI is lacking. There doesnt appear to be a button for diplomacy short of clicking on an AI world and initiating from there. Planet listing doesnt highlight which world you are currently on. Selecting a planet doesnt take you to the building panel, instead shows a pretty useless picture of the planet that you then need to continue past to get where you want to be. Unnecessary tedium.
- Research fun while it lasts, but once it ends all your research buildings are useless and have to be torn down and replaced manually, one planet at a time.
These gripes and many smaller ones add up to one thing: this game is lacking in a great many places and it simply gives nothing to the 4X genre at this time.
Has potential but... definitely needs more work,

SteamWorld Heist is a 2d turn based XCOM-like game, taking place in a universe inhabited by robots. You control a small team of so-called steambots with unique abilities, in small, tactical confrontations against enemy bots, where you have to kill the opposition, grab the loot, and get out.
There is a story present here, but it is rather underplayed and not the main focus of the game. You're essentially just finding new opposition with every chapter, and the script focuses on what you're doing to muck up their plans/steal their stuff. There is some enjoyment to be had with the story, but don't buy it if that's the only thing you're interested in.
The presentation on display is really damn impressive considering this is a game originating from the 3DS. The game runs gracefully out of the box, and supports 60+ herz framerates without any tinkering in the cfg. files whatsoever. This is genuinely more impressive than a lot of triple A games that I've played. And don't get me started on the graphics. The 2d art here is brimming with detail and, just, pure effort. Every pipe, valve and rusty backdrop has been gracefully drawn, and are beautifully colored. Animations are superb as well.
As mentioned, this is a turn based strategy game, rather similar to XCOM. You are given a set distance you can move with a character; move a short distance and you can fire your gun afterwards, but if you move further, you will need to fold until the next turn. However, where Heist differs, is with its ditching of certain chance-based actions common in other strategy games. One example being aiming and shooting, which is done manually by using the mouse/joystick. This eliminates lots of frustration, as most deaths are your own fault, because of your poor aim. Attacking like this is incredibly entertaining, especially since you can bounce bullets off of walls, resulting in some awesome trickshots.
In addition to this extra layer of gameplay, you have access to a set of teammates you can bring with you on a heist. They can specialize in heavy weapons, sniping, punching, and my personal favorite, flanking. You need to play around these quirks and use positions wisely, like placing the heavy on a top floor, or placing the flanker far ahead, as to make it easier to get behind the enemy and deal extra damage. The gameplay is deep, but simple and easy to learn. And most importantly, the game is fun, incredibly so. Hitting next to impossible shots, blowubg up 3 guys next to an explosive barrel, or figuring out new strategies or abilities is extraordinarily rewarding and entertaining.

There's an inventory system present here, deciding how many weapons/items you can have a hold of at any-one time. The problem is that it's incredibly harsh in terms of space, only allowing a very small amount of items to be stored. You can upgrade the availible space, but they get exponentially more expensive with every purchase. Deleting items almost after every mission got a little tedious and annoying.
This is a criminally underrated game, considering the overwhelming quality and effort present here. I plead you to give this game a try, even if you're new to turn-based games. SteamWorld Heist puts an enjoyable twist on a solid foundation, and succeeds with flying colors, and is 100% worth a purchase.
