The Force is not strong with this one:
I got this game because of so much hype I read online and of course being a massive star wars geek. The idea of a squad based FPS in the Star Wars Universe especially Clone Wars sounds amazing on paper, but the execution with this game makes it in my opinion completely unplayable:
1) Horribly Optimized for PC: I know it is an old game, but no matter how I manage the settings I always get choppy frame rate (which is weird as my FPS counter shows up to 400 FPS)
2) Bad squad AI: With a game that prides itself on your squad, its amazing how bad they act: They get killed all the time, do not really support you in combat, and are mainly used for story based segments (hack this, destroy that) which only hinder your experience as you have to revive them constantly
3) Weak weapons + ADS aiming: I only played the first mission, but there are no other weapons you use except for your assualt rifle/sniper combo and pistol (which a pellet gun would have more damage than what they give you). The assault rilfe is extremely week, and the sniping is hard to master with the choppy frame rate. As well when a game has better accuracy aiming from the hip rather than ADS, you know theres a problem with your shoooting mechanics.
4) Bulllet [or Blaster] sponge enemies: Second to worse offender in this game. Super droids,  Genosians, and Genosian Elites (main enemies around the part of the game were I quit) take so much ammo I would run out of ammo and be forced to use my pistol instead which would take sometimes 3-4 minutes of shooting at one enemy of which there could be 3 or 4
5) Respawning enemies + level difficulty: This in my opinion finalized my decision to stop playing. In the beginning of the game, you have to go across a bridge while destorying barricades with little to no cover. On top of this you have continuously spawning enemies, one of which has a beam weapon that can sap your health down to zero. Add to this your teammates dying left and right causing you to respawn constantly.
Do not pick up this title.

Star Wars: Republic Commando is a squad based shooter set during the Clone Wars. You and a crack squad of Clone commandos navigate a number of high risk operations in a bid to turn back the endless tide from the Confederacy forces. But is the game enjoyable to play? This is what I think of Republic Commando.
Republic Commando is a fantastic game even today. It's such a shame that it never got a sequel, or that no one has made another Star Wars game with the same concepts. Battlefront lets you play as a normal soldier on the ground but this game goes one better by giving you a squad of unique elite clone troopers and running you through a fantastic, if far too short, campaign from Geonosis right through to the invasion of Kashyyyk. The graphics haven't aged too badly in my opinion and some of the level design is exquisite. You can expect the usual excellent Star Wars tracks playing during the game, as well as some unique to the game. It is all suitably epic. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it.
The story starts with you growing up as a clone, along with your squad, and showing the squad develop into the efficient killing machines they are in the game with some starting cutscenes. You are then thrown into the maelstrom of the Clone Wars as the Republic begin the war in earnest on Geonosis. You are Delta 38, Boss, voiced excellently by the definitive clone trooper voice Temuera Morrison. You lead the rest of Delta Squad, 40, 62 and 07 known as Fixer, Scorch and Sev respectively. Each trooper has his own personality and the banter between them is excellent. Together, you fight through hell and back and you can really get behind this band of brothers.
Republic Commando doesn't do anything radically different to shake up the genre but commanding your squad and using the rudimentary tactics feels great. You have an assortment of weaponry to use in your battles, as well as being able to set your squad up in sniping positions or grenade points whilst you flank the enemy and performing breach and clear maneuvers. The level design is excellent, with a number of well done set pieces complimenting the strong gameplay. There is a good variety of enemies as well, each with different strengths and weaknesses. I always found it odd that it was so easy to take down Super Battle Droids in Battlefront but here they really earn the "Super" title as they are heavily armoured walking shields that shoot at you. A negative is the short campaign, clocking in at just under 8 hours. That itself isn't a problem, but the game has three acts each set in a location. Geonosis, on board an abandoned Republic ship and Kashyyyk. With the entire Clone Wars conflict, they could have included more locations whilst still keeping it fresh. A missed opportunity there.
Another complaint can be made about the AI. Too often it feels like you have to carry the rest of your clone brothers and it's hit and miss whether they'll be effective or not, especially during some of the set pieces. They can often wander out into the open and get gunned down, won't do as they're told and other silly little things you probably have come to expect from AI in a video game. It's all par for the course.  This isn't a negative, but the cameo is strong with Star Wars games. If it doesn't have a character from the films, is it even a Star Wars game? All jokes aside, they are done well and integrated nicely in the story.
Overall, I think Republic Commando is one of the best Star Wars games period, right up there with Kotor, Battlefront and the Jedi Knight series. It makes me a little sad we probably won't see the likes of these games again but we are lucky to have them available here on Steam. With its great level design, enjoyable campaign and decent FPS gameplay, this is one Star Wars game you need to play. You won't regret it.

Neverwinter is a fun free-to-play MMO that can be played without spending a dime - if you are okay with an endgame that is an incredible grind (even for those who pay). Choose a class and enjoy some decent MMO combat and story-telling as you progress to the game's max level. At this point, I recommend creating a new character or uninstalling.
Unlike Star Trek Online, the endgame content is separated by releases rather than into different skill tiers, so players new to the game will need to either purchase upgrades (with real-world money) or grind their way into gear that is competitive with that of the diehards. To be fair, new players in STO are not able to compete with the diehards there either, but the separation of content into difficulty tiers allows free players (or mostly free) to slowly progress. With Neverwinter, you'll be able to purchase good gear from the auction house the moment you turn level 70 at a reasonable rate, but adding enchanments to all of that gear, buying companions and fully upgrading them, buying a mount (or mounts for different buffs) and the mount enchantments; well, it is a lot. This is what happends with old MMOs that suffer mudflation and without the difficulty tiers of STO, Neverwinter's endgame content is impenetrable to new players - unless you are willing to throw a good deal of money or time at the game.
If you're like me, someone who likes paying about what I'd pay for a subscription service (like WoW) for free-to-play games, then you probably want to get an epic (purple) mount as the speed bonus is huge for out-distancing mobs so that you can ride through zones without being dismounted. That's going to cost a good $35 or possiblly a bit less if you use a coupon or buy during a sale.
The game has loot boxes and all kinds of silliness around leveling up enchantments for every piece of gear too. The bugger-bear with these is that you have a risk of enchantments not leveling up and you lose all reagents if they don't. Plus, of course, the gambling involved with loot boxes. I don't get all up in arms about these mechanics, but I do refuse to play with them and, in this case, they do ruin the game's long-term viability for people who don't want pay-to-win progression and who are late to the game such that they haven't slowly built up their character's fortunes. No judgment against people who like these systems, btw; if you like this kind of thing then this may be a great game for you.
Finally, the game's engine is aging poorly. While not ugly, the visuals are dated and I was disconnected from the server due to server lag on numerous occasions. Plus, the Foundry (a game system that allows player-created content) has not been up at all since I came back to play this again - well over a week. The calendar shows that they plan to publish new featured content for it next week and they have a tab for it, so clearly their engineers and/or hardware are far below par.
Having said that, Neverwinter is a crunchy MMO. You can make mistakes on creating or gearing your character and most games don't allow that. It also has really strange combat with builds that play strangely compared to other MMOs. Some of the time this is good because it adds a layer of complexity to progression and at other times it is bad because some combat strategies are far superior to others which can lead to playing the game in the optimal way instead of playing around with powers or feeling like your play-style is supported. Every ranger who has a Legolas fantasy is going to suck in endgame unfortuantely and it has been that way since the class came out. They could add a class feature that adds 50% to archery (or melee) damage but prohibits players from switching between the two, but I think they think this MMO will last despite the aging visuals and are holding this kind of change back so that they have other classes to create. Just a guess.
In any case, I recommend you try Neverwinter and have fun with it as if it were a single player game. If you feel like you are enjoying it by level 20, pay for a mount and then don't buy anything else until you reach the endgame and play it for a few days. You'll soon realize the amount of work required to gear up into this complex mudflation mess won't be worth it. They want hundreds (not tens) of dollars.

You can spend months or years grinding epic dungeons and epic trials to get good gear or you can pay money to get it right away.
If gear isn't your goal, but achievements and accomplishments, then Neverwinter has got your back. You may spend months grinding away for those hard won achievements and accomplishments or you can buy an item from the cash store that gives 80% of that to you right away. Great options abound for the avid adventurer.
The game is either grind for months every day or pay money to finish right away. The choice is yours.

Stars in Shadow is easy to learn, fun to play, full of great tactical warfare, and has just enough micro to allow for customization and meaningful choices. If it's not the "best" space 4X of the last few years, it's definately the most fun.
This game is sleek, beautifully illustrated, and full of easily-grasped systems that enable meaningful short- & long-term strategy without a steep learning curve. But while the systems are easily grasped, the depth of strategy possible in this game is outstanding.
Some players might not enjoy the small number of terrestrial buildings. I think it's very close to the sweetspot between micro-intensive planet-customization and stream-lined empire management. Each planet can support 3-6 buildings (usually) depending on size, S,M,L. Choosing what to build, when, where, has a huge impact on the early game, allowing for a focus on population growth, industry, research, or wealth. Planet quality also influences these resources, and while a huge, core, industrial planet can switch from farming to reserach to commerce with great ease once it's developed, back-water planets can take so long to develop, that early choices and well considered diversification and focus can be vital to late game.
Planet management is fun, simple, yet meaningful, and a sense of identity and importance develops around key industrial worlds, centers of commerce or reserach, and worlds with rare and unique charactersitcs.
The alien races have particular strengths and weaknesses. Players will, I think, find a favorite race that boosts their preferred play-style, or one that is weak in their preffered style and offers a greater challenge.
The tactical combat is a particular strength of Stars in Shadow. As most reviews have noted, it's a cornerstone of the game, and players who want to utilized ship construction and formation combat will find a lot to play with.
Ships can be customized in very profound ways, allowing for long range missile cruisers behind mid-range gun-boats behind heavily shielded point-defense screens ... or whatever. The range and efficacy of all the weapons can be brutally effective and effectively countered, so a war against two alien neighbors could require some very different fleet compositions.
For those who don't want to fiddle with lots of ship designs, focusing research on a few techs can work well against most enemies .... most of the time.
The recommended "huge" map size feels small at first, but 99 stars with all the factions in play creates a very big game. If your computer can handle it, you can play on a map with hundreds of stars ... but it will lead to a very long end-game where everyone has all of the techs researched.
There are some nice customization options, along with map size, including distance between stars, likelyhood of habitable planets, speed of tech/building, and a few others. All together, these options can make for some very different games, increasing even further the replayability of SiS.
If you're still reading, then I would also recommend this game over Stellaris and Distant Worlds, because what Stars in Shadow does, it does very, very well. What it lacks in scope compared to Stellaris, it makes up for with excellent combat, meaningful ship customization, and actual strategic gameplay. What it lacks in size, detail, and lenght-of-gameplay compared ot Distant Worlds, it makes up for with sleek, easily grasped systems that don't require either automation or a huge investment of micro-management and constant structural fiddling.
If you think you might like this game, chances are very good that you'll love it.

I can’t stress this enough – If you love MOO II, buy this game.
For 20 years, we’ve been asking for a game that had the same charm that MOO had, and here it is. It doesn’t have the same customizability as MOO II did, but the tech tree is pretty fleshed out and I burned through 2 hours with a huge grin on my face.
Planetary micromanagement, something that always was boring and time consuming is automatically taken care of when you get the next level of requisite tech – this lets me focus on designing warships, and conquering/enslaving the enemy.
There are decisions to be made, for example, Humans do not start with a homeworld, so your population is rather light. I immediately encountered a slaver… do I purchase some slaves to bolster my fledging economy, or do I leave. Notice, I didn’t say “Destroy them all” because my pitiful fleet in the beginning is garbage. However, 30 turns later, I returned with a fleet.
Diplomacy is novel and interesting, using diplomacy points rather than arbitrary background numbers.
But most importantly…
Space battles are outstanding. If you were at home with tactical combat in MOO II, you will instantly love this.
Support this Indy developer – it’s worth it.

For me, it's a game that's not without its faults - the day/night cycle was more of a hassle than it's worth, and the fast-travel system gets introduced way too late in the game. There's a whole lot of walking around you'll have to do before it presents itself. But I guess you could argue it at least gives you more time to listen to that amazing soundtrack. These are all minor nitpicks though, and I'm glad I gave the game a chance.

The Wolf Among Us : a brilliant and mature Point & Click thriller taking place in New York City. It narrates the story of a community of Fairy Tale characters (called "Fables"), exiled from their Homelands and trying to start over in our world. Since most Fables don't exactly look like humans, there's an expensive magic spell called Glamour that alters their appearance, allowing them to blend in and not to get noticed by the "mundies". Those who cannot afford a Glamour are forced to go the the Farm, a place rather seen as a prison.
You play as Sheriff Bigby Wolf - the Big Bad Wolf ; your duty is to protect Fabletown and its inhabitants. Until one day a murder occurs and you have to investigate to find the culprit. As you progress, you discover that it's something bigger, it goes beyond murder ; you also realize how much most of the Fables struggle to adjust and make a living. The plot thickens...
The story is well written and thrilling ; the more you play, the more you are immersed and intrigued. You ARE the Sheriff, you want to know what's really going on and make your own decisions. And this is one of the many pros of the game : you have the choice - not only in the dialogues, but also in the actions, such as where to go first, stay silent or just beat the crap out of someone... Those choices will have an impact, not only what you choose to do, but when too.
The gameplay is pretty intuitive, like most of the Telltale Games. Other than the usual Point & Click aspects, you'll face quick-time events. Imagine a scene in which you have to fight someone ; you'll have for example to press the Q key repeatedly until your opponent lets go of you, then click on an item you want to grab, click on the person to attack him with it, press A to dodge his attack to the left, etc.
Along with the story, there are many other catchy ingredients : a great character development, an amazing voice acting, plot twists, a beautiful artwork that feels like a comic book, an awesome soundtrack, a simple gameplay, a noir detective style, Book of Fables entries to unlock by playing, decisions that have an impact ; as a whole, the game is simply brilliant.
Telltale has without doubt managed to create a spectacular dark story driven video game. Unless you don't like that kind of game, I suggest you take a huge bite and taste this stunning piece of work that will hold you spellbound until the ending. I'm really looking forward to the Wolf Among Us 2, hoping it will be up to its fantastic prequel.

I feel like someone who is intimidated by the massive scope of a zelda would like this game as they can just concentrate on going to dungeons and beating the bosses. You can see my playtime above which is how much time I needed to complete the game, although there is a little bit more you can collect.

Shipwreck is a great example of how retro is done right.
All these indie games with pixel graphics are becoming tiresome.  They aren't much to look at, and honestly they never were, but in the 80s that was all we had.  You don't simply slap pixels onto a 2D map, add clunky controls and call it "retro" if it doesn't actually evoke memories of a classic while you play it.  That said, if you ever played any Zelda games on the GameBoy Color, you will likely enjoy the top-down dungeon exploration in which you avoid traps, find chests with keys or giant hearts that add to your health meter, and fight bosses with a sword or bow.  The music is definitely better than anything the GBC ever chirped out, and it's short enough to complete in an afternoon or two.  There isn't much replay value and the achievements are all fairly easy to get, but clearly the developers had a very specific experience in mind that they wanted to emulate, and they totally nailed it.  9/10.

Emily is Away is not the kind of game that you play because you're looking to hone your legendary skills, improve your flawless strategy, or evaluate the potential of society through a hypothetical dramatization of the political landscape. Rather, Emily is Away is the kind of game that you play to have closure with a bygone era, to say farewell to your childhood or college days once and for all, knowing that life--or at least instant messaging--will never be the same again. The variance in chat decisions leads to an interesting difference of interactions, emulating the reality of a regular online chat. After twenty years of AOL Instant Messenger, the dismantling of an internet icon is commemorated with this refreshingly simple yet well-executed mini-story to peacefully send it to its final resting place.

Great game for any Star Wars fan.
Back in 2005, there weren't a whole lot of games that incorporated the squad tactics that this game had. So from a 2005 rating, this game was great (and even now it's still a fun game). The characters were entertaining and the storyline that followed them was great. Though many say the gameplay is boring and repetitive, I found it to be fun. By using the F1, F2, F3, and F4 controls, you could easily change how you and your squad handled certain tasks. For super battle droids (AKA bullet sponges) you could use different weapons, such as the anti-armor gun, that could easily bring them down rather than unload 300 shots from your primary weapon and take down one or two. This game isn't like the old Battlefronts (both great games by the way) where taking down a couple droids is no big deal. It's only your four-man squad, so you have to use different strategies.
From a 2017 perspective though, many people try to compare it to newer games such as Battlefront 2 (2017). These are games that use different strategies, so someone who likes the playstyle of a game like Battlefront 2 (2017) might not like a game like this.
On a side note, I do wish that the Geonosian Elites weren't so... OP. It might have been better if their weapons did less damage and shot in bursts rather than beams. But this is just a small nitpick to an otherwise great game.
All in all a great game that provides a different play style that's fun and unique. Hopefully in the future a sequel will be made, though I'm doubtful.

Here's an interesting little game. One intertwined with a lot of childhood nostalgia, and the cause of a lot of memes amongst my old school friends. Birthed in an older era, it's quite unique in its qualities:
-6-7 hour long singleplayer campaign with linear level design, fairly obvious pathing
-From 2005, a time unmolested by DLC and weak core gameplay dependent on patches and premium content
-Decently intense at times; gives the player a sense of urgency once in a while
-When you kill jetpack enemies, they go flinging so hard and high into the air they smash into the skybox and stick there
-If you want the mouse sensitivity in the menus to not be 9999999 dpi, or if you want a resolution wider than 4:3, or a different FOV, you're going to have to edit either some text files or some binary.
-The main variant of your rifle hits like a wet noodle, and the only time you ever use it is to sink extra damage into tough enemies, or shoot at distant targets when you can't just whack them upside the head.
-Although the commanding system can be enjoyable, you'll likely come to a point where you wish the AI was smart enough to assist you without being constantly ordered around to do so; your squad are a bunch of headless chickens.
-While the "blood splatters on your screen when you get a melee in" feature was neat the first couple times, it gets very irritating when you're fighting in an area swarmed with enemies and you can't even see where you're going for 3 seconds.
-The game is far too oriented on "interact with this item for X seconds" and slows everything the f*ck down, constantly. Need to plant a charge? 10 seconds. Open a door? 10 seconds. Crack a console? One minute. This is most of the entire game.
-Remember when I mentioned the terrible AI? They'll kill you in cold blood if you stand between them and their target. this includes things they see as enemies which distinctly are not, and are sometimes that thing you have to interact with. Good luck with that.
-Super battle droid deployers are absolutely awful to take down, as they constantly spam out juggernaut-tier enemies around them as you try to rig it to blow in a 20 second long sequence whilst shidding yourself.
-Every room is basically just "tell teammate go there" with a healing station either before, in, or immediately after it. Health kits would be far better, as they at least wouldn't waste your time to bring you back to health.
-In most situations, you're relying on your teammates to sit at their commanded spots and spam their infinite power weapon ammo until you make the odds favorable.
-The Geonosian elite flies around with a death ray, and is bs.
-The Trandoshan elite kills you if you even look at them funny, and is double bs.
-The scavenger drone, a tiny, flying, stupid little part-collecting robot
, zaps and melts you with ungodly damage whilst being a microscopic target whizzing all over, and is triple-quadruple-QUINTUPLE bs.
-If you haven't caught on by now, some of the enemies do an unbelievably and unjustifiably high amount of damage. They attempt to excuse this by the fact that your team can revive you.
-Soundtrack: "Can we listen to something besides Episode II trumpets?" *thrown from LAAT gunship*
-Maybe not the best story or ending around
-Voice lines can be campy and repetitive
It's aite, just hasn't aged terribly well.

Chains is a game about linking 3+ bubbles of the same colour. It features 20 puzzles, each different from one another. Rules, objectives, layout change from one puzzle to the next, sometimes even the gravity is modified.
Basically though there are two types: puzzles that make you think a little, and puzzles where you have to act fast. Unfortunately there is much more of the "act fast" ones. When I got this game I thought it will be relaxing & laid-back. It wasn't most of the time. Chains require focus, reflex and speed, which makes it rather tense experience, stressful even. Hey, I'm old ^^>
I finished the game, although that turned out to be a test of patience. The progress I made was wiped a couple of times or rolled back (I had severe saving issues for some reason), so I was forced to repeat each puzzle at least a couple of times. Without all that repetition the game is very short.
I'm recommending this because "on fence" or "so-so" is not an option. Plus Chains isn't bad, so thumbs down would be unfair. Also, I like the music/ambiance, the art style/ design choice and the variety. I appreciate each puzzle being different (even though not my speed), as I'm often tired with games that have hundreds of carbon copy puzzles with barely any modifications. Ideas for some puzzles/ level design are neat as well :)

I am basing this game review solely on my experience with the game, that stems up to colonization of planets, setting up a new universe, race selection, and option setup. That's as far as was playable as it isn't for anyone who has a custom monitor resolution, as the story and smaller prints of the game are not legible without any video options.
I didn't get to actually playing this game, because the text was so small, and within 10 minutes I was rushing to the refund process. Out of all the 4x games I have played over the last decade, this one has the least options I have seen of any. The layout and gameplay is that of what I would expect from a browser game, or a 5.00 game.
This is 2017, not 1995. I expect a game in this era to have video options, this one does not. It doesn't have a single graphics option, it doesn't have a resolution option, no UI scaling. Which is a serious problem when you decide to print out all information in the screen in fine print. I found myself squinting to read anything in the actual game.
But before that, we were on the typical 4x, select a race, then select universe.. ect.. screen. This is the most simple one I have ever seen. You get a handful of races, there is 0 customization for which race you choose, you do not get the option to make a custom race, you do not get an option on which traits you get per race.
The universe selection is How many planets, and what difficulty, and about 6 options for things like pirate raids, habitable worlds.. ect. Total, the amount of choices you have to make before creating the universe is a whopping 9. Most 4x games I have played, such as civilizations and stellaris have at least 40.
The universe itself seems as 2d as possible, the ships are pictures, the planets are animated pictures, there is no 3d element to this game, and while the art is great, it feels cheap without depth. The only depth to this game I could see was the storys, which were again, so damn small it was hard to read. Don't believe me? click the screenshots provided above, if you have trouble reading those, I gaurantee you will have issues with reading in this game.
I am more angry at the blatant lies of all these reviews, than I am of the devs of this game though.  It's mind boggling to me how anyone could even dare compare this to any of the greats. It does not come close, and doesn't have the capacity to even try.

I've been following this game since early stages.
Highlights were two very responsive developers that stayed in touch and addressed bug reports personally. You don't get that often.
For the game itself, it takes the best features from many 4x.
Planetary management is similar abstracted like Master of Orion 1, slightly different but less of a micro burden than others.
My impression of the way diplomacy is implemented is refreshingly good. Your empires statistics like military strength, personal chemistry and previous actions influence the relations directly and you are getting told that exactly, you're not left in the dark.
Most importantly ship customization and tactical combat feel both very good. Ship design is similar to "Sword of the Stars" which took a slot based approach. You can drag and drop your available components and weapon turrets or fixed weapons into specific slots.  Master of Orion gave you a little bit more freedom but in this game you still have plenty of that.
Tactical combat feels responsive and fluent. It's turn based similar to MoO2, except on steroids. Rubber band selection allows you to give orders to multiple ships at once speeding the inputs up by a lot if you want to. Visual indicators like movement and  weapon ranges are clear.
Visually the game is a combination of traditional very beautiful hand drawn 2D art, stylized but mature enough,and 3D effects like shaders, lighting etc. resulting overall in good mood and atmosphere.
Audio seemed fine to me, weapons have their oomph, music sounds a bit retro but I personally quite like it.
Of course there's always room for improvement.
First of all the visual representation of the otherwise good research tree can be improved. Right now it's a long list, a few people been saying that but this ain't super critical.
Secondly the game allows you to refit your built ships. At the moment the process is tedious in which you directly edit the design. I'd personally have preferred picking an existing design from a list. This is repetitive if you intend to refit more than one.
Overall very good impression though, recommend buying it!

For a Early access game, it is still fun to play. Yes, there is some missing content, other stuff they are fleshing out and improving but the base game is fun and interesting. What I really like are the fleet battles. I actually feel like I have control of the ships I take into combat.

In my opinion, this would be a great investment for a future game that should turn out great.

In the world of adventure games, Dropsy stands out on so many levels that it deserves to be considered a classic of the genre. The art is amazing, the characters memorable, the soundtrack is astonishingly perfect, and the story will pull at your heartstrings in all the best ways. That the game manages to tell a story and guide the player through it without any written or spoken dialog* is a quite a feat.
For me, it's a game that's not without its faults - the day/night cycle was more of a hassle than it's worth, and the fast-travel system gets introduced way too late in the game. There's a whole lot of walking around you'll have to do before it presents itself. But I guess you could argue it at least gives you more time to listen to that amazing soundtrack. These are all minor nitpicks though, and I'm glad I gave the game a chance.
(* ok, not quite true, but you'll get what I mean)

Overall I would give this a solid 8/10

Hints for Windows 10 users:
Make sure you select a resolution that is x32 instead of x 16. The x32 resolutions are at the top of the list rather than the bottom where one would normally find them.
Don't even mess with the graphics settings in game, use your Graphics card to set up effects and aa values. The only thing you need the launcher or in game settings for is to set the resolution.
No matter what kind of hardware you have, chjoose the rendering option that mentions direct x.
If you wanna use a 360 or Xone controller you will have to set the control option to KEYBOARD and then press the buttons on the controller in keyboard settings. KAMUI is the third and final chapter in "The Tale of Alltynex", and also the oldest game in the series, just bought from the 2017 Steam Summer Sales and fell in love with it. Here some pros and cons for the game:
The pros:
+ The story is simple and dark, takes place after the events of RefleX.
+ The graphic looks really old (as a 1999 pc game) but notstagic. Yeah, pixels in HD.
+ Very well-level designs (although just 5 stages) with high and low altitude environment.
+ Like the 2 previous installments, the soundtracks are top-notch.
+ Responsive control scheme. Still recommend to play with a controller. And can be rebinded by using Autohotkey to match your play-style.
+ More complex and unique gameplay mechanic, your Kamui fighter got 2 offensive weapons: The Vulkan Shot can be powered-up by picking up the green gems and the AOE Lightning Attack for the enemies below your ship (likes the lock-on laser of the Ray series). And a combination of these two attacks will create a powerful beam attack which deals massive damage and has many useful abilities. Switching between these 3 weapons and managing the energy gauge at the left corner of the screen will help you survive throughout the stages.
+ Pretty simple scoring system, use your AOE Lightning to attack the enemies at the low altitude and the multipliers will depend on the level of energy gauge (up to x16 at maximum energy). Picking up the power-up gems of your fully upgraded main shot or shield will grant bonus points.
+ Like RefleX, your ship can take several hits before exploded.
+ The game has 3 difficulties from Easy to Menace, enemies and bosses will be more aggressive.
+ The game is very optimized, runs smoothly with constant 60 FPS.
The cons:
- Sometimes the laser shots from enemies still hit you although your beam attack was still activating.
Overall, this is a fun and challenging game with unique tweak gameplay. The long war between human and machine is end in this chapter. The Tale of Alltynex will keep your gameplay mechanic fresh throughout 3 games, with great level-designs and awesome OST albums. Recommend those who want to seek for challenges and even for beginners of this genre. Wait the game for sales, worth it.
Oh, and 1 more thing, play KAMUI first and then Reflex and finally ALLTYNEX Second, if you are interested in the story.
P/s: This game should be deserved an upgrade graphic. (Seriously, this game looks really, really old :)) ).
_Final score: 9/10.

The Wolf Among Us is an episodic, interactive point and click mystery, focusing on the main character Bigby Wolf's exploits and interactions with various members of Fabletown, where he and many other storybook characters live.
It is most certainly a personality driven story. How you chose to present yourself effects how the town perceives you and the general tone of the story as it moves forward.
While not every choice in this game actually impacts the direction the story will flow (a common complaint among the various Telltale games), there are enough key moment differences to make a second play through of the game fun and new.
The game isn't perfect - it’s relatively short at around 9 hours a play through, some of the controls are a little clunky and for people unused to walking simulators, there may feel like not that much to do. But what it does well, it does really well. The voice acting, tone, dialogue and art direction are top notch. It has an incredible amount of heart. It feels like the comic that spawned it.
If you enjoy well crafted interactive stories, this one is a can’t miss.
The story is brilliant. It's worth to buy.

In the dry run between when the Nintendo 3DS came out and when the games started really rolling in, one neat indie game on their E-Shop took off: Steamworld Dig. It was a pretty simple Motherlode-style platformer, but it had charm and a satisfying gameplay loop. The only problem was its length, which was short enough to beat in just a few sessions. The game was successful, but rather than do a direct sequel, Image & Form decided to make one in a different genre altogether, a strategy RPG. That means you won't beat Steamworld Heist in just a few hours, and it also resulted in a fantastic game to me.
Heist is set a while after Dig, following the Earth exploding and its robot inhabitants moving into space on barges. You play as Captain Piper and her crew, who operate as space 'pirates', although you never steal from anyone who isn't also a pirate or evil in some other way, so they may as well just be bounty hunters or something. Pirate attacks in the outer regions of space have become more vicious later, and it's up to them to find out why, and make off with as much loot or hats as they can carry.
Combat is clearly inspired by X-COM: all the ladders, drops and cover are there as you might have seen them in Enemy Unknown/Within, but set in a 2D backdrop. Also like that game, you can move and shoot or use an item, or use your entire move dashing. The most unique wrinkle though, is that there is no RNG in Steamworld Heist, at least on your end. When you go to attack at range, you're allowed to freely aim your weapon, and spend as long as you want aiming the perfect shot. Your bots' don't have perfect stability, so the sights waver a bit, and there are things like ricochets to factor in, but if you hate when a 90 percent shot turns into a miss in X-COM or Fire Emblem, this might be the game for you.
That doesn't make the game easy, of course. Even your most bulky party members can't just tank fire, and it's safe to assume enemies will hit them if they're ever out in the open. Your team is made up of all unique party members, so they're not gone forever if they bite it, but that means they don't receive experience (which is doled out for fulfilling mission objectives rather than killing enemies), and your rating for the mission will drop. It's a good balance between encouraging you to be careful, but not punishing you horribly if something happens to go wrong. There are also multiple difficulties so you can fine-tune it however you like.
Despite being in just 2D Heist has a lot of tricks up its sleeve, such as enemies who only melee, ones with shields you have to flank, and ones who charge up piercing lasers. It's also able to replicate things from X-COM that work with it, like flanking (at least with two characters), and a running timer on some missions that will spawn extra reinforcements, keeping you from just turtling up. There are also some interesting boss battles, which X-COM doesn't really do.
Heist also has a DLC known as The Outsider, which adds another character and a couple more missions to each map (of which there are three, with different ships to invade and enemies to fight). It's not necessary by any means, but the extra crew member is interesting to use, and it has some useful, but not game-breaking items. I like that it's not cordoned off in its own little area, and it's only five dollars as well.
Overall, Steamworld Heist was a very pleasant surprise for me, and a huge step forward for the people behind it. Moving between genres can't be easy, but they produced something not just good, but a huge leap forward compared to their last game. If any of this sounds interesting to you I'd recommend picking it up now, and especially if it's on sale. Really looking forward to Image & Form's next game, whatever genre it happens to be.

Be aware, as of July 2016, the playerbase is small: I recommend picking this game up with friends for maximum fun.
Full review:

Arkshot is an arena-style online FPS. It can be played for hours or in short bursts, due to the rounds being done in max 10 minutes. However, the game is not flawless, and the controls might be hard to pick up, if one choses not to try the tutorial.

Chains is a combination physics-based and tile-matching puzzle game, in which the player creates the eponymous “chains” by connecting brightly colored “bubbles” to other, like-colored bubbles. Once a chain of 3 or more is created, it's removed, and the remaining bubbles fall in place.  The “physics” portion comes not only from that, but in certain levels that are designed around the weight of each bubble, and thus introduce a new element of strategy.
There is no finite goal to the game; each stage has a different objective the player must reach, with each level changing to reflect the current task. Some tasks require more pause, like “Match the given amount in one chain.” Others are a race against another mechanic, such as, “Clear 200 without losing any.” by which the weight of the balls are pulling on a counter weight that, when overwhelmed, will mean the balls can fall out of the level, and the player fails the current stage.
The game is controlled via the mouse alone, and even if there were controller support, it probably wouldn't be wanted. As is, the mouse isn't terribly precise, and one can fail levels solely due to the fact that the “link” of the chain didn't register one's mouse movement.
There are 20 stages, each with varying difficulty. The player may find one level to be as easy as using the game's core mechanic until the goal is reached, while others prove substantially more challenging, with failure encroaching even before the player has a chance to counteract it.  The varying difficulty seems like an odd design choice, as one can also change the difficulty setting of their profile, creating two separate points of variable difficulty. It's also jarring and frustrating to have a difficulty curve that looks less like a steady climb, and more like EKG waves. One is also barred from moving to the next stage until the current one is completed, a perplexing choice given the erratic challenge levels. It would feel less like the levels were simply thrown together if they were ordered, or at least grouped, by relative difficulty.
Further disorientation comes from the
also changing for the different stages. For example, the stage to clear a specific amount is very strict about which direction one can go in order to create a chain.  This is directly followed by a stage that allows one to clip halfway through another sphere in order to create a link.  As a result, the gameplay is left feeling haphazard, as the rules the game teaches the player initially, aren't necessarily the rules for the next level. Mechanics can often feel as if they aren't consistent in-level, either; a notion exacerbated by the fact that connections can be made while the bubbles are still moving.
The sound design is similarly strange: it's not bad, but it seems either too similar or out-of-place. The sound effects for clearing bubbles are fine, and the “fail” noise is also adequate, but the “You're about to fail.” and “Hey, you're #/# of the way there!” are nearly indistinguishable from one another. This is a negative because the more fast-paced levels require the player's utmost attention, and they can't look away to the HUD or text in the corner without losing focus.  Further, the music is also not bad, but it's oddly dire for a simple puzzler. It engenders the feel of a Mission Impossible sequence more than it does shiny neon balls rolling around.
I can't recommend Chains.  The puzzles don't build off of each other at all, leaving no coherent tie between the stages; the game feels more like a tour of the applications of a game mechanic, rather than a cohesive experience. I also noted a hiccup where I was green-lit to go to the next level, even though I hadn't met the requirements for the stage I was on, and could find no way to replicate it. Collectors will also be disappointed to note that there are no achievements and no cards available for the game. I can't see this appealing to anyone but diehard fans of Meridian4, or those who simply must have this experience in particular.

The game itself is pretty simple: Shipwrecked on an island that has troubles with the frequent storms. You'll need to defeat the entity that causes this by collecting 4 special seals.  Each seal is in a dungeon with different biome, with unique bosses.  (There are 6 dungeons - 1 tutorial, 4 seals + final boss' dungeon) The dungeons are pretty good - enemies are different, there are some nice traps, and a puzzle here and there. Sadly the enemies doesn't respawn at all, so in my opinion this turns the dungeons a little too easy. Bosses are also varied, for example the guardian of Earth Seal gave me a really hard time (wanted to kill it without using healing food)   Speaking of food, you'll get LOTS of gold in the game, and in my opinion you will only want to buy food, maybe a few arrows - so if the game is hard for you, you can simply stack up with food between dungeons making fights and dungeon-lurking easier.
I mentioned arrows (maybe bolts, as you'll use a crossbow): you'll need to complete a minigame to prove you're good enough at fighting to use the crossbow. It's a really nice idea! Sadly this is the single minigame or activity you can do between dungeons - the world is utterly empty on the surface. Trees, bushes (smack them for possible loot!) and butterfies.

Shipwreck is a retro style top down adventure game that is quite obviously influenced by games in the Legend of Zelda series. It's a fun experience. Basically, your ship gets wrecked on this island, so you need another to leave. You adventure to get one, but the only way to do so is to use the one ship on the island once the mayor allows it. So you end up having to help the mayor solve the island's problem. A ghost showed up recently, locked itself away in the island's lighthouse, and has been causing storms which disrupt the people's way of life. You must stop this evil ghost. To open the lighthouse, you need to obtain four seals, each in their own dungeon protected by monsters. Typical adventure stuff. Go to the dungeons, get new items, use the items to complete the dungeons and fight the bosses. Get the seals. Do the final dungeon, beat the final boss, and win the game. Also, you more than likely will be able to get all the achievements just by playing normally, which is good if you care about getting achievements I suppose. The music is alright. The retro style is nice if you're into that. And you get to run around hitting things with a sword. What can I say? It's fun. However, I feel this game has some rough downsides. While it's clearly inspired by Zelda games, it seems to lack a lot of what makes Zelda games so entertaining.
There's not much story in Shipwreck, instead just surviving on a main plot. That's fine by me, but some people will see this as a point of disconnect. My point of disconnect was moreso from the fact that there's a distinct lack of characterization. The main character has no personality or lines, but that's because it's YOU. The part that bugs me is that none of the people in the game have any real personality. Everyone is rather bland and most of the townspeople will say nothing of consequence to your journey or the world building. It makes them feel very forgettable and doesn't motivate you to help them. All the villain does is cause storms, so there's not a lot there to make you really hate them or understand them as a villain, which is sad for the main villain of the game. So your only real motivation to beat this villain is to leave the island and beat the game. Kind of a weak motivator.
Another strange thing is the overworld. Zelda games have overworlds, but... they have things in them for you to do. In Shipwreck, there are a decent number of screens on the overworld to explore, but there's no point in exploring those extra screens. There are no enemies to fight in the overworld. No secrets to find. I believe there are one or two houses to enter. One has an item you'll need, the other might just have some treasure. But there's a desert, a swamp, a forest, even a graveyard in the overworld that are all empty. There are dungeons in four of the areas, a town in the center, and the final lighthouse to the North. That's it. The areas leading to the dungeons are just small mazes. I can understand this being cool for one, possibly two areas. But all four? It feels a little bit like padding. Why not put some enemies in here? Thow in some puzzles or terrain I need my new item from the previous dungeon to overcome. Something more than just a change of scenery would've been greatly appreciated and give the overworld more purpose.
The dungeons aren't too bad. I just can't help but feel like the dungeon bosses could've been cooler. Maybe that's just me. The puzzles in dungeons were also a bit lacking. There could've been more or just trickier ones that required more thought. Still, I will admit the dungeons were probably the best part of the game. I think having more items would've opened up a lot more possibilities here. You can equip any two items at a time, but there are three empty item slots. I can't imagine why. Perhaps I've missed something, but it just feels like there was supposed to be more items than what we ended up with. Plus, none of the items were that creative. Sword and shield are basic. So is a bow. Having two slots for healing items, one for each specific one, is a bit silly since this is the only way to heal on the go. I like that you keep all the health you pick up because of this, but switching to the healing item every time can get tedious. And the pickaxe is probably the saddest item because, while it's cool for the dungeon you get it for, it serves no putpose outside of that. Why wasn't breaking rocks to get to new areas or breaking walls in other places part of the gameplay? Why was the pickaxe a one and done dungeon item? It just seems like such a missed opportunity. Also, while I liked the retro look, I wasn't too fond of some of the art and color choices, but that's not a big deal.
Overall, Shipwreck is a cool little game. It just could've been so much more. There's lots of good ideas here, but they need to be explored. The adventuring in this game isn't much, even though the gameplay that IS there is solid. It is also fairly short, as I beat it in one sitting.  It's only three bucks at full price. I'd say that, if you're a Zelda fan, or want to get into Zelda games without the stress of learning all the references or paying full game prices... this is a good start. But if you're a Zelda fan... don't come into this expecting Link's Awakening 2. It takes the basics of Zelda games and cuts to the chase, sacrificing most of the charm. If it was more expensive I wouldn't recommend it, but it's not bad for the price. If you're looking to test out Zelda basics, or if you're already a big Zelda fan, you'll probably appreciate this game. Otherwise it might just be too bland for your taste. Make a sequel expanding on these ideas and I'm sure I'd give it much more praise. I'm easily suckered into Zelda type games so make those improvements and you have a sale right here already.

Sometimes I wonder what anyone could see in an old game like Kamui. This STG was released in December of 1999. This was back when everyone had to walk fifteen miles through snow and broken glass, just to find quality shmups. Kamui runs at a pitifully low resolution, and there aren't any tanks that turn into robot-girls. There isn't even any fanart. Why? Because the protagonist is a brain in a ship! That isn't kawaii, not in the slightest.
Seriously though, who cares about all of that nonsense? Kamui is just as awesome as it ever was. It's a tremendous game that delivers everything fans expect from the genre. This game tends to be compared to titles like the Ray Force series, though it has other elements that help set it apart.
Risk Vs Reward is an adage older than time itself, and it's the entire basis of this game. Aside from the main cannon, your most important weapon is lightning. This weapon can be used to power an exceptionally strong laser, that also cancels enemy projectiles. However, using the laser tends to negatively impact your score. Your other weapon is the targeting bolt. Enemies destroyed by bolts offer up a multiplier bonus. Depending on how much meter you have remaining, this bonus can go as high as 16X.
While Kamui gives you a generous supply of hit-points, you're constantly putting yourself into bad situations, just to get the highest possible score. Bolts can only destroy enemies that are below you, and that applies to bosses as well. You might find yourself keeping the boss alive, allowing them more chances to kill you, just so you can get the massive multiplier bonus. As for the stages themselves, your attention is almost constantly divided, due to the prevalence of enemies both below and in-front of you. If you approach this game strictly intending to survive, then it probably won't be that difficult. However, your score will suffer, and eventually you'll give in to the temptations of 16X.
Kamui is a very short game, and doesn't make any attempt to pad things out. Each stage creates scenarios that are fresh and interesting, without straying away from the concept that drives the game. The enemies you face are varied, and the bosses employ numerous strategies in order to take you down. This isn't like some STGs, where you deal with giant pieces of garbage that do nothing but fill the screen with bullets. Every second of this game is creative and dynamic. It's loaded with energy, and has just enough challenge to keep gamers compelled.
In short, Kamui is a classic. Give it a go sometime.

Kamui is a vertical 2D shoot'em up released exclusively for PC (Windows) in 1999 by japanese Indie developer Siter Skain. This game is part of the trilogy " The Tale of Alltynex " composed of  the games: Kamui, Reflex and Alltynex Second. Kamui is considered one of the best shoot'em ups released for PC, something I have to agree, because the game is really great! Kamui's gameplay is heavily inspired by the games Rayforce, Raystorm and Raycrisis made by Taito  Corporation. In Kamui you have three types of weapons at your disposal: the front gun that can be upgraded;  the ray gun, seeking and hitting the enemy in the lower layers in relation to your ship and finally a powerful, concentrated shot that smashes the enemies, but that depends on an energy bar in a scheme similar to the classic R-Type. The game has a nice and fluid gameplay, very tasty and fun. The controls work very well with the Xbox 360 controller and the music is wonderful and very engaging! Pros:
- Good story, keeps you guessing throughout and there are a few twists and turns that keep you engaged
- All the characters have their own personalities and view on the world. The fables all have real world problems and each has their own story to tell.
- The world is interesting and leaves a lot open for a sequel
- Game mechanics are easy and do not require much skill or practice.
- Decisions will change how you as the player character act, where you decide to go, and how other characters react/treat you, however it does not alter the overarching storyline (can be a pro or a con) so you don't need to worry about making "the wrong decision" in terms of the main story
Cons:
- Gameplay is limited, mostly story with various choices for dialogue, occasional 'search the scene for clues' and QTE fights
- Not very challenging
- Does not touch on all the plot points or character arcs that pop up
- Visuals and animation can be a little off putting at first
- Needs more world building
- Some dialogue cues are not what they seem to be. You may be thinking one way but it comes out differently than what you intended. This can cause some unintentional results.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game. The story is interesting, the characters are very fleshed out with varying personalities and stories, you get to play the protagonist how you want to play him, and characters will react differently based on how you play. The only major gripe I had was that some of the dialogue choices were not written well in that they make you think you're going to say/do one thing but you end up saying/doing something else. It's not something that will ruin an entire scene but it does mean you really have to think about what the devs really meant. It's a very film noir/murder mystery type game and is worth having in your collection

The initial artwork makes you think this would be a decent title.  I loved the Wipeout games, is this a modern take on it?  Sadly not even close.
The first problem I encountered is that there are no insturctions on how to play.  I selected the first of what appears to be 3 stages, got in a match against three other racers... and sat there.  The other ships zoomed off, and I was pressing my keyboard and mouse trying to figure out how to move.  I quit out of the game and looked for help, tutorial, anything.  In the end trial and error by pressing every key on my keyboard I discovered "X" was the magic key I needed to press to figure out how to go forward.
Alright, so no controls are posted.  That isn't a great sign.  Still, now I finally know how to play.  Get ready world.... Wipeout clone here I come.
Oh, no, wait.  You only can choose from one ship.  The controls are sluggish.  The tracks are boring.  Wipeout used the vertical element in its track design to great effect.  This game has only a few race tracks to try, and they are bland and no fun to race on.  And at all times I felt like I was fighting poor controls.
The worst part though in this generic knockoff tragedy, worse than the lack of instructions, the poor controls, the bland music and the boring race tracks.... is that even once you take the time to really master the game it isn't fun or satisfying.  Hitting an enemy ship with a weapon does not have any sort of satisfying impact.  Hitting boost arrows never leads to those "breakneck speed chains" you would expect in a title like this.  In fact, at the end of the day you don't seem to be able to go very fast at all.... in a racing game.
I liked some of the particle effects, and it about ends there.  This game is a chore to learn how to play, and even once you do there is no fun waiting to be had in the mastery of the mechanics.

I remember seeing this game getting well reveiwed when I was a kid, but I never was able to play it since all I had was an original Playstation. I also remember walking out of Episode 2 in theatres, and even then at 6 or 7 years old, thinking it was one of the worst movies I'd ever seen. I loved Star Wars back then.
Flash forward to 15 years later, and Republic Commando is on sale on Steam! That game that was set in one of the coolest fictional universes, where you control a group of elite clone soldiers and use tactics and weapons from across the galaxy! The game I wanted to play as a kid but couldn't! It's also constantly heralded as one of the best and most interesting Star Wars video games, and there are a lot of those, so that's got to mean something. Not to mention it was made in a sweet spot for video games, one of the generations where technical accessibility for developers matched with graphical and artistic advancements that meant that many different types of games could be made, where interesting visions could be brought to life, and developers could take risks and not lose trillions of dollars like they do now. It's gotta be good!...... I haven't been this dissapointed by a game in a while. Republic Commando has aged like milk.
The story is pretty by the numbers, but it establishes its characters well and some of the dialogue is charming enough to get by. If you're familiar with any "color coded action heroes team" media from the past 20 years, this'll be more than familiar. But the art and sound design are excellent enough to push you forward (Shoutout to classic LucasArts games, they never went wrong in those departments). Unfortunately, the entirety of what I played was predicated on 3 gameplay loops that soon became unbearable. Shooting, which is broken beyond compare. Enemies are either so easy to kill all you need to do is run up and melee them, or such ridiculous bullet sponges that you need to focus all of your squads firepower on them, and usually use special weapons (that you don't have, or if you do, have EXTREMELY limited ammo for, whilst there are dozens of heavy enemies) to defeat them. Or you can go up and melee them 30 times. It does more damage than your primary weapons. Grenades are an option, but you run out quickly and at a certain point towards the end of the 1st act, The game stopped giving me refills.
The combat is some of the worst I've experienced in an FPS, and ultimately what made me quit playing before the end of the first act. I couldn't do 12 hours of it. It was like Chinese Water Torture. If you think games now take 5 hours of content and stretch them out for 90 hours, this game does the same with 45 minutes of content. The second gameplay loop is disabling and bombing doors, each which takes 10 seconds. There are hundreds of these, every new room is locked off by a door. MY GOD. Yes you can get your squad to do it but it still takes 10 seconds and you're usually leading them so you might as well do it yourself. Horrific, I would say at least an hour or more of the game is just opening doors. finally, especially on harder difficultires, you're constantly getting your health back. The enemies still take 10000000 shots to kill on hard, but you only take about 5. It's horrible. Is it easy to get health? No. You have to stand at a console and wait for your health to be refilled. The moment to moment gameplay is already languid enough because of the invincible enemies, but you have to take 10 second breaks every minute to open doors and restore your health. I couldn't make it past the first act. Some of the squad commands and strategic elements are impressive and streamlined for their time, but it doesn't matter when the gameplay is so bad. I can't recommend this to anyone with a working brain. Unless you enjoy repetitive opression, in which case, you should just go to work all the time.
Side note: The graphics are good enough for 2005, but the PC port is junk. No widescreen, resolution is capped, and display is overall funky. You'll have to download a mod to play this game and make it look halfway decent. But the graphics haven't aged that well either. Look at Half Life 2, which came out a year before and still looks fantastic (I know that was developed for PC, and this game was developed for X-box, but you could at least give some options to make this game look better)
Anyways, do not buy this game. Thanks.

Good concept, but you can't "beat" it - you can only hope that it gives you the right bubbles in the right order, and that you're fast enough to notice that order and make the right chain. It sounds kind of exciting that way, but in reality, some of the levels are just too difficult because of the random allocation of colours.
It's a puzzle game that you can't solve; a supposedly calm and relaxing game that often comes down to your twitch-reflex and your ability to spot when the game hands you the solution after hours and hours of combinations that make it literally impossible to pass the levels. And when you get stuck on a certain level that you know how to beat *in theory* but can't actually beat because the game keeps sending down purple bubbles into the middle of the yellow-bubble chain you've been building... it's just not fun.
The music is ok, and that's about the best thing I have to say for Chains. The level ideas are cool but poorly executed; so much so that a cool concept becomes abject torture... the graphics are quirky and somewhat artful the first time around, but after thirty attempts at the same level it loses any of interest from trying to figure out the "flow" and you're left staring at something that looks like childrens' scribble... and even when you do manage to pass an impossible level on a lucky run, it's only a matter of 1-2 more levels before you're stuck again and don't come back to play for months at a time...
seriously, the only reason I'm writing this review now is because I came back to Chains again because I had nothing else to do, and realised that this game held no interest whatsoever for me. I can't find any reason to reccomend this game to play, let alone to buy. This should have been a browser game; and even then it wouldn't be a very good take on its genre without some major balance adjustments.

So with a few hours so far played what can I say about SiS... well simply put it is a interesting concoction of MOO 1 and MOO 2, sprinkled with a dash of beautiful retro artwork. If you liked those two titles, you will quickly find that there are many things likeable about SiS.....yet in the same vein it is constantly comaparable to both titles, and this is where I found myself struggling to click "next turn".
I understand it is early access, and many things are yet to have descriptions or even be totally complete; but SiS feels like a clever pretender, trying hard to mimick what made MOO2, in particular great to go back to....... I desperatly want to love this game, and I will persevere; simply because the things that could set it apart and possibly greater than the original 4x masterpiece is the very concepts dashed into the game that give me hope that SiS is going to do what MOO 2 never tried to do.
Diplomacy. It feels the same but SiS is just starting to break out of the sandbox and give real possibilities of giving this game more than "conquer thy nieghbour" which ultimatley most similar 4x games become to any experienced player.
Priates, Mercenaries, and Minor races. Love this aspect, as it gives so many more strategic posssiblities and challenges, and of course deepens the diplomacy.
Rebellions. As with the above, any junior conquerers are ultimatley going to suffer from constant strife as they maintain a war with a race, as they assimilate thier populations, even peacful citizens become ardent militias in the face of your rolling war machine.
The above three things are elements that give me what I really didnt know I wanted from MOO2, yet now understand what really could have been. I just hope that Ashdar games sees what this could be and make it truely great.

Definitely a Beta Game as it stands right now. A deal of clever game mechanics and ideas were utilized as compared to other space strategy games. Plus as you can undo any mistakes you have made, it works very well for any laid back types out there like myself.
However, there is room for improvement. I am just going to leave it to five good areas to improve.
- One notable area is detailed area of a solar system, perhaps instead of using the Polaris Sector/Endless Space formula of showing planets in a system, you could instead consider showing system regions and then put planets into those regions, followed by moons of course. Lets utilize our own Solar System as an example, notably you would have a maximum of four regions: Inner Planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth + Luna, Mars), Asteroid Belt (Ceres, Vesta, Pallas, Hygiea) Outer Planets (Jupiter + Io & Europa & Ganymede & Callisto, Saturn + its four biggest moons, Uranus + its four biggest moons, Neptun + Triton & Proteus) Kuiper Belt (Pluto + Charon, Haumea, Makemake, Eris + Dysnomia). This could work by having two new size categories of worlds (dwarf and petite) in which a planet can have a moon so long as the moon is one size smaller than the planet unless it is a binary planet (Pluto and Charon). Asteroid belts are likely to have only dwarf and petite size worlds. You also have the prospect to join structures within an increasing system dynamic as you progress through techonology. So you may start off with your moons being structured independently from their host planet, but as your technology improves, you can then group the investment and aspects of your moons with its host planet making it easier to use all of your labor from each moon in support of its host planet. This could proceed further to an entire section of a solar system to the entire solar system it self.
- Another could be varied solar systems such as having multiple stars or having a neutron star, pulsar, magnetar or black hole. This may involve building certain structures around stars as well as certain stars to grant you more bonuses and unique gains for your system and overall empire.
- Another good idea is a section manager, now this I would argue should be optional as should be any automation in general. When you have the prospect of having a very large game (500 systems), it can be kind of daunting to say the least in managing that many systems. Easier would be to manage sectors, which in turn manage systems for you, but this is after you have a good number of systems under your grasp. Again, optional as you have people who love micromanaging.
- Succession Manager. Think of Crusader Kings 2. Now this is quite ambitious, but it can be kind of basic (more like the animated mods of Crusader Kings 2). This is due the fact you will have the same leader even when a thousand years have gone by.
- Lastly, you can spend a great deal of just clicking the "next turn" button just to advance in the game and that can ruin the game play immersion as each turn should possess its own relative importance. Therefore, you should have events that transpire and can alter the dynamic of the game during each turn. I suppose you can use your own imagination, but think about games you have already played that are space oriented and think of what exciting events could transpire to give you a decision in how things might proceed as you continue that click the "next turn" feature desperately waiting for something to get built, enough money to rush it or just the next available technology. Explorating events is also a good idea as well, including an exploration feature when you reach a solar system and you have to spend time to actually explore the solar system rather than know what is there the very turn you show up.
Ultimately, I highly recommend this game, both to help out the developer, but also a new refreshing taste at how to design a game about colonizing and exploring space.

First, I would like to say that this game
indeed an actual game worth the price, and
actually satisfying to play. However, I cannot reccomend this game because although it may be worth your money, it is not worth your time. Why? Well, after finishing the main adventure and dabbling in the other game modes, I've assembled a list of reasons why I think this game is ultimately somewhat insulting to the video game medium (I know that sounds harsh, and I really don't want to insult the dev, but this is honestly perhaps the best way I can describe my feelings toward this game). Here it is:
The story is not great. You control Cally, a young girl who must save her parents from an evil scientist before she can go to school for the day. She has over a wide array of guns at her disposal to help her do this. Along the way, she talks to a few characters who are halfway interesting, but the only one who really stuck out to me during my playthrough was Bera. Bera is a bear cub who you control at several points throughout the main story, and in her own sidestory available from the start. That was the most interesting part of the game's story IMHO. Really, her parents just serve as a plot device to thrust Cally into an adventure. There's so much that's left unexplained, and it honestly started to aggravate me after a while. For instance, why can Herbert, the mad schientist, fly? Why is he so hellbent on kidnapping Cally's parents? Why does Cally have a gun and sword when the game begins? Granted, these points may have been properly explained in the series's previous installments, but I feel that they should have been more properly elaborated upon in this entry since its the only one the dev has made avaible on Steam right now. So the story is not mentally engaging in the slightest, and is just there to get Cally (and ultimately the player) in action.
Unfortunately, the game's art design is mostly bland and uninspired as well. Sprites are simple, clear, colorful, and effective, but certainly don't exceed expectations and quickly get old since most enemies only have three different animations (walk, attack, recoil). Music is not memorable. Sound effects are bland (and unmutable, another aspect which frustrated me). The only element of the art which really stook out to me was the weapon sprites. They were somewhat interesting at times.
This is what really annoyed me. This is not a game of skill. It is honestly just a glorified idle game. All you have to do to beat most of the game's foes is just click the shoot button a dozen times or so. This levels up your weapons, which makes their damage increase as well as occasionally adding some often trivial effects. It is not difficult in the slightest, especially since you are able to easly grind for consumables which make you darn near invincible extremely early on in the game. Weapon balance is not there, as you can honestly just stick with the rocket launcher (again, given to you extremely early on in the game) for dispatching foes for the whole game. While it is kinda fun to experiment with the different weapons, there is ultimately no real point in wasting time upgrading all of them since you only really need to upgrade one to get through the game. Most enemies have little vertical movement, and the ones that do have low health and follow extremely simple attack patterns. This is a game that you can "do well at" and "see your character improve" without actually improving as a player. It's just grinding. That's all there is to it. This is a game for people who just like seeing numbers get bigger; and honestly, if you'e that kind of person, then I reccommend playing Cookie Clicker or some other free idle game. At least those games are free, and can be left on in the background while you do something more productive with your time.
Very few of the levels are downright bad. Very few are outright good. Most are (following the motif) bland and uninspired. Often, they are lacking in wit, and some of the design choices just make little sense to me. Here's some examples:
Ultimately, this game is just that - a game. Nothing less, and nothing more. It's like bubblegum for your mind: fun to chew on, but has absolutely no nutritional value. If you have too much time on your hands and a few bucks burning a hole in your wallet, then by all means go ahead and buy this game. You'll probably enjoy grinding for more than a dozen hours. If, on the other hand, you prefer games that are a bit more challenging, mentally engaging, and valuable as a work of art and not just a source of entertainment, then pass forget about Cally's Cave's 3.
All this being said, I am actually looking forward to Cally's Caves 4. The dev is quite prolific on Twitter, and it seems like has learned from many of CC3's mistakes. If  CC4 manages to have the same kind of addictive fun as CC3 as well as heightened difficulty, craftstmanship, and core mechanics, then I believe it has the potential to be a masterpiece.

Fidel Dungeon Rescue is a challenging puzzle game in which you move around a randomly generated dungeon of monsters without crossing your path. Everytime you "attack" a monster you lose some health, and everytime you move over a health pack you restore health. As you collect experience while you progress through the increasily difficult dungeon floors, you level up, causing the amount of health you have to increase, providing an incentive to maximum the experience you gain on each floor. While this may sound like a simple concept, there are enough secondary mechanics, interesting monster behaviours, and challenging trade-offs you must make to keep the gameplay varied and interesting. If you lose all your health or spent too long on a level, the ghost will appear to keep you on your toes. This provides a very fast-paced gameplay, while forcing you to pay careful attention to every move you make, even if there is an undo command.
Unfortunately, the game is not without its flaws. The ghost can be an annoyance to those who want to take their time, or experiment without worry of having to start all over again. Furthermore I was unable to get my controller working with the game (although I suspect things like this will be patched in the future..?). Regardless, this game is highly enjoyable and I would recommend to anyone interested in puzzle games!
