SteamWorld Heist is a side scrolling, turn-based, tactical game where you're the commander of a group of space pirates drawn into unavoidable conflict against the Empire while performing routine heists. Although the game is in side-scrolling 2D, it encompasses the familiar genre staples such as a cover system and terrain variability while displaying some of its own mechanics such as bullet ricochet which add some depth to the simplified systems. While the game delivers an entertaining journey and tense combat, it suffers from a lacklustre story and somewhat repetitive mission structure in the latter half.
+ Dialogue and interactions between characters is really enjoyable as characters often share their entertaining back-stories with you after missions.
+ Combat is extremely well done, I've heard it compared to a simplified mix of XCOM/Worms.
+ Bullet ricochet is highly enjoyable as you can kill enemies hiding behind cover by ricocheting bullets in the blind spots where there is no cover. Getting unassisted ricocheted kills feel extremely  satisfying.
+ A lot of effort was placed into the audio and visual aspects of the game and it shows as the game oozes polish from every nook and cranny.
+ There's no grind for what amounts for a tactical game and that's surprising for me. Lower skilled characters can be carried and get essential 2 bars if they survived the mission easily bringing them up to the rest of the squad.
+ There's no reliance on RNG during the combat it's all skill. If you missed shot, YOU missed the shot as have full control of where you aim. If a character is out in the open then the chances of receiving damage is 90-100% and it was fully based on YOUR decision.
+ Combat while not difficult is often times tense under certain situations depending on your difficulty.
+ The difficulty curve is rather smooth. I played on Experienced and even though I got wiped on a few missions, it wasn't difficult to complete the game.
+ A unique-ish loot system that's literally all of the items found lying on the floor in missions plus the epic swag bonus which is often placed in a mildly inconvenient room forcing you to explore all rooms. Don't feel like managing your small inventory to store mission loot rewards, fine, simply go for the epic swag and leave all other items alone.
- Story is kind of lacklustre and forgettable.
- You can't equip weapons/items outside of missions.
- Missions are too repetitive, you're often stuck doing the same things mission in, mission out and while enjoyable it does get tiresome.
- Limited inventory results in management feeling extremely tedious as you're given generous amounts of loot as reward for completing missions.
- Aborting missions cost 50% of your current money/water. Why is this a thing, there were times where I accidentally retried missions I'd completed instead of selecting the next mission and I had to slug through it again because I'd be penalised for nothing.
- The game feels a bit too long and drawn out, almost like if it was padded with unnecessary content e.g. the 1 character missions.
- There are times where the enemy AI is too accurate. This is clearly evident during the boss battle against the Queen. The general's bullet will ricochet a number of times and the result is a perfect shot no matter what. I've had this happen to me a lot during that battle to the point that it's unfair and too perfect.
- Battles can become drawn out as result of the alert system which spawns a number of enemies of increasing difficulty when the counter has elapsed. I get why this is here but boy does it get annoying.
+/- Hats...why are they a thing? They serve literally no purpose, no added stat benefit or complexity.
+/- Loot is kind of boring as it simply boils down to +1 this or -1 that.

My nominee for "Villian most in need of a hug" award 2016.
Um, what can I say.  This is a fantastic indy adventure game.  The storytelling manages to capture emotion and make you empathize with a protagonist and characters in a way I haven't seen too often.  I also have to say, I haven't met a protagonist as admirably selfless as Dropsy in a long, long time.  If you enjoy adventure games or want to find good and imaginative storytelling experiences, this is a game that belongs in your library.
The game follows the story of Dropsy, an overweight, horrifying looking clown who is so mentally disabled he can't speak except to laugh or mumble, writing looks like unintelligable squiggles to him, and he can't understand a single thing other people say.  The story begins on the anniversary of a tragic accident he caused which resulted in the death of his mother and affected everyone in the city around him.
There are only a few ways you interact with the world around you.  The most useless, is speaking since you can only understand generally what they are saying and everything comes out as unintelligible.  The second, is by using the assortment of items you find.  Third, is by having several animal friends you make interact with them.  Finally, and most usefully is hugging - you should hug everything.
The puzzles for the main story are not too complicated and you should have no problems figuring out where to go and what to do.  The real meat and most enjoyable part of the game are the interactions you have with NPC's on the side and solving their problems, the game does quite a bit to push you to these people.  Dropsy has this interesting gift to see how depressed people are around him and the game nudges you to do something about it - since Dropsy wants to do nothing more than make the world a better place.  The result is almost always heartwarming and satisfying to watch.  Finishing these side missions and finding out how connected all the people in the world are to each other and how they connect back to you is more rewarding than the story itself and makes the story that much more enjoyable.
The game isn't without its problems, the pointing and clicking can sometimes be a little off and the soundtrack can sometimes be a little...grating.  Travel times, in the early game can be a problem and even after you get fast travel you may find yourself walking around...a lot.  None of this detracts from the overall experience as far as I'm concerned though.
There is only so much more I can say about this without spoiling it.  Suffice it to say Dropsy is a wonderful little game and a satisfying experience I will not likely forget.

There's way too much game here to be able to write a comprehensive review, so I'm just going to go with a simple list of pros and cons:
Cons:
-Instanced, very instanced.
-Character customization is "eh."
-World feels static, NPCs are forgettable.
-Cash shop is a little steep, certain upgrades (IE companions) REQUIRE cash investment to advance beyond a certain point.
-Bank / Inventory space is very small (though a couple dollars will remedy that).
-Story is disjointed and bland.
-Game doesn't explain it's systems very well, campaigns are cryptic (I actually still don't get exactly what they are).
-Item upgrade system is positively dumpster.
Pros:
-Graphically the game looks good enough.
-Combat is super fun, daily system / skills feel really good.
-PVP is quite good, though there is f-all for balance.
-The cash shop doesn't feel required for the most part. I invested $20 once, wound up with a fast mount, heirloom weapons, and bunch of cash shop currency (to buy bags etc). Also did premium for a month, that gives you a loot crate key and some silver bars (a special currency) daily, which is pretty good.
-It's free to play (you won't feel the cash shop draw for at least 20-30 hours).
All in all, if you're eyeballing it, give it a shot. Once you get to the point where the cash shop starts feeling necessary, either invest or don't EZPZ.

Pros:
- Fun Gameplay
- Tons of Free Content
- Good Variety of Classes and Races
- An okay Dungeon Que System
- A Reasonable Campaign Grind
- Awesome looking mounts
- Lots of mounts to choose from, same with companions
Cons
- A huge progression wall after a certain amount of time playing
- An absurd grind to get over that wall
- The wall is where pay2win complaints come from
- I agree, it's pay2win, hard.
- The Random Dungeon que is so broken it's crazy
- Some races are priced absurdly high
- Mounts and Companions increase your stats in certain ways so you have to build around certain ones, really limits your choices if you want proper stats
There are a decent amount of classes and races to choose from, and more to come from what it seemed like to me. The character customization is awesome and really feels like you're creating your perfect D&D character from your facial features down to your characters backstory that other players can read. It's awesome and really gives the player a ton of freedom to mould their character in any way they want. After creating your perfect character you're thrown into a massive world of lore with a crazy amount of free content. Eventually, after playing for hours and reaching max level, you'll reach the next level of progression which is campaigns and gearing up. Campaigns are daily quest grinds for boons which give passive stat boosts. They are reasonably paced with some taking up to 30 days of dailies and others being like 2 weeks. They are basically placed there to add new content for new players to enjoy while they begin doing the normal MMO thing of grinding for better gear.
The game is great and is all fairly reasonable until you finally hit a massive wall of progression. This wall is so insanely high that if you don't throw money at the game, discover some secret market manipulation, or grind for Astral Diamonds for months until you can pay for the ladder to climb over. Basically, the progression at this point is grinding/paying for Astral Diamonds to gather enchants for your gear, buy/upgrade companions, and buy mounts in order to up your gear score and stats, as well as buying companions and mounts. These enchants go for over 200k+ Astral Diamonds for the good ones and the good companions/mounts go for well over 300k while you're only able to refine 36k astral diamonds a day. You are able to buy/sell more than 36k on the Auction House a day, there is no limit, but unless you are manipulating the market it still takes ages to get enough AD to buy your upgrades. Basically at this point it's either stick to the grind for a couple of months or throw like $300 at the game.
I was able to get through all but 2 of the campaigns and get to around 8.8k gear score without spending a dime before I couldn't take the grind anymore. If the grind wasn't so smack in the face about it, I might have stuck with it, but it's just way too insane and crazy how fast it sneaks up on you.

Also, another minus for me is that the crafting is an idle mini-game. You hire a supposedly worker npc and they do the crafting from you. From the gathering to the crafting of equipment.
In short, this game is pretty much about adventuring with your friend, so if you like to just jump into an adventure and fight bosses in dungeons, this game is pretty much for you. This is the classic Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver that you, like me most likely, played on the original Playstation! It's still the same, and still rather good, though there are two major problems with this port that you should know:
FIRST: This is a direct port of the Playstation version, not the Dreamcast. This won't trouble many people, but.....
SECOND: The sound issues with this port are deplorable. Music won't work correctly and will reset when the game is paused, sound will cut out or altogether be delayed and sound static-like, and, the worst sin, there are songs missing from the game. From my own play through, these are the missing tracks: all of the spectral music, boss music, various combat loops, and the puzzle OSTs.
I'd actually recommend getting an emulator and playing the Playstation or Dreamcast version over this.

Well, it appears I changed my mind on this title in retroperspect. My initial points still stand - the game's camera system often is nothing short of awful, and the Steam version is a very lackluster port that is wildly inferior to the original PS/Dreamcast versions.
That being said, the game has plenty of good sides - there's an entire set of spells that sort of act as a side-quest in that you will never run into them if you just follow the main mission. The platforming generally is solid (so long as the camera doesn't get in your way), and although the combat system has its issue (with enemies thrown onto the stabby bits necessary to pernanetly kill them often magically landing next to them rather than on them), its still rewarding in its own way - the fact that you usually fight no more than 2-3 enemies at a time shows that you're fighting against powerful vampires, not jut plain old mortals.
All things considered, Soul Reaver is a neat specimen of classical jump'n'run adventures, but suffers from the camera and collision issues games of its time often had to deal with. If you can tolerate the latter, it is nonetheless an enjoyable experience.

This is probably the last Legacy of Kain game that had open exploration, you start off without the means to get to certain areas, but once you have them, there are quite a few optional areas and collectables to pick up. If you're terrible at puzzles in general...you might want to bypass this one, if you want to do them as well as figure out where to go, where to jump and navigate a path through a dying landscape, then this is worth checking out.

=========
The Review:
=========
It's nowhere near done but it already scratches the MOO2 itch better than any other space 4X game to date, including the recent remake which was 'meh and didn't really feel like it was designed by somebody who really understood what made MOO2 the game we can't let go of but also the game that many of us would have liked to have seen improved on by a sequel or spiritual successor that didn't drift as far away from the good stuff as most did.
For the record, I am one of those nerds who has not stopped playing MOO2 since it came out with 2-3 binges a year in more recent years. I've also tried a lot of other 4x space games hoping they'd match up or provide an equally worthy but totally new experience. So far I've been most impressed with Sword of the Stars which I loved for a lot of reasons but found it lacking on the longevity factor.
So trust that when I say this is the MOO2 foundation with improvements you, or at least I always wanted that it is for realz.
===============
And now for the TMI
===============
Acronyms:
MOO/MOO2 - Master of Orion 1 & 2 - bothe excellent 4x (civilization-style) galactic expansion strategy games but with MOO2 widely regarded by many as the best ever
MOM - Master of Magic. Developed by the same company as the above way back in the day but more of a fantasy Civilization-ish game with a brilliant mechanic where you mixed the sort of wizard you were with your starting and ultimately conquered races and other advantages/disadvantages that all layered very nicely  to make for a ridiculously replayable game.
What the game borrows/retains from MOO2:
* Graphics: 2D sprites + some 3D here and there (mostly the planets). Speaking as a programmer and a former pro game reviewer, I love this. It keeps the team small, independent and free of publisher stupidity, which are all great things when they're clearly as well-dialed in on what made MOO2 great and also see all the neat stuff worth lifting from more recent space 4x games.
* Extermination/Combat: Pretty much the same deal  + new tech to play with and cool music, effects, and fun.
* Expansion/exploration: Same exact wide open exploration and colonization scheme with fuel limiting distance you can explore from your colonies but no starlanes, or any of that jazz. At least not yet. The dev/designer is inspired by SoTs apparently, which excites me and I can already see some of that influence.
* Exploitation/industry and economy on a planetary and galactic scale. But with many enhancements/improvements.
Improvements Over MOO2
* Colony improvement: Now you build generic structures (factories, economy, mining, industrial, research, agriculture) on improvement slots which very from planet to planet I believe on the basis of max pop. Smaller planets have as few as four. My largest planets so far seem to have 6-8ish. I assume you can improve this with tech. The six generic structure types can improve with tech but they auto-upgrade and always represent the same generic function. They also operate to varying degrees of efficiency depending on how much pop is freed up to operate them. There are no food guys, research guys, and labor guys to drag to differents specialties. Colonists in the current iteration of the game appear to do everything all at once, I assume, to varying degrees of efficency based on the race they represent with the structures adding a nice bonus - it's possible I'm not 100% correct about this.
* Resources and production are no longer a glued-together abstraction: Resources are something you have to build up through mining (if there's a name of the vanilla/generic resource, I don't recall atm) and currently matter a great deal to early-game fleet-building. With a ton of resources you can build large fleets fairly rapidly even at early tech levels in the current iteration of the game. The cool thing is that your largest colony can be lousy for farming and mining but still a great place to build a ton of factories to be the ultimate ship-builder that relies on sipping that other stuff in from smaller more specialized worlds. That also makes for a lot more strategy to consider in times of war. Do you go for the factory planets or that one awesome mining planet that appears to be providng the bulk of what they need to build those fleets in the first place?
* The freighter system: Now you can build freighters and also use troop transports to ship colonists or troops around manually or you can set them to trade, vanishing them from the map and making them more like MOO2's behind-the-scenes freighters which can be used to transport pop or handle food. However, unused trade freighters contribute to your economy through automatic trade so there's incentive to keep planets reasonably self-sufficient for things they're good at providing for themselves when they can. Being able to convert the troop transports to civilian needs is a nice touch making them feel like less of a waste of space when wartime is over and less of a liability when it makes sense to start building them when war is on the horizon.
* Racial balancing: Races have a lot more unique traits that would be hard to break out into a 100% customizable race scheme which I find agreeable. I'm only 10 hours in but every planet has multiple biome types and every race is optimal on those biomes to highly varying degrees, making it a huge advantage to diversify colonies when you get the opportunity to. Also, each race has its own unique tech options and ship hull types which I believe can be traded/stolen. It also just adds a crap-ton of new things to think about when faced with the prospect of going to war (so you can diversify your races for optimal colonies) or selecting one colony over another. I haven't seen this level of incentive to get one of everybody that synergizes well with your race since MOM.
* Art/Design: They weren't weak in MOO2 and I'm still torn on one of the font-choices but the music and the art direction overall are both surprising and very very cool/welcome. I can't believe this game is just two guys and as a programemmer ex-game-reviewer/avid strategy game player I could only dream of working with people this talented and with instincts this good.
Criticism?

Full review:
It is October 2016 as I write this review. For the record, this game came out in 2011  March 22nd. I've over 675hrs in game, much of that flying with a virtual Sqn.
I am writing this review now because I can but also to highlight that this title is still the 'go-to' title for WW2 Warbird flight sim enthusiasts.
In short, this ugly duckling has grown into a relatively elegant swan (I know, ducks and swans are two different biological lines .... but take that up with Hans Christian Andersen  ....)
The ugly duckling part:
This is well written and reviewed and I am not going to go over old cold coals other than to say that the then developer of IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover released a flight sim that was beautiful, full of promise and quite badly failed the performance test when released. It was full of ugly bugs, ran terribly and was soon consigned to the 'what a load of rubbish ... and it could have been so awesome' bin.
The grown into a relatively elegant swan part:
Enter the Team Fusion mod group. Mod groups do their thing and take released titles and polish them up. They often are responsible for taking titles what had been set to 'end of life support' status by the original developer and keep them supported. There are plenty of cases also of Mod group essentially taking over from defunct developers such as Falcon 4 by MicroProse and Richard Burns Rally by Warthog Games. Both these developers are no more yet their titles live on being developed even to this day.
Team Fusion are the effective custodians of  IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover's continued development. The developer, C1 Company, to be fair, did make a final last ditch effort to iron out the show-stopper bugs before they abandoned the project. They succeeded in that effort and thereby can be credited with a base game that is today ... playable.
However, the salute goes to Team Fusion, for taking this almost but not quite product and dragging it kicking and screaming through 4 patches of development into what I will describe as the shining star of multiplayer WW2 warbird flight simulators today.
The name "IL-2 Sturmovik" can be found today in other titles. Sadly, these title do not, in my opinion, represent positive forward evolution of the genre.  IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover with Team Fusion still reigns supreme if a truly immersive flight simming multiplayer experience is what you are looking to achieve.
There are a number of servers still running with two servers standing out. ATAG, basically a dog-fighter server, known for it's association with Team Fusion, (Team Fusion needed a virtual home and ATAG server, an independent entity provided that ) is a server that new folks and returned players regularly go to for fast turn PvP experiences.
ACG is a long time realism server group which are regular stopping in places for the more experienced CLoD flight simmer. With missions and campaigns from time to time and large multiplayer sessions, ACG youtube videos are famous and beautiful.
The last server of note is Storm of War.  SoW replays the BoB campaign. Every reply is unique in many respects. Presently in SoW Season 4, it is the goto server for the more experienced sim pilot which is seeking a multiplayer campaign experience. This is particularly true if you have a group of friends you like to fly with. SoW has developed it's own statistical system which provides Sqn level statistics as well as individual sortie reports even and  accommodates groups of players with their own dedicated operating bases, custom airfield configurations, managed airframe stocks, real life TOPHAT in fighter command... the list goes one.
So 5 years ago, no one could have imaged that in 2016, IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover would still represent the top of the pile of WW2 Warbird flight sim experiences.
Newer titles, some even with "IL-2 Sturmovik" in their names (e.g. BoS & BoM) fail to match what IL-2 Sturmovik: Cliffs of Dover brings to the table today. In terms of multiplayer, BoS / Bom are not yet as successful.
If asked, my recommendation could not be easier or clearer.
Forget any reservations about CLoD being 5 years old title ... it really isn't that old due to Team Fusion patch updates.
Enjoy the fact that you will save money and have a superior product (assuming you install the team fusion patches!)

OK. You bought the game and followed the updates. Now get the Team Fusion Mod and patch it with that. I have Win10 64Bit, and it works fine.
Ok having said that. It's not an easy game, it's very hard.  Once you learn to start the various aircraft, and get them in the air, then you have to learn sharply about what your aircraft will and won't do. They spin if you look at them the wrong way. They get shot down. They fall in holes at the aerodrome and crack up. Then you want to take off. It's pure fluke if at first you manage it...practice makes perfect. Oh, and then there's landing the crates. That is a real task....that takes time and practice to learn and get down. The English and French countryside is gorgeous. The aircraft are a treat, so realistic. For a sim you pay less than $50 for it's remarkable how good it is. Of course you can wait and get it when it's on special. You get to fly Spitfires. Did I mention that the game has Spitfires? Oh yes, it has Spitfires. There are several flyable craft, from fighters on both sides to bombers. And then there's the player communities. Great bunch. You can interact with them by in-game chat or voiced with Teamspeak. There are websites you can visit. There are squadrons you can join, or jastas if you want to play for the German side.
So all in all, while the learning curve is damn steep. Kinda like a church spire steep, it's worth it.

Now I'm sure there are many reviews that will tell you the history and poor release of IL-2 CloD, but I'm going to keep it brief.
IL-2 CloD has possibly the best community of any game I have ever played; helpful, understanding and serious.
To access this however you must install Team Fusion. To play this game without Team Fusion is simply not worth it, just go and play IL-2 1946, you'll have a better time. In any case, you decide to buy or not.

Graphics: Look a bit dated (the game first game out in 1999), but I think they add to the charm of the game
Soundtrack: Amazing, So good in fact I will by the soundtrack (also on steam) when I get some cash to spare
Gameplay: Great with some interesting elements which I will explain
-The game has two layers the main(upper) layer which you are on, and a lower level.  There are enemies on
both layers, but the ones on the lower layer can only be killed with a certain attack, you also can't crash into to enemies     on the lower layer.
-You have three attacks, you primary attack is a basic machine gun attack that can be up-graded with power ups.  Your other two attacks are special lighting attacks.  The 1st of these attacks is a multi-enemy lock-on attack, this is also the only attack that can hit enemies on the lower layer.  The 2nd lighting attack is a powerful beam attack, this attack can also block enemy projectiles, making this attack you you most powerful offensive and defensive tool.

Kamui is a vertical shooter that was made by Siter Skain in 1999 for Windows.
Well, I actually didn't know any of that until I got this game a few days ago. I had never heard of Kamui before, being a fan of shmups that is rather out of the loop on the world's favorite shooters.
The ship that the player pilots from start to finish in this game is, if I'm correct, a Kamui fighter: a powerful machine controlled by the daughter of the game's antagonist. The story of Kamui remains very simple throughout, with the game's beginning scene and ending credits being the only points of plot. I don't believe story is usually focused on much when it comes to shooters, but I do wish the plot was at least a bit more fleshed out.
Coming from 1999, Kamui's graphics are predictably not at all impressive by today's standards. The game shows its age in this aspect with its pixelated designs - it gives it somewhat of an arcade feeling (though I think its only current platform is Windows). None of this bothers me much, as the dated graphics work well as far as the gameplay goes. One of the most frustrating issues I tend to have with shooters is trying to distinguish just exactly what is going on at all times amidst the chaos. Nothing is worse than dying to one tiny bullet just because you couldn't see it very well, and were in the middle of focusing on something else. During my time with Kamui so far, I have never encountered this. I have been hit by small individual bullets; but they were bright yellow, and running into them was my fault. Overall, Kamui's colors are distinguishable and bright enough that it is easy enough to tell what is happening most of the time without them being distracting and looking out of place.
As far as sound goes, I really like Kamui's soundtrack. It is hard to focus on it while actually playing, but watching videos of this game gives a great opportunity to hear its music. It doesn't stand up to Ikaruga and Mushihimesama, in my opinion, but the tracks seem fitting and immersive with the game's action.
The best part of Kamui is, as with all great shmups, the gameplay. Along with movement and pausing, Kamui only makes use of two other buttons in its control scheme, keeping it simple but effective with the game's mechanics. One button is used to fire the main shot and the other is used to release lightning. Kamui uses, throughout the game, a two-plane system: enemies and objects are in either the foreground or the background, and may change planes. The only way to hit enemies in the background is to use the lightning system. A meter at the corner of the screen shows how much charge the lightning has, which will slowly fill on its own or will increase greatly in speed if the player holds down the lightning button. When a bolt destroys an enemy in the background, you will receive a score multiplier of up to x16 based on how full the meter was upon use. The amount of lightning to actually be released is based on a charge orb shown in front of the Kamui ship, which will grow when the lightning is not being used. The third weapon of the Kamui is used if both buttons are held at the same time, which results in a very powerful laser that will destroy most bullets it comes into contact with. This does effect the lightning meter, however: the blue meter will be pushed back until the laser's red meter depletes, limiting the score multiplier of the lightning. Correctly using these weapons is essential to surviving and scoring. Destroying enemy bullets with the laser will hurt your score if used too copiously, forcing you to think and time uses of each power.
If there's one thing that I really love about Kamui, it is its difficulty. Kamui is both forgiving and unforgiving, which is something that I usually cannot say about other shmups. There are three difficulties: easy, normal, and hard, each of which starts you with two lives and four bars of shield. Taking a hit will result in losing a piece of the shield, and will destroy the ship if it has no shield left. Taking a hit will also reduce a level of the ship's main shot, which is powered up by green drops from particular enemies throughout the stages, some of which also drop a blue power up that will give you an additional bar of shield.
The main part of Kamui that surprised me though: unlimited continues. This is one aspect of this game that makes it extremely enjoyable - I was actually able to play through the entire game on my first try. Of course, getting a game over will reset your score to zero, and very quickly my goal in the game became trying to score as high as I could. A very important part of scoring that I have yet to focus on is (I think it’s called) deathlocking. Certain enemies that you’ve killed in the foreground will have a few frames before they explode in which you can finish them off with lightning, allowing one to get a massively high score if used right.
With 3 hours put into the game as I write currently, the improvement I’ve experienced has been very satisfying. I still haven’t completed the game without a continue (on easy, too), but I’ve gone down from 6 continues to 1 since my first play, and my highest score has grown from around 2.6 million to almost 11 million. To see such a jump is rewarding and motivational to keep playing the game and improving. I haven’t had it for long, but I would definitely recommend Kamui to anyone that likes shmups, casual or not.

This is a game I only played recently even though it is an original Xbox game. I was not disappointed though as it holds up surprisingly well.
The graphics are quite good, and the sound design is impeccable and very true to the franchise. I found in some "makings of" the game they even used foley artists which I thought was fun. Each teammate is supposed to be specialised, but they can do anything. The squad mechanics, however, are well developed enough that you still feel as though you are controlling a special team and not just four clones. It helps that each character has a unique personality that works pretty seamlessly into the gameplay as there is no real cutscenes either.
The game/gunplay is good as well although I found some weapons weren't very satisfying like the stock blaster rifle. Some weapons felt like you were shooting a bb gun. There was no real impact, enemies would often just not even react. All the weapons, however, were quite distinct from one another which added some good variety. Enemies had fairly decent variety, but nothing crazy with only a dozen or so different enemies.
The levels are very linear, but they often open up a little to provide some nice variety in your appraoch to the situation. Whether you want to set up a couple sniper posts and jump on a turret; lob some grenades; enter a room by hacking in silently or breach it with some blast charges.
It's a real shame that this game never got a sequel as there is a lot more potential here to an already stellar game. It definitely gets my thumbs up.

Cally's caves 3 is a mixture of platforming game and shoot-em-up adventure game. You control Cally across different stages and levels to reach the final boss to rescue your parents. The game is decent overall, but there are some improvements that can be had.
Storyline - it's a pretty short storyline so don't expect any story rich scenes. Imagine Mario where you are constantly travelling across different stages/levels to reach the end.
Weaponry gameplay - there are a wide variety of weapons to play with and they do upgrade themselves as you continue to use them to level up. While this is nice in that it keeps the player entertained, I find this large weaponry a hassle as I don't end up using each of them equally. Some weapons are more useful than others and I think others are just plain useless in a lot of the cases when you are trying to shoot at an enemy. In addition, having to cycle through all the weapons consistently was a nuisance. I wish you can deselect which weapons you don't want to use or have an easier system of accessing the weapon you want to use at a specific time. Next, the amount of money needed to purchase weapon upgrade is ridiculously high. Even with multipliers, I don't see myself wanting to keep playing the game to complete the collection.
Gameplay - the game is easy enough and forgiving considering how many checkpoints you have. It is even more forgiving considering the HP regen and consumables you can buy overtime as well as the lamp to restart at a specific stage of the level if you die before you reach the next checkpoint. Althought the price can be steep, once you get the multiplier stacked up, it becomes slightly easier to purchase the consumables. There are some areas during the gameplay where enemies or items will clip through walls or fall through the "cracks". That or you are stuck being walls and are forced to restart from the last check point as you can't get out. Sometimes, it's annoying since it can be a heart that you need, consumable, or it's the boss fight and you have to restart it.
Overall, Cally's Caves 3 is an amusing game to play, but it's definitely a completionist's nightmare. The soundtrack is exceedingly repetitive and even with just 3 hrs in, I really don't want to hear anymore of it right now. I've collected all the regular weapons and I don't even envision myself wanting to max-level and get the final weaponry via the collectibles (which is an ordeal all by itself). In addition, I rather not encounter more buggy gameplay throughout the game, which seems to be more frequent in the new game+ and Melvin's Zone. Luckily, getting it on sale for $2.99 doesn't make me too bummed out with the game, but I don't think the replay value is that high for a game like this. 6.5/10.

When Cliffs of Dover was released, it was frankly a mess, the publishers made efforts to improve it, but then lost confidence, leaving the game pretty much a half finished affair.
Since then Team Fusion have taken up the reins and set to work improving the game, to say they succeded is an understatement, improvements in all areas has led to a game that is nothing short of the pinnacle of WW2 flight gaming, and this from a volunteer enthusiast group of programmers!
So have they rested on thier laurels, hell no, Tf5 is in the wings being readied for release, with new planes, a new map and a huge number of yet more improvements, add in a great community and you have a game for real flight sim enthusiasts.
Would I reccomend this game? as it comes from the publishers no, but download the TF patches and it's a whole different ballgame, I spent years on the old IL2 1946 and was dissapointed when I changed to the original Cliffs, but since following the majority and joining the Team Fusion game it's left the old 1946 in the dust, is it perfect, no, but it's improving alll the time and I could not go back to 1946 now, nor have I been able to migrate to other sims, I tried  then came back to Cliffs of Dover!

In a media environment oversaturated by "hit in the feels" games like Undertale, I'm suprised fans haven't gotten onto this game's bandwagon.
This game is, at its core, one of the ultimate "don't judge a book by its' cover" games. I bought the game thinking it would be about an evil creepy clown that does crazy stuff... I couldn't be more wrong.
Dropsy is a charmingly short and simple point and click game that follows Dropsy, the scary looking clown with a warm heart and even warmer hug for those in need. The game itself hardly has any text or speech, leaving the actions and animations as the only thing to progress the story. This game pulls off this method of storytelling quite well, so well that I would call it a staple to the genre on which other sorts of "hit in the feels" games should be measured.
Only downside for me was the fact that it was a point and click adventure, and sometimes the plot moved around alittle too slowly for my liking.
However, for the price, I would strongly encourage anyone even slightly curious about the game to give it a try and experince the quaint, charming experience that Dropsy offers!  *Gives Hugs*

Nice, decent game. Anyhow it's design seems to be out of the 90's...rumors tell the devs are doing it from that time till now. Well, it is not an overall good game...but also not a bad one. Percieved I'd rate it in the same division as MoO2 or GalCiv2, while other games have allready moved on from that design style.
Highlights are the tun-based fights and the ship designs, which are quite interesting.
At current stage (EA) I'd say the balance isn't the best. Research is really really fast and you could re-design your ships nearly every other turn, while it's not that easy. Let's say you build a starbase, then you research the next bigger model...well then you have to scrap your old one to get a free slot for the bigger one. It's ok for EA, but I would really like to see such problems be gone, once the game is finished. Plus, I like to see some inventions and new ideas to contrast with other 4X games a bit more.
I would not rate it negative, but honestly I'd rate it counterbalanced. But, as I didn't find any mayor problems and the devs do a good job to upgrade any now and then, the final rating is positive for now.

Fidel is a game in the style of The Witness and Stephen's Sausage Roll, where the game has a certain set of mechanics, and the consequences of those mechanics are explored. Sometimes this results in great comedic effect -- particularly with the Alien boss.
Gameplay is super fun and not stressful. Each run lasts about 5-10 minutes, so dying isn't aggravating, since it's usually pretty quick to get back to where you were last run. All of the rooms feel very fair, and it's possible to progress through them without a perfect route.
The art and the sound effects are excellent, and really contribute to the feeling of joyful exploration.
There's also a good amount of replay value, since the game has plenty of optional challenges that stack on the difficulty. I found the default mode pretty easy, but the challenges get pretty tough.
I recommend this game. It's a lot of fun.

This game is cool, as are all Alltynex games. Pretty difficult - but it's fun to play even if you fly the first level 20-100 times. Never gets old - and is fun to play even when you lose.
Graphics/Technical:
Graphics are... well they are good in the way they are done - but comparing to todays standards sub-par. The fact that it only supports a 800x600 resolution which is then stretched (to fit your vertical resolution) does not help much. Also the game only takes up 1/10th of your screen, when you are playing on a 16:9 monitor because the aspect ratio is locked in 4:3 and even then puts borders inside the 4:3 screenspace! There is an option to flip the display by 90° which lets you play sideways - yet sadly this does not enlarge anything. In fact it does nothing but confuse the crap out of you if you ever played the game normally. What a shame, because the game uses like something close to 16:9 flipped by 90 degrees. But these are technical problems due to the fact that the engine is badly optimized for today's standards. Essentially the graphics are great if you take it down to 16bit-era or more likely 32-bit era standards. They are "Aesthetic" and the explosions do satisfy (because this word has been getting the hype recently - like gamers never knew what looks good or something...!..!).
Sound:
The music is, well... just as the graphics, oldschool. It's something better than MIDI but not quite much more. The soundtrack is great though. Fast paced music that makes you want to dodge those bullets and shoot everything down. The music is an essential part of the game, like in "Wipeout", "Olliolli" or "Need for Speed: The force unleashed", which - to me - is proof of good sounddesign in the music department. Without the music, the game would be like 33% less fun. Yea, i can do maths with fun. The sound design itself is fairly decent as well, gunshots and explosions - there isn't much to differ anyways - it gets the job done.  It's even in stereo! Idk if the stereo applies if you flip the game by 90° though, maybe your speakers start flipping as well. If you dislike the music, for whatever reason, put some Yngwie Malmsteen on. He is just about as much over-the-top as this game is to fit in there nicely.
Gameplay:
Well, why put up with all this oldschool ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t? I mean i play this game not to be cool or retro or oldschool or anything. But yea it makes me feel cool. Like a real badass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's hard, yea. It's bullethell - or whatever they declared it to attract those niche shoot 'em up pros incarcerated in the nineties trying to blast their way out. But there's like nothing better than a good SHMUP! Like seriously. It's like therapy. It's just you, nearly infinite enemies and bullets to dodge, and your trusty little ship with the ability to shoot infinite bullets - fly the ♥♥♥♥ all over the place and shoot rockets and freaking laserbeams across the whole screen (which is like only 1/10th of your screen, mind), all without having to collect powerups in this one! But yea, there are powerups to broaden the firing arc of your main gun. Also i think there are unlimited continues - as i managed to "die" myself thru in the first playthrough (and i'm not a real hero, more like a shmup up). Which took like only 30-90 minutes, i can't tell, it was freaking short. But that's not what it is about, it is about perfecting the levels and memorizing every last freaking bullet. There's only 5 or 6 levels i think, but beating the game using continues is like running across the field from left to right in FIFA Soccer 199X - that's not the point. Well yea it is the point - but it's the point to do it flawlessly. So if you're a perfectionist, but not a "collector" and not an "explorer" or a "grinder" - but a real man that loves to master skills and kick asses with the crap he's got - then this game is for you. Controller support is good enough (xbox360 wireless). I love every pixel of this game!
Story:
Mind stories in arcade-video games?! If you are expecting anything here, forget it. The world design in itself is coherent. The visuals make sense in the scenario imposed. It is all "canon" for whatever that may account. But the story is like only a skeleton. It's just "oooh terrible♥♥♥♥♥♥has occured, kill everyone and fix it." - that's fine by me! If i want story, i read a book, play baldurs gate or listen grandpa.
Conclusion:
My playtime is low (somedude in the back: "excuses!" and leaves) - that is due to the fact that i got "the tale of alltynex" compilation and play the titles in rotation. All in all the games are similar in gameplay quality, though different enough to switch over to when one of the titles has siphoned your concentration and endurance. Luckily in graphics quality the titles have improved over the years - Alltynex Second is actually in 2.5D and technically quite sophisticated compared to this one. I suggest getting the whole package, i'm sure you can spend well over 20hrs with them altogether - and that is the case even if you give up before you actually turn into anything near-pro. Well i know i will be spending 20hrs with the titles for sure - and i tend to get bored of stuff very quickly. Also the games, in core, never feel old. SHMUPS never die!
The technical problems mentioned subtract nothing from the masochistic pleasure this title provides. Clear recommendation for anybody on the look for true gaming. You know... like people who are sick of Third-Person-Stealth-Action-Roguelike-Sandbox-RPGs with climbing elements.

KAMUI is a pretty fun top down, even more so for its low price and inclusion in the Humble Bundle. It has very fun mechanics that allow you to fire into the fore and background, hitting enemies before they can get on your level and cause you a more direct threat. This also goes for boss battles, where bosses will have entire stages in the back or foreground requiring you to use your lightning weapon to hit them. Its a solid game, but lacks a focus mode that I feel would greatly benefit it, similar to Touhou. I often times found myself getting lost in the quickly moving backgrounds, as they caught my eye more than my own ship. Another negative, is that the game itself is only about 30 minutes long, max. Despite having some negatives, it is overall a very solid and fun game.

A top-down shmup eerily reminiscent of Raystorm. I wouldn't really call it a Bullet Hell; the bullet count and speed are far more tilted towards the likes of Gradius than Mushihimesama or DoDonPachi, but nevermind that. This is a fast-paced shmup in which you have three weapons: the normal machinegun, which is rather underpowered; a screen-clearing shower of targeted lightning that only hits enemies on the plane below you; and shooting both at once releases a huge forward laser that clears bullets, deals ginormous damage and will be your best bet to survive the fiercer bullet spams. Both lightning attacks deplete a 'Lightning' gauge, but the lightning shower can be spammed even if your gauge is empty (though you'll get far less points per enemy destroyed).
Kamui is moderately hard, though you shouldn't feel discouraged, as the game offers infinite credits (though a 1 credit clear challenge is there if you feel like it, and it's bloody hard). Clocking in at about 30 minutes per run, I'd say the $8 price tag is slightly salty, though the game is VERY replayable and definitely very good. If you can get it on a sale (or a Humble Bundle, as has happened in the past), it's a no-brainer.

As a bullet hell fan, I can very safely say that this game has gotten very close to the top of my favorite bullet hell games. The combination of the lightning and the bullets to make a multi-dimentional game forces you to focus on two different fronts which ultimately makes it VERY complex, yet simple at the same time.
And for those of you who fear that it will be too difficult, the easy setting is quite generous to newcomers of the series.

I recommend the game, but if you havent played yet Reflex or Altynex Second, I think you must play them before. Kamui is weaker than the other two. Particularly Reflex is a great game once you give it several tries.

Kamui is the first title released in the "Tales of Alltynex" trilogy, a trio of 2d shoot em ups focusing on cinematic presentation, offbeat gameplay mechanics, and a strange and melancholy storyline about planetary warfare and rogue super computers.
In Kamui, players have access to a standard machine gun for destroying hordes of small enemies, a homing attack which only hits distant enemies attacking from the background, and a powerful beam weapon that focuses damage on a single target and nullifies enemy fire. The last two weapons are dependent on a recharging energy meter that must be carefully managed, because running out of energy can result in being overwhelmed. Destroying enemies with a charged homing attack also awards greater points, but requires players to leave dangerous enemies alive for longer and find perfect timings to blast them all, forcing mastery of the mechanics to achieve high scores.
I find these mechanics give Kamui a sense of chaos. Not only do players need to dodge and shoot the usual enemy formations and attack patterns found in shoot em ups, but they also need to be careful of enemies in the background and simoultaneously juggle three weapons with precise use. Beyond the mechanics, the game's actual execution of stage and boss design is refreshingly unique. Kamui has a slightly larger hitbox than most bullet hell shooters and an emphasis on agressive enemies and bosses with quirky attacks that go beyond the usual bullet ballets of the genre. The chaos and agression combine to give Kamui a very visceral feel.
There are drawbacks to Kamui's design choices, though. At times, the bullet cancelling beam dominates the game a bit too much, turning evasion into a matter of simple timing and placement instead of complex manuevering, reflex, or strategy. Playing for score alleviates this somewhat, forcing you to hold off on cancelling some attacks, but I still wish pure survival play wasn't as simplistic. I also don't like the vast amount of health players are given. The difficulty is balanced around it, but the sheer amount of life points the player has means that no matter how bad you do on any one stage, you're pretty much guaranteed not to die till at least the next stage, removing some of the tension from the game's first half.
However, when its playstyle clicks in the end game, Kamui truly shines. The last three stages offer one of the most intense and memorable climaxes in the genre, and the intensely visceral action throughout generally make up for some minor issues. For those looking for something a little different, Kamui is an excellent change of pace from shooting game norms.
The single BEST doujin shooter EVER. Nuff' said.
A very impressive Taito-inspired doujin shmup with a lot of Rayforce cues. Spectacular presentation (within its idiom). Steer clear if you hate bendy lasers though.

Even little details like how the stages connect together are clever in design; there’s no obligatory rolling out of background tropes like the jungle level or the factory level just so boxes can be checked. KAMUI is a seamless journey stitching each of the six stages to each other, offering a rare glimpse of chartable progress from cloud-covered sky, through depths of earth into the outer reaches of the planet to take on an orbiting weapons platform. It’s a real labour of love that not only does credit to its esteemed source material but manages to out-perform it. It’s more forgiving, more fluid, more concise.

x = accelerate
arrow left  = turn left
arrow right = turn right
z =enable bonus
Not much to it.

I did not expect to like a game in this format - it's not normally something I would have chosen if I came across it on casual browsing, but I love werewolves and a friend said 'this is technically a werewolf' so I thought okay why not. I'm so, so happy I tried it.
I haven't read the comics this is based on, but personally I don't think I need to anyway. This stands by itself as a fun and quirky story. And now feels like as good a time as any to review this first part, since we are FINALLY GETTING A SEASON 2!
PROS:
1. The art design. It's beautiful! It's one of those games that looks just as good in-game as it does in animated gifs on tumblr. The comic-strip style art really gives it atmosphere, especially since it's a story primarily about fairy tale characters/creatures.
2. It has great characters with voice acting. Whether you like or dislike someone, they still have merit as a character. I found Snow White pretty sanctimonious and annoying, and I was frustrated with Beauty and the Beast. But looking at it objectively, I wasn't playing an angel either. In my usual pattern, I was a giant jerk for my first playthrough. Hey now...if you're gonna play the Big Bad Wolf, why not do it with your whole heart? I chose every rude, violent and all around antisocial option available and it was the most fun I'd had in a long time.
The voice acting was great. You might even recognise some of the voices from other popular games like Skyrim. This is my first time really noticing Adam Harrington, though, and his voice is a real treat. He's an amazing choice for Bigby.
3. I like the effects of your choices, although I feel it could have been a little more fleshed out. I was still able to achieve a decent ending even though I'd been a complete monster to everyone and their mother the whole time. I felt like I should have been punished a little more for my actions, with a slightly differing ending sequence depending on just how much of a POS you were. But what the game does have is still interesting, and it makes it worth replaying again to see how doing the opposite of your previous actions will affect the story. Who knows - this time around, you just might save someone.
4. The werewolf overtones were hammed up here and I loved the hell out of it. I know, Bigby's technically not a werewolf, but it plays that way at certain points and it made my werewolf nerd-self dissolve into violent happiness. Violent as in, I always chose the violent options, and it took me a long time to realise that I hadn't unlocked certain achievements because doing so would require me to choose non-violent options for a change.  This kind of game brings out the worst in me, I guess.
5. The statistics that would show up at the end of finishing each chapter were hilarious. Let's just say that many others who played seem to be far better people than me. You go, guys!
CONS:
1. If you're looking for a game with some roleplay-esque elements, this probably isn't for you. You're playing a character from an already-established comic world and I'm guessing (haven't read them) that you're still operating within those storylines in this game. For example, Bigby's interest in Snow White is clearly expressed at multiple points. I myself did not like Snow White, but I was still hemmed in to certain dialogue options and results. No matter how hard I tried to make them fight until I had the option to tear her head off, it never happened. It's a shame, but then again this game isn't advertised as some blank slate roleplay, so it is what it is.
2. I felt like more consequences should have happened due to your actions in the game. The ending does change a little depending on your choices and your final 'battle', but all in all I felt I got off waaaaay too lightly for all the ripping and glassing and insulting I did. People I was truly terrible to seemed to miraculously forgive and forget at crucial moments and it disappointed me. I think that several different versions of the ending scenes should have been available to really highlight the 'karma' level of your Bigby by the time you hit the end credits.
This is possibly the shortest list of cons in one of my reviews so far. Roll on season 2!

Overall 10/10 for storytelling and immersion.

Soul Reaver was my- well most peoples introduction to the Legacy Of Kain series and holy hellblazes did it leave an impression on me. Not a bad port. Always loved this game, so I'm a bit biased. Take it from me, this series has one of the best stories in gaming period. Try it out if you like it I defy you not to play all of the others just to unravel the tale. Destiny, time travel, interdimensional conspiracies, vampires, and false gods this game is the best place to enter into the series. Between the voice acting and the writing this game is good enough, but Soul Reaver boasts the most enjoyable gameplay in the whole series.
The enemies and the environments work togather to create an interative playground for you to test out different and creative ways to clear out rooms. There are several ways to stun enemies from beating the hell out of them, to psychokenetic force balls to throwing rando crap at their faces. And once you've gotten them stunned they're your toys. You can grab them and throw them at hazars like spikes or flames, off cliffs or into the brimy deep. Impale them from afar or up close. It's just too much fun to experiment with.
The big plus that always had me entranced with this game is there is no death and no fail state. Your experience flows and remains fun regardless of how good or bad you are doing. While in the physical world if your health is brought down to zero, the world is transformed into the spectral realm. This changes the shape of the world and the enemies that spawn. Devour enough souls and you can return to the physical world die in the specral realm and you are transported back to the first room in the game. This would be frustrating if it werent for the fact that along your journey you discover way gates, and there is a gate right after the first room. So you rarely actually lose progress and through all of this there is nary a load screen.
All and all I've played the whole series and love each part for different reasons but this the the best in terms of the total package. If you haven't tried it yet start here.

So this is the very first time I've ever played through any Legacy of Kain game, and after beating down Soul Reaver, I am overwhelmingly impressed.  Soul Reaver is an action/adventure/puzzle solving game in where you (Raziel), are harnessing a deep hatred for your former leader and pseudo-father figure, Kain, that runs so deep that an elder god decides to  utilize you as his weapon of destruction against Kain and his forces, as they have left the entire world in shambles from centuries of war and butchery.  So let's get down to it!
Definitely one of the high points of this game (and there are many) is just the overall gameplay.  The controls might be a little loose, but the targeting and the executions are spot on.  And fun.  Like, suprisingly fun.  Nothing quite like taking a spear from a wall and impaling a demon/vampire creature straight through the abdomen, while absorbing it's soul afterwards for sustenance.  If this sounds like fun, definitely get this game because you will be doing this a lot.  Don't misunderstand though.  Incredibly, this game actually focuses more on puzzles rather than direct action.  Even boss fights are generally a small puzzle that needs to be solved, rather than directly assaulting the giant, horrific monstrosities (because let's face it, that immediately doesn't sound like a good idea as soon as you see any of the bosses).
Oh, and this game is not exactly easy.  Some of the platforming can be very difficult due to the loose controls, and the world does not exactly hold your hand.  It is very open-ended.  Very few hints are littered throughout the world to guide you on your way, but just enough is given to you if you really pay attention to what is being said.  In an age of games that practically play themselves, this particular type of difficulty in a game is a very welcome feeling.
The only slightly negative part of this game are the overwhelming amount of block puzzles.  Block puzzles.  Block puzzles.  BLOCK PUZZLES.  At any point in time through the game, it's a good bet that a block puzzle is within at least two rooms of where you are currently located.  They are interesting, but the developers really went all out with these puzzles.  None of them are too overwhelmingly difficult, but when they're in every room, it becomes mundane and repetitive.
Fantastic graphics for it's time.  Remember that this game did come out in 1999.  A mere three years after Super Mario 64.  There are a lot of clipping issues obviously for this particular period in time when this game was developed, but overall the game is pretty gorgeous.  Animations are very smooth, enemies are interesting, environments are gloomy and downright spooky, and bosses are horrendously disgusting looking.  Even for today's games, those bosses are the things of nightmares.
So the sound in this game is phenomenal, and probably the highlight of the entire game (at least it was for me).  Every movement makes a sound that is very adequate for what it is representing, but the sountrack that kicks in every once and a while is perfect for the theme of the game.  Dark, gothic, and eerie.  Partners perfect with what is happening on the screen at all times.  Especially the opening cutscene music, that also just happens to play near the end during a particularly important part of the game.  Oh, and the voice acting talent is, for lack of a better word, incredible.  Tony Jay is still severely missed.  The script is so well written that several games that are released these days, could learn a lot from sitting down and playing this game.
So the total game took me about 12 hours to beat, and that's exploring a good amount of the world.  Didn't go for 100%, but pretty close.  Beyond reliving the adventure again, there is not too much reason to revisit this game after beating it.
TL;DR - Great gameplay with a few flaws + decent graphics + fantastic audio + incredible story = 8/10

My hours for this game on Steam are slim...but the hours I put forward on my original playstation version are far greater.  I was gifted the Legacy of Kain collection for my birthday last year and I'm thankful for that because I enjoy having digital copies of old beloved games.
As a warning, I find this difficult to play with just a keyboard and mouse, although it is possible. I’m currently looking for another way around this, as my controller does not hook up well either.  That is my only complaint. Keep in mind, as well, that this game was released almost 20 years ago so it has clunky graphics and textures but this makes me love the game even more. Nostalgia.
Even with it’s old graphics, I find this game quite eerie and creepy, although it has no horror tag. The characters, the story, the vampires/creatures and the music, ambience has always given me chills.
I think what makes me recommend this game is the plot.  It’s hard not to love a game with deep and captivating storyline.  Kain raised Raziel (the protagonist, whom you play) and his brothers from death, turning them into undead vampires. Kain saw an unfortunate fate in store for him in the future, and had plunged Raziel into the Abyss to save himself.  The vampires depicted in this game are supposed to evolve over time, becoming stronger, while gaining new abilities. Unfortunately many vampires were left weak, with few valuable skills after Kain took over Nosgoth. The “Elder God” brought Raziel back to life but not in his original form nor his vampire form. Many centuries had passed and the God deemed Raziel as his  ‘soul reaver’, to hunt down Kain and seek revenge, to save what was left of Nosgoth, which Kain had left in ruins.
You are given an option to switch between the living world and the spirit realm.  Raziel doesn’t necessarily have or need a weapon either. You can pick weapons up when you find them but you can also use your claws and tactics such as tossing your enemies in an open flame, sunlight spots or into water.  There’s also some strategy involved - mostly block puzzles - and you can collect glyphs to gain new abilities.
TLDR; 7/10 overall... Rich storyline, confusing controls at first. Worth a try if you like classic oldies, or dark fantasy/gothic adventure games.

Simple Zelda-like game, although about as short as the price tag implies (2-3 hours of playtime even if you go for 100%, assuming no deaths).
+ The dungeons are good and atmospheric. They're complex and involve puzzles, but not unreasonably so.
+ The boss fights manage to be unique and engaging even though you're mostly just fighting them like you would normal enemies. However, some of them are awfully short.
+ Gorgeous pixel art. The game never stops looking good.
- The item selection you're given throughout the game feels uninspired. The crossbow sees very little use outside of combat (and it tends to be impratical
combat, too), and the pick becomes worthless the instant you're done with the mine dungeon. There could've been done a lot more with riddles involving clever use of your items.
- The overworld is maze-like, empty and boring. There are no enemies to fight, no secrets to discover, and on your search for the various dungeon entrances you'll often have to backtrack a couple of screens because you'll run into arbitrary dead ends with nothing in them.
- Combat has hitbox issues and as a result feels very rough and somewhat un-fun. The game often registers a hit on you when the enemy/projectile didn't even visually touch you, and some enemies (the small slimes are the most obvious offenders) will sometimes
register as hit even if your sword clearly went through them.
- There are several points in the game where you're forced to take damage to progress, something I've never been a fan of.
Overall, I did have my fun with this game, but... So much more could've been done with it. I'm a little disappointed.
Is it worth getting? At this price, yes, if you like the genre. Just don't expect too much.

Crunchiness rating: 6/10
Crunchy things:
- Turned based everything
- Combat is grid based allowing for easier executed ship tactics
- Variety of weapons/systems allowing for different strategies
- Changing of ship loadouts
- Renaming planets (some space 4x don't allow this much to my chagrin)
- Variety of racial populaces on planets, each with their own morale.
-- An example I bombed a slaver planet and killed some slaves of a certain race, citizens of that same race took a morale hit on all of my planets.
Not so crunchy things:
- Diplomacy is shallow at the moment.
- Some tech in in the game but not implemented code wise (I want my super-dreads)
- Ground combat is very shallow.
- No modding support. (This could lead to EPIC mods)
- No custom races.
- No faction color choosing.
- Computer combat ai consists only of charge forward and shoot, with a chance of trying to board your ship. Maybe this changes at higher difficulty levels?
-- This leads to not needing advanced tactics for the most part except when dealing with very deadly enemies.
- Computer strategic ai is not too smart either (again this may not be the case at higher difficulty levels)
-- Example: I had a massive fleet and conquered most of the galaxy. There was one race that had been my ally from the start that I isolated in one star in the corner through my expansionist tactics. I made a huge fleet to go against one of the slaver planets. Apparently having slaves really paid off because their one ship mauled my fleet, leaving me mostly defenseless. The only race that thought to take advantage of the situation (there were two much larger ones on my "northern" border) was my erstwhile ally with his one star and puny military. That race declares war, but doesn't move any fleets, 1 turn of instabuilding some massive battleships thanks to me hoarding money through trade, and I conquer his star within 10 turns (most of which was ship travel time). Not. Real. Smart.
- Humans do not have a hard start contrary to their description.
Given this I still recommend this game. It reminds me of the old Master of Orion II game I played as a kid.
This game has immense potential and from what I see, I know they will get there. Most of the non-crunchy bits I mentioned will be addressed by the end of development, I am sure. Support the dev so they can get there!
I will update this review if I hear/see more.

Subject to editing as we go along:
With the 20% discount I can be real sport about buying an Early Access game.  As with many EA games these are really beta versions working out the final kinks and adding the polish to allow this rough cut diamond to shine among its peers in the 4x space genres of games. For those who play games such as MoO (Masters of Orion 1/2/3/new) or the GalCiv (1/2/3) there won't be a steep learning curve here.  Despite at this time a lack of tutorial, the interface while not being super intuitive, does the job and with a bit of experimentation you can find what you need quickly.
The artwork, is a treat, a real homage to early space games with it cartoonish feel. That does not detract from the game one bit.  The game in my opinion is a lighter 4x affair with a limited building options for planets, there is really only a few resources you need to manage, like Food, Money, Minerals and Research.  Want more money build transports, and send them out to trade, trade is very abstract, you don't have to pick a destination just works.  Minerals, mine them off our planet by building mines. Want more food build a farm. Want to increase levels find a technology and research it.
The tactical space battles are enjoyable and better than MoO or GalCiv3 where you just watch and hope that you are bigger, better, and faster than the next guy.  Here in SiS  you have a chance if you play your tactics right.  Ship design is easy you pick a shape, drag the components, rename and save.  More technology, gives you new choices and technologies you can add.
At this time aside from a crash or two, it does give you the "Just One More Turn" feel we all love.  The developers are active on the forums and respond to many posts, for the crashes and suggestions.  While not everything may not get into the initial full release, it should offer some great time wasting play value.
Right now I will give the game 8/10 for EA to entice those on the fence to buy the game and post the issues and suggestions that could make for a fantastic game.
I mean obviously this isn't a finished product (some descriptions appear to be missing and what not) but I am really enjoying it so far. If you're into 4X games? I'd suggest this.

I expect it's only going to get better, and is well worth $20.

Dropsy is a beautiful game. It borrows the best traits from old school point and clicks and melds them into an emotionly heavy story you'd expect from a new tell-tale style adventure. They put so much love into this one, it's one of the best i've played in a long time.

Dropsy gets my nomination for the "Villain Most in Need of a Warm, Damp Hug" award. Having grown up in the golden age of Lucasarts and Sierra adventure games, Dropsy appeared tailor made for my sense of nostalgia. Happily, its appeal goes beyond its gorgeous pixel art backgrounds and animations; it's a brisk, rewarding, charming, and surprisingly moving work of art. Its characters communicate clearly through actions and emoticons, and only on the rare occasion did I feel that the lack of written or spoken dialog made it difficult to infer a goal. I never had to resort to a walkthrough to finish this game, which puts it head and shoulders above the majority of adventure games I've played. I did find myself reaching the point of having to try every possible combination of actions towards the latter half. Despite a quibble or two, it's highly recommended and an absolute must-play for fans of the genre.

Great game, one of the best SHMUPS I've ever played. If you're familiar with Layer Section/Gunlock/Raystorm, then you'll have some sort of idea of what to expect with Kamui.
As with Layer Section, the gameplay is split into two layers, the plane you're on, and everything beneath you. On your plane, you can shoot a machinegun-like weapon and a  powerful laser that uses energy, but also destroys enemy bullets. On the layers beneath you, you can attack enemies with a lock-on lightning weapon - this can be used to destroy or damage enemies before they become a threat, or attack enemies shooting you from below.
The more you use the bullet-soaking beam, however, the less energy you have for the lightning attack, so it's a double-edged sword. This makes the gameplay significantly about energy management in the short term (as you do recharge quite quickly). The scoring system ties in to this, as kills with the lighting attack recieve a multiplier.
Gameplay aside, it's a nifty little game with an amazing soundtrack - and while the graphics are a bit dated, they're well made; there are really neat parallax and explosion effects to see.
If you like shmups, check out Kamui. It's a good'n.

According to Steam, I played this for twenty-one hours. I could say that isn't really the case. A lot of that time was spent trying to get it to work. The game would work perfectly one day, then would just stop working on another. There are even times where it crashes taking a few steps after the game lets you play. Not to mention the amount of times I had to reinstall this game.
Although I'm totally fine with the game only being 30FPS, I tried SRHook to play it at 60. Doing so will make the game skip all the cinematics. I asked on the Game's Discussion page if there was a way to still get the cinematics to play while using SRhook, and was told that there isn't anything that can be done. So, I just decided to remove SRHook when I got to parts that had cinematic cutscenes.
I used a Dualshock 4 and Inputmapper to map the controller buttons to be keyboard inputs since just using an xinput controller won't make it work properly.
It's really a shame that this game suffers from these problems as it's still pretty solid during the times when it actually worked. It felt like it did when I first played it on the Playstation, I never finished it then, which is why I got it here on Steam. Besides the problems stated above, I didn't encounter any game breaking bugs or glitches. Just make sure that when using SRHook, cap the framerate at 60 as it'll mess the game up a bit when played higher than that, specifically with some puzzles that need the constrict ability. But that's not the game's fault. The gameplay still holds up, each boss isn't just a straight up fight, and are themselves puzzles (except for two). The story is a big part of the whole Legacy of Kain saga, and is still in my opinion one of the best in gaming to this day.
If you can put up with the crashing, and are lucky enough to not have the game stop working at all, it'll be a good experience. If you have very little patience with these things, you may want to pass on this version and play it on the PS3 or if you still have your PS1.

Sequels to games I really like usually struggle in my eyes: I like small, enclosed games that have endings and don’t try and explain away the small mysteries that make the worlds seem much larger than they are. Portal is a perfect game ruined only by the existence of Portal 2, for example. Emily is Away, the AIM simulator spanning five years of a young person’s life as the chat with the titular Emily, absorbed me for two hours as I worked my way through its five chapters to get every ending. Now, with its sequel Emily is Away Too, I find that I don’t want to play any more.
The sequel takes the gameplay of the original and applies it to a new story with new characters. The five chapters are back, but this time everything takes place over senior year of high school. This condensed story works a lot better, since I always found it a little strange that the two characters from the previous game only seemed to talk once a year despite being best friends. Also changed from the first game is the addition of a third character, Evelyn, and some of the story choices revolve entirely around picking who to talk to.
Some of the old tricks from Emily is Away are joked about in Too, my personal favourite being something we’ve all done: writing out a message, and then deleting it and replacing it with something completely different. In the first game - and this is a pretty heavy spoiler for a free game you should definitely already have played - you lose all freedom of choice and no matter what you choose, you’ll type some of it out, then delete it and write the same answer. In the sequel, one of the two girls will pick you up on that in a lovely throwback to what was legitimately one of the most heartbreaking scenes I’ve played.
