Soul Reaver was a timeless classic. Rich voice acting and a dark enthralling story makes the journey a compelling experience. You play as Raziel, a reborn, immortal, vampire on a quest for vengence against your vampire brothers who betrayed you at the command of your former master, Kain. Slay your enemies, solve puzzles, and slip in and out of the spirit world as soul reaving wraith.
Sounds really cool, right? Pity, this game is completely unplayable. The PC port is worthless, controller compatible is non existent, graphics clip in and out, and crashes randomly. If you want a somewhat playable Soul Reaver experience try Legacy of Kain: Defiance. Watch the story on youtube.
It's almost a perfect metaphor for the character Raziel, immortal and undying thanks to the steam port, but in such a grosteque form, it may as well be dead.
Don't buy this game.

I remember wanting this game as a kid, so I jumped at the chance to get it. Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver is a great game. The agency, while it takes some time to become competent with due to poor but doable controls, feels really good. As you play you become better at playing, almost as if mirroring Razael's revival and strengthening. The game has a steady drip of interesting lore and a plot that leaves you wondering what the next part is. The puzzles often have you stumped until you remember that you can change the world by changing planes, which adds a layer of depth to them. The combat feels pretty decent but simple and can take a bit to become good as different enemies actually have slightly different approaches. The boss fights though are almost all amazing in that they are not blunt fighting but more puzzles. When you die you simply shift to the spectral plane, giving you a chance to come up with a new plan. The platforming, much like the typical combat, is simple. Unlike the combat though, gets more depth as you unlock more abilities.
Obviously the game has its flaws: dated graphics, occasional crashes with no catalyst, poor controls, and the such. But those really do come with older games and are outweighed by the better aspects of this game. This game isn't long, but it certainly isn't short. If this game has caught your eye at all, I'd definitely recommend it.

EFLC fixed everything GTA IV did wrong or lacked, and added even more. TBOGT made up for GTA IV's mediocre weapon variety, something that Vice City and San Andreas had already perfected. Some new weapons include the AMT Automag, the Explosive Shotgun, the P90 SMG, Yusuf Amir's golden Uzi 9mm, the M249 and a few more. Also expanded is the range of vehicles and 3D-era features that were missing in GTA IV. Back from San Andreas is the parachute. Back from Vice City Stories is the golf range. The tank is still missing, though. In its place is an APC, a vehicle that was *almost* featured in GTA III.
Both TLAD and TBOGT take place in the same setting at the same time as GTA IV, though their storylines begin a little while into GTA IV's story, meaning the entire map is accessable from the get-go. TLAD follows Johnny Klebitz's antics with the Lost Biker gang in LC. TBOGT follows Luiz Lopez and Tony Prince doing similar things, though the main background is in night clubs. Some missions, like Buyer's Market in TLAD and I luv LC in TBOGT tie in with certain missions from GTA IV, but they are played from the perspectives of Klebitz or Lopez, depending on the game. I will not spoil what happens in these missions.
However, don't be mistaken. Unlike GTA London which was a mission pack and needed GTA 1 to play, these games don't need GTA IV to be playable. Since these are side games or sorts, the story of both games is a fraction of the length of the storyline in GTA IV. I highly recommend all three games in the GTA IV trilogy.

I have a lot of point and click games to go through and they all look a little samey when searching through the list.
Whilst looking for something to play a bit earlier, Dropsy stood out and instead of me wasting a whole lot of time just trying to decide what to play I decided to just give this one a go.
I’m very pleasantly surprised with this game. It has little features that don’t seem like much but I actually quite enjoyed.
For example, this is a classic point and click game with various puzzles involving the towns people. As per usual in a point and click if you want something from someone you’re going to have to do them a favour first. That’s pretty standard, but this game throws in the extra level of thinking by adding in a day to night cycle. Some people are in different places depending on what time of day it is and others may not even be around at all until a certain time.
It’s an interesting way to add to the puzzle of the game.
Something else that I thought added to the game was the communication between you and the characters. I have to admit that as much as I adore point and click adventure games, sometimes the long blocks of dialogue can get on my nerves.
This game lets you understand characters, their needs and their emotions just from little pictures and signs. In terms of story, you find things and figure things out for yourself more so then the characters waffling on at you. If they want something, If something is wrong, if they feel a particular way, you’ll know by the signs they use. Someone wants you to go somewhere and talk to someone? They’ll use a picture of legs in motion, a picture of a place, a picture of someone speaking and a picture of who to talk to. It’s simple, but effective and somehow enjoyable.
The graphics in this game definitely brings balance in my opinion. You can tell that this game has a slightly sinister and peculiar quality to it. The bright, upbeat, minimalistic pixel graphics give it a bit more of a light hearted feel despite the story being about an extremely creepy (yet loveable) and maybe a little deranged clown whose mother died in a circus tent fire. The almost cartoon-like animation on Dropsy being a perfect example of that.
When you start this game, everyone and everything seems to hate you. Part of this games charm is that you can choose to help and win over everyone in the game by solving their problems and doing them favours. I liked this feature of the game as it extends our creepy little clowns personality a little. He may look horrifying but really he’s a sweet and helpful little chubby monkey.
In terms of achievements this game wasn’t too bad. In the 9 hours that I played I played through the game once with great detail on the characters and once kind of half way through to sweep up left over achievements.
All in all really I adored this game. It was very fun and I’d definitely give anything else this developer came out with a go. If you are a fan of the genre definitely try this one.
TL;DR : Unique with some interesting features such as a day to night cycle and communication through pictures. Great graphics, a loveable character, not too bad to 100% and generally a decent play for those who enjoy the genre.

Although Cally's Caves 3 was released before Cally's Trials, this is actually the sequel to Cally's Trials (Cally's Trials is actually Cally's Caves 2). And just like Trials, Cally's Caves 3 is a mobile-to-PC adaptation.
Like Trials, this game is a solid platformer, but this time with a lot more content. The story is that, yet again, Herbert kidnaps Cally's parents and she once more sets out to find them. Lloyd returns to help her again, but this time she also gets help from Rupert (Herbert's son) and Bera (a cub bear, the daughter of Mama Bear from Cally's Trials). While the story is once more kept simple, this time there's actually a little more development, including the ending, which is pretty cool.
Gameplay is the same as before: kill enemies to acquire money and XP, get more health upon leveling up, guns level up as they're used. You'll find a lot of similar enemies and actually fight a lot of similar bosses too. There are a few differences this time, however. There are more interesting choices of upgrades to buy, this time you don't have to buy shortcuts (yay!) and you can also buy consumables to use on the way. Some of the upgrades are actually found throughout the game rather than be purchased with money and guns will level up to 20 this time, rather than 10 - though you'll need to find each gun's Final Form to be able to level them up to 20, otherwise they'll only go up to 19. The Final Forms do actually change the guns quite a lot - the Assault Rifle, for instance, when leveled to 20, will start to shoot grenades besides the usual bullets. Some of the most expensive upgrades in the game are the weapon mods, which add an extra effect to each gun (Fire, Poison, Shock and Freeze), though they're far too expensive in comparison to how actually efficient they are (basically, only Freeze actually makes a difference).
The game is also longer this time around. Not only it takes a little longer to beat the game, but there's also the New Game + mode, which changes the enemies found throughout the game and brings new enemies as well, besides new upgrades to find too. And while the level design in this game is still a litle too repetitive, this time there's actually the occasional secret to find (even if not too many of them) and 4 types of collectibles to obtain - upon obtaining all collectibles of one type, you'll be taken to a bonus level.
One important thing to mention is that, besides the forementioned fact that you no longer have to purchase shortcuts, this time the game has actual checkpoints and you can teleport between them on the map. Also, environmental hazards are no longer instant-kills - they cause damage, but that's it. While this may make the game seem to be too easy, it needs to be considered that the game is somewhat more challenging this time around.
On the note about challenge level, some of the enemies in this game are harder than they were in Trials. Smokey, for instance, will turn towards the character when shooting and shoot twice, instead of only one shot and always ahead of him. The Turret will aim for the character when shooting, instead of also only shooting in a straight line - among other examples. Bosses are somewhat harder this time as well. Just standing in place and shooting will no longer work and there are a few bosses that might actually require a few tries to defeat or understanding their attack pattern.
Besides all the collectibles to find and New Game +, there are also 3 other gameplay modes: Bera's Quest, where you'll play as Bera as she tries to return to her mother; Melvin's Zone, which happens right after the main game as Cally goes after Melvin, and Survival. They each add a little more content and gameplay time to the game, Survival actually has an unique reward if you can beat all 150 levels and Melvin's Zone also include three new weapons as well.
The only issues worth mentioning in this game are, once more, regarding controls. Just like Trials, you have to constantly tap the fite button to quickly shoot guns, except for the Assault Rifle and the Flamethrower and that will tire your arm out quickly, and you only have one key to switch guns so, yet again, trying to choose one specific gun will be a problem. It could also be mentioned that achievements require a lot of grinding (max out all guns, kill X of an enemy type, die 250 times, etc), though that's just a detail.
Overall, it's quite an improvement over Trials and a highly recommended platformer. Graphics look even better this time and the soundtrack is quite good too. If there's another Cally game in the future (and I hope there is), what I would actually want to see from it is better controls (better switching guns and no more fire key tapping), more secrets (hidden levels, secret walls to break/walk through, easter eggs, etc - maybe secret guns?) and better level design (more variation). Perhaps less grindy achievements and a little better cost/benefit relation to some upgrades (mainly the weapon mods)... And definitely more Bera, too. She's pretty cool.

Downloading the Team Fusion patches for this game is a must. My favourite combat flight simulator with a great representation of the Battle of Britain. The TF patches also add a Luftwaffe campaign as well which I am having an absolute blast on!
There's nothing like going on a sortie in a BF-109E-4 and feeling the adrenaline rushing through your body as you prepare for battle. Once you cross over the English Channel and see the White Cliffs you know you're flying into a sh*t storm.
The game is a must with the Team Fusion patches, otherwise, it's a mediocre combat flight simulator with little content. I would personally recommend buying it from somewhere else though as the price on Steam is a little steep,

First let me say that I LOVE IL-2 Sturmovik and IL-Sturmovik Pacific and 1946.  They are great games and insofar as I can tell, not being a pilot myself very accurate flight sims. Alas, IL-2 Cliffs of Dover is not up to their previous efforts. It feels like they got bored halfway through development and never really finished. There is only one campaign (British) and it is lamentably short. The German side is just a series of missions.  There are no promotions, medals, et hoc genus omne as there were in the earlier games. Also missing (at least I can't find it) is the small HUD display that gave you airspeed, direction and altitude when you were in cockpit view. Accurate though the instrument panel may be, trying to read it in flight without spending two hours memorizing the layout first is . . . inconvenient.  The flight sim enthusiast who is truly dedicated (for which read 'crazed') can be expected to do this. I just want a quick indicator of airspeed and so on while still in cockpit view. Also missing is the time skip control so it's necessary to put the plane on autopilot and advance speed or else fly an actual two hour mission in real time. See comment about flight sim enthusiast above.  The trouble is when you run into the enemy when the speed is at 16x normal things can get a bit hairy . . .
The quick mission builder is also nowhere near as good as previous versions where you could select almost any plane and a variety of maps and situations. In this one there are set scenarios and as far as I can tell you can't really adjust them. There is a full mission builder, but I never messed with that in the old games and I'm not touching it now as it was pretty complicated.  When I just wanted to shoot things down, the quick mission builder worked fine, when I wanted complicated, I started a career.
Honestly compells me to admit that I actually bought this game two or three years ago, only to find my computer's graphics wasn't up to running it. So I've really only played it for the last week or so.
Do I recommend it?  Yes. it's still a good flight sim if you buy it cheap. But it could -and should-have been so much better . . .

I bought this game when it first came out in 2011, played it thorougly through and have returned to it occasionally since. Let me start with a frank but fair summary; if you're a fan of the IL-2 franchise or simply looking for a suit up and fly yet realistic flight simulator, then this is not your cup of tea! Windows 10 users will need to get a series of 3rd party mods to even start the game!
If you want a complex and somewhat demanding, realistic flight simulator with a WW2 setting and are prepared to spend some time on optimizing and training. Then by all means, give it a go.
My initial reaction back in 2011 was that it felt old, a bit like mid or late 90s combat sims. Slow, somewhat blocky or even cartoony graphics and optimized for the past generation of hardware. Which it probably is! Definetly unfinished. It has since improved some, not least in terms of performace (like a much needed multi core compability). Which is a bit of a shame since it actually has a lot going for it like the beatiful interior modeling, the lighting and the weather simulation. Exterior models unfortunately look a bit flat. As do the effects. Terrain varies from "rather nice" to "something a bit 2003". Flight models are fine. With a good joystick the flight experience become really enjoyable.
The user interface is still one of the things that could scare people away. It is downright terrible! And confusing, escpecially in the mission menues. Here's where the 90s feeling really shows and not in a good way, I wouldn't be suprised if it was actually designed 10-12 years ago for a low budget strategy game and simply shoehorned in because they didn't have time to make a new one.
Another issue is that there's isn't really much to do in the game except for casually flying around, unless you want to spend a lot of time in the mission builder (which is a heritage from the Il-2 and Su-27 sims of the early 2000s) or engage in multiplayer matches. The latter can be rather fun though if you end up in the right crowd. There is a short, linear and amusingly poorly written single player campaign. I won't even comment on the translation errors!
Quick missions come in heaps and can be pretty fun once you get the hang of the game, but thanks to the clunky interface they are a bit frustrating to setup and the actual missions aren't very exiting.
So would I recommend the game? Uhhhmm. For the hardcore flight simmer that has to own every sim on the market, it's a decent if a bit frustrating WW2 era simulator. It doesn't make up for the abstinence left by the original Il-2 series. But it has it's moments and there's still a small, yet thriving community around it.
For the casual simmer or people without a special interest or experience with complex flight simulators, especially W10 users. Save your money! While there are plenty of decent arcade aviation games and modern, working, flights sims of all eras to go around. This isn't one of them.

Legacy of Kain is a well known franchise amongst many oldschool players. Some were introduced to the series with Blood Omen, others began with Soul Reaver. While the core gameplay was different both of them shared rich story and nice voice acting. Soul Reaver is the second game in the franchise and is a direct sequel of Blood Omen.
The gameplay consists of exploration, battles with vampires, boss battles, platforming and puzzle solving. While I do like the franchise I also do not have bias due to nostalgia and do not like to see the game through pink glasses. Exploration is fairly nice, game offers interesting locations and architecture and there's a lot of backtracking and hidden secrets. Battles (at least at first) are interesting, but quickly start to get redundant and boring. While the game introduces a couple of new enemies the core battle mechanics stay the same, as you advance more through the game you get more power and enemies aren't a real threat, just an annoyance to stall you a bit. Boss battles are good, but short. They're not the "win by brute force" type of battles as you need to find a weak point / solution to defeat the boss. Platforming is fairly frustrating as the camera and controls are far from perfect. Nothing is impossible and can be mastered after trial and error, but jumping onto series of tiny ledges can be painful, especially if you fall down and are forced to redo the entire segment. Puzzle solving is fairly Tomb Raiderish, but also gets too repetitive: "Block puzzle A is introduced, now do it a couple of more times. Block puzzle B is introduced, now do it a couple of more times again.". The best part of the game (aside from story and voice acting) is the soundtrack. It's great and memorable, a lot of people know Soul Reaver's "Ozar Midrashim".
The PC port has flaws. It runs on newer systems, it's possible to run at 1080p and 60fps. However, it suffers from audio issues. The music has crackling noises, dialogue skips. The only solution is to play it in software, texture unfiltered mode. Another flaw is that the hardware mode goes up to 1080p, while software mode goes up to 2160p. Makes sense, right? When compared to PS version the soundtrack is pre-recorded. It has less tracks and doesn't really change according to what's happening around you.
Should you get this version of the game? That's up to you. If you can oversee no texture filtering then go for it. If you prefer better overall experience, but lower framerates then go for the PS version. Dreamcast is supposed to be the best version.

Dropsy is a gross clown, but he loves you.
Cool game, not a puzzle oriented point and click, more about observation and deciphering what the townspeople want(there is no readable text, they communicate with pictures).
If I had to say something negative about it, the menus are slightly confusing.

A unique and memorable point and click for sure.
I have a lot of point and click games to go through and they all look a little samey when searching through the list.
Whilst looking for something to play a bit earlier, Dropsy stood out and instead of me wasting a whole lot of time just trying to decide what to play I decided to just give this one a go.
I’m very pleasantly surprised with this game. It has little features that don’t seem like much but I actually quite enjoyed.
For example, this is a classic point and click game with various puzzles involving the towns people. As per usual in a point and click if you want something from someone you’re going to have to do them a favour first. That’s pretty standard, but this game throws in the extra level of thinking by adding in a day to night cycle. Some people are in different places depending on what time of day it is and others may not even be around at all until a certain time.
It’s an interesting way to add to the puzzle of the game.
Something else that I thought added to the game was the communication between you and the characters. I have to admit that as much as I adore point and click adventure games, sometimes the long blocks of dialogue can get on my nerves.
This game lets you understand characters, their needs and their emotions just from little pictures and signs. In terms of story, you find things and figure things out for yourself more so then the characters waffling on at you. If they want something, If something is wrong, if they feel a particular way, you’ll know by the signs they use. Someone wants you to go somewhere and talk to someone? They’ll use a picture of legs in motion, a picture of a place, a picture of someone speaking and a picture of who to talk to. It’s simple, but effective and somehow enjoyable.
The graphics in this game definitely brings balance in my opinion. You can tell that this game has a slightly sinister and peculiar quality to it. The bright, upbeat, minimalistic pixel graphics give it a bit more of a light hearted feel despite the story being about an extremely creepy (yet loveable) and maybe a little deranged clown whose mother died in a circus tent fire. The almost cartoon-like animation on Dropsy being a perfect example of that.
When you start this game, everyone and everything seems to hate you. Part of this games charm is that you can choose to help and win over everyone in the game by solving their problems and doing them favours. I liked this feature of the game as it extends our creepy little clowns personality a little. He may look horrifying but really he’s a sweet and helpful little chubby monkey.
In terms of achievements this game wasn’t too bad. In the 9 hours that I played I played through the game once with great detail on the characters and once kind of half way through to sweep up left over achievements.
All in all really I adored this game. It was very fun and I’d definitely give anything else this developer came out with a go. If you are a fan of the genre definitely try this one.
TL;DR : Unique with some interesting features such as a day to night cycle and communication through pictures. Great graphics, a loveable character, not too bad to 100% and generally a decent play for those who enjoy the genre.

Yellow and green. They're very similar colours, and for a colour blind player like me, that's a *big* problem. But even if that weren't the case, the difficulty curve on this game is highly erratic. Level 1: Match up 100, no biggy, they don't fall too fast, and none of them drop off the bottom of the screen. Level 2? Get 200, they fall fairly rapidly, and if you don't clear them very quickly indeed, a hatch is opened by the pressure of the balls, and you inevitably lose.
Considering you can't move on to the next level without beating the previous one? That's a difficulty spike that's just going to turn people off this game. Just as it turned me off this game.
So, in summary, this game is distinctly colour blind unfriendly, has highly erratic difficulty, and it's a case of "too tense, too early", a bad trait in an action puzzle game. Not recommended.

While the campaign is alright, this game proves EA needs to be disbanded. I had played the multiplayer (which is ruined because of all the servers that just GIVE you XP, you'll never tell the difference between an actual veteran player and someone who just started.) and I was playing on the laptop before it got destroyed. I finally got it repaired, and decided to come back to the game only to find out I had to use the serial key again, only this time it didn't tell me I'm good to play. No, instead it said "Serial Key is already in use"... Excuse me? I'm on the same account I was using and everything... I tried using EA Support but as expected they're just as bad as expected. Now all I can do is replay the campaign for this game. What a waste. Do NOT buy this game! I've seen people who had my same problem and didn't even have a busted computer or use a new one. It just didn't work for them. This is a disqusting waste of space and I regret buying it. Would never recommend to anyone unless they just want a campaign.
Now, on to talk about the campaign instead of complaining that the campaign is all you can play. You play as one of four unique soldiers in a squad (I forgot the main character's name, and it doesn't matter as the only time he ever even speaks is in cutscenes). You're trying to stop Russians from making and using some form of doomsday device. Now let's be honest, this is a game you can complete in a few hours if you binge-play it (Trust me, the day I bought it for the 360, I was sad that I almost already beat it) and the game has some nice features that couldn't be executed better. The soldiers you play with don't feel like just some gritty soldiers. There is one soldier who is a living cliche that somehow doesn't become the cliche. And that's the leader of the group, sergeant. He's the living cliche of "I'm so close to retirement, better hope nothing happens to me" and *SPOILER ALERT* nothing happens to anyone during the campaign, because the game ends with a sequel bait. The other two characters seem like children who mess with each other and Sergeant is the parent who tries keeping the operation serious. I won't spoil what happens at the end but I can explain what or who you're hunting: Some russian bald guy who's the leader of the operation. You saw him kill one person and figured out he's the leader.
Now onto the gameplay: This game features a weapon collecting system, which I think was a beautiful plan. In a game where you can carry only two weapons, I find myself debating on which weapons to get. thankfully, you can just pick up a gun and drop it and you'll still be able to take that gun later on. A lot of weapons are found secretly, adding an exploration reward to the game. And exploring will happen a lot because you will get confused as to where you're supposed to go. It can be made easy after a battle, however, because by the time the fight is over, buildings will be knocked over which makes it easy to see what you're doing and where you're going. The gunplay feels good and sometimes satisfying. Not Killing Floor 2 levels of satisfying, but more like using the AWP in CSGO and hitting a sexy shot levels of satisfying, but only with the awp and SOMETIMES with a scout.
Multiplayer (Or what little I've played). I've played a few hours of multiplayer on PC (Couldn't play much on Xbox, I got the game after EA shut down the servers). So I haven't had much experience. What I can say is if you're wanting to have a hardcore grind to build up your status and become a hardcore veteran: It's not happening. Almost every server will give you 50,000 Exp for killing one guy. So I looked past that, and found it to be a lot of fun. Hitting nasty shots with a sniper is the most fun you can really have in the small servers there are, however. But I found some chilling moments when I had a sniper fight with someone and it was horrifying when I lost sight of him. Overall the game is fun but you won't be able to tell if someone is a Veteran or a new player (as I said before).
I still wouldn't recommend the game, however. The campaign is good but I wouldn't pay 20 bucks for it when I can't play multiplayer as well. I would only recommend the game if someone only cared for the campaign. Therefore I must vote no for this game.
(P.S. please don't let my hours confuse you. As I mentioned a lot I have played this game many times on the Xbox 360 so I do have more experience than it says on Steam)

Cally's Caves 3 is an interesting platformer, but one bogged down with extremely low difficulty and dubious grinding mechanics. It controls well and offers a wide variety of weapons - 15 guns (and bombs), plus a sword - for you to use against your opposition, but its origin as a mobile port seems to show in that actual platforming skill is rarely ever required. There are essentially no difficult jumps and very few timed jumps, and enemies can almost always be defeated at no risk to yourself by choosing a gun that can hit them while standing in a location where they can't attack you. Even if you manage to get hurt, by the end of the game you'll have 20 health (with no enemies dealing more than 2 damage in a single hit), passive health regeneration, and four or five full health refills in your inventory at all times if you somehow need them. In addition, your sword stuns all non-boss enemies, rendering them harmless in melee range as long as you hit your sword button every 1.5 seconds or so.
Despite its low level of difficulty, Cally's Caves 3 is still a rather long game: 111 short stages, a NG+ version of those 111 stages, then a 150-wave survival mode, a short "Bera's Quest" mode where you play as the melee-only bear you occasionally have to play in the normal game, and a 33-stage Melvin's Zone which is supposed to be a final post-game challenge. It took me about 12 hours to complete, though I took a break with the game running at one point, so it's probably more like 11.
The gun system is likewise neat - fifteen different weapons, including the basic pistol you start with, a heat-seeking rocket launcher, a gun that shoots slimes that bounce along the ground and up walls, landmines, and a gun that shoots harpoons that you can use as platforms, including while they're in mid-air - but they all level up by hitting enemies, so once you've maxed out a gun, you tend to stop using it, especially since there's no real difficulty that would cause you to need your good guns. Given that all the guns get a final upgrade when they hit their maximum level, I thought this was an annoying oversight in design.
Cally's Caves 3 isn't a bad deal at $5 for a game that takes more than 10 hours to beat, but it never really hooked me into wanting to play more or actively enjoying it, as opposed to just feeling that it was something to do and that I was, I supposed, making progress. Given the wide variety of indie platformers on PC, many of high quality, I sadly can't recommend Cally's Caves 3.

Cally's Caves 3 is one of those games I'm not really sure to recommend or not. Unfortunately, I have to go with 'no' in this case.
First the good:
-Platforming controls are extremely tight. I never felt like I missed a jump because of the game.
-The art style is very nice. It has a kind of cutesy-retro fell. The developer didn't go for a cash-in 'retro' faux 8-bit style, but still managed to capture an oldschool charm.
And the bad:
-The difficulty is almost entirely of the 'nailed by an off-screen enemy' sort.
-Weapons lack any kind of punch or impact. I was never really excited to get a new gun, because I just kind of assumed is would be as bland and uninteresting as the rest. I was usually right.
-Many weapons rely on you slamming the fire button as fast as you can to be effective. This gets old quickly.
-Level design often punishes exploration. Certain paths might lock you out of a large part of the level, but there is no indication they will do so. Choose the wrong path and miss all the tasty gems.
-Level design is bland. They're around the size of a Mario 3 stage, but with none of the appeal. Just platforms with enemies on them.
-There are quite a few weapons, but the only way to scroll through them is by pressing the 'change weapons' button. This will allow you switch through all your weapons, one at a time, in sequential order. If you accidentally go past your desired impliment of destruction, you're going through the list again. An odd design decision.
Despite the bad, I did have quite a bit of fun with Cally's Caves 3. But that fun was often punchuated by both minor and major annoyances. If you're really, really into platformers, then give it a try. For everyone else, I'll have to regretfully give this game a 'no'.

A terrible Wipeout clone. Decent music, graphics and gameplay out of a mobile game, absolutely no support for any kind of controller, and some of the worst keyboard driving dynamics I've ever had the misfortune to play with.

The races are grindfests, since winning is almost entirely luck, but you can replay the 6-lap time trial for 3 points each time. Only 3 opponents means the tracks are largely dead, there is rarely any other vehicle around you to use your weapons on.
The graphics are passable. Very simple geometry and detailed, low-res textures give it an early 3D look. The machine designs look great and overall the handling isn't bad, machines are responsive and turn quickly. Nailing the apex is pretty satisfying, especially when you have a boost in your pocket for the exit. It would be easier and a lot more fun with analog controls.
The keyboard seems to like to ignore or lock input, resulting in a quick tap sending the machine hard into the wall. So you can be impressed for a while until you start racing hard, until you find deploying powerups through a turn will cause you to crash.
If you crash by brushing a wall, your machine will phase through it and continue out into space before respawning.
You will have more fun by running the 20-year-old Wipeout 2O97 in Dosbox, I guarantee it.

Easily one of my most favorite games of all time! I remember playing this on the original Playstation like it was only yesterday. In my mind this game set the bar very high for what video games were capable of. Wonderfully written script and rich dialogue, Extremely clever puzzles that make you consider all possibilities. A unique and large open world game that managed to pull off one of the first concepts of streaming data directly from the disk, cutting out loading screens from area to area. Crystal Dynamics had outdone themselves when making this game, and it's a shame that we don't get games like this more often.
By today's standards this game would be considered a little rough around the edges (remember, this is 1999 we're talking about), but if you can look past its dated graphics and very rare glitches you will find a well crafted story with unique characters, all of whom are well rounded and are even pursuing their own goals.
Following the noble vampire Raziel, now turned undead wraith, on his journey to seek revenge for the betrayal of his creator Kain, you will find that the world they inhabit is dark and desolate, but not without reason. As their destinies unravel, you soon realize that there is more at stake than just Raziel's personal vengeance.
The Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver is heavy on storytelling and puzzle solving, but the combat isn't the best (in fact the combat is terrible). Many of the puzzles are far from obvious. Some are on such a large scale that you may have to visit several areas just to solve one and move on, but they are definitely rewarding as the further you go the more you learn of kain's actions, Raziel's resolve, and this dark, slowly dying world and how it came to be the way it is.
I have tried this on several computers and can easily say it runs quite well on modern machines. It runs on essentially any resolution, although I'd recommend playing at 4:3 resolution as that is what this game was made for. Widescreen works, but the game stretches. If it doesn't run well on yours then there may be a complication or something affecting its performance.
There is a problem with the audio, however. Sometimes the audio suffers from problems and you may miss some dialogue and key ambiant effects without realizing it, but it's easy to figure out as you can identify it when the sound starts to get choppy or, say, when you jump and the grunting noises you normally hear are missing. It's an easy fix, simply quit and restart. Now I know some people might find this a daunting task, and all I can do is assure you that this game is well worth the time and patience.
When I saw this game on steam, I was a little apprehensive to play it at first, as I was afraid my nostalgia would cloud the fact that this may be a terrible game after all. But once I ran it, I fell in love with it all over again. It can stand on it's own merits, and comes from a time where people were more worried about clever storytelling and breaking new ground than trying to introduce exclusive features and new DLC packs to increase product longevity. It's a masterpiece from another era, and shows that video games can be more than the generic "Action Adventure" label that is used to describe them.
I
recommend this game and any other in the Legacy of Kain series.

Star Wars Republic Commando is a product of the many Star Wars licensed games to come out during the early 2000s with the release of the prequel movie trilogy, movies known for being torn a new ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ by Star Wars fans over the years. Republic Commando takes the premise of the Clone Wars era of the movies and places you in the role of Delta 38, leader of the titular Clone Commando squad known simply as " Delta Squad ", consisting of Delta 07, 40, and 62, all of which have their own distinct character traits and personalities. Throughout the three primary acts of the games which take place on Genosis, a Republic Ship, and Kashyyyk the wookie homeworld, you'll be progressing through linear levels and shooting and blowing up Droids and the occassional Trandoshan or Geonoshan enemy type. Delta Squad is equipped with primarily with a laser repeater which is the base of the other 2 weapon modes (Sniper and Anti Armor Charges), you are also equiped with a basic pistol that recharges its infinite supply of ammo after a couple of seconds , and you are also given access to numerous Wookie/Trandoshan/Geonoshan weapons which can only be carried one at a time. The primary standout of the game is the squad control system that allows the player to seamlessly issue various tactical commands to your squad in the middle of battle while still allowing the action to go unhindered. Now you're probably wondering why i'm not reccomending this game and that can be summed up with the fact that this game suffers from numerous gameplay issues that make the game simply frustrating at times. The games AI is often polarizing, with your squad mates being able to effectively breach a door, retrieve bacta, or detonate a obstacle, yet the other half of the time the AI can't handle focus fireing or effectivley avoiding damage from the heavier enemy types, the AI also seems to get lost or simply stuck in geometry from time to time with no real way to free them other than reloading a previous save. The heavier enemy types are also something of a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ being more akin to a bullet sponge than any actual challenge. The players weapons also seem to lack any real impact or power to them, causing the numerous gunfights against super battle droids or trandoshan heavy gunners to become increaseingly frustrasting. The confrontations against multiple droid dispenseries and heavy enemy types often require you to rely on your AI squad mates to focus fire or place a charge, which they often struggle performing, usually requring multiple revives from the player. Now i'm not just going to heap♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game, there a definitely some great things. I like the cheesey squad banter of your squadmates. The soundtrack is pretty damn good with tracks composed by John Williams and Jesse Harlin, with the former being well known for his work on the film franchise with some iconic tracks making appearances in the game. The inclusion of a tactical visor that effectively provides and displays all the information you need is also great, with the must have mention of a visor clean sweap that removes blood and innards from your visor when you perform a closeup kill. Theres quite a few other touches here and there that help bring the game together. But theres just so many frustrating irritations (Bullet Sponge, Lackluster Weapons, Team AI) that really make the game a frustrating experience. Its honestly suprising how most people who remember this game praise it like it's this masterpiece spin-off game and let nostalgia play a huge role in their opinions, but I just can't agree with a game thats many issues hurt it fundamentaly. I can't find myself being able to reccomend this game, especially since it hasn't really aged all that well and doesn't really provide any new or rich lore and is basically just a squad of commandos blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up every level with hardly any character development or connection. All this aside it still is a somewhat decent shooter, giving you the opportunity to jump into the boots of a Clone Commando and fighting alongside Wookies.

This game is something of a mixed bag, but at its core there is a really enjoyable (and addictive) game if you can tolerate its various faults.
Cally's Caves 3 is a simplistic high-paced action platformer that has you explore a fairly diverse and colorful set of locales. Along your way you will discover a ton of different weapons, each with its own strategic use, and each that can be upgraded simply through usage, which results in bigger, badder weapons that do more damage, have more range, increased projectile count, etc depending on the weapon and upgrade level. Weapons not only perform better through upgrading but have several different visual forms, so the satisfaction from upgrading is very much apparent.
Through your progression you will slay tons of enemies, which drop your usual EXP and currency. EXP increases your character level, which only determines how much life you have. The game's currency is used to buy an assortment of upgrades, including gold drop modifiers, weapon modifiers, health regen and others. There are also a variety of collectibles hidden throughout the game, with high-level weapons upgrades unlocking as an incentive to collecting them.
The game is quite long for the price, offering easily 15 hours of content for completionists. The main story consists of 110 levels, which can be repeated in a new game plus mode that features different and more challenging enemy layout and minor differences in physical layout as well, making the content still feel quite fresh. In addition, there is also a survival mode where you must survive 150 waves of enemies in one sitting, and a collection of post-game levels that are best experienced once you have fully upgraded everything.
This is all held back, or held hostage it sometimes feels like, by some baffling design choices. In a game that has 15 odd weapons once you've collected them all, there is only one single button to swap weapons. Skip by the weapon you wanted? Well, you'll have to go through the entire loop again, to get back to it. Don't accidentally skip it a second time. (This will happen A LOT.)
The user interface is clunky and poorly designed. Accessing your inventory and the map are arduous tasks, with both hidden behind multiple menu options. Cursor selection on the map screen behaves erratically with directional buttons often not going where you'd expect them to go or being outright unresponsive.
The game's soundtrack is bland and completely forgettable and does nothing to add to the atmosphere of any of the levels, as all of the levels have the same set of tracks that play continually on a loop. That is not to say that there isn't a variety in the music, as there is, it is just an odd choice that each level has the same loop of tracks rather than selecting a different track from that loop to correspond with each thematic set of levels.
Finally, the platforming is extremely basic as you can only move left and right, and jump. You cannot aim up, or move up, or duck, or shoot down, or jump down through platforms. Doors are even entered automatically, which can be quite frustrating if it was not your intent to change areas. Enemy strategy is thus a fairly straight forward matter of avoiding standing on the same plane while you jump to avoid projectiles.
Overall I would call it a good action platformer that is lacking a professional level of polish, with the price tag being justified by the amount of playtime you are likely to get out of it.

I have played this game in a normal run without any of the bonus areas. I know it says only 5, minutes, but that's because I was beat the game while in places without internet, so forget about that.
CC3 is an empowering jump and shoot game~ If you like doing those two things, this is well worth a run! The fundamental controls mentioned work very well throughout the entire game. The pixel art is colorful and the animation is nice and bouncy. The use of sfx is quite characteristics of the era I believe the game was trying to emulate as well. The soundtrack is alway randomly changing, which keeps the feeling of the game a focus of interest. In a technical sense, jumping-and-shooting is buy-in-large what the game is about, and it might sound as if this would get boring over the course of the many worlds in the game, but the game spaces out the new weapons just right so that by the time you've gotten tired of shooting your old gun, you've got a new toy to enjoy all over again! If anything this just goes to show that the "less-is-more" school of thought on game design can work very well!
I do wish to bring up points of the design that I didn't seem to resonate with. Do keep in mind though, I'm in no way asking you to make any changes, but I do believe that it is important to bring up these kinds of things in a review. Since this is the third game, I will leave suggestions, as I am excited to see what you'll do next.
1) The inventory is not very streamline, and accessing it necessarily slows down the gameplay. Since there are only six items, I would suggest simply putting them all in the initial pause menu, so as to make them instantly accessible.
2) The boss battle design is at odds with what I am conditioned to do when fighting normal enemies. Blitz seems to be the best way to fight enemies. However, trying to do this against bosses has gotten me countless defeats. The bosses are instead designed on a predictable, almost turn based, experience that involves them attacking while it is not safe for you to strike back, but are in a fairly good position to parry, and then waiting for that long winded attack to be over such that you can move in and blast with all you have for a brief moment that the enemy is vulnerable. In theory this difference is interesting, but I just wanted to point out, that all of my encounters with normal enemies has trained me to fight a completely different way, and boss battles betray the logic that I have been conditioned to use in combat.
3) The fundamentals are the best option. The game will grant you a bunch of abilities, like charge shots, and rolling, and changing your weapons, but none of them seem to be viable options in the middle of combat. I found myself a more adequate player when I did nothing but focus on jumping and shooting with the occasional sword slash, rather than try to manage and think about all my options.
My suggestion has to do with both of the 2 mentioned above. I think my main issue with the combat is that I have no control over the enemies. Or rather: I have little to no idea what the enemies are going to do, and when they are going to do that, and this fundamentally makes reaction based play a bad option. Let me give you an example of the opposite, as it appeared twice in the game. There is a point in the game where you have "control" over the Balding Eagle, by being able to determine where he will crash into the ground. There is also a similar "control" that you have over the queen bee. This, to me is exciting, as it make it to where there is a well telegraphed amount of information that I can use for formulate a fun strategy against the enemy. In contrast, I often found the behavior of the Knife Bandit, Smokey, and the Bazooka Hulks to be unpredictable. Sometimes they would pace back-and-forth, sometimes they would turn toward me, and they would attack without warning, sometimes doing so while still moving forward. My suggestion here, would be two things. I think that reaction and strategy can be encouraged if the enemies are designed with attacks that are more telegraphed, a kind of visual cue to let the player know that an attack is coming.
I do have one additional moment of confusion about the enemies. The bazooka hulks shoot green rockets at you and you cannot parry them. When I fought Melvin, and saw him shooting green rockets at me, I must have died 20 times before I figured out that these are different rockets than the Hulks' and instead that this boss battle required the opposite logic of actually parrying the rocket--- This is the kind of thing that I mean when I say that the I am "conditioned" to play in ways that don't work during boss battles.
Rolling is not intuitive. (side note, there is a glitch where you can perform a "wave dash" by hitting roll and then mashing the direction forward, this will let you zoom right past all of the enemies and clear the game in a more pacifist manner) but aside from the wave dash, I could not at any point use the actual roll as a dodge, and a lot of this has to do with the above mentioned lack of encouragement for reaction/strategy based play. But it also has to do with how the controls for the roll demand a few too many steps: 1) keep cally perfectly still on the ground, 2) think of the direction you want to roll, 3) make cally face that direction, but remember that you have to keep her still because she cannot roll when running, 4) mentally figure out which button you have to press to roll, because there is one for each direction 5) press that button to roll.
Indeed, I would oft find myself being chased down by skeletons where I only want to roll back to get behind them, but never have enough time to actually input it, usually instead getting me both run down and hit by a projectile.
My suggestion is this: simplify roll to be a single button, and have it to where you are allowed to roll both forward, and also backwards, while maintaining the direction you are pressing. The controls for this would work like this:
1) if you have a neutral standing position, then you will roll backwards.
2) If you are running, you will roll in the direction you are running.
The result is that it should make rolling a much more reliable option in the middle of combat, and if back-roll maintains the direction you are facing, it could make for some very cool scenarios where in being chased by an enemy, you can just boost behind them while giving them a scattershot to the back.

If you're out searching for a pixel art app, I recommend giving Aseprite a try.

I really enjoyed the game.
If you like classic graphics adventures with gorgeous pixel artwork and are looking for a game that leaves the trodden path then this may be something for you. Dropsy really pulled me in with its atmosphere that was both foreboding and light-hearted at the same time. The nightmarish beginning draws the player right into the world of Dropsy and keeps them guessing whether the plot will develop into a horror story with you being the monster or maybe something else entirely.
The game pulls something off brilliantly that few games dare today, and that is to tell a story without words. Dialog is presented in pictograms only and they are so well-designed that it is a lot of fun guessing what the characters are saying. I played the whole thing through in one sitting and was motivated enough to try and solve the puzzles myself, even when I was stuck. This was largely due to the fact that there are a lot of optional tasks you can do when stuck and some of them may lead you to places that get you back on track for the main story.
These days it's been getting more and more difficult to find an indie game that actually bothers setting the mood, creating a dense atmosphere and bringing something new to the table. Dropsy was a nice surprise in that regard and has been one of the best story-based games I've played this year.
There may be some quirks in the game mechanics that may put sensitive players off, but if you are used to old school adventure games and enjoyed some of the newer indie adventure games then you should be pretty much used to the other imperfection. And really, overall the game was super stable for me, so I didn't get the feeling I was stuck due to a bug.
My only gripe is that I bought it cheaply off a sale, because Dropsy is worth every penny.
I really feel like buying it again and gifting it to someone who can appreciate it.

"Dropsy" in my experience is a casual point and click pixel graphics game. The animations and music are actually quite good for this kind of game. The idea of a homely clown figuring out tasks and then giving out hugs is brilliant. The gameplay is mostly exploration based, and figuring out what to do is tough sometimes, I would say it is too abstract. Sometimes great artwork and music aren't enough if the gameplay isn't fun.

Dropsy is really one of the best games of the genre. Feels both warm and cold at the same time, it's like it tries to balance out the overwhelming darkness of the plot and  people, with a lovable main character that uses hugs as his main weapon - which is a very nice
to current trends, and for that I applaud.
During play, I saw indirect commentaries of many, many things that are wrong about today: media manipulation, violence, hive-minded people with wrong facts, seemingly nice corporations, slave-like working conditions; also there's a town full of people that don't want to help you in any way unless you give them something in exchange first, not unlike what's happening today everywhere.
Then again, you have a fat, ugly clown (how can he be more alienating!) that wants to hug you because it's his primal need: just being nice, regardless of everything else. Dropsy, in its own way, feels insanely more human than any of us, which we are already lost in hate and overall discomfort of society.
On the negative side, I feel a bit disappointed with the gameplay itself: I thought Dropsy was going to experiment with some kind of new modes on how to develop the story, but the branching is quite linear and standard. Yet, Dropsy innovates with its surrealistic storytelling and non-verbal communication (though already done by Botanicula and probably others before).
And I
to mention the superb OST made by Chris Schlarb. I've even put "In The Court of the Junkyard King" on repeat for a whole day while I was doing other stuff.
This game is really what's good about games today: the way you can say a thousand things in a way no other medium can do. It's a must play, and I recommend it to anyone who cares just a little bit about games overall.

Got this as a gift from a friend. The art style turned me off at first but I quickly I got into its story and style. Puzzles were great and funny. I wish it ended differently, but other than that, a great point-and-click experience.

I don't think I've ever come across a game that is as satisfying as this one for its genre. Amidst all the rpgs and roguelikes that proliferate the atmosphere of Steam, Dropsy is that one point-and-click adventure that I'm glad to have stumbled upon. To this day, the game's story and music grow fondly in my heart.
Pros:
-Dropsy is an amazing, unique, innocent character that you can't help but feel for.
-Gamplay mechanics are intuitive and well-placed (as opposed to clicking everywhere until a solution is found).
-Storytelling is utterly satisfying and surprisingly deeper than expected.
-Visuals are rendered in a delightfully pixelated world, and are no stranger to a day-and-night cycle.
Cons:
-The game is relatively shorter than expected.
-The deeper aspects of the story remain hidden in crypted text, but does not harm the integrity of the gameplay itself.
I would happily enjoy going on more adventures with this one-of-a-kind character.

So, after over 20 hours of gameplay I finished the game on the third out of five difficulty levels - Experienced.
And wow, was it a fun ride.
I guess it's time to write a review, huh?
Then let's start.
Steamworld Heist is set in a universe where humans went extinct (not quite, but... spoilers) and Earth is now inhabited by steam powered robots. Actually it WAS inhabited by them, because Steamworld Heist takes place hundreds of years after the first game, when Earth explodes and all that is left of it are big shards floating in space. Luckily Steambots learned how to build spaceships and managed to escape.
Soon began the new era in their history, a era of Cowbots exploring the endless frontiers of Universe.
But their life isn't so simple. Cowbots have to face many powerful threats: space pirates, diesel powered robots who formed strong military and consider themselves superior over everyone else, and an alien, powerful threat lurking somewhere in Deep Space.
In Steamworld Heist you play as Piper Faraday - a pirate captain with a golden heart and assemble a crew of different colorful characters, like a jolly adventurous grampa who is a great sniper, a soldier with a love for blowing things up or a robot sailor with a fish head who can only communicate by saying "Blub".
The gameplay is a bit like 2D XCOM - you play in turns, there's full cover and half cover, you also can choose if you want to move a few tiles and shoot, or use up your turn to sprint. But there's a very important feature that makes Steamworld Heist much better than XCOM.
You aim each shot manually. When you play your shots are not calculated by RNG - everything depends on your skill. Another cool thing is that your bullets can bounce off walls and objects. You will use ricochets often, because enemies rarely can be hit with a straight shot. If someone hides behind cover, you can just shoot at a nearby wall or barrel to hit him in the back of the skull. When you pull off a risky shot and it connects, it feels really satisfying.
The game has a wide selection of different weapons you can use as well as many different items you can equip for missions, like medkits, armor or sidearms. But that's not important.
What's important that this game has hats.
Dozens of hats.
What are they for?
Nothing. Absolutely f*cking nothing. They don't give you any stat boosts, they are just there to put on your head.
So does that mean that they suck?
No! They look great and it's fun to collect different hats and put them on different characters.
Also, a really good band called Steam Powered Giraffe made several songs for this game.
Check them out on Youtube, they are fantastic.
So, in short:
Steamworld Heist is almost perfect. It runs well, the graphics look good, the gameplay is really fun, it offers a lot of replayability, and the music is super catchy. This may be the best game I ever played in the last few years.
Highly recommend.
Also, get the Outsider DLC. You will get a awesome new character, more missions, new weapons and even more hats.

To describe Cally's Caves 3 succinctly, I would say "2D Ratchet and Clank"; it's an action platformer with a large array of guns which level up as you use them, hideous amounts of money pickups and multipliers for them, and the requisite extremely expensive weapons mods on which to spend them.
For what it is, it's a competent little game that's quite moreish thanks in no small part to the weapon upgrade system. Anybody with completionist urges will end up wanting to level the arsenal to the max, and the guns are fairly diverse (although there are issues with the selection; more on that later.) The graphics are quite crisp and appealing.
On the soundtrack, I feel more or less neutral. While the songs that are on there are pretty decent, and suit the game well, there are no specific 'stage' tracks; for much of the game, the library minus the boss fight songs will just be looping in the background, no matter where you happen to be. Because of that, it feels like there wasn't too much conscious design behind it all from the game's devs. On the plus side, though, this means you can easily turn the music to zero and then play your favourite album or listen to a stream in the background. And again, what's there is pretty decent.
The weapon arsenal both benefits and suffers from the Ratchet and Clank syndrome the game has going on. At first it feels like all weapons are viable but some weapons are more viable than others depending on the situation. You might dps with your pistol, and use your shotgun to chip away at enemies you can't quite reach without putting yourself in danger, for example. By the end, however, you have the R.Y.N.O element coming into play -- i.e. there is a single gun in your arsenal that will outclass any other given gun in almost any situation, and the only reason to not use it is because you're trying to level up a worse gun. This is actually worse in Cally's Caves than in Ratchet and Clank games, however, because the developers have helpfully furnished you with infinite ammo -- meaning if you don't want to change weapon to use something worse, you never have to. Let's just say that you'll probably be using the Laser a lot, and leave it at that. That said, some of the guns are genuinely quite novel, particularly the spike gun, which has a lot of outside the box applications for the creative.
One annoyance is that most of the guns fire faster if you spam the button than if you hold it. I don't really get why this is the case (it isn't hard to mash buttons, although it can become a little tiring and unnecessary); I'd love there to be some kind of endgame upgrade that pulls the auto fire all guns come with up to a reasonable human button speed, if only to save the wear and tear on my controller.
I also feel like the expected difficulty of the game is off. I'm not great at action platformers; I play sloppily, I tank damage for convinience, I jump in the lava to skip obnoxious moving block puzzles, the whole shebang. I've 100%ed this game, with the exception of two achievements: one for dying 100 times, and another for dying 250 times. How many times have I actually died, in the course of the game and new game plus and survival mode and the bonus Melvin Zone and Beara's quest segments? 12, and all of those came quite early in the first run. You get so much more powerful than the game can effectively handle, and it just sort've runs out of tricks halfway through new game+. It doesn't feel like a stereotypically 'kid' difficulty game (especially not considering your protagonist has a vast arsenal of firearms, and it ends with
. Some of the tricks used to hide collectibles are stuff that usually you'd see more often in the Mario romhacking community, like leaving the ceiling open and expecting the player to walk outside the edges of the screen, and enemies in the lategame get pretty bullet spongey. I think you just scale too hard for the game to effectively kill you, regardless of how sloppily you play.
Overall, the game is pretty enjoyable, in a kind of mindless, rompy way. If it goes on sale, you're unlikely to regret reaching for your wallet. Recommended.

TL;DR - If the "thumbs up" sign for the recommend option on this review means I can can shove said thumb up the developer's ♥♥♥♥♥♥, then yes, I recommend this game. Otherwise...
Gameplay:
I've only played a solid seventeen minutes of Ampersand; the rest is me idling for trading cards so I can make a profit off of this abortion (update from the future: I tried idling for a little bit but didn't bother doing so long enough to get cards. I ultimately decided to cut my losses and get a refund). The game doesn't reveal to you the utterly enigmatic controls: left and right arrow keys to turn, X to boost, and Z to use power-ups. You have to get "points" to advance to the next stage which requires placing in the top-three of a given race...
So essentially, you're grinding for points on the same
tracks on the starter grid in order to finally progress. Also, I don't know if you have to use the points to purchase vehicles, but the vehicle selection screen
If you do indeed have to use points to unlock vehicles, there is no such indication. Furthermore, the powerups are awful; you get a two-second boost ability that does practically nothing, some lock-on machinegun that does even less in the way of destruction than the Death Star in Return of the Jedi, landmines that are more detrimental to yourself than others, a shield that breaks more quickly than your father's condom, and a rocket launcher that, surprise, launches rockets. Your ship also has some arbitrary health system that gets chipped away by taking damage from volleys of enemy pea shooters and ramming into walls--the later of which is inevitable thanks to the aforementioned wacky controls. Essentially, my most recent encounter with a red light at a main-street intersection was a more action-packed racing experience than Ampersand.
Story:
You are a bored 17-year-old male who watches more pr0nz than television and wanted to buy a slipshod racing game as a joke. You come to regret your ill-advised decision
(nevermind the strikethrough section; at the time this review was written, I didn't realize that the point at which trading cards started accumulating was the point at which you cannot get a refund. However, you can still sell off trading cards and potentially make more money than the amount you paid for the game).
Graphics:
This is a PS1 port. Don't let anyone tell you otherwise.
Overall:
This game gave me breast cancer even though I'm a dude.

If you're reading this review, then you already know that Neverwinter is a terrific online MMO game. It's a fast-paced adventure that leads you through a wide variety of lands and kingdoms. From a busy city (Protector's Enclave) to a land of Pirates, a spooky graveyard, dungeons, and beautiful pastures (Shandahar), you're sure to enjoy them all.  It's easy to lose hundreds of hours playing Neverwinter. It just never gets old.

I absolutely recommend it, but there is a lot of content that will take you weeks upon weeks of grinding to unlock.  You do have the option to purchase to complete most campaigns - the ones that provide you crappy items and are essentially not worth the weeks of grind - but you'll effectively cheapen your experience with that.
You could put $2000 into this game still would have to grind to not be inadequate; So, I would not recommend to those who read this review to do that.
It has an active and experienced community.  The stronghold and alliance features provide a great long term shared goal.

I don't think I've ever come across a game that is as satisfying as this one for its genre. Amidst all the rpgs and roguelikes that proliferate the atmosphere of Steam, Dropsy is that one point-and-click adventure that I'm glad to have stumbled upon. To this day, the game's story and music grow fondly in my heart.
Pros:
-Dropsy is an amazing, unique, innocent character that you can't help but feel for.
-Gamplay mechanics are intuitive and well-placed (as opposed to clicking everywhere until a solution is found).
-Storytelling is utterly satisfying and surprisingly deeper than expected.
-Visuals are rendered in a delightfully pixelated world, and are no stranger to a day-and-night cycle.
Cons:
-The game is relatively shorter than expected.
-The deeper aspects of the story remain hidden in crypted text, but does not harm the integrity of the gameplay itself.
I would happily enjoy going on more adventures with this one-of-a-kind character.

A cute little open world point-and-click adventure about a hideous but happy clown who just wants to make the world smile. It's not always intuitive where you're supposed to go, but the world's not huge, so you won't spend hours trying to figure one portion out. Pick up everything, hug everyone, and walk everywhere, while uncovering the mysteries of both your little town and yourself.

If you're looking for a light-hearted point and click adventure game with barely any creepyness or violence, then this game is for you. The animations are absolutely beautiful and the music is quite good.
If you are expecting a game with a dark and twisted story, then this game is not for you. The game is overwhelmingly happy and tame. There are some (rather interesting) dark parts to the game, but they are very very few and far between. The game is mostly about small subplots with the characters you meet, but the game really stuggles to make the player emotionally invested in anyone, and as a result most of the gameplay is tedious. The real killer for me was how incredibly bad the ending was. Its like the writer came up with this interesting story, and then only elaborated on all of the least interesting parts of the story. To give you an idea of how bad the ending is without spoiling anything; the main antagonist is only revealed within the last 5 minutes of gameplay. Needless to say the game doesn't elaborate on the antagonist's motives, or really what is happening at all. This game had so much potential to delve deeper into the darker and more interesting parts of te story, but it just never happened.

Buy? Yes. It's a SURPRISINGLY and REFRESHINGLY GOOD match 3 (or more) physics puzzler. Normally, I'd shy away from either of those genre's, but it was a small download thanks to the Indie Royale Prarie Dog bundle. The main mechanic is linking adjacent, like colored orbs together in chains of 3 or more. Left click to link, right click to cancel - those are your controls. The goal widely varies from level to level - the first level requires you to just make enough chains, the next requires to continue making chains on a weight based door before it becomes too heavy with constantly falling orbs. One level requires you to keep a stream of orbs falling while preventing clogs in a "pipe" level, another has you try to make a big chain as orbs fly from the edges of the screen to the center based on gravity. Another has you link different sized orbs that are worth points relative to their size, and you have to make a chain with the exact score. It's surprisingly clever and very enjoyable with a great soundtrack (A link to the artist's page is on the game's site). The cheap gradient effect of the orbs kinda clash with the crisp, PixelJunk-esq background graphics (which look good IMO), but it's not the worst thing in the world. I got through half of the game in about 30 minutes, so you can probably beat the game in a couple hours, unless you get stuck (I'm stuck on Level 11). A very neat title that I'm glad that I found.

Recommendation - Puzzle fans, pick up when on sale.
This game is interesting, and requires a different type of thinking than most other puzzle games out there, but it's insanely short, and the difficulty is not very even.
The first few levels are simple, but the difficulty ramps up fast, and it never stops. You will likely be able to beat this entire game in around 2-3 hours, and most of that will be spent on the last few levels. For example, there are only 20 levels, and I was up to level 16 inside of one hour, then hit a wall. There is a nice variety in the levels, but I wish there were simply more of them, and the difficulty took a more gradual progression.
The graphics are fit their purpose perfectly, except that I wish there was a more drastic difference between the yellow and green colors. I'm not colorblind to any degree, but when you're frantically trying to manage multiple areas of the level, it really helps to have a stark difference between all the colors, so as to see them all at a glance. Speaking of which, the game does include a colorblind mode, although I didn't try it.
The music is pleasant and non-distracting, but don't expect to remember any of it once you've exited the game. It, like the sounds and graphics, is there merely to serve a purpose, then be forgotten.
I liked what I've played so far (I'm on level 18 right now), but even as an avid puzzle game fan, I can't recommend this for $5. The premise is just slightly too basic, and gameplay is just slightly too short. It feels like a free Android game, where you have to purchase additional level packs.
Overall, the game is pleasant, but not overly enjoyable. I would probably give it a 70/100.

I have been a fan of Legacy of Kain series but never did play this game when I was a child because the game was too simply too dark for me but the whole lore of the series has intrigued me in the longest time (my dad played this game and was immediately hooked as am I).
I played this game after playing Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain for the PC(Why didn't they have this on Steam?) and like Blood Omen, the story is clearly superior to other games of its time, having a superior voice acting talent in this game with a proper direction of the story to boot. The characters in this game are pretty likable in telling the story of the game, the character you play, Raziel, often tells you, time to time, his views of the current world he is in, in a pretty elaborate and amusing way during his journey. I have to say the character development regarding him is well done once you are done with the game. This game's story takes you far into the future, centuries after Blood Omen. There are few references from Blood Omen that are mentioned in the game, I'd say it's not that important to play Blood Omen, but it's clearly recommended for future references in the other games.
The gameplay seems fresh for a PSOne/PC(1999) title, 3D Platforming is a notable element of the game, jumping around the place feels very organic in a way that it paved way for future 3D action/adventure to takes notes on basic things such as climbing using the ledge to reach another platform. Gliding feels pretty organic too because of the big and high places you will venture to, it proved useful in Raziel's journey.
This game also has puzzles for you to uncover while most of them are cube puzzle where you have position the cube like objects to its correct positions, although it feels pretty ridiculous as God of War's Kratos doing the same thing(and Thank golly, it was this game that started this element of gameplay), it felt pretty fun and I had the feeling I have to finish it right away, but I can't help that I'm thinking that Raziel would be better off as a "Plumber" of sorts, he certainly has a great talent for it, *snicker*.
The fighting system feels that it contributed a lot to upcoming games such as Devil May Cry, Dark Souls and other action/adventure games that have a feature for you to lock on the enemy in close combat while holding a button. While holding the "autoface" button, you automatically focus on your current adversary and anticipate his move. While in this state you anticipate his upcoming attack and dodge with the proper directional button and the jump button. This would lead the enemy to be in the open, off-guarded. It's a simple mechanic that does its job well in the starting stages but as you progress, you uncover more skills you can abuse to your enemies such as things from side quests.
Side Quests in the game does make the game a little easier but it is no easy task to uncover them blindly though. The side quests contain powerups that would increase your health, your magic and your arsenal such as glyph spells. The game would be little more of a challenge if you play without the powerups, but just a little because of one little thing.
This game setting has you going into different realms time to time in real time. I'd say it's an impressive feature back in the day, because the 3d setting changes/transforms IN REAL TIME as you change from one realm to another and it is needed for you to do in order to progress more into the story.
The enemy designs are pretty grotesque and scary, it is what repelled me from playing it as a kid. I think third boss and its minions takes the cake that will keep preventing me from getting a sleep for a day, two or three if I was dealing with this game back then. Dealing with the bosses require you to analyze the environment and take it as an advantage to defeat you adversary, it will take time figuring it out but you will accomplish it nonetheless.
The sounds are fit the setting but the ambience of the setting puts me on edge especially when the game decide to bugs regarding the sound such as sound loops and what not, you know I just have to reset and load the game from where I was. Voice acting is top notch, it is dramatic but it does its job pretty well for a video game of its age.
This game has certain bugs/glitches such as game crashing suddenly during lengthy play times in a sitting, enemies going T-Stance on you all of the sudden, sound loops that are pretty scary and nerve wrecking. They are pretty minor and not necessarily would break the game render unplayable.  Just save consistently, you can save anywhere. I MEAN IT.
