This game was one I had vague memories of playing a demo of. So, when I found the collection was available on PC for $5, I quickly scooped it up because Gaben.
TLDR: Moar Puzzle, Less Fight. Like? Buy. Not like? PASS
Overview: This game takes place in a land called Nosgoth. You play a death angel who turns into a zombie-vampire hybrid who can't die now. Your job is to get revenge on Kain, for leaving you in this ghoulish state, and then ruining Nosgoth while you were in the underworld. The game truly is an Eidos title in more ways than one.
Pacing:
The game's pacing is nonexistant. It managed to feel the same during all 10 hours I played. Maybe it picks up later on, I don't know tbph. Once could call it postapocalyptic.
Gameplay-Combat:
The combat just seems to lack flow. Many many areas are full of enemies that respawn so constantly that it's almost not worth it to fight them every time, and just run+jump past them. Or use Spirit Realm if you can get away with it. The first boss of the game is a puzzle boss. Bleh. Without spoiling anything, I had to use a walkthrough in the same manner I used a walkthrough with HeXeN.
Gameplay-Puzzles: BLOCK PUZZLES, SON. Also, stuff that isn't obvious. Painful and requires a walkthrough beyond the first twenty minutes or so.
Story: The story is an odd thing, one that doesn't irk me or compel me. Perhaps it's because the first game in the series isn't available for PCs. The game manages to advance the story without drowning you in exposition too much, although there are a few too many cutscenes for my liking.
Controls: Standard clunky PS1-ported-to-PC controls. Can't even use a mouse. A shame, because i'd love to LOOK UP.
So, in conclusion, I can't wholeheartedly reccommend or deny LoK:Soul Reaver, in spite of me being forced to put a NO. It depends. Do you like Tomb Raider and other similar games? Liked HeXeN? Dive right into this gem. Want a more actiony thing to play? AVOID. The puzzles get to the point of feeling forced, imo.

Pros:
* Nice mix of the recent XCOMs 2-move strategy with Worms like aiming with different gun types, such as sniper "rifles", pistols, grenade launchers, SMGs, and shotguns

Cons:
* The game became quite repetitive towards the 8 hour mark.  There weren't enough things introduced in the late game that kept the gameplay fresh.  As a result, the game became stale
* New Game + is literally just playing the game over again, except you get to keep your hats and unlocked characters.  I only played the first stage of NG+ before quitting.

Notes:
* If you would like to get credit for beating the game on a higher difficulty, make sure to stay at that difficulty! I played most of the game on the Experienced difficulty, which is like the 2nd to hardest, but I only got credit for the lowest difficulty that I played it on, which was normal for the first level because I didn't know how hard it was going to be.  So I feel a bit ripped off there.
Final thoughts:
It was a fun game, and I would recommend it to others, but I probably won't be coming back to it.  Definitely buy it if you are looking for about 8 hours of enjoyment out of a 10 hour playthrough!

Not to sound insulting, but Image & Form games often feel (to me) like one notch above games with mobile developement in mind. Overly simplified to a fault. When you build a game that begs to be compared and described as something like
, you have the potential for tons of customization and sandbox-like creativity. Let me explain further.
When you reduce a tactical game down to 2D, you already lose a bit of strategy, which is fine - to a certain extent this was made up for by the brilliant bullet-bouncing/aiming system. Thats great, and beyond the superb graphics and music, thats about where the greatness ends.

But alas, it is also so far. I want more. I want strategy like
. Whether it would be more base-building elements, better equipment, character customization, etc. All of this is possible in this game. In fact, the hard part of building a brilliant combat system is done. I think we just need more bells-and-whistles.

A very lightweight Run ‘n’ Gun platformer. The platforming isn’t particularly difficult, you start with Double Jump and then get Triple Jump very early on. The games controls are responsive and almost all the weapons are semi-automatic with no delay in-between shots. This gives a very satisfying 1:1 ratio of button mashes to shots fired.
All your weapons gain exp and level up. The exp is gained every time a weapon shot hits, rather than it being based on kills or pickups. This makes failed levels and boss attempts not feel like a waste of time as you retain the exp even if you die. The weapon leveling gives a nice feeling of constant progression throughout the game.
The game is very simple, you pretty much just jump and shoot things the entire time. Don’t expect a Metroidvania, the game is very linear with very few side areas and doesn’t have much in the way of secrets to find. I never really got the sense that I was exploring anything, mainly just collecting all the money and then looking for the exit to the next area. But this game is very fun for what it is, it’s great for when you don’t feel like thinking and just wanna hop around and blast things.
The game uses the Dpad rather than Left Stick for movement so be prepared to fix this with your favorite third party program such as xPadder.
-Playtime-
8-10 hours for first play through. New Game+ is substantially quicker because you retain your weapons and their levels which makes things much quicker even though it has tougher enemies.
-Achievements-
Nothing fantastic here, mainly just getting all the collectables. Only 2-3 of which I would consider to actually be hidden, most are just found with a thorough exploration of each area. Finishing up the Max All Weapons achievement took less than an hour and didn’t feel too grindy. I did however use Turbo on my controller to speed this up quite a bit. The biggest grind was the 250 Deaths achievement, I only died maybe a dozen times playing though the whole game and New Game+. I ended up just going to a boss fight, setting up a macro and leaving for an hour to get this.
Recommended on sale.

This game gets a positive from me - but only barely.
First, the pros and cons:
The graphics are nice and the game plays well, but the game is very easy, and the level designs vary from okay to tedious. There are blocks that can only be destroyed by certain weapons. You won't encounter these blocks until you've found the corresponding weapon, so there's no backtracking to find secret areas you couldn't access before. These blocks are placed randomly and without thought, which would be okay if it wasn't for the biggest pita in the game: weapon selection. The game has 14 weapons, and you can only cycle through them one by one - and only in one direction. This gets tedious really fast; especially when there are multiple different types of weapon-destroyable blocks in one level. When weapons level up, they often change graphics, which makes them even harder to find again when cycling to find the one you need.
There are no areas or spots in the game where you have to puzzle or use skill to get. You get triple jumps, but they are never required in the game. Everything is easy to reach. You also get a lot of health, which makes dying an actual achievement.
And talking about achievements - they seemed to have been added as an afterthought by someone who really couldn't be bothered. Most achievements are "Kill 25/100 of monster X". The others are equilly as uncreative. The worst are "Die 250/500 times". As dying is time consuming and boring, this one is too tedious for me to attain. It's not even an achievement.
The melee weapon, on the other hand, has an important function in the game. You can stun enemies and return bullets to sender. There could have been some really good achievements attached to the melee weapon, but none were.
Overall the game is mediocre, and fun for a while for some mindless platforming. I don't think it's worth full price, as there are better, similar games to be had for that money.

Today, for my 200th review, I'm going to be looking at
! For over 20 years, this game has been considered one of the all-time best, but in my opinion it... oh... wait... really?! Actually, for my 200th review, I'm going to be looking at
. Huh. This is supposed to be a momentous occasion, so I should be critiquing an important & highly-regarded game. I guess it wasn't meant to be.
Oh well.
Seriously though,
is actually pretty decent. I haven't played either of the previous games, but I guess that isn't really important. Cally's parents have been kidnapped by a Mad Scientist. In her quest to rescue Mommy & Daddy, she jumps and shoots through dozens of levels, while putting together an arsenal to rival World War 3. There's a simplistic charm to this game that's hard to ignore. It reminds me of the kinds of videogames kids would imagine. Cally has a shotgun so now she's shooting wolves, skeletons, and bandits. Is that a giant hornet? She better blow it away with her rocket launcher. Cally triple-jumps and has a pet bear that knows kung-fu. It's aspects like these that make the tone light-hearted and amusing.
At first, the game is rather slow. The enemies are placed in locations where you can easily get away, or shoot from an advantageous position. This is mainly to counter-balance the fact that enemies take a bit of punishment before they go down. This becomes a common theme of the game. You can make the process of killing baddies more efficient with different guns, and using the sword to stun them for a brief moment. What you'll be doing more than anything else though is grinding. This is bound to put off more than a couple players, and speaking for myself, constant upgrades can be just as much a detriment as a boon for many games.
That said, I think
works well with this system. It's similar to the weapons in the Ratchet and Clank series. While they're not as creative, the guns acquired throughout Cally's adventure, recieve substantial upgrades. Aside from shooting more powerful bullets, these guns can adopt new properties, such as a heat-seeking add-on for the rocket launcher, or a piercing effect for the blade gun. It also helps that there's a constant rate of positive reinforcement throughout the game. You're always finding new weapons, acquiring strength boosts, leveling up, or purchasing something useful. I also like that whenever a gun undergoes a major upgrade, the screen showcases the newly-kitted out weapon along with a flurry of explosions.
This is one of those games that also makes New Game+ interesting. The enemies recieve a substantial health-boost, and their numbers are bolstered due to an influx of fresh-faces. Aside from having a massive arsenal, you've likely also purchased a number of coin multipliers, so you should be able to afford the weapon mods. These mods are elemental, and can as much as double or triple the player's DPS when used with the right weapon against an enemy weak to its effects.
You probably won't notice due to the steady stream of weapon upgrades and other amusing aspects, but
is a really easy game. There might be a couple stumbling blocks early on in the form of certain boss-fights, but after enough upgrades you'll enter a "How could you ever die?" state. On one hand, I appreciate this, because there are more than enough hardcore, rogue-like, one-hit-equals-death, spike-laden platformers. On the other hand, becoming so overpowered in this game makes it feel menial. When you play Survival mode in this game, you're not worried about your life, you're more worried about having the patience to sit through it for so long. At least the cash rewards are pretty nice, and they're good for farming achievements.
While this isn't quite the masterpiece I was hoping to write about for my 200th review, I have to admit that
is well-done. It lacks the challenge found in other contemporary platformers, but it's still thoroughly compelling. It reminds me of something that would have been popular back in the shareware days. A simplistic yet charming shootemup with a nice soundtrack and a lot of content.
It's worth looking into, I think.

It's a good classic game. I love that dark dirty atmosphere, the mythology and the design of characters (especially bosses). I love the puzzles. I love boss fights, where you can have time to think about their weak spots. Finally, I love the idea of two planes - if you're too weak, you move to the spectral realm and you can do other stuff before going back to material realm. Feels good, no immersion-breaking "you died, try again" scheme. However, the game is still far from perfect in my opinion.
The camera and controls are just messed up. Seriously, it feels like they weren't tested enough. For example, seeing Raziel's butt zoomed in when you need to judge distance is nothing but good gameplay design. The level design often doesn't conform the camera movement, which, combined with camera-dependent movement direction, makes it very easy to fall off narrower platforms.
I understand that many of those issues were common in that gaming era, especially the camera work, which apparently was a plague of TPP games back then. On the other hand, it's weird that noone complained about that during testing stage. It just feels bad and makes the game unnecessarily repetitive and frustrating on some locations (especially Rahabim clan's).
Anyway, if you're immune to frustration, you should play it just for the atmosphere. It's so dark I sometimes felt like I didn't want to go any further into that darkness. It's like you never know what you're gonna meet in the next chamber/corridor. The graphics is also good, just low-res. Good colors, good textures and good models. It's still immersing, even though it's so old. The music makes you sink ever deeper.
That ugly world, corrupted with pure evil, makes me want to drink fresh human blood.

I want to like this game. I really would. I'm a sucker for sci-fi, I'm a sucker for strategy, and I've got a nostalgia spot for flight combat simulators.
But I have enough bones to pick with this in just four hours of gameplay that I just can't give it my seal of approval. Let's start from the top.
Stability
I am stunned that this was considered stable enough to be allowed past beta. The game has crashed six times thus far for me. Twice was something to do with the main menu, which found itself caught in a submenu and attempts to return to the main menu crashed the game, twice (reliably) had to do with removing scaffolding construction commands (more on that later, I was trying to place gun turrets), and the two other crashes I can't attribute to anything besides spontaneous software autocannibalism.
Controls & Interface
Alright. The devs were going for a mashup somewhere between the grand strategy of Homeworld combined with the individual ship combat mechanics of something approaching EVE or maybe Starpoint Gemini. Designing a control scheme that allows a player to fluidly transition between these two very disparate modes of thinking is pretty bloody hard.
Perhaps the first recommendation would not be to try and overturn the WASDQE mechanics that so many other flight games have used: if your A and D are for left/right strafing, Q and E customarily are for rolling, not... up/down strafing? Yeah, fine you can reconfigure your keyboard bindings, but coming out the door with an intuitive control scheme is much less frustrating, especially when there are twenty other someodd functions that also intuitive control keys that are conveniently in reach.
Ship controls in small craft aren't too bad. The larger the ships get however, the more difficult it becomes to keep track of velocity, orientation, targeting, fire control, and fighting the god-awful camera behavior. The camera doesn't seem terrible at first, until you start trying to target anything faster than an anemic snail. The clever sort might then leave turrets to be crew-controlled, but between their tendency to split fire across multiple hostiles and the low average damage per turret, your vessel end up soaking enormous amounts of unnecessary damage.
The mouse orbit in strategic view operates on a hair trigger. For a nausea-inducing psychedelic effect, right click and drag the cursor all the way in one direction or the other and watch the screen snap around somewhere between five to fifteen times. The camera also manages to never go where you want it to go, and you spend more time orienting your camera than maneuvering your ships.
In strategic view, the game can never decide what markers to apply to allied and enemy ships. Half of the time, all of the markers in the strategic view have white arrows. Sometimes it will acquiesce and return to the red/green dealio when Saturn is in retrograde, and then suddenly it'll switch back to its ambiguous, ivory mystery.
Ship movement commands in both pilot and strategic view are somehow incredibly clunky. In strategic view, they took half of the Homeworld formula minus the pieces that make it work. That's the only way I can describe it. In pilot view, the 1 through 5 movement commands take too long to use, and you can't seem to integrate them together: it just becomes easier to fly the ship yourself, which for a capital ship is much like trying to direct a peanut butter avalanche. Most of my other complaints here are related to keybindings, which can be chafingly tinkered with. Mine look like very close to what I had for SP:G.
Buildings! Buildings should not be as difficult to place as they are. When you click on the entry of the structure you want to place, it should not default to scaffolding. I don't want to place scaffolding, I want to place gun turrets. I want to place trade stations. I want to place literally anything besides scaffolding. Removing scaffolding crashes the game. Stop with the scaffolding, I will stab you in the cloaca with a blender if you try to place scaffolding again.
The way the text scrolls onto the dialog box makes me want to gouge out my eyes with a ladle. This might just be me, but man is it painful. Much spacebar spamming ensues. Somewhat related, I really would rather not admit to how long it took me to figure out how to close out of that dialog box. The escape key is reserved for opening the main menu, not progressing chat windows. Scoundrels!
TL;DR: The UI chafes my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like an angry meth'd porcupine.
Graphics:
Not much salt here. The game feels like its trying to chase Borderlands' coattails with its quasi cel-shading style (Maybe it's actual cel-shading, but it seems a bit polished for that) and while I give it a minus on originality, it's still alright. It gives the game a certain visual immortality that keeps its appearance from nagging at the player. It's nothing breathtaking, but it's not detrimental either, and that's all I really ask.
Physics:
I like me some fidelity to Newtonian physics, and the ship velocity mechanics scratch this itch fairly well. Beyond that, the scale of things is small enough that there really isn't much to do here. A lot of the potential here is lost thanks to the collection of hemorrhoids that is the user interface, because as much as I would like to tractor beam an asteroid into that there cruiser at 300 meters per second, the controls just aren't elegant enough to let me do that.
Speaking of tractor beams, these things are wonky. Something escapes your tractor beam? It stops. On one hand, that might be convenient for not slinging something important off into deep space, but on the other hand, I want my makeshift mass driver. LET ME HAVE MY MAKESHIFT MASS DRIVER.
Tutorial & Plot
If I were to take the tutorial and attach it to a control scheme that didn't induce a stroke in its users, it would qualify somewhere between "meh," and "Oh, OK." It's basically a quasi-organized controls crash-course tethered to some low-key hit-and-miss attempts at humor. It works, ish, but it has much potential for improvement.
I can't speak to the plot. It might be good, it might not be, but with the game stability having all the reliability of diarrhea farts combined with a user interface that can induce the berserker fury of distant ancestors, I just couldn't be bothered to soldier on and find out.
Overall:
If the devs hadn't moved on to VD2, I'd have said this game had potential pending some bugfixing and interface changes. As it stands now, well, simply refer back to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chafing.

A fundamentally broken game. I bought this game because the gameplay video made it look skill-based and action-packed with lots of bullets, dodging, parrying, etc. Unfortunately, the maps and damage sponginess of the enemies completely ruin that design.
Most enemies will stay on their vertical level without moving up or down. Almost every time, you'll be able to approach them, completely risk-free, from a higher or lower level and simply spam them down with your weapon of choice. The sword cause enemies to go into a full second and a half hitstun, so once you hit an enemy once, you just have to keep swinging the sword until they die. Either way you choose to unfairly dispatch the baddies, make sure to pack a lunch; it'll be a while.
Enemies have so much HP that these tactics don't feel "pro" or even "cheap" - it's just tedious. Spam from a distance or stunlock up close; either way you'll be sitting there with no risk for 5-10 seconds per enemy. And there are a lot of enemies, and a lot of stages.
I get that the enemies have so much HP so that when you get bigger, better weapons cutting through them like butter will feel great; but you're asking a lot out of your players, who have much better games sitting on their shelf they could have fun with immediately, without having to grind up weapons.
Speaking of weapons, the levelling is completely uninteresting. Weapons get more damage as you use them (very incrementally more) and occasionally 'evolve'. This sounds cool, and could be if the evolutions were meaningful or changed how you used the weapon. Alas, they're almost always "fire extra bullet", "bigger bullet", or "more damage". What's the point? Why not just balance the weapons around each other so that you choose weapons based off the level, the enemy, or your personal preference? When you really get down to it, who cares whether your shotgun does 1.00 damage per pellet or 1.05 damage? These are actual numbers from the game, I'm not even exaggerating for effect.
As for the other RPG mechanic, the money/shops, that's broken too. From the beginning one of the first things you can buy is a drop that lets you get more money; obviously this is the optimal thing to purchase, since you can see that later upgrades cost hundreds of thousands of gold, and enemies drop between 10-100 apiece. Unfortunately, maxing out the gold-dropping multiplier takes hundreds of thousands just by itself, which means that your first few hours of this game will be doing nothing but making it so that later you'll have enough gold. What's the point of cool upgrades if they're all so expensive I can't buy them without spending hours either farming gold for them, or farming gold for the gold-multiplier upgrade?
The writing, plot, characters, etc are all mediocre but that's to be expected, so no points off there.
All in all, a game that missed its potential by bad design. A lot of the pieces of a good game are here. Pretty decent art, sound, the controls are tight and feel right. Some of the fights I had, when the level didn't allow for cheesy tactics, were pretty challenging and fun. Just needed better playtesters.

Cally's Caves 3 is a sequel to free Cally's Caves platformers from mobiles made by yet unknown indie studio VDO Games. You play in a role of a young girl Cally, whose parents get abducted by an evil scientist and you, as other girl would do too for sure, take a gun and shoot through hordes of enemies to save your parents.
It's a platformer with focus on shooting and weapon variety. You'll be able to pick from many weapons, may it be pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, RPG launchers or laser rifles. Every weapon acts a bit differently and every weapon can be leveled up. The game strongly focuses on the fact that using your weapon will make it stronger by the time. As far as the crazy nonsense story goes, you'll also see Pokémon-like evolutions of your weapons. Congrats, your shotgun has evolved into Terminator! (But don't get your hopes high, it's just a better shotgun.)
Graphic style seems to be similar to Cally's Caves 2 with slight improvements, the sounds feels more annoying after some time. What's worth praising, is the game length, as the developer really tried to make a lot of levels to make it worth the 6,99 € price tag. You'll wander through those in metroidvania style, as levels are connected through the tunnels and you can return to any checkpoint anytime.
Cally's Caves 3 is not a bad platformer with a lot of content, but on its own it still didn't get rid of the freeware game feel. It may be not appealing to platformer newbies with a little raw and unpolished menu design. It can be an entertaining experience for some time but I don't think it's worth recommending with so many other great platformers in the store. This just keeps being an average game and weapon variety + upgrades (damage boosts) are not enough.

I paid: £2.99 (Bundle price, normal price: 4.99)
I expect: 12 hours of play
I rate it 83/100
Story-driven: no (but there is one)
Demo available: yes
Worth the price. Review below.
"Overall, I think the game will offer you a solid 10-15 hours of gameplay for a very reasonable price. I certainly enjoyed the experience more than I was expecting."
I picked up Cally’s Caves 3 as part of a bundle on
for £2.99, and I was surprised to find that it was quite competent. Casting my eyes down the list of games that I just purchased and downloaded always fills me with buyer’s remorse.  Games which are presented as ‘indie’ titles have been so over-done that they have moved completely out of vogue, and knowing that a game has been developed by an independent entity is no longer impressive.
That being said, I decided to try it out anyway. I will begin with the negative points.
The game looks nice, the sprites are very crisp and clean, but it lacks that last little bit of aesthetic polish. The ground and terrain is built up using tiles but as far as I can see, there is only one multi-tiled geographical feature and that is the soil corners. What this means is that the environment looks blocky and un-natural when it could be much richer; the best comparison that comes to mind is the mega drive Sonic games – they have floating islands that look none-square despite being made entirely of square tiles. The damage text is clearly just a basic font – arial? – and considering the frequency of its display, one imagines it would have been given a little extra attention. I like the fact that the game has a world map that allows you to freely teleport to checkpoints and shops, but the actual map looks as though it was made in mspaint, which surely could have been improved with a small amount of work.
The music is very pleasant. If it was to my taste, I would download the sound track quite happily. Unfortunately though, the songs are not in sync with the game itself - instead, they play as though it was a playlist on repeat which I found a little jarring. The controls are generally quite sharp with the exception that rolling is needlessly clunky. For some reason, you have to come to a full stop before you can roll and there are two buttons depending on which way you are facing.
These complaints are either minor or aesthetic in nature and have almost no bearing on the gameplay. The game is extremely competent despite these flaws, but it breaks no new ground. Platform games that include shooting components are tried and tested, and this game brings nothing new to the table. If I hadn’t recently decided that I was actually going to play through some of the drudgery on my Steam account I probably would not have even considering installing this game. What I found in place of a boring game that failed to hold my interest was instead a game that draws together the elements that it claims to work with and polishes them to a mirror-like sheen. Nearly everything about the game is tight and it just feels great to play. No falling to your death because your foot nudged the platform corner; no weird Mario-like momentum; no throwing your character into a wall of spikes for no reason; no trying to control a crosshair on screen while also jumping from platform to platform. Everything simply works.
Let not these complaints deter you, however. The positive aspects of this game far outweigh the negatives. The difficulty scaling is essentially perfect, for example: there is enough of a slow canter towards challenge that people unfamiliar with gaming can ease themselves into it but this is not so long as to bore those who are familiar with platforming. The deaths are frequent but fair. I did not feel as though the deaths were undeserved (with one exception) and they were infrequent enough to avoid being annoying. The exception to this is that early on in the game, you rapidly learn that water is actually made of a kind of magma, and stepping into it causes an instant death. There’s no reason that the game can’t just damage you and allow you to jump out, but this is ultimately a minor gripe.
The game has a sense of progression about it that places it somewhere between a Mario game and a Castlevania game in terms of RPG elements. There are enough McGuffins to collect for completionists to come back and take a second look – one of them unlocks a secret level – and the weapons all have growth and upgrades for those who get a kick out of those sorts of minor rewards. Indeed, just looking at how many weapons there were impressed me when I first opened a shop dialogue. To add to this, there are special blocks that require you to use a specific weapon to interact with them. It was truly a mercy to find out that these weapons were actually useful in their own right. Nothing kills my enthusiasm for a weapon system than a clumsily handled switch because you are forced to use something that sucks.
The levels are laid out in such a way that you will see secrets before you have the means to obtain them. This is pretty standard, but for an indie developer it is a sign that some extra thought has gone into the design of the game; something that too many indie titles are lacking. In addition, there are extra game modes for once you have finished the main game which is a nice reason to pick the game back up again.
Overall, I think the game will offer you a solid 10-15 hours of gameplay for a very reasonable price. I certainly enjoyed the experience more than I was expecting.

Here's the short of it - it's my GOTY 2016.
It's a bit like Worms, set through the filter of a sweet space western. Everything is done almost perfectly, and i'd like to express how much i've come to love this game here.
The mechanics are extremely satisfying. It's a turn-based system on a 2D plane where you have to maneuver and aim shots, using various mechanics to insure that you're hitting without getting hit yourself. Taking cover, using line of sight(such as ricocheting bullets and arcing projectiles like grenades), and calculating damage so that the enemy lines are either crushed or so scattered that they can't muster a threatening retaliation.
But the combat is only part of what goes down when boarding a shuttle. Half of the fun is just assembling a proper team, utilizing the loadout system to either boost the strengths or cover the weaknesses of your various crewmates. Aboard the shuttles themselves is treasure, or 'swag', to find and gather. The swag itself is generally the game's currency(water; it's good for you!), but occasionally it will be weapons and items of various rarity that provide either a new mechanic for your arsenal or some kind of statistical boost. Collecting the stuff also gains you bonus experience after you get out, so there's multiple incentives to get in and out as quickly as possible. I've redone a ton of stages just trying to find rare stuff and level out characters, experimenting with new character and loadout combinations. Pro-tip, Payroll is awesome.
There are a few major arcs to the story and level design, each offering some solid enemy types that consistently add more to the shenanigans as you proceed - you've got standard mooks, but some start coming at you with shields that provide them regular cover, enemies that will scatter oil on the ground to ignite under you, melee enemies packed to explode when they die, snipers that attempt to utilize the ricochet, and so much more that I dare not spoil. They're all initially kind of intimidating, and demand that your playstyle adapt quickly to each incoming threat. It provides a pretty meaty challenge, and can feel so satisfying when a plan comes together. Better still, if you're really hurting to get through an objective, the difficulty has five or so settings that allow you to get past a mission and let you build yourself up a bit before tackling it again.
I can't emphasize enough how great it feels when you can clear a room or a threat by sheer wit and skill alone. Things like needling a rocket through a cluttered hallway to hit a target before it can kill an ally, or forcing an enemy to turn around by getting into melee so that a flanking character can crush its health bar. What helps is that most maps are randomly generated, and a lot of stages will spawn in more enemies from various entryways, so it helps to build up the adaptability and skill required to handle later stages. It's very smart about how it both teaches and rewards players.
Oh, and there are bosses, and they all kick♥♥♥♥♥ They're all super distinct and memorable, with some kind of added gimmick that may or may not hint at stuff you might encounter more regularly as the game proceeds. They can be a legitimate struggle, as more and more enemies start forcing their way into the engagement, putting pressure onto the player to finish the boss as quickly as they can before they get overwhelmed. And when their health reaches zero, and the sparks fly, and their body blasts in every direction, the soundtrack kicks in, letting their sweet melodies follow you out; one arm carrying the swag, and the other raised in victory.
On the subject of audio, this game has an excellent soundtrack - mostly played very quietly in the background, picking up when enemies are nearby, it's a very western and sci-fi series of tracks. Steam-Powered Giraffe did a great deal of the music, which you hear as fanfare for defeating a boss and in the various bars spanning the game. On more than one occasion i'd found myself stopping to just listen, which I think says a great deal more than what i've done for ambience in the past. The weapons and sound effects are also all very crisp and excellent, very distinct sounds that leave you satisfied when you scrap some poor sap thinking he's safe behind that barrel.
The visuals are a mixed bag, but I think they do a great job of showing you everything you need to see. There's even a minimap you can deploy, in case you ever get confused about things like swag, doors, etc. All of the non-mook types of robots have very memorable designs, and they're given a little more creative freedom since everything is a robot and doesn't have to conform to any particular type of body. Note again the aforementioned character Payroll, whose legs are literally just a big wheel, like Gizmoduck.
The story isn't particularly grand, but for a game like this, it only needed a modest amount to get the player going - the gameplay was enough to keep me involved, but the presentation of the story was quite excellent. So many little touches with the dialogue and the direction the robots were taking in design allows it to stay fresh all the way through to the end.
There are some other little disappointments, like character features switching sides when they turn around(Piper's 'hair' shifts from either side of her head), or maybe a thing or two about the story itself, but honestly if that's the worst I have to say about the game then i'd say you've got a pretty solid game on your hands...at least, for me.

Pretty much the perfect example of how to make a good turn based strategy game. XCOM fans will feel very comfortable with the mechanics in place. One strange downside is that the game has a fantastic OST by Steam Powered Giraffe but rarely uses it, and the standard combat track gets old very fast.

Highly enjoyable low-stress XCOM-like. Very interesting hybrid of the aforementioned game and Worms: It's got great customization, inventory management, good weapon variety, and very well put together leveling-up system. The gameplay itself may seem very simplistic but it has interesting depth; chiefly with unit position (As all your battles take place aboard usually cramped spaceship interiors) but more entertainingly enough with bullet ricochet. Pulling off a well-executed (Or outright lucky) trickshot in this game is incredibly satisfying. The different characters also fulfill traditional class roles that we all know and love (Specific abilities and access to specific weapon types, as well as suitably different stats).
Apart from the game itself the art style, animation, and catchy soundtrack really tie it all together. It's *loaded* with character and I absolutely adore how charming (And surprisingly bleak) the setting is. I was also surprised by how satisfying the sound effects are.
Anyways I'm enjoying this game a lot. It's charming and easy to get into without being shallow and repetative: There's a surprising amount of depth both inside and outside of the combat. An easy recommendation for strategy game fans.

What's not to love? It's humorous, turn-based, and has gorgeous artwork and more than enough depth to make it fiendishly addictive. Oh, and the 'hat thing' was inspired; because to the fashion conscious one's choice of headwear at loadout will quickly become an important consideration to make. It's also family-friendly, and a great game for parents/grandparents to play with  the kids; but make no mistake, when the kids have been consigned to their beds the grown ups will be fighting over who's playing this one!

I will be honest to you from the start - I am biased towards this game. It has been a fundamental pillar in my gaming life, it was one of the first PC games I played and I love it. Just look at my avatar - it's Raziel. First time playing it was way back in 2002 but I have fond memories of how awesome this game was. Yes, I can see the flaws it has today, it did not age that well ... but please hear me out. Soul Reaver is a game that was revolutionary in it's time. It combines combat and puzzles in the big post-apocalyptic world of Nosgoth. Both are difficult so if you like more casual games I guess this one is not for you. The game does not take your hand, you have to try stuff out for yourself. And die a lot in the process. But not really die since this game created a great mechanic of shifting between physical and spectral realm. So if you die in the physical world you shift to the spectral one. If you die in the spectral world you reset at the Elder God. You can however shift when you want and this gives the game it's dynamic feeling. Boss fights feel very satisfying when you finish them. You also get a power from each boss you beat, adding extra layer of gameplay each time. All of this was fun, but the story and narrative is why I LOVE this game! The story telling is what this game nailed - from the writing to the voice acting. Plus it has a really cool soundtrack as well. Some downsides are here as well, the game is old so graphics and compatibility are not that great, though it runs fine on my Win7 laptop. The open ending can also be annoying for some people, although it is not that bad (and continues well in SR2). And I could write all day about this game but I will stop right here because you already know if you want it or not from what you have read. I will end this review and give one of the most true and heartfelt recommendations I ever gave on Steam!

is a hack&slash classic that specifically shines in storytelling and oozing atmosphere. Originally released for PS1 this was one of most groundbreaking games due to a mechanic that allowed you to switch between 2 different realms with different physics. You play as a fallen vampire who seeks revenge against his comrades that condemned him into a burning abyss. When it comes to PS1 games you always need a little bit of nostalgia for old graphics but if you see SoulReaver for $1, give it a chance.
It certainly has its own share of glitches and problems, especially on new systems.  You won't be able to use modern controllers without third party software. Some people have issues with operating systems like win 8 and 10. It is also a notorious game for bad camera angles and potential glitches that may force you to reload save files. In fact, it is a common knowledge that Soul Reaver is not a finished game which shows through unfinished areas and lack of elemental upgrades for the soulreaver.
Soulreaver is formatted a lot like Metroidvania when it comes to progression. Each of your comrades has a power that is required to progress further into the game. For example, you have to eat the soul of Rahab ( a water-resistant vampire ) before you can swim and access new areas. I hope you like block and physic based puzzles, the game has a lot of those. Switching realms changes how the world behaves which creates complex scenarios. Although the combat is satisfying you can skip almost every enemy. It also has a lot of platforming gameplay which can be kind of a chore.
It is very easy to invest yourself into the story because the narrative is so good. From amazing cutscenes to engaging dialogue it always kept my interest. The entire game has a chilling soundtrack, one of my favorites. You will explore a post-apocalyptic version of vampire kingdom full of sinister locations and labyrinths. Although it aged visually, it was one of the better looking games back then.

These days it is hard to find a hack&slash game with a strong focus on narrative. SoulReaver is a prime example of a good storytelling and is still worth playing despite its old age. If you did not grow up with PS1 you might have a hard time enjoying graphics.

I fortunately got this game on humble bundle for $7 recently. After the first couple missions I was hooked. I love the Homeworld tactical feel along with the more hands on sim modes and many options the game gives you for type and level of control. I think if your looking for a versatile space sim or RTS game that you can't beat in 4 hours, I think this is worth a shot.
Yes, its true, I only have 15 hours on the game, and loved all of them so far, and since I only payed $7, that's already down to less than 50 cents per hour, and ive barely touched the storyline campaign let alone tried any of the scenarios.
There are a couple "cons" to the game from my perspective.
1. Sometimes it is difficult to get your fleet to do exactly what you want it to, especially if you don't experiment with the little AI settings on them. If you want your ships to stay in line and not get baited into the enemy too deep, you have to set them on "do not engage" or similar, then remember to change that when your ready to move in for the kill.
2. Not totally a con, but anyway, the game can be frustrating. Event triggers can smash you. There are times when you've built a big fleet to send over to the enemy base, and by poor timing the enemy hits your base at exactly the wrong moment. Or, you just dont know what you need to do to defeat a particular fleet or event and you just get smashed... Either way, at least the game has 5 autosaves it saves 1 per minute in a cycle, and also at key points seperately, so you can back up to anywhere from 1 to 5 minutes ago, or to the beginning of that mission or event, or to a previous mission/event. Once I needed to capture a base, but my marine ships got wasted enroute. There was no way to build more until I captured the base, so, I had to back up to the previous area, losing like 30 minutes of play, and then redo everything until then making sure I kept those marine ships from getting wasted.
Overall, I say that this game is very challenging, fun, and rewarding, but if you don't want a game thats challenging to the point of frustration sometimes, this may not be the game for you.
p.s. Save manually often because even the best laid plans can go awry.

Highly enjoyable low-stress XCOM-like. Very interesting hybrid of the aforementioned game and Worms: It's got great customization, inventory management, good weapon variety, and very well put together leveling-up system. The gameplay itself may seem very simplistic but it has interesting depth; chiefly with unit position (As all your battles take place aboard usually cramped spaceship interiors) but more entertainingly enough with bullet ricochet. Pulling off a well-executed (Or outright lucky) trickshot in this game is incredibly satisfying. The different characters also fulfill traditional class roles that we all know and love (Specific abilities and access to specific weapon types, as well as suitably different stats).
Apart from the game itself the art style, animation, and catchy soundtrack really tie it all together. It's *loaded* with character and I absolutely adore how charming (And surprisingly bleak) the setting is. I was also surprised by how satisfying the sound effects are.
Anyways I'm enjoying this game a lot. It's charming and easy to get into without being shallow and repetative: There's a surprising amount of depth both inside and outside of the combat. An easy recommendation for strategy game fans.

What's not to love? It's humorous, turn-based, and has gorgeous artwork and more than enough depth to make it fiendishly addictive. Oh, and the 'hat thing' was inspired; because to the fashion conscious one's choice of headwear at loadout will quickly become an important consideration to make. It's also family-friendly, and a great game for parents/grandparents to play with  the kids; but make no mistake, when the kids have been consigned to their beds the grown ups will be fighting over who's playing this one!

This is a fun game. It's a combination shooter and platformer with really high energy. The story is minimal, and the soundtrack is rather repetitive, but overall, the game has got some really entertaining qualities. The controls are consistently responsive, but it was a bit awkward for me to get used to using the D-Pad and not be able to use the left joystick for movement. The scavenger hunt for weapons and upgrades is definitely a plus and enough to keep most players entertained.
There are a lot of levels, but I didn't notice anything spectacular in regard to level design. Most new levels were variations of others, but the introduction of new monsters and weapons meant that this didn't detract from my gameplay.
It's definitely rough around the edges in some ways, though. I'm the type of gamer who is busting every destructible and searching for every possible hidden area and surprise. In doing this, I found an oddity very early on. Upon entering the first doorway (level) I jumped up to the platform on the upper left and started hopping around to see what was there. In attempting to see if my character could walljump, she "fell" through what should have been a solid barrier all the way through to the previous area. When I walked back through the door, my progress had been reset as if I'd restarted the level. This oddity was easily repeated a number of times, but I could find no real purpose for it, so I was forced to conclude that it's simply a design flaw. I also noticed a placement issue, which was most noticeable to me on the second map. There are a certain amount of destructibles that can yield coins or hearts which grant healing. I found one of these green plant destructibles placed above a doorway to the left of the shop. However, it's impossible to get the heart that was dropping from this destructible. It seems to go either behind or through the doorway, and getting too close to the doorway takes you back a level, where there was no heart waiting.
Overall, this game has a lot to enjoy. It should appeal very easily to casual gamers, as well as fans of shooters, platformers, and arcade games. There's a combination of permadeath with checkpoints, meaning that you only have one life and that while you might have to go back a few levels, you won't have to go all the way back to the beginning of the game. In that respect, it's very much like Giana Sisters: Twisted Dreams. The addition of a consumable lightpost also helps to reduce rage and allow even young and new gamers to enjoy it. Though I would encourage the developers to revise the store interface so that it's clear that the lightpost is indeed a consumable. I definitely recommend giving it a try.
Edit: Just wanted to add that the level design gets more interesting as the game progresses, and the placement issue is consistent throughout. Pretty much everywhere there is a shop, there is a doorway with a destructible over it, and I saw this on some standard levels, too. I also noticed that there are several monsters that you simply can't kill in a good area to ensure the coin drop. Many of my drops have ended up in the water or falling in front of one of these doorways. Easy come, easy go, I guess.

As I recently began to make a game with a few of my friends, I also began to find out that I am not just bad at Pixelart. I am absolutely terri- Ok jokes aside, I am not all that bad but I have much to learn. After a while a friend had shown me a browser pixelart tool which I used for a while but didnt help all that great and I came back to using Gimp. Shortly after I see a person on twitter writing on how to make a custom brush in a program that looked like it was mainly used for Pixelart and I was already interested. After asking this person, I was redirected via name to steam where I then bought it only one day after and used it for about 10 hours straight with varying results.
Overall, if you want to get into Pixelart and you dont want to pay a buttload of money for some high-end program, Aseprite is perfect for you. At first, like with any program, you will have to find your way around but after a while it actually becomes quite easy to use. Or in other words: You do not spend 5 hours on figuring out the basics unlike with some other high-end programs *cough*Photoshop*cough*. What? I didnt name any programs. You are hearing things. What? This is a written review?
...
LOOK A PERSON ON THE INTERNET WHO IS WRONG!
(Too soon?)
The program gives you a full on working layer and frame system. Layers work as intended. Human base, then ontop a layer of colour and ontop of that a layer of hair and another one for clothing. But what about animation? Here is where the frames come into play. Lets use a chest as the best example that I will give you now. A container. You have the chest right infront of you but you want to put in content that you dont want to redraw everytime? Then simply draw the chest without the top, put the top on another layer and only animate said top part. That way, one copy of said chest bottom part is enough for you as it will stay stationary no matter what. It is only the top part that moves.
Other than that, the program also gives you alot of colours to work with. Unlike your usual painting/drawing programs you can not only choose your own colours, but you can also choose from wide variety of palletes. You can make a real oldschool game look-alike or you can go in and create Pixelart Mona Lisa in the colours of the rainbow. You can even customize and create your own palletes to your liking. And those then can also be saved and loaded for later use.
There are a few different modes that I have yet to find out but one mode, the "Tiled" mode is honestly one of the best if you want to make continous tilesets. It mirrors every side of the tile you have on display and from there you simply pain as per usual. But at the same time as you paint on the basetile, all other tiles will be painted the same way and even overlay each other. This way you can make tilesets that add on to each other very easily and that, thinking about how hard that can be, is very very appreciated. I nearly ripped my hair out once due to a trial on actually making such a tileset in gimp. It became so frustratingly hard that I gave up until I found this tool.
Other than that, there are also a good amount of brushes. Not too many to say "Oh Lord, where just where is the pencil?". But also not too few to say "Where is the eraser?" You have what you need for the task that is pixelart. A pencil, spray, line, box or circle, eraser, fill and even a blur tool. You heard me, a blur tool for pixelart. Now doesnt that make things a bit easier?
Overall, this program saves me a lot of time going around trying to find out which colours to use because it is all in two windows. Oh yes, another point I nearly forgot is the second window afterall. You gain a second window which is the review window for your pixelart. While you go deep and dirty into the finest details, this review window can still show you, your masterpiece in its full glory. No more zooming out. Just a look to the right and you are up to date on how the mistake looks you just made. Well, or should I call it a happy little accident? Either way, its all there.
And that is about it. Another small point I would like to mention are the easy access keyboard shortcuts that make it very easy for righthanded people like me who mainly use their left hand on the keyboard. You are able to rebind them but the default layout works quite well for me~
And that is about it.
I would certainly recommend this program to anyone who wants to get more into pixelart. Actually have done that already with a friend of mine who bought it a day later. Do not know of the results but I doubt they will be worse than what I have done so far~
Just get it. It is the best on the market!

I got Aseprite as a birthday present, one month ago.
It's a very simple tool to use with many unique features.
Want to challenge yourself by using the NES palette only? Aseprite has the palette built-in! Want to rotate things without having them look jagged? Aseprite has RotSprite! Want to make your very own MissingNo? Aseprite has the Scramble Tool!
While it's easy to draw something in any sprite editor, Aseprite has "Pixel-perfect" drawing, so you don't get those weird jagged lines when you try doing something like a curve, and "linked cels" which don't change with every frame, so you don't have to do any cut-and-paste into all the frames like I used to. The downside is that, if you accidentally forget to unlink something, it changes in all the linked frames. The good news is you have unlimited undos, unlike some of the other spriting tools I've used.
There's also things that other spriting tools have, like layers and palettes, and while Aseprite has some cool layer stuff, I haven't used it much, and if I were to talk about the palette editor, we'd be here all day.
Aseprite is worth the $15. I may have gotten it for free, but the amount of quality put into the sprite editor is enough to give away the price tag by itself. It's a nifty little thing I've already spent 100+ hours on, in the month I've had it for.
The best pixel art editor I found. And I've already tried PS, Graphicsgale, own pixeledit and many others. Aseprite consolidates many tools in one program.
It's sick.

If you are looking for a definitive, dedicated package for producing pixel art, or sprites and animations for game development - this is absolutely THE best software out there.
Every single feature is designed so thoughtfully, it just seems like the developer really knows what people want out of the product. It's rare that I use a piece of software and simply navigating the interface makes me smile, and Aseprite does that. It's simply a joy to use.
The basic interface works like Photoshop, but everything is tweaked and optimized with pixel art in mind. You have every drawing tool you need right there, ready to go - as well as layers, frames (for animation) and a TON of really cool, intuitive tools designed to make your life easier - and they do! Take, for example, the shading tool: This pen-type cursor auto-shades the hues on a block of colour you draw on. Aseprite is also very light on resources meaning it runs like butter on basically any machine. Great for those long hours of drawing whilst watching films or listening to music. The interface itself is beautiful to look at, kind of like a nu-retro version of classic mac os aesthetics.
I cannot recommend this software enough. I spent years trying all manner of pixel art packages (or tweaking up existing ones) to find the best software for my game development hobby. Now that search is over. Aseprite is a stunning app at a bargain price. The more you use it, the more you love it.

In some sort of insane design choice control groups and formations are separated - you can't grab a swath of units and tell them to do something because they won't move or stay in formation, and so will arrive piecemeal at wherever you send them, neatly forming a line so enemy forces can eliminate them a few at a time. You can control group formation leaders, but if they die - you lose the control group. There's also no way to see the overall status of a control group at a glance. Unlike in Warcraft / Starcraft, you cannot see individual unit status with the group selected; you have no way to know who's close to dead without pausing time and examining each unit individually, and there isn't even a good interface for doing that much.
Nothing is taught. Prime example: in The Hub mission, you have 3 bases full of enemies bearing down on you and you can't even generate resources to make anything. So you have to tell a Tug ship to go over to a nearby asteroid to pull it closer to the base for resources. Except I couldn't figure out why commanding it to go to a extra large asteroid or a medium asteroid did nothing. As I finally found out from the forums, it's because it only works on a "large" asteroid and no other size category. Not only does it not make any sense, game doesn't even bother to tell you.
I absolutely applaud Chaosavy (the dev) who is very active on Void Destroyer 1 and 2 steam communities and seems like a generally swell guy, but there's no way I can recommend VD 1. At every turn I'm reminded of how Strike Suit Zero Director's Cut, Freelancer, etc ... did everything about ship mode better, and how Homeworld did everything about RTS mode better. I really, really wanted to play through VD 1 to learn the backstory of VD 2, but I'm just not going to♥♥♥♥♥♥away my time trying to beat this 1 single mission that's 9000 times more difficult than every mission before it. I'm sure it's possible, but I simply don't think it's worth the investment of time to wrestle with all that is bad about this game to see what lies beyond it.

Pros:

It’s somewhat shocking that the first two Cally’s Caves games never made it onto Steam – they’re only available from the iTunes Appstore and were made for mobile play only. Consequently many PC gamers may never have heard of this outstanding franchise by ZDO Games. To bring you up to speed the Cally’s Caves franchise has always represented outstanding platform gameplay with heavy does of elements from adventure and RPG games. It was with much delight when it was announced that they were going to be making the third game available on PC.
The Cally’s Caves games have always utilized intelligent retro style platformer graphics. The characters – both Cally and the other NPCs both enemies and otherwise – are all very well designed. Although the music is energizing and suits the game it becomes a bit too repetitive. The game could have been improved by having a larger soundtrack.
The game play is traditional platform style action but features a weapon upgrade similar similar to that found in the Ratchet and Clank games. As you use your weapon you will find that it gradually upgrades itself. At each upgrade level the weapon will increase damage and add effects that make the game easier to play without ever really breaking the game to the point where it feels like cheating. The biggest negative to the actual gameplay is that the enemies are damage on touch. This can be very frustrating early in the game to non-advanced players when they reach the first boss level and accidentally land on the tip of his tail which can very quickly cost the player their life and force a start over. IT makes the game to be a rhythm game at times. The most significant advantage to the gameplay in my opinion is that although there is no tutorial the game design teaches you the mechanics as you traverse through the first levels of the game. This is outstanding game and level design and is a highlight throughout the entire history of the franchise.
Another highlight for me is that the game has a metric truck load of weapons and upgrades. Finally, and definitely worth mentioning is the amount of content – good content – that makes up the game. In complete honesty not many studios release games in this genre with nearly as much content as what VDO Games put into Cally’s Caves 3. When you think you’ve completed the game it feels as though you’ve really just started. At $6.99 it represents an absolute bargain.
If you’re interested in metroidvania type platform RPGs then you absolutely should buy Cally’s Caves 3. We can only hope that VDO Games is able to port the first two games onto Steam so that we can have all three parts of the trilogy – to date – on Steam. Although Cally’s Caves 3 certainly improves upon what the first two games accomplished Steam players definitely deserve to have access to all three games on the PC platform.
Go out and buy this one.

After having not played this game in awhile I thought I'd see whether or not it still holds up to nostalgia. I'd say it absolutley does! While this is certainly not a perfect port with a mod fix (especially to fix the horrible mouse acceleration) the game runs amazingly well and really the graphics are not too bad!
I'd say the gameplay is really the heart of this game as you truly do need to use your squad in order to win and as the game goes on you get many opportunities to use them in various positions from turrets to sniper postions to using grenade launchers. There's just enough depth that making tacticul decisions feels good but it's also very streamlined so that you're never confused or overwhelmed. For the most part your ally AI is pretty damn smart! Many times they will take cover on there own and can very much handle themselves in battle. There are not many games where I can actually rely on AI companions and them actually protect me!
The story is pretty good but it definitely takes a backseat to the whole experience. Really just the reason for you and your squad to be going in and kicking serious♥♥♥♥♥ The game takes you from Geonosis where Attack of the Clones starts, to an awesome mission reclaiming a captured Clone Assault Ship, to the final missions on the Wookie home planet of Kashyyk. The squadmates (and your PC as well) are very well voice acted and very likable. Each with their own personalities that make them easily identifiable. Granted while they all have their own "expertise" that really doesn't show in gameplay as they all can do every task equally as well. But hey I'm sure that's part of why the gameplay goes very smoothly.
Now for stuff to nitpick about I'd say that the later levels definitely have some bugs and problems as well as general problems throughout the game. For example if you alt tab and go back into the game more often than not the textures un the game all suddenly stretch and look incredibley ugly. The main assault rifle of the game is really damn weak to the point of frustraion at times. It gets the job done though if you're out of ammo for the other weapons which are all basically top notch EXCEPT for the Trandoseon SMG. That gun is so damn worthless. Might as well be farting at the enemy and hoping they'd be offended.
All in all I would say Republic Commando is a very solid experience and frankly for a rated T game it's pretty dark and gritty. Would definitely rank this as one of the best Star Wars games up there with Knights of the Old Republic and OG Star Wars Battlefront.

This game is pretty incredible, and so is the dev.
When I first found out about the game, I was super excited about it. The idea felt like a wonderful "best of both worlds" experience. For the first few missions, it really was. Loads of ways that I could successfully approach the situation, both in the strategic view, and with piloting individual vessels.
For the first few missions, you quickly find yourself up against a learning curve. The learning curve is real, and it is steep in places, but the learning curve for the UI goes away soon after (I actually like the layout, after I spend a while getting used to it). And the learning curve for functioning your units, and piloting tapers off soon after that.
Basically, once you give yourself time to get comfortable with the UI, then it's not all that bad afterwards. While you’re still getting used to everything, take advantage of the help that is offered for navigating the UI. It’s very thorough and very helpful if you want to know how to do something.
After the first few missions, you briefly get a place where you can, more or less, just easily go on, and progress through the game. Once you get through those missions, the difficulty starts ramping up. Although, I greatly enjoy the fact that the way to beat the game isn't just about numbers. Apart from the obvious strategic difficulty, the majority of the game's difficulty comes from the different situations you're in, and how well you'll do in the mission is proportionate to how well you can adapt to those situations. Some of the situations are "caught with your pants down" situations, in which you have no real way to preempt them. But, I've found that many of the situations that you will find yourself in are situations that you'll either blunder, because you weren't watching your perimeter, or succeed in, because you are familiar with the strengths/weaknesses of each vessel and how it's best used in battle.
Remember: Your Capital ship isn't a god. It's more like a mothership. Protect it, and use it strategically, that's what it was made to do.
There are always two (or more) ways to finish each mission, the 'brute force' way, and the 'right' way. There is always a solution to each situation that you're put into that maximises your effectiveness in battle. Find it, and the mission won't be nearly as difficult. Also, if the AI gets to be too much, you can try to bait it or kite it.
Though, the campaign missions are great, they are heavy on the RTS side of things. So, if you're in need of a quick break, or want to experience the space combat side of things, flip over to the skirmish mode.
Skirmish mode reenacts your previous missions, but has some twists, as well as certain missions that aren't in the campaign. Skirmish mode was made for flying around in a fighter, or piloting one of the corvettes. It's great fun, and you'll soon find that there are certain situations that you can turn the tide of war by piloting some of your smaller ships.
It also has a wonderful sandbox mode, where you can create your own maps.
There also is another sandbox mode, and this is a bit different. It's a test of the new, and soon-to-be-released Void Destroyer 2. In that game, you will be able to start as a mercenary, and fight/trade/pirate your way up to owning a decent ship, and even being a fleet commander. I'm very excited about Void Destroyer 2, and if you're interested, I'd suggest giving that test a little play through, too.
This game is wonderfully made by a dev that is incredibly passionate about his work, and he does the best he possibly can to help form his work to the desires of the community. Many things that are in the game today are because of ideas that were shared over the steam forums. I think this game is worth it, and I'm certain that his next game will be even better!

I see alot of "I wanted to like..." which really should tell you all you need to know. That sentence could also be: "My own expectations ruined what could have been a unique, enjoyable experience."
Go ahead and watch the first 30 seconds of the first video on this here store page. Do you see all the red diamonds? Those are enemies. See all the bullets flying set to the epic music? It's a hailstorm, literally. Void Destroyer is absolutely the best space game I have ever played. Void Destroyer was so incredibly epic, I explored the entire genre. I hadn't played a space sim since microsoft's flight sim 95. RPGs, RTS, FPS, TBS, 4X, etc are more my wheelhouse. Because of Void Destroyer I tried Rebel Galaxy, Starpoint Gemini 2, SPAZ 1+2, Space Rangers 2, Starsector, even X2:AP. All fine games, some excellent, nothing quite like VD.
So what is Void Destroyer? It's a realistic space combat sim with rts functions, realtime pause, and giant setpiece missions. Example: Second mission kicks you in the nuts, because a ship with a giant drill on the front is literally ripping though you, oh my! Hmm, try to turn and shoot the drill?♥♥♥♥♥♥ that drill is armored. Pause, click fleet, click frigates tab (your giant ship killers), click enemy drill ship! Proceed to kite giant enemy drill while your hitters pound the drill ship in the back for 2 minutes. Feel accomplishment! You just exhibited problem solving! What follows is about 15 missions that range from attacking and capturing bases, building ships, attacking enemy lines, navigating through minefields, defending those bases, tactical retreats, saving the universe, etc etc.
Now to rebut some of the top rated complaints: I have finished the game, I believe I even got that sweet 0.4% ending.
You can select groups of ships, in tactical (rts) view: click fleet, click their tab, done.
Shaky Controls? Likely ghost input from another controller, etc. There's an option to disable.
I had no experience with bugs or crashes in main game, no stutter. Game is very very smooth.
Capital ship abilities? Awesome. Hilarious that the dude who listed 2 of my favorite: pull ship and capture ship didn't think to put them together. Almost every ship can be captured until the very endgame enemies. Remember that drill ship? You fight a similiar one later, I pulled and captured it and he helped me save the universe. Shield does block lasers, pudge style rot(radiation), use retreat skill, use heal skill and you just did massive aoe damage.
Super weapon on first ship? Secondary weaponfire is "X", check controls.
Just a ton of bad information and whining.
Teardrop drones? Kill their carriers before they swarm you (called frogs), or switch over you one of your smaller ships and shoot them off like a cleaner fish does for a whale! Don't forget you can pause at anytime to look around, take stock of your situation, evaluate, plan, execute.
The combat controls are tight and responsive, there are tutorials and text guides. There is nothing else like this where you have an excellent 6DOF shooter combined with rts scale battles. It really is amazing, if you have half a backbone give it a chance. It won't let you down. Hell if you still can't beat the drill, it's not the game, it's you. :)

As of this review, I have logged 440 hours in this game.  I think the lack of extra features (decals, skins, huge selection of weapons) is actually the reason I have so many hours logged.  After decades of playing AAA titles made by huge companies all throughout my youth, I found the LACK of things to be extremely refreshing.  There aren't airdrops, perks, rewards for killstreaks, and other gimmicks that the gaming community has come to expect from every FPS.  It's just you, your team, the enemy and a gun.
You won't be rewarded for venturing ahead of the squad nor will you find that to be a satisfying experience.  You will find, however, a game that strips away all pretense and just allows you to engage in high tension, collaborative, and insanely fun gameplay against enemy AI or other players.  This stripped down experience was exactly what I had been waiting for in a FPS game, without even knowing that I was waiting for it.
A few bullets will take you out and a few bullets can turn the tide of a match going badly for you.  One well placed grenade can save you and completely ruin the tactical advantage of the winning team, all while having a crazy amount of fun.  The conservative nature of play can lead to extremely high tension moments that you will replay in your mind later on when you close your eyes.
Finally, the file size is only 5-6gb and it can run pretty smoothly on most machines, even on Macs.
TL;DR
BUY THE GAME.

Cally’s Caves 3 is an action platformer with a Ratchet & Clank-style weapon upgrade system, and a karate master bear cub sidekick.
tl;dr It's a lot of fun with only superficial gripes. It focuses on gameplay far more than story as well.
The good:
This game oozes with style and takes good game design from some of my favourite Ratchet & Clank games.
The music is bumping with energy
The characters are cute and look good
It's has an interesting combination of level design and the combat system thats lend to natural advantages and disadvantages for the player or enemies. EG: The heights of platforms, sizes of enemies, positioning of everything.
Any early complaints I had with the game were quickly solved as you gain EXP, level up your weapons and generally get better at the game.
Learning the mechanics as you go makes a huge difference and the game doesn't baby you with tutorials.
That said it does a good job of encouraging you to learn the mechanics naturally through level design than obtuse or forced tutorials.
There are a ton of weapons and abilities.
Weapons can be upgraded a LOT through using them and they become really, really cool. Very R&C.
There are also weapon modifications although costly so will take some time to get.
The game does give hints towards mechanics that you have previously had chances to figure out, in case you didn't by yourself it will tell you not too much later. EG: Parry mechanics.
Options menus are good enough without complaint.
Lots of control options and remap the keybindings even for your controller if you use one.
The cons:
Music feels a little repeative at times but you can
Damage on touch with enemies can be annoying at times
Many weapons have a random spread instead of fixed-spread, may not be a con but it can make choosing a reliable weapon favourable at times.
Why does the lamp only work once? It wasn't listed as a consumable implying it was something you could always pick up. Although understable because it would negate the checkpoint system.

Cally's Caves 3 is a port of a mobile game to PC, but don't let that scare you away.  It's ported relatively well.  It's an action-platformer with some powerups that can be earned throughout the game to give it a sort of metroidvania-like feel.  It's not a metroidvania though, since it lacks the interconnected open world of a metroidvania.  Everything is upgradeable in this game through level ups.  Every gun, your health, your sword.  There's a constant feeling of progress throughout the game.
It's a pretty solid game.  The amount of weapons and worlds means there is a lot of content in this game.  Add in an alternate adventure or two, new game+, and a survival mode, and you've got a pretty solid investment if you enjoy the gameplay.
For me, the gameplay wasn't enough.  It felt grindy because of the nature of leveling up and constantly working toward evolving your guns.  I felt more focused on getting the next evolution than I was on completing the level, and that kinda ruined my experience.  However, the gameplay is responsive and works well, just because I didn't enjoy it doesn't mean it is bad.  If the gameplay and constantly leveling up for favorite guns looks compelling to you, you'll probably really love this game.
I have some more technical gripes.  The soundtrack sometimes feels out of place and feels like it lacks something.  The sound design leaves a LOT to be desired.  The jumping sound annoys me.  The frame rate is capped to 30, which is more obvious in a fast, high-contrast sprite game like this than it would be in some other games.  The movement through menu elements with the D-pad is capped to a certain rate, such that your input when trying to move around the menu WILL be swallowed.  None of these things by themselves are too bad, but all of them turned me off of this game.  The enemy AI is incredibly basic.
In spite of all that, it's not a bad game, hence my recommendation, but only if all of this sounds fine to you.
Key was provided by VDO Games and Dietrich Online Services.
