I played SteamWorld Dig quite a while ago mainly because, despite the fact that it looked like something I’d enjoy, people kept praising it. Unfortunately the game didn’t meet my expectations but I still found it to be a good game overall. All this to say that when I heard that there was a new game of the SteamWorld series coming out I got a little bit skeptical. When I eventually saw the game itself I knew the chances of enjoying this were far greater than the previous one.
, they caught my interest right there.
In SteamWorld Heist you get to play as Piper, the captain of a ship of Cowbots which is on the run from Royalist forces due to alleged acts of treason, piracy and smuggling. The Royalist forces are led by the Queen and are committed to rebuilding their planet that was shattered a long time ago but, despite their noble intentions, they tend to extort other Cowbots for resources in order to achieve their goal.
Our brave heroes decide it is enough and it’s time to help out the common folk so they start their journey by ridding the Outskirts of the Scrappers, a group of cowbots who use any spare parts of their fallen enemies to either upgrade themselves or increase their ranks. From there forward, the story escalates at a steady pace and along the way you’ll meet other friendly cowbots which can join your crew, each of them having their own unique character and background.
As I’ve mentioned before, the devs were inspired by games such as XCOM and Worms, but in essence I’d say they only took 2 key elements from both of those games. From the recent XCOM reboot, they’ve took the 2 moves per turn system in which you can move a character twice within a certain range, move once and then attack or use an ability or simply attacking which will cancel the second phase of that turn. From the Worm series what they’ve adapted to their formula was making it so that, in contrast with XCOM for example, instead of relying on a percentage chance of hitting a target, it is actually the player who aims the weapons and the various different items and abilities. This not only imposes another layer of skill on the player but it also makes the combat more interesting and fun due to the fact that a lot of projectiles (bullets, grenades, etc) can ricochet from walls.
The combat itself revolves around taking cover behind shields and other obstacles, tactics rather than pure luck based on hit chances, keeping an eye on alarm countdowns which make you proceed faster in order to not get hit by enemy reinforcements or turret emplacements. There weapon and enemy variety is just enough to keep things interesting, from close quarters weapons and enemies to long range fights and even teleporting enemies that can surprise you. The same goes for your crew, given the fact that each has their own set of abilities and play style.
As far as controls scheme go, i the game is a lot easier to play with a controller rather than with a keyboard and mouse, simply because with the controller you just move your right analog stick in the direction you want to attack, while on keyboard and mouse you have to click with the mouse and play around a bit in order to get the proper trajectory you want.
Besides the combat part of the game, which is what you’ll spend most of your time doing, between missions you can walk around your ship and talk to your crew and go to the space map and select your next destination. On the space map you can go to shops to buy new equipment (including hats), go straight for the main missions or do some side missions. Each mission takes place on a ship with a randomly generated layout and it can consist on collecting
(loot containers), killing a certain amount of enemies or rescuing someone and after that you need to move all your crew to an escape pod in order to evacuate.You can always go back and replay previous missions in order to level up your crew if you’re having trouble. Upon completing a mission you’ll get EXP which enables you to level up your characters, thus unlocking new abilities. Depending on the amount of swag you gather during a mission you’ll also be able to open containers which can either have water, which acts as a form of currency, treasures or weapons and other equipment such as hats.
As far as visuals go I don’t think there is really much that needs to be said, they are clean, good looking and fit the theme perfectly. I don’t think I’ve ever seen such good looking steampunk robots ever before. The change in scenery as you move to new zones is also very notable and the game never loses its charm.
Now, one of the biggest things about this game for me is the music. I looked it up and apparently the devs have worked with
, a group which I had never heard before but after looking them up I’m even more glad I played this game, they do an excellent job in setting the right mood at the right times in the game, mainly when you visit the bars and you can see the actual group there playing. Yet, one thing that I wish was in the game was voice acting, I feel like it could add a whole new level of character to the various characters in the game but alas..
If you’ve read this far you’ve probably got the feeling that I thoroughly enjoyed SteamWorld Heist, if you just skipped until the end then let me fill you in.

This program has some incredibly frustrating idiosyncracies, but also a strong core featureset, and a lot of potential.
First, am I the first to say this? The chunky 8bit stylization wastes an ungodly amount of screen real estate in the GUI. The minute I saw it in the trailer I thought it looked gaudy, gimmicky, tacky,  unnecessary and wasteful. I'm trying to draw some basic sprites in an efficient interface, not pretend I'm using an ultra lo-res monitor with an 1980s microcomputer. Lets keep in mind I paid for every inch of panel space I have, and if a program just throws it away, I'm basically losing money. I also finds this stylization highly distracting, though that seems to have been the opposite of its developer's intention.
Intention vs. Implementation:
The first problem is that it wastes so much space.
Another problem is the icons become cryptic. It was very hard to figure out very basic things about the program, which doesn't yet have a huge community online do draw knowledge from.
Here's the big one, something the dev probly didn't consider.
This interface looks *nothing* like any productivity program I have running on my computer.
And herein lies the big issue, I am constantly having my eyes pulled to the GUI elements looming in my peripheral with their (as of 2016 at least) highly sylized blocky pixels. That bold, jagged, upscaled unicode font is constantly screaming at my eyes to look at it.
I would love to just have this look like my normal computer, which is running in Classic mode, AKA it looks basically like Windows 98.
I edit video in a program that doesn't look like a piece of glass candy. My eyes ignore the UI and focus on the content I'm making. It's lovely. Importantly, the interface doesn''t *match the content*, so my perception never blurs the lines.
There are some serious concerns I have with the default layout. I was unable to find any way to change it on Google and the program does not make anything about itself obvious. I was finally able to change it thanks to developer response(thank you), and I can finally get to setting up a workflow.
Overall the program performs well, hasn't crashed, and the thing that has frustrated me the most is that these issues stood in the way of me using a program that does have basically all the features I need.
UI scalling has steep gradations only. Everything is too tiny or too huge.
Same with zooming in/out. Going from 100-200% in a single scroll-whell step is not very helpful.
Preferences menu will hopefully see some expansion in general.
a "Dark" skin would also be a godsend, as with all productivity software.
I have only used this program for a couple hours. I will likely update this review with more notes once I hit hour 40.

An interesting concept ruined by a hopelessly shallow combat system. Paint the Town Red is a sandbox game where you are thrown into a level and asked to eliminate everything that moves. The levels in the game include a bar, a dance club, a prison complex and a pirate cove. To accomplish your task, you can use just about anything in the environment, including chairs, bottles, dumbbells, electric guitars and more.
At a surface level, it reminds me of Dead Rising, where you have a decent-sized sandbox filled with trivial items that can be used as deadly weapons. Unlike Dead Rising, however, every item has the same moveset, save the very small number of ranged weapons available to the player. Clicking the left mouse button does a thrusting attack, while holding it down repeatedly performs a horizontal swing. Right clicking allows you to block enemy attacks, which greatly reduces damage inflicted on you. Throwing weapons and objects is a viable tactic too, although it often causes them to break. You can also kick enemies, which reminded me of Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. Unlike that game, however, there are not enough environmental hazards to kick your enemies into. Killstreaks are present too, giving the player three different supernatural powers that are gradually unlocked as they slaughter enemies. The first power is a simple shockwave that knocks enemies over. The next one is a berserk mode, that allows the player to deal massive damage to enemies with their fists for a short period of time. Finally, there's "smite", where the player shoots a finger gun at enemies, and a bolt of energy from the sky decimates them into thousands of tiny voxels.
This combat system may sound sufficient for a game of this type, but given the large arsenal of melee weapons, I was hungry for more variety. The aforementioned Dead Rising series also has a huge variety of weapons, but each individual weapon has at least one unique ability. The player character does not use baseball bats in the same way that they use a power saw. Not only are there a plethora of toys to kill enemies with, but picking up a new weapon instills a sense of giddiness, given that the player does not yet know how it will function. Paint the Town Red lacks this magic, because all of the melee weapons function in the exact same way, except for some differences in how damage is inflicted on the enemy (sharp weapons can slice through enemies).
It's a shame, because this game has a very entertaining damage system. Enemies are made up of tiny voxels, each making up a layer on the enemy model. There's a surface layer, a muscly layer, and a bone layer. Bashing an enemy's head repeatedly will cause it to slowly fall apart, eventually revealing their bloodied skull. I'd be lying if I said that the gory spectacle of Paint the Town Red didn't captivate me while I was playing it. However, gleeful violence isn't enough to save the game from being a major letdown.
There's only four sandbox levels available currently, and none of them really stand out from the others. They all have the same formula, where there are numerous, easily-defeatable creep enemies, and a handful of special enemies with unique weapons and a great deal of health. After completing all of the levels, I can't say I've felt the urge to go back and replay them, despite the inclusion of a timer, challenge mode and leaderboards.
It's worth mentioning that there's also an arena mode, where you're thrown into a colosseum and are tasked with killing off every last combatant. There are multiple waves, and the layout of the arena changes between each one. Sadly, the arena loses its charm very fast thanks to the same issues present in the sandbox levels. In fact, I'd argue that those problems are more apparent here, where the environment is relatively barren. Despite the inclusion of some environmental hazards like spinning blades, fiery tiles and spike traps, utilizing them usually just requires some cheap exploitation of the AI. This can become incredibly boring, as your kick has a cooldown that requires some brief waiting before you can kick an enemy into an obstacle again. Some levels feel designed around the AI's incompetence. One arena map requires you to lead a lone adversary into fiery tiles, which slowly dwindles down his very large health bar. It's painful, and it's made even worse by the lack of weapons lying around and the fact that some enemies can't be kicked into environmental hazards at all. Instead, you just have to hit them a few times, avoid their attacks and repeat ad nauseam for 5 or so minutes.
Player levels are interesting, and I'm glad they opted to include a level editor. The community levels are arguably more fun than the main game, taking you to interesting locales such as a rock concert, Christmas town and a Roman market. Even though they use the same weapons and environment pieces present in the developer-made levels, their larger scale and varied structures make them more fun to play through. There are also numerous secrets scattered throughout the better maps, with power weapons like shotguns hidden in hard-to-reach places.
In conclusion, I was very disappointed by Paint the Town Red. It's only in Early Access at the time of this review, and while I feel like it has some enjoyable qualities, the overall game becomes a slog too fast to warrant a recommendation. If the developers put more time and effort into the combat system, and designed the stock maps to be a bit more varied, this game could be a fun little gore-fest. Sadly, they seem more interested in developing new modes for the game, some of which (the arena mode) being completely at odds with the game's best concepts. Neighboring Islands is a pirate-themed visual novel from indie developers, BAD Team (Blue Angry Dog Team).
Neighboring Islands tells the story of the crew of the Siren Santy, a pirate ship plying its violent trade in the Spanish Caribbean waters in the early 18th Century. The game begins with the then-unnamed protagonist locked in the ship's hold, the last remaining of a group of prisoners. He's weak from hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, as well as torture and beatings. The other prisoners, it seems, have already been dealt with by keelhauling, and the protagonist knows that his fate will be even worse: left defenceless and alone with nothing on a deserted island in the middle of the ocean.
Neighboring Islands uses the Ren'Py Engine and a fairly traditional visual novel style throughout, with posed characters and portraits overlaid on mostly still painted backgrounds. The story and dialog are displayed in a semi-transparent text box towards the bottom of the screen.
It diverges from most other VNs in the style of the graphics, though, with characters and some foreground objects being posed and pre-rendered -- some even including animations -- giving the game a much more three-dimensional appearance. For the most part this looks pretty good, but character expressions are few in number, and many of them look somewhat comical. Some scenes are too dark, with the details hard to discern.
The developers have added a large on-screen button to access the menu, which is unnecessary and obtrusive. A standard small button on the main text box or even no button at all would be preferable. The little pop-up windows explaining certain piratical terms are okay, and might be useful for someone completely unfamiliar with them, but they seem unnecessary in my opinion. I found the title screen quite ugly, too; the black-and-white skull sketch part just looks out of place with the rendered part.
Typical of the genre, there are no graphics options beyond full screen / windowed mode.
The music in Neighboring Islands is very good. There's quite a large range of instrumental tracks and at least one with vocals: a haunting melody in the opening scene. The title music has a sort of dark, piratey feel to it. I noticed one very out-of-place track at the start of Chapter 2, but other than that the music was well chosen to complement the scenes of the story.
As with most VNs, the sound effects are limited to the occasional scene-setting sounds played at certain key points in the story. They're appropriate and well-made, but somehow still seem out of place at times, probably just because of their rarity.
There are no voices, which is a bit of shame.
Neighboring Islands doesn't diverge from the tried-and-tested VN formula used by almost every game in the genre. Visual Novels are a blend of two types of media: visual art and writing. To my mind, for a VN to be good overall, it really needs to have good visuals and good writing. I've discussed the visuals already; though perhaps an unusual choice for the genre, the combination of pre-rendered 3D, small animations, and drawn backgrounds actually works quite well. So what about the writing? In short, it's terrible. Simply awful. Cringeworthy, even.
"Viscous half-darkness wraps over most of the room. Dust dances in rare rays of dim light, somehow filling the premises with resemblance of life. Grated door encloses this uncapacious place ..." And it gets worse.
The story seems to have been very poorly translated from Russian and is desperately in need of a professional editor. It reads like something written by a pretentious, but illiterate, English major, who copied down a whole lot of fancy-sounding words and approximate meanings, but doesn't know how to string them together properly. Or perhaps it began life as a machine translation, and someone has had a go at fixing it. In any case, there are a lot of big words that don't quite fit, the tense is all over the place, there's incorrect punctuation and spelling, and so on. The grammar is really very bad. I can normally see what the writer was trying to say, but it's genuinely sad to see it jumbled so badly.
I will say, though, that I grew more attuned to it as I read. I suspect the writing might have improved ever so slightly, but I think I also became more versed at plucking out the important details from the Pidgin English text.
Some choices are included, but the non-linearity introduced by these choices is almost always short-lived, with most ending up with the protagonist dead and a new achievement awarded, or simply moving the story along the same route, usually with only minor temporary flavour differences. While the death scenes are sometimes amusing, the game really only offers the illusion of choice from most of its decision points.
The game has adult themes running throughout, including violence, gore, sexual themes, and even a little bit of nudity, but for the most part these themes are part of the story, rather than being merely gratuitous.
Finally, the story is currently unfinished. There are two chapters and the end of the second chapter is quite sudden, the game finishing with "To be continued". The third chapter was announced in June and work is ongoing; I'd expect it to be a free update for owners of the current game, since that's how the second chapter was released, but I haven't seen any official announcements that confirm this.
Pros:
+ Interesting style for a VN, with some very nice graphics
+ Pirates!
+ Steam Achievements and Trading Cards
Cons:
- Ruined by poor English translation
- Currently unfinished (but development is ongoing)
I struggled to make it through Neighboring Islands and then felt a rude shock at the abrubt second-chapter ending. The subject matter is interesting and the story should have been gripping in places, but it was ruined by the English translation. Though I would dearly like to recommend it, in its current state I just can't bring myself to do so. If an adult, pirate-themed visual novel interests you, then by all means take a look, but if you're planning on reading the English version, be prepared for a really rather awful translation that makes it hard to take the game seriously.

TL:DR - Extra-thick nostalgia glasses required.
Had this recommended by a friend who is way into star wars, and it was advertised as a tactical shooter.  Was on sale for like $2, so I figured I'd try it.
Long story short, it's like Halo, except not fun.  And I'm not even that big a fan of Halo.
It's a pretty average shooter, except it manages to be both frustrating and boring, as the game just sends seemingly unending waves of stupid enemies who eat up all your ammo.  The most challenging part of the game was finding enough ammo to kill everything, which isn't too difficult.
Weapon options seemed pretty lacking.  I got a couple bonus weapons, but ran out of ammo for them almost immediately.  90% of the game seems to just be full-auto with an incredibly inaccurate battle rifle.
As far as the 'tactical' part, there's setpieces around every map where you just tell your squad to entrench and do an action - like man a turret, snipe, throw grenades.  It sounds better than it is, and it sounds pretty boring.  And each squad member seems to be able to do everying equally well.  They were introduced as being some kind of specialists, but for the life of me I couldn't tell you who was supposed to do what.
Maps are just you running along a tunnel from point A to B.  There's no exploration, setting up ambushes, flanking, finding sniper perches, nothing.  Just move foward, shoot, repeat.
It just wasn't any fun.  And it's hardly a star wars game, there seems to be almost nothing I recognized, except the dorky skinny battle droids.  You could have slapped a MLP skin on it and it wouldn't have been substantially different.
In the end, it feels like a cheap halo clone, but is much, MUCH worse, despite being 4 years newer.
Could not recommend.  Couldn't make it 2 hours before getting bored.
Soundtrack is pretty good.  That's about the only positive thing I can say about it.

Please bear in mind, this is not an action packed game, it's pretty much a sim, which means some aspects of it can be mundane; but if your too broke to actually afford a pilots license, and unable to Uncle Rico your way back in time, then this game will do fine. It's easy to learn, and not nearly as painstakingly thorough at some of the other air combact sims out there (which are fun, but require a lot of time, and aren't exactly jump on when you get off work games).
If you're using a joystick, you'll need to assign all of the functions, including the X and Y axis. Don't forget to assign a key to the map, or you'll get lost like my dumb♥♥♥♥♥and get scolded by the AI squad leader in his oh-so polite English accent.
The flight controls are nice and fluid, they don't snap into dead-zones like some games, and they are quit comunicative if you have a force feedback stick. Even at medium the graphics are good. I still need to learn more about the games options, because in the 'cockpit' some instruments, especially important once like your heading compass are completely blocked by the stick. Again, the gps/map will save your butt. As good as the game is, it still leaves you wanting something more, but for a 4 year old game that's been modded to function much better with really good patches, you can't beat it for the price. Out of the trio of pixel art programs that I've used (GraphicsGale, PyxelEdit and Aseprite), Aseprite is definitely the easiest to get used to if you intend to do any animation. Gale is great usually but it can be a bit hard to get to grips with. PyxelEdit is great if you want to do tiling, but it's not very good for animation (no frame manipulation, movement, no cels).
On the other hand, Aseprite has all those things and more - it can open anything you can throw at it, it has a very intuitive timeline feature, it even has a fancy pixel-style interface.
It takes a little bit of getting used to, since the controls are quite a bit different than something like Photoshop (which Pyxel Edit's control system is based off of), but once you do get to grips with it, you can come up with complex animation in record time.
Here's a couple of examples I've made in it:

Another great advantage is that the developer keeps a close eye on what people ask for and does a good job introducing well-tested new features regularly. You can opt into the beta program via Steam, and I recommend doing so, as it allows you to export your animations at larger scales without having to change the size beforehand.
Probably the best program for spriting out there.

SO on the fence about this one! Short version: Homeworld meets X3, with big bugs and frequent crashes, but frequent auto-saving and short loading times to partially compensate. There are achievements for each of the endings - highest is 0.4%, total is 0.9%; that means less than 1% have even finished the game... Maybe the fact I have will add a little authority to my review.
Update: You know, I might go so far as to say ignore the positive reviews because they don’t know what they’re talking about. If you look at them, notice how many hours played and the fact these reviewers haven’t finished the actual game: xsmasher, Morally Bankrupt, templelord, and Cyrus (90 hours, must be a beta tester). I know this makes me look stuck up “I've finished the game, I'm H@rdc0r3!”, but we can see the highest-rated helpful positive reviews are likely beta testers. And if anyone else gets the game, they’re less than 1% likely to finish.
Longer:
Graphics: Cell shaded. Nothing special, but the models don't get boring or look ugly. Good.
When contolling ships (only in the first few levels) the ships will shake alot, like when you try to glitch through a wall and your character oscillates rapidly between two positions. The dev says this is due to "Intel graphics chips". Well I have a graphics card, but almost everybody has an Intel processor. Bad. When placing stations, icons for some items are very small (and the build method is unintuitive).
Story is alright, gets into improbable coincidence territory, but alright. Need to find if there's info on the character/faction backstories.
Ship-to-thip combat is ok. Like a flight simulator. Flight modes are kind of whacky. Cockpit, camera chase 3rd person, and 'command' view where you control the turrets. For fighters, cockpit view. For everything else, chase view. Command view is pretty worthless since you won't be dodging fire well that way. Turrets do auto-track with Shift+A, I think. There's also a view to move the camera around your ship and admire it. There are some command ship specific issues I'll address later.
Tactical mode (Homeworld) is eh. An issue that only appeared toward the end is that engagement rules and ship orders will revert. You'll see dudes fly halfway to a target (target's still alive), and they just turn around and go back. I don't know what causes engagement rules (tiny buttons!) to revert, but I've given the same order 5-6 times to a group only to watch them stop caring until I gave up. Ouch.
The command ship is also iffy. At least 4 of its abilites are worthless except a few parts in the story. Command: take over enemy ships! Except about 1/3 the way through enemy ships stop being capturable. Radiation field: damage yourself and anything right next to you! Useful for two engagements where enemy drones are trying to saw their way through your ship. Quick-ish reverse: accellerate backwards sorta fast. Rarely could that benefit you. Right side shield: temporary energy shield on the right side of your ship. By the time you get this, the enemy laser weapons seem to ignore the shield. Worse than having a million bucks on a desert island. The other abilities are also iffy: tractor beam the enemy, but make sure they don't hit your ship; rapid repair, but lose control of engines and inertia takes you to wherever. The ship does passively repair, too, which is way more useful. The main gun of the ship is only useful when upgraded 5/5 during the last 1/3 to 1/4 of the game.
Extra: The game is continuous - your fleet, ship upgrades, etc are preserved between areas/levels. It does feel like one big activity - first fighting miners, then running from overwhelming aliens, then fighting back against those aliens that were supposed to be overwhelming. Upgrade progression is awkward. Would have rather gotten most (except shield and the main gun) as soon as you got the command ship. Instead it's "you're at this point in the game; here is some research that should already have been done and some upgrades/repairs you should have already been able to access". The game is supposedly focused on numerical superiority, but your fleet usually forms up with the command ship and it feels like your fleet is really just one really big gun turret. The rare few times you send ships away from the main group is so you can control one of them, to act as distractions, or two instances where enemy fleets just sit there and you can irradiate part of them to death with a Bear. You'll lose/reload a lot, part from crashing, part because the game gives you a bunch of "FU" situations - the digger Cruiser you can't control, and figuring out how to keep it from drilling you to death (hit 'F'); Teardrop drones that latch onto your ship, and figuring out how to keep yourself alive (you die fast); aliens that can warp into the map wherever, and realizing they just completely bypassed your defenses. You do get an additional cruiser and carrier through the story, and the carrier's pretty boss, but they'll mostly chill far away from the fight so they don't die.
Awesome idea, but ultimately you just end up loading a lot to argue with your units that refuse to reposition correctly. And the dev is working on the second game so these issues are here to stay.
Thumbs up if the review is helpful.

Awesome game.  I had it on my wishlist for a while and finally had the extra money to buy it and I'm really glad I did.  There is a lot of control given to you in the game.  You can move your entire fleet with ease, set up formations multiple different ways, pilot each ship in your fleet or fire an individual turret.  The dev gives you multiple different control schemes; each one has benefits depending on the ship you're piloting.
The campaign has been challenging so far but you learn a lot in the earlier missions and you'll apply this knowledge to the missions to win.  You can tweak the difficulty if needed too.
There is a skirmish / quick battle mode with a bunch of scenarios.  You can set up base battles or just a 10v10 epic dogfight bonanza! Go nuts!
A guide is accessable in-game to check up on topics while playing.  It's pretty in-depth and reviews almost everything in the game.  Part of the fun is also figuring out how things work and experimenting.  I had fun sitting in a ship, equipped with a flamethrower (yep a mutha♥♥♥♥in' thrower of flame in space) clearing out an area of space while I parked the rest of my fleet back at the gate, told them to rest up for the next big fight.  There's a few ways to accomplish each mission, are you an RTS player?  Fine, go HAM on the Tac Map and RTS the♥♥♥♥♥♥outta this game, or you can #quickscope420blazit and pilot a fighter to go all Maverick on the enemy.  You can do both, almost at the same time.  Speaking about time, you can slow it down.  Well, you actually speed your brain up which gives the illusion of everything else slowing down, think NEO in the Matrix.  This bullet-time lets you set up your RTS strategy and then resume rocking enemy's worlds in a turret on your capital ship.
The dev is also very active in the forums/discussion boards, so drop him a line and you'll get a response.  (Well I can't guarantee that because I don't know the guy, but he responded to me within a few hours).
Great game, check it out.  I don't know of any others that give you this amount of control.

The Earth has been broken into a million pieces and the steam-powered residents that had lived on its surface have taken to the stars.
You are a gentle cowbot, a moisture farmer by trade, and your attempts to eke out a living are thwarted by the Royalists and a gang of vicious bots known as the Scrappers alike.
And so you turn to a life of adventure, the liberation of the common folk, and more importantly, heists!
.Gameplay.
You can use your keyboard and mouse or a gamepad. I prefer the latter, so I’ll be talking about those controls from here on out. The majority of gameplay occurs on the battlefield, though the moments between battle will be spent on the main map, which exists as a series of space ships connected. You can travel to each location by selecting it and more open up to you after you beat the preceding level.
There are two types of areas: battle field and hub (where you can buy equipment and recruit units). So, if you’re looking for a game where you can explore the rich universe, then this isn’t the game for you.
Before the quest begins, you’re given an information screen that shows you three icons at the top: whether you collected the Epic Swag, the number of units you can take into battle, and the number of stars you can get/have gotten respectively. Underneath that, you can find the objectives that you need to complete and are also given the option to change difficulty.
The different difficulties include casual, regular, experienced, veteran, and elite. Changing difficulty effects the penalty for failing a mission (you lose a percentage of your stored gallons from 0-50%), the number of enemies, how much damage enemies do, and their health. The higher the difficulty, the higher these stats, but also the more bonus experience you’ll receive at the end of the battle, so there’s a measure of risk versus reward here.
Once you’re satisfied with the difficulty setting, you can change your loadout. Here, you select the units you want to use as well as their equipment. Units have four equipment slots: a weapon, two utility slots, and a hat. The utility slots can be used for armor, grenades, first aid kits, etc, while the hat is purely cosmetic.
Quests consist of one main objective plus one (or two side, depending on the number of stars you can get) objective that usually (read: almost always) has to do with gathering the Epic Swag available on that level
And now, combat.
Combat is turn-based and you can swap behind units mid-turn if need be. You need to aim in order to shoot other units, so if you aren’t very good at estimating distances and line of site in pixels, then you’re SOL. Some guns have a laser sites available, however, so you can play with those until you get better at eyeballing distances.
You’ll  lead a small team—two to three units—through the bowels of an enemy ship and teamwork is key in order to make sure everyone makes it to the extraction point in one piece. Objects such as barrels can be used as cover. When attacking, you’re told exactly how much damage you’ll do (or a range if applicable).
After your glorious victory, you get to open up all of the swag bags and containers you picked up. Inside you’ll find Gallons, equipment, and objects solely for selling to make a profit. Epic Swag containers cannot be picked up more than once.
Experience is awarded at the end of every successful battle. It’s divided evenly between your units.
You’re also given a star rating based on: objective(s) (two stars), Epic Swag collected (one star), and any casualties (subtract one star per death).
*If a unit dies, they are reassembled once you go back to your ship. These units receive no experience.
Reputation is used to hire more crew. New crew starts at level 0, so it’s a good idea to go back to earlier stages in order to get them up to speed.
.Atmosphere.
SteamWorld ‘s brightly-coloured sprites are detailed and nice to look at. The Scrappers’ ships’ mechanical innards are appropriately dismal, and the pubs and bars that serve as your information hubs are contrastingly warm and well-lit. They also feature fantastic music via a “live band” of bots that sing wholly original tunes.
The game does a wonderful job of creating a grungy, dystopian world where the general populace consists of steam-powered robots and something as commonplace as water has become a currency. The bots “speak” in gibberish reminiscent of the older Legend of Zelda titles or even Animal Crossing and the script is rife with humour.
.Longevity.
It’s taken me about five hours to beat the first area—including the challenge stages, which are unlocked by playing through normally—on “experienced” and I managed to get all of the stars while I was at it. I could easily see sinking the promised 15-20 hours into this game, however.
The difficulties would normally offer greater longevity, but given that the difficulty can be changed at the beginning of a battle without affecting the reputation rating you got previously on another difficulty, there’s no real reason to play on a more difficult setting except to challenge yourself.
I’ll update this with my final verdict once I’ve completed the game.
.Pros and Cons.
.Bottom line.
The pros outweigh the cons for sure and, if you can forgive repetitive gameplay and a linear world, you’ll enjoy SteamWorld Heist. The cast is quirky and loveable, the music is great, and strategizing is fun.
With a range of difficulties and additional challenge stages, there’s something for strategy lovers of every skill level here. The game is definitely worth a look if you’re even a little bit interested in the genre.

Coming from the indie studio Image & Form, SteamWorld Heist is a delightful take on the turn based strategy genre. The pseudo sequel to 2013’s SteamWorld Dig, Heist shares many elements from the modern XCOM and Shadowrun series, albeit in the 2D space, and is just as good as its contemporaries.
Having never played the first game in the series, Heist was a great introduction to a world that is very reminiscent of the Borderlands and Firefly universes. The wonderful meld of western/sci fi and steampunk is a great match and is wonderfully realized in Heist. Special shout out to Steam Powered Giraffe who orchestrated a tremendous soundtrack that only enhances the setting of the game. Tonally, the game is very consistent and forms a solid identity.
One of the main hooks for Heist is that every level is procedurally generated. This allows for multiple playthroughs and grinding to avoid getting stale as fast since level layout and enemy location will be different each time. The other back of the box feature is that unlike XCOM, Heist’s gameplay is based purely on skill rather than luck. Don’t get me wrong, I love XCOM, but boy is it frustrating when you miss a shot with 95% accuracy and you have your gun square in the alien’s face. In SteamWorld Heist, you aim your shots, so the accuracy is completely up to you, which is quite refreshing. The game allows for both long and short ranged characters, but I found long range to be much more successful (especially when you have a rifle with a laser scope).
The game throws enough environmental and enemy variety at you to keep the 10+ hour adventure fresh and well-paced throughout. There is a story there for those who want it, and while charming, I found it took a backseat to the rock solid mechanics that the game presents you. Speaking of great mechanics, I especially loved the fast forward feature when moving your team around. When you select a teammate to move around, you can skip the running animation entirely by holding down a button. This was a wonderful addition as it can make certain missions much less tedious as a result.
SteamWorld Heist is an entertaining sidescrolling, turn based strategy game that can be played as casually or as hardcore as you’d like. The art and music are lovely and the world is quite amusing. There is plenty of game to be had here, especially if you plan on doing New Game+. In addition, there is a somewhat sizeable DLC at a nominal price that is well worth the investment. I greatly enjoyed myself with Heist and hope to see more games from this universe in the future from a great up and coming studio.

is an action, strategy, adventure turn-based strategy role-playing game. In
the primary objective is to start from your home ship, navigate through the map towards your next destination and fight off enemies known as scrappers. The aftermath is to survive each mission, fulfill all objectives and gather cool swag which includes points to buy weapons, upgrading storage space and buying repair kits, only one each wave per character which can be used once on each mission. It is published and developed by Image & Form, a company I have not heard of until now.
The story consists of two main ways in which it seems to be told, one primary way and then one through still cutscenes. The still cutscenes are told through a very old narration style, radio broadcasting. The other way to get information about the community and what is going on with the scrappers is to interact with the non-playable and playable characters on the ship. The two starting characters are Captain Piper Faraday, practically the strongest member at the start of the game located on the ship and throughout the game in my opinion, the main character; and Gabriel " SeaBrass" Stubb. According to the game SeaBrass " lost everything he held dear when the Royalists monopolized the whale oil industry." Each character in the game have different strengths and weaknesses. They are divided into different classes which determine what weapons are compatible for them to use.


It has a system where you collect epic loot and bags of gold call ' swag' which earns you reputation, normally water which is used as a resource giving you your in-game currency. The loot can range anywhere from weapons of different rarities and types; items that sell high in the market to be able to purchase more weapons; inventory slots; armor and things like grenades. You gain reputation by fulfilling either most or all of the objectives during each mission. Most missions at the beginning are very short while increasing later on in enemy types, increased weaponry and increased shields on some enemies for protection.  Reputation is used to hire more members to be on your crew during tougher missions while also at the same time being used to unlock more areas to explore on the map. This means that if you are short of reputation, you will have to fulfill certain objectives to increase your overall stars at the end of the mission adding more to your overall reputation.  The experience points system is based on how many current members are on your team and any casualties that have occurred.

The primary shortcoming within this game is the turn-based strategy aspect of the game that is mundane and boring for some people. I am one of the people included in that minority that finds the game too simple with a lack of complexity that I held within my preconceived expectations before initiating the game. While the shooting mechanics are fun, and as many have said, the aiming and cover system is purely identical to the Worms series, it fails to deliver much action which I was expecting much more since this game combines action, strategy and role-playing within it. While it is a good game, the gameplay mechanics seem to me, average at best.
Since it is a turn-based combat system, you are instructed to take turns moving your characters having to pre-select which direction and position you want to go. Your movement is limited by the distance you can travel in one given turn. The trick is to move once, and then try to aim accurately at the opponent, the scrapper's heads in order to do an increased amount of damage through headshots. It is also wise to use environmental objects to your advantage in order to take out enemies quicker such as fire barrels. One thing I enjoy and like that this game does right is the physics and ricochet mechanics of propelling bullets in different directions, especially when using weapons with laser sight.

The user interface is very simplistic. Once you return back to your ship upon exiting the escape pod, you are able to access the pause menu which brings up your inventory. Inside your inventory you can sort your weapons, utilities which give you boosts and advantages in combat and even sell your highly valuable collected treasures to receive more in-game currency. Other than that, mainly equipping weapons and utilities is the only main function of the whole interface. The 'Outsider' downloadable content is worth it for new missions, new loot, a new character named Fen and great new weapons.
•Excellent use of gun selection and aiming mechanics
•Great use of physics, cover and character design
•Missions are quite short in duration
•Controls are simple to use without overdoing it
•New Game +
•More content from the ' Outsider' DLC pack
•Mundane and repetitive gameplay even though I am in the minority for this, primarily boring because it follows the Worm system of tactical positioning which I have never been a fan of
•I wish the game was much more complex for a turn-based strategy game
•Combining the role-playing elements in this game with turn-based strategy in the way the story is presented distracts me from all the good things this game attempts to do right
•The downloadable content should be separate standalone content that should be available within the main game menu so those players that might not want to spend many hours playing this game will not have to wait until progressing gradually in the storyline having to know of Fen's history in order to be able to play the new character Fen and the new missions to unlock the downloadable content in-game.
•Honestly, the pricing for the main game would sell better I think at around the $14.99 price range full price while the downloadable content should stay at the price it currently is.
While the game is good in my own opinion, I do recommend it as a nice arcade game. However, it feels average at best mainly due to the simplicity which just disencapsulates the intellectual side of me.  Graphics seem average to me, the storyline seems mediocre and the turn-based combat lacks depth as far as positioning and options. While the controls are fantastic, the music is decent and the Charlie Brown type inaudible dialogue that relies fully on text, captioning is brilliant, it suffers most for me by not seamlessly blending these elements in together as well as I think it could have been done ported to the personal computer. It executes itself ok, but I expected much more from a $20.00 title for other people to sink their time into.

As i think you have already discovered from trailers and game description that SteamWorld Heist is an Turnbased 2D game where tactics are like in XCOM series with obstacles where to hide, move to certain distance and you can shoot or sprint and be done with the turn and then shooting mechanism (for most guns) is like from Worms series where you can aim and see where the bullet will land and you can use walls, objects, etc. as a way to ricochet your bullets!
Basically game's objectives are mostly breaking into ships and do objectives (and side objectives) and you can adjust your difficulty before entering mission (more harder difficulty you choose more exp you gain so being greedy can cause you death and lose lots of currency) and replaybility on same missions is huge since every time you do the same mission the ship is procedurally generated so no ship is alike. There is also limit how many crew members can you have per particular mission. After you defeat mission you are given stars (1-3) depending on how did you do and it is also used as currency for certain things, so there is real incentive to get your missions done perfectly. Games story is pretty good (with lots of humor) and graphics and sounds fit very nicely to this game! Also helping with replayability is that after you complete the game you get new game+. SteamWorld Heist: The Outsider DLC is recommended purchase since it adds new character, items and missions with storyline!
This is pretty unique game and if you like turn based games that require tactical thinking with some RPG elements mixed in with good story (and humor) and good replaybility and DLC's worth their prices you should buy this ASAP!

At first, it seems like a simple idea on paper, Half-Life with multiplayer, no biggie! However in execution it can fall flat on its face rather quick.
Lets start off with the good things,
1. It's Free: you dont have to worry about paying anything in this game and its highly mod-able which allows you to edit the game the way you want it to be.
2. Graphic Boost: Everything certainly looks alot prettier along with some new weapon reskins and the models look pretty gorgeous even when examined up close.
3. Better AI: Half Life 1's AI was almost ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the AI had a hard time going around corners, had trouble targeting more than 2 NPC'S or Players and the Grunts completly forgot that a grenade was under their feet if they got hit by you. Now its alot more consistent.
4.New Enemys: Throughout Half-Life 1, and Blue Shift, you would constantly fight the same aliens and zombies over and over again, sure they would throw a new enemy like the Tentacles but even those were practically a joke. Sven Co-op makes the enemies more varied and even brings back scrapped enemies and cut enemy features from the original Half-Life (such as the scrapped Kingpin, Panthereye and the Human Sergeant and for enemy features, Aliens slaves able to ressurect their partners and so on).
5. New Weapons: Most of the original Half-Life weapons were changed to be unique in their own way (such as the MP5 changed into a M16 assualt rifle with M203 grenade launcher) and new weapons were introduced (such as the Uzi and the scrapped XM213 Microgun or otherwise known as the Minigun in Half-Life 1) .
Now, lets start with the bad things,
1. Framerate Killer: In maps where NPC's and lighting effects are heavily used or there is more than 6-8 players, your FPS can significantly kill itself in the process causing FPS lag and other problems. The FPS can be "slightly" boosted through lowering the aspect ratio but it still dosent help for bad computers.
2. Playing a new game by yourself is suicide: Excluding certain maps, Every map you go on when you start a new game will be put on survival mode (You take much more damage, but you recieve more health and armor regen and if you die you have to restart the current map your on and you only have 3 tries). This is especially terrible in maps where high damage NPC's or trapping NPC's such as Barnacles (You cannot shoot back at them if you get caught in their tongue),Grunts or any bullet/laser based enemy which are commonly used in most maps, is horrible for unaware or oblivious players. You cant even turn it off without very, VERY complicated setups and commands.
3. Easy to troll: I remember numerous times where a player would block a crucial air vent for progression and wouldnt move away, and most servers dont even allow voting which makes them impossible to move.
4. Everyones a weapon hogger: Literally just about every player I've come across will make a bum rush to a weapon or ammo pack  just so they can keep it to themselves before dying 5 seconds after they got it, its terrible on maps like the Half-Life 1 campaign maps (or other maps for that matter) where weapons and ammo dont respawn and your left with a dinky little healthpack.
So overall, I would say just buy the original Half-Life games and mods, sure the half life games are kinda pricey but trust  me, you will have a lot more fun playing by yourself than with multiple people. Sven-Coop encourages you to play with a friend or more but honestly, its just such a bad idea when executed that it just simply trips over and hit its face flat on the ground.

I like the concept of the game, top down heist game is a great idea. The execution however leaves a lot to be desired. This game has a lot of balancing issues. The starting guns are very poor, the stealth pistol cannot be used effectively against heavies since it just doesn't do enough damage to them to put them down before they shoot back. The gameplay is also heavily biased towards stealth, you are far less likely to succeed if you go loud. This is partly because the weapons come with a very limited amount of ammo, the rifles and the SMG's only only carry two spare mags which you would go through very quickly if a few heavies show up. That wouldn't really be an issue if the available arsenal reflected that but that's not the case. At least half of the guns are loud and stealth guns come saddled with lower damage. You will also quickly discover that there is a meta for a good loadout, there are two or three guns that combine stealth and good damage and that means that the rest of the loadout is almost worthless. Tacticals also have only a very small number of viable options, for example you would be crazy to take grenades over throwing knives.
Another problem with the game is that there are no intermediate saves. This becomes a major issue if you decide to go for "Completing primary objective undetected" challenges of which there are 15. Say you stealthed 95% of the mission but the last guard spotted you? The entire attempt is down the drain. This brings me to another problem, usually in coop shooters, if stealth goes badly your partner can back you up and you can complete the mission loud. This isn't the case here since the MP is completely dead. You stuff up here, you better place mines and grab loud weapons quickly and hope for the best.
Lack of content is another issue with this game. There are only 15 heists spread between 5 different areas so not only is there a very limited amount of missions but the areas are also recycled between those missions. Games like Payday 2 get around this by introducing procedurally generated layouts, this helps the replayability value immensely. This isn't the case here, the areas and even the guard and item placements stay exactly the same.
On a final note, I would like to make a warning for achievement hunters, there is at least one broken achievement in this game. "Bags for life" does not unlock for on either of my two PC's. It does not unlock while meeting the minimum requirements of the achievement or even by picking up every single loot bag in the map and it does not work on different heists either. This is unlikely to ever get fixed because the game has been abandoned by the developer.

Overpower
Still In Early Access
Overpower can be best described as a combination of MOBA and MMO genres. It is a third person shooter where you have multiple game modes at your disposal. The game modes available here are Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Last team standing, control points and critter capture, all of which are pretty basic affairs for a multiplayer focused game. The gameplay of Overpower is fast and fluid where there is little to no complaint about the standard shooting. There are 4 classes available in Overpower which are the main selling point. They are as follows:
Assassin
Mage
Rogue
Archer
As is visible, all of the classes play very differently and bring a lot of different abilities to the battlefield. They all have choices of different weapons and a class ability. There is also a gem ability aside from the class abilities which are more unique such as cursing an assassin’s knife which does huge damage to the opponent. Each hero comes with his/her own 5 special gem abilities which if used correctly can turn the tide of a battle. There are 10 maps in total to play around in which is a fair amount considering it’s still in early access. The graphics of Overpower reminds me of games like Orcs must die, which I adored. There is a cartoony feel as you play the game and even when it is low-res, it looks lovely. There is a very serious lack of players online which might not be that big of a trouble when the game comes out of development. There are a couple of bugs here and there too but nothing game breaking. The game is receiving patches and updates at a fairly fast rate which makes it look like a game with high potential. Overpower caters to a lot of gamers needs with good graphics, a fair amount of maps and game modes and fleshed out character classes. This is a game which can take the full and proper use of early access and be a great game when it comes out.

Filthy Lucre is a Top Down Shooter with tactical, stealth and espionage elements, that also plays as a Heist game set in a crime-filled London. You have to recover "Stolen" goods for an old man named Lucre, who has hired you to do his dirty work. It's up to the player to quietly, or loudly, retrieve those goods in 15 missions scattered throughout 5 different locations, with an incredibly smart AI that certainly won't forgive the smallest of mistakes.
Now, if it weren't for me telling you about it, you wouldn't be aware of the controls and mechanics. This game doesn't do what many others do of giving you a tutorial sequence. Don't get me wrong, there are tutorials that teach you about the game's mechanics like the HEAT system and  bigger threats like unkillable Elite Attack Squadrons that will stop at nothing to kill you. But these tutorials are shown under the pause menu during gameplay and in the hub world. If you don't know this, you are basically throwing yourself in without being aware as to which button does what. In the early stages, the game gives you plenty of occasions to test out new ways to execute enemies, or work on your accuracy. Thus, it’s teaching you how to do the basic stuff through its own level design, and as such, I'm so glad to see that there are games out there where you’re treated with respect instead of teaching you how to do everything in a sloppy intro sequence.
This, however, will not prepare you for what could possibly be one of the most tense and difficult indie games out there. The game is hard, very hard actually. As soon as the first stage begins you'll see many of the aspects that make this game's Artificial Intelligence look like it's going to viciously hunt you down. First off, corpses don't disappear. You have to dispose of them with Body Bags and to be 100% in the clear, you gotta take that bag all the way back to the place you started at. Otherwise, you risk another guard finding out about his buddy being stuffed in a bag, and he will start calling reinforcements. Then, the AI has a keen eye and can see a lot and has some hard to tell patterns that will make you start planning things 3 steps ahead. Otherwise, you'll risk being spotted by another random guard who is walking by as you murder one of his friends.
Even with its technical and gameplay hiccups, FIlthy Lucre is a great example of how a game can be challenging and teach players the ropes of the game with its level design. The AI certainly won’t slack off and it’s going to keep any gamer considering their strategies the whole way through. There might be glitches and technical issues but these are a few and far between and shouldn’t mess with your gaming experience as a whole. The graphics and sound are gorgeous and with the game being such a bargain of costing around 7.79 dollars at the moment, it certainly is a great addition to the collection of any heist games fan. I can’t in good faith recommend this to a casual player or someone who wants to be entirely reckless with top down shooters, since there is almost nothing that will welcome them to the genre. But I can certainly recommend Filthy Lucre to the hardcore gamer that loves their fair share of challenge every once in awhile and is open to trying new things and mechanics. With all that said, this game is simply great.

is an indie tactical stealth game, that challenges you to sneak around, staying to the shadows and silently take down enemies, or else bring out the big guns and blast through anyone who gets in your way.
Each mission explains who you are dealing in with and as you slowly steal back your patrons treasures, you will be able to display them proudly within a vault inside of your hideout.
You will be forced to deal with different types of enemies, and a host of different technological security measures such as cameras and lasers. Find inventive ways around them, or hack the systems and disable the alarms before causing chaos. There are also always a number of secondary objectives to complete, such as never being seen or robbing extra, hidden stashes in optional areas.
The game is displayed in a typical top-down, isometric view. The visuals are good and pretty modern looking. And whilst parts of the UI and menus do look a little clunky and lack polish, the animations are smooth and the backgrounds are absolutely excellent.
The audio is generally of good quality, the voice acting in particular is excellent and this really works well to flavour the murky London underworld you are exploring. The sound effects are likewise good and plentiful, whether you are picking a lock or destroying electrical conduits.
is a fantastic addition to the indie stealth genre. The missions are varied and memorable, the large choice of weapons and equipment are excellent, and the addition of co-op play is just the icing on the cake.
All in all,
is just a lot of high quality fun.

1.It's more like a novel with variations in the narration then a choice novel.
2.It is very well written and the author style is his own choosing, I personally don't mind MC not having quote because his thinking actually melt with what he says... and you understand this at the end of the game, can't spoil you more.
3.Well ok you don't make any choice and don't leave any real impact but the narration DOES vary upon your choices. I'm afraid I can't recommend this product. As the author of Fatehaven seems to have missed the point of interactive novels, namely the part where they're interactive. I will admit that I haven't finished the whole game, as I'm hoping to get a refund, but judging by the first four chapters, the story flows more like a novel, and, to be fair, is well written and enjoyable. But that's undermined by the fact that the 'decisions' you make in this story have little consequence outside of choosing the gender, sexuality and name of the MC.
Otherwise, all choices lead to the same conclusion, with a little varying dialogue beng the only real difference between them. Entire pages will pass by without a single decision at all during the "serious" moments of the story. Your characters personality is also set in stone, with them constantly being a pervert (which can get kind of annoying) or automatically having certain opinions on things.
But the biggest example of how linear this game this would have to be the inclusion of the "corruption" stat. As the name implies, it determines how evil your character is, starting at zero, but steadily rising the more you kill people, or the more people die. There's only one small problem, as listed above, none of your decisions matter, so the corruption stat will simply raise automatically, independant of any choices you make. No really, mine rose from 0 to 20 during one of the earlier mentioned moments where pages pass without there being any decisions from you.
Worse yet, is the illusion of free will they try to create in the game. For example, in battle, you have two choices, kill the opponent with X, or kill the opponent with Y, that's it (Either choice raises your corruption level, btw). Why not have an option to knock them out or restrain them? Especially if you're going to have this "corruption" stat be a part of the game, you could have choosing a non-lethal option lower it instead of raise it. But no, that's too much interaction for this interactive novel.
Final verdict: 3.5/10

Neighboring Islands is a corny, weird visual novel that I actually enjoyed because of how odd it is.
You can tell the creator put in a lot of effort to flesh out characters, the world and storyline. They clearly cared about what they were making.
The game follows standard visual novel formats. The only gameplay involved is the occasional choice that can either lead to your death CYOA style or it will slightly alter the dialogue.
The story and characters are not incredibly well written but it's clear the developer tried to make it interesting which I respect. It feels very much like a visual novel you would find on a flash website back in the mid 2000's.
The character designs look very odd, especially the faces. It's that weird 3D model look that is very cheap to utilize but never makes anything look real. Kids especially look very off.
The game took me roughly an hour and a half before it cut off chapter one on a cliff hanger. You might as well wait until all the chapters are released if you are at all interested.
Overall it's hokey, corny and kind of weird, but it was actually kind of entertaining because of all that for an hour or so.

Neighboring Islands is a pirate themed visual novel. With the first chapter currently out it can provide around 2 hours of gameplay/reading.
The story is about as classic, as a pirate story can get. There's a pirate ship, a greedy captain, a mutiny, a shipwreck, and a tropical island. The main character, a reasonable Irish man O'Sallivan with natural leadership skills, is sick of the insane plans his captain keeps making. There comes a point where he can take no more, and along with some of the crew, he decides to rebel against the reckless leader. Things don't go so well, and O'Sallivan along with a French cook, and Tim, the young powder monkey, ends up on a mysterious tropical island inhabited by huge snakes, crocodiles, and savages.
For a fan of the pirate theme, this game is a light form of entertainment. A little easy reading, when you have some time on your hands but don't feel like actually playing a game. Like many visual novels this game does not have voice acting, therefore the reading is all on you. Whether you find that to be a flaw is entirely subjective. I personally prefer reading myself, over a voice actor going through the text, therefore I enjoyed it.
The art is pretty high quality, particularly when showing ships at sea. My personal favorites were the panels showing sharks, as they were done really well, and left me feeling slightly uneasy.
The music is simple, and slightly repetitive. It's mostly reminiscent of typical tavern music in a pirate movie. You can almost imagine a bunch of drunk men singing along to it. It fits the theme, and doesn't get in the way, or distract you from the story.
The big downfall of this game however is the writing. Clearly not made by native speakers, the English is somewhat flawed. There's grammar mistakes, there's misspelled words, and there's just words used incorrectly in context. For a visual novel that you have to read yourself it's a big problem. Since the game is still worked on, I'm hoping these things will be ironed out soon.
To summarize - the game is a simple pirate themed visual novel without voice acting. It presents a classic pirate story, with good quality art, and neutral music, that doesn't get in the way. It's biggest flaw is the use of English in the game, which is full of mistakes, and makes it more difficult to enjoy the story itself. However this may be soon fixed, and it doesn't make it impossible to understand.
For the price, and with the note that it's still being worked on, I would consider this game worth buying if you enjoy visual novels and pirates.

A pirate-themed Visual Novel! Now that’s something you don’t see everyday, on Steam or otherwise. Intead of another cookie-cutter love story between awkward highschool students or Japan in general, off we sail to the Caribbean for a good ol’ fashioned journey motivated by greed and revenge. Developed by the rookie BAD team, their first Steam project is anything but bad.
You know the drill, especially if you’re fans of this gaming genre. In the case of Visual Novels, the gameplay revolves around the storyline. They fuse together in fact. I will still avoid any spoilers but I can reveal to you the main characters at least. I’m glad the developer didn’t draw inspiration from any pirate movies or novels and went for an original plot. Neighboring Islands’ hero is the pirate helmsman Robert O’Sallivan, a mutineer against his uncle, the pirate captain Richard Habbard (who serves as the game’s initial antagonist).
The mutiny goes horribly wrong but before Robert can be executed by his ruthless relative, an unusually powerful storm damaged Habbard’s ship, “The Siren Santy” beyond recovery. Slowly sinking but close enough to a mysterious island, the captain flees along with a few of his loyal subordinates, leaving O’Sallivan trapped on the doomed vessel. Luckly for our protagonist, he still has friends of his own and makes a daring escape from the Siren and onto the same island as his murderous uncle. You can discover the main plot and its subplots on your own. Hopefully I got you intrigued already.
The visuals reminded me of the Myst series. 3D artwork that is skillfully rendered and also a far cry from the classic look that the vast majority of Visual Novels (VN) go for. One thing is certain, the game looks great even without anime-style drawn characters. It’s also not the type of 3D that might put a strain even on low-end PCs so you musn’t worry that Neighboring Islands will not run on a laptop, for example. The fact that it scales around your monitor’s native resolution is a big plus in my book. Far too many VNs seem to hit the ceiling at 1080p for some reason. Even at 4K, the fonts were crisp and large enough that they could be read from a distance. The artwork is featuring enough diversity and attention to detail, that I can’t find a single flaw to it. You even have certain maps and events during the storyline, displayed for future observation in the Extras tab from the Main Menu.
I like what I saw but I couldn’t say the same about what I heard. More precisely, what I DIDN’T hear. No voice acting at all? Not even a few words at the beginning of each phrase? C’mon BAD team. I really wanted to praise you guys for not sticking to the generic VN formula, but only the soundtrack and occasional sound effects will never replace some proper voices actors giving life to the colorful cast of characters already present in Neighboring Islands. There are apparently Russian dubs, but they cannot be set from the in-game settings. It's a region lock issue and the dev team should at least release an update that might allow worldwide players to read the English subtitles while listening to the Russian voice acting. I know it's a compromise but frankly, any language is better than silence. I am really disappointed that I couldn’t hear some nice English, Irish, Scottish or Welsh pirate accents but at least we have AC IV: Black Flag to cover that front. Still the finest pirate-themed video game of recent years.
The gameplay is so simple, to the point of becoming too easy. You read either on auto-speed or at your own pace, what the character have to say and from time to time, you can choose from several options that translate into a branching course of action. From my experience with these choices, they are mostly just an illusion. Only one choice shall yield the outcome necessary in progressing the storyline. The rest of them invariably result in death and Game Over. Why should you even bother?
Because most of the game’s Achievements can be obtained by “rewinding” the story or loading a previous save file and experimenting all the choices and their less pleasant results. So you shall have to appreciate at least the attempts at creating replay value. The buttons to skip or rewind the dialogue, remind you at all times that you’re playing a Visual Novel. Is "playing" the right term? You are mostly witnessing the events play out before your eyes. Never really understood how you can refer to VN gameplay but that didn’t stop me from owning and giving some of these titles, a well deserved chance. Curiosity killed the cat though…
Even if you’re not a fan of Visual Novels in general, you will still find Neighboring Islands’ story to be worthy enough to warrant a purchase. I’d say that it’s decently priced, considering many other VNs out there. Sure, there’s no nudity or big-eyed females, but you will still find an interesting tale regardless of how the characters are rendered. You get Trading Cards and easy to unlock, Achievements along with future plans for free DLC to expand the existing plotline. You really can’t ask more from this developer.  Once they straighten out the few lingering typos, you can overlook the absence of voice acting at least partially.
+ Interesting graphical style.
+ Captivating storyline and characters.
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards.
- Some typos within the English subtitles.
- The illusion of choice.
- No voice acting.

I have played the story, but not the multiplayer as it doesn't work. I'll review the story, enemies, weapons, ect.
My opinion on the overall game is about an 8.6/10. Only because some parts seemed a bit repetitive.
Main Story:  The main story was pretty good in my opinion, some parts of the levels seemed repetitive, but enjoyable. The main goal is straight forward. Your the leader of an elite commando squad, Your job as commandos are to infiltrate, kill, destroy. No questions asked. I don't want to really talk about the story so I don't spoil it, but I'll say where you go to for each mission. The first mission is quite obvious really, you start on genosis. There you experiance the first battle of the clone wars, and go into depth on a part of what happend. The second mission is on a ghost republic ship, it's your job to find out what happend to the ship. The third misson is near the climax of the clone wars, on the planet kashyyyk. There you take the fight to the jungle and fight along side the wookies.
Characters:  Delta 62 is by far my favorite character, very enthusiastic and funny at times. Delta 07 is your very dark and brutal character, he's enjoyable aswell. Delta 40 is your tipical soldier, he doesn't have that much intresting diologe, but still a great part of your team as he's extreamly loyal.
Enemies:  As far as old NPC's go the enemies are actully pretty good at killing you, they swarm you and your team so you have to out smart them which is fairly easy most of the times. You fight your typical battle droids, battle droid's (Light Infantry), Super battle droids (Medium Infantry), Droidaka's (Heavy Infantry), spider droid (Tank). Then you have your Geonosian's light and medium variants, Finaly we have Trandoshan's, they have  light, medium, heavy variants in their ranks.
Squad Gameplay:  This is by far the best squad based game I've ever played, and the squad mechanics are very basic and smooth aswell. Move there/Place bomb/slice or heal, Come to me, kill anything you see, Cancel/Get off equipment, kill specific target. These are most of the squad commands I can think of off the top of my head.
Weapons:  For this being a star wars game, there aren't a lot of weapons. However I like the way your standard blaster changes into specific weapons. These vary to sniper rifle, to granade lancher, to basic again. you then have your simple pistol. Theres certain weapons you can pick up through the game if wan't to use them.  You'll probably use the pistol the entire/most game like I did as it seemed to do the most damage at times. It also has unlimited charge.
Graphics:  I'm the kind of person who doesn't care about graphics, so in my opinion they looked quite well for their age (14 year old graphics, and they still look decent). If you want to run this game on a laptop you can do just that. I ran this game on my laptop and desktop. I got and average of 16-30 fps on my 6 year old laptop with ultra graphics on, and well over 60+ fps on my desktop. You should have no problem running this game if you're on a 2009 computer. I don't see why you wouldn't.
This concludes my review, I'm sure I missed something that I can't think off the top of my head though.

In detail: a gorgeous steampunk robot Firely XCOM without the RNG shenanigans. The theme is fantastic, the art beautiful, the characters great, and the gameplay fun and rewarding. You manually aim all your shots, so you miss not because you didn't pray to RNGesus, but because your aim was off. The ricochet mechanic means you can do insane shots that involve bouncing a bullet off two pieces of cover, taking some poor bot's hat off (because it's shiny and you want it), and then hitting some other bot square in his face. Weapon design has good variety with enough special guns with unique characteristics that it's always interesting, and unlike XCOM (where you field your A-team wherever possible), mixing up your squad composition is necessary as squad size varies between missions, and different characters' strengths will play into different level layouts. Also, most of the levels are prodecurally generated, so you'll only see the same ship twice on special missions (ie, boss fights).
Overall a fantastic game.

It's a
great animation tool for 2D animation. I'm mainly a 3D animator, with over
hours of experience in Valve's Source Film Maker (as of writing this review) but this software is really simple to use. Just Incredible, really, I can't believe how good this is.
Many other software can do what this software does - but Aseprite does it with the best user interface I could ever find. It never gets in your way, you don't feel like you are using some tools to draw and animate. You just feel like you are... Drawing and animating.
I am not an artist, but I could do the best walking cycle I ever did in my life, in just around one hour, because I was just doing animation, not fiddling around the software trying to figure out things.
If you know the basics of frame animation and know the main Photoshop keyboard shortcuts, you are ready to do some great stuff with this.
I recommend this to anyone who wants to make animated pixel art, for games or whatever reason they want.
I think it is also a great tool if you want to draw static sprites, but you won't be using it at its full potential.
Even if you already own Spriter, I would also highly recommend this, since they work with very different kind of animations and could really complement each other.
