What at first appears to be a statistically average looking puzzle platformer (following the linear and predictable path from left to right) Metrico+ soon begins to experiment with your expectations. Skewing the results of your actions and forcing you to change your methodology in order to reach a satisfactory conclusion.
In other words - jumping for that platform may not go exactly as you planned.

Digital Dreams infographic puzzler, Metrico, makes the leap from handheld platform to consoles & PC in the mathematically appropriate - Metrico+.
You play as a seeming ordinary man or woman traversing a world built on charts and graphs. Where in a clear (if a little strange) demonstration of cause & effect every one of your actions is liable to change the puzzle infront of you in some way or another. Be it jumping, running backwards or even resetting the level the platforms & obstacles react differently. And you must piece together the right order for these actions in order to clear that section.
Thankfully the developers have got rid of some of the goofier controls that were present on the PS Vita version but there are still some little niggles present. Like aiming with the analogue stick is way too sensitive. You can use keyboard and mouse but then you are left running around with trajectory lines cluttering up the screen. And there's not a lot you can do to change all this in the fairly anaemic settings menu.
That said this is an incredibly engaging little game. With some cleverly constructed puzzles, a beautiful low-poly aesthetic and a wonderfully ambient soundtrack. It's not for everyone and it maybe a little short but if you are into your puzzle games this is certainly one worth checking out.

Originally released exclusively for the Playstation Vita in 2014, Metrico was so heavily entwined with the Vita’s hardware that it was difficult to imagine how developer Digital Dreams would replicate it on other platforms. The short answer is that Metrico+ both is and isn’t the game released on Vita just over two years ago.
Its first half remains largely unchanged, though the visuals are now noticeably more robust, to the point your character will even stop at times to take it all in.  Metrico’s art direction was always eye-catching, but Metrico+’s enhancements make it outright beautiful. Low-poly mountains and sonically synced environments pulse and bend around pastel colors and bold shadows. Walking through a level and watching it come to life around you and because of you was already awestriking on the Vita, but when played on a larger screen at HD resolutions Metrico+ is finally able to fully encapsulate the player, and the experience is like being inside a piece of digital art. Which, of course, is what Metrico is and always was, but it has never felt as alive as with Metrico+.
But though Metrico+’s visual upgrade is welcome, it is the reinvention of the original’s control scheme that truly elevates the port over its forbearer. On the Vita, Metrico utilized every input method available to it, from touch to tilt to light and all the idiosyncratic spaces between. It was a marvel of hardware specificity, but in execution was not only clumsy but actively uncomfortable. Much as I attempt to champion the neglected Vita (whether out of a legitimate love or mere delusion, I couldn’t say), it’s an incommodious piece of plastic at the best of times. With a game like Metrico, I routinely had to set aside the game to uncramp my hands, as the act of playing for more than 15-20 minutes proved more than mildly painful.
Metrico+ avoids this, of course, by being playable with a standard controller or mouse and keyboard. But though a few of Metrico’s mechanics map cleanly to more traditional controls, others like those utilizing the Vita gyroscope and camera, required a more specialized approach. Rather than attempt to retrofit new controls onto these levels, Digital Dreams simply built new ones in their place. And while that does mean Metrico+ is forced to move away from the original, in the end, the loss of these levels make it a significantly better game and their replacements feature some of the game’s most phenomenal puzzles. Gone is the finicky color sensor, replaced with teleportation and ricochet puzzles, which make the most of Metrico’s mathematical setting while merging invisibly with puzzles carried over from the original. Metrico+ is the best kind of rerelease because it doesn’t just repackage the original game, it edits it and makes it better.
To some degree, the removal of Metrico’s quirky control scheme has caused Metrico+ to lose a bit of the original’s personality and abstracted magic. But when the end result is a game that is incomparably more playable, it is hard to argue for the Vita’s originality. Metrico was always an enjoyable platformer hosted on an unfortunate platform, so even if it took two years and the rebuilding of half the game, it is a welcome sight to witness Metrico+ finally save the original game from itself.

It's a testament to how well nailing an aesthetic can produce such an engrossing and enjoyable experience. Steamworld Heist conjures up a lot of fond memories for a Firefly fan, it wears it's influence proudly, and there are obvious analogues, the main character Piper Faraday is the captain of a small smuggling vessel, the villainous Scrappers who are pieced together from parts of dead robots are this verse's Reaver counterpart, and Royalists being the obvious stand in for the Alliance. The game permeates a Firefly vibe, but it's all got enough of it's own identity that it is far more than just trying to be Firefly: The Game and is very much it's own space western, there's some obvious love for the Western genre as characters will spout references to movies like The Good, The Bad and The Ugly. The music is also terrific, and I'd be remiss not to mention it, seeing as the band Steam Powered Giraffe who provided the soundtrack were an initial draw for me, and right from the title theme you can tell why their talents were sought.
Gameplay wise, it's been touted by many as XCom meets Worms, that's a fairly succinct way of putting it but I really don't like this trend of comparing nearly every turn-based strategy game to XCom, that's fairly reductive and the differences are more than apparent. But that aside, the gameplay is indeed extremely competent turn-based strategy, and landing some critical shots with bullet ricochet can be incredibly satisfying, or for that matter firing a grenade that bounces with a metalic ping before hitting it's mark doesn't seem to lose it's spark. You'll have many different crewmembers being recruited for you to take on various missions, each with their own particular traits and abilities, as well as unique personalities. It's a hell of a lot of fun.
Well recommended if you like turn-based gameplay, and if you are a fan of Firefly, this'll be right up your alley.

This game is extremely good. I wholeheartedly recommend it. It's like the developers took X-Com's combat system and made it 2D.
Pros:
-The Combat System
SteamWorld Heist was able to take everything good about X-com's combat system and make it 2D. It also made some tweaks that I like more than X-com. One example is that shots are not based off of dice rolls. What that means is that when I line up a shot, it will hit whatever I'm aiming at. If you line up the shot correctly, you can shoot enemies that are behind cover.
-The Art Design
The game looks amazing. The robots are detailed and cool looking. Space looks awesome and colorful. My favorite part has to be that you can collect a bunch of different hats for your characters to wear.
-The Soundtrack
The music is really good. It's well composed and it fits the space western theme that the game is going for. I really wish that it was available to purchase.
-Boss Fights
I was honestly surprised when I came across the first boss. The games that I have played similar to SteamWorld Heist did not have what I would call bosses. The bosses that I have fought each have had special abilities and multiple phases.
Cons:
-The Story
Let's get this out of the way first, I'm NOT saying that the story is bad. What I'm saying is that the story is the weakest part of the game. The beginning, middle, and end of the game felt really disconnected to me. I can't go into more detail without spoiling the plot, but know going in that it's not the best.
-Lack of Mission Variety
My biggest problem with the game is that a lot of the missions feel the same. Most of the time it's go in, kill bad guys, collect loot, escape. The game adds things like doors that won't open until you destroy a generator, but it never feels any different. I can't tell you which mission would be my favorite (excluding boss fights) because they all feel so similar. This is somewhat solved with The Outsider DLC, but that felt more like a bandage instead of a fix.
There you have it. Like I said earlier, I recommend SteamWorld Heist. The Cons section is a bit nitpicky because there is honestly not a lot wrong with the game.

Wow, where to begin. First of all, this is without question not only my favorite First Person Shooter of all time, but my favorite video game of all time. In fact, Republic Commando is the game that got me into PC gaming in the first place. I still remember years ago when it came out, seeing one of my friends playing it on his gaming rig, and being absolutely blown away by the concept, sound, graphics, and atmosphere. Now of course, this was back in 2005, so it may not blow people away any more with its graphics, but it is still an incredibly satisfying shooter experience. My steam hours in this game pale I'm sure to the many hours I poured into this game before I had steam and when I had the game on disc.
First of all, with Republic Commando it's the details that matter - and this game gets the details right, every time. You play as the leader of an elite spec ops squad consisting of four clone commandos called "Delta Squad" during the Clone Wars, and each Commando has his own distinct personality and traits. They even got the guy who played Jango Fett in Attack of the Clones to voice your character, a nice touch indeed. To this day, years later, I have been unable to find a game that has a more intuitive, responsive squad command system. It's simple, but effective, mostly because your squadmates are not the helpess AI that most games tend to have, but they can actually get the job done, regardless of if you're there or not. Take a round to the face and fall to the ground? No problem, the commandos of Delta Squad will carry on the fight, often engaging in hand to hand combat with the enemy (which is incredibly fun to watch) before they come back to revive you.
I won't go into all the nitty gritty details of gameplay. Suffice it to say, any fan of first person shooters and squad based games will be immensely satisfied. What I will focus on for the remainder of my review is the fact that this game gets every detail right, time after time.
First off, your squadmates. Holy hell, Lucasarts hit the ball out of the park with this one. Each commando has his own personality, and the dialogue between the four of them, including the commando you play as, nicknamed "Boss", is very entertaining.  They'll banter back and forth, often joking with each other and comparing dead enemies to each other's mothers (I mean, they
clones who don't have mothers, but still, it's funny). The game also has a cool feature where if you die, you stay there on the ground, waiting for your squadmates to revive you, and you can either order them to maintain their current orders or come rescue you, a nice touch for sure that makes you avoid the usual frustration with AI in games. You can also revive your squadmates if they go down, and the only time you have to go back to a save is when every commando has gone down - if one clone is still standing, the fight goes on.
And then, of course, there's the sound and the atmosphere - from the moment the game starts on Kamino to the brutal ending firefights on Kashyyyk, the sound design in the game is simply flawless. It's over ten years later, and this game is
a joy to crank up and enjoy with surround sound. The game takes place over the course of three large missions - one that takes place on Geonosis (and later in a Confederacy droid factory) at the beginning of the Clone Wars, one that takes place on an abandoned Republic ghost ship in space (my personal favorite), and one that takes place on Kashyyyk at the very end of the Clone Wars (tying in nicely with Revenge of the Sith, which came out right at the same time). Each environment is very well-designed, even by modern standards.
Beyond the commandos and the atmosphere, there's something else going on here too, something a little deeper. This is a
game. And Lucasarts got every detail right. There are no Jedi in this game. There is no "save the day" moment where the fate of the galaxy rests in your hands. You're simply another grunt, albeit a well trained one, in the long and brutal conflict of the Clone Wars. This is not just a Star Wars game - this is a war game. The Commandos get tired, they complain about the waves of enemies they face, they even seem to suffer from mental exhaustion sometimes, firing extra rounds into already dead enemies as if the stresses of war have become too much, even for a special forces clone. I'm still shocked that such a gritty attention to military detail was put into a Star Wars game, as you actually see the clones experiencing combat fatigue as the war goes on. Now, this isn't some super-deep Apocalypse Now or Heart of Darkness story, but it's still compelling nonetheless. Heck, the game even ends with a rock song, a sharp departure from the style of other Star Wars games, but a very fitting one nonetheless.
I'll quickly touch on the enemies you face, too. You fight waves of Trandoshan slavers, mercenaries, battle droids, super battle droids, droidekas, and other even larger enemies. And, on harder difficulty settings, it can be a challenge. Super battle droids can annihilate your entire squad in a matter of seconds, and that chubby Trandoshan with the shotgun running at you? Yeah, he can pump one blast right into your face and you're a dead man. Super Battle Droids in particular are nasty enemies in this game - they have much deeper voices than the movies, and fire what basically amounts to a rapid fire cannon out of their arm that can flatten you in two or three hits. Overall, the diverse enemies in Republic Commando contribute a great deal to the gritty feel of the game.
I could go on and on - about how awesome the weapon choices are, how immersive the ambient sound in the game is, how jarring and frightening some of the enemies you face are, but I'll leave that to you to discover when you buy and play this game, which I very much hope you do. To recap, if you like:
-Squad Based Shooters
-Any type of Shooter, for that matter
-Star Wars
-Shooters that get that gritty war feeling
-Immersive, intense single-player campaigns
-Sci Fi in general
-Sci Fi shooters
(You get the idea...)
Then buy this game for the cheap price it goes for now. One reccomendation, search for "Republic Commando graphics fix mod" on google when you get it, and before you play it install the graphics fix mod that pops up when you search. It updates the resolution of the game for modern PCs, improves the textures nicely, and fixes some minor bumpmappping issues the base game has.
This game gets Star Wars right, it gets military sci fi right, it gets squad-based shooters right, and in general it gets everything right. Get it, play it, and enjoy.

Fun so far. Think Xcom: Enemy Unknown, but with Co-op and RPG elements.

Updating after completing the main game, minus challenges:
Things I liked-
Soundtrack
costmetic customization (so I can change my look without altering effectiveness)
simple but effective controls and UI
an interesting story (coming from a newcomer to Shadowrun in general)
Things I didn't like-
Limited class abilities
limited gear
recycled maps and missions (understandable for side quests)
The majority of the voice acting, which is oddly only present for about 1/5 of the conversations in the game.
Overall, this game is excellent for the money (especially on sale) and very impressive considering the size of the team behind it. I've dumped a couple dozen hours into it and definitely have gotten my money's worth and then some. My largest complaint would be the way gear unlocks are staggared. Toward the middle of the third act, you unlock access to a myriad of new gear, but after going 15 or so missions since the last unlocks, you'll probably have enough cash to just pick up the best items for your build. It's not like it's a "this thing has better stats in these categories and this thing has better other categories," as much as this is better than that. This takes a relatively large selection and narrows it down to a single choice (maybe two), imposing an artificial limit to your decision.
There are a couple "boss encounters" in the game, but only the final Boston Lockdown story mission stands out as a "real" boss. The difficulty curve up to that point was pretty static: ♥♥♥♥ up a movement early in a mission and you MIGHT end up taking a couple extra hits. The final Boston Lockdown mission, the curve jumps up 3-4 notches. It took my buddy and I (who usually steamroll stuff like this) a couple tries to work out mechanics and strategy. Definitely a standout moment in the campaign and left us wishing there had been more of that than recycled maps, but again with such a small dev team, I understand why.
A note for the future: If there was weapon customization, I think I'd have creamed my jeans.

General Overview
Grand Theft Auto: Episodes from Liberty City is an expansion pack for Grand Theft Auto IV and while you don't need to own the base game to play, I would recommend you play through that first so the narrative makes more sense and you will also see how all three stories from each of the characters connect and intertwine with one another which I found to be interesting.
The Lost and Damned
In the first story, you play as protagonist Johnny Klebitz - a man who is second in command of a notorious biker gang known as The Lost. There are 22 missions in total with three (or four) random character missions. This will take you around 10 or 15 hours to complete depending how much you focus on the storyline. There are mid-mission checkpoints which were not present in the base game and also new weapons including the sawn-off shotgun, assault shotgun, pool-cues, grenade launchers and pipe bombs. New vehicles include Johnny's custom-made Hexer motorcycle among other bikes not found in the original game. You will also be able to call on your Lost brothers for bikes, backing you up and discounted weapons or just to hang out. Gang wars and bike races are the unique activities included in this episode. Activities you can play with your Lost brothers which were not present in the base game are arm wrestling, hi-lo cards and ever air hockey! Several new songs are added to the radio stations in TLAD - LCHC (Liberty City Hardcore) and Liberty Rock Radio saw the biggest additions of tracks to fit in with the expansion's biker theme in particular. The story itself is dramatic, the voice acting is excellent and motorcycle mechanics have been vastly improved.
The Ballad of Gay Tony
In the second story, you take control of protagonist Luis Fernando Lopez. An ex-member of the Dominician drug dealers and personal bodyguard of Anthony "Gay Tony" Prince. "Gay Tony" is a name well known throughout Liberty City and very high up on the social ladder as owner of the two biggest nightclubs in the city. Throughout the story, Luis has to aid Tony in battling drugs, debt, mafia families and attempts on both of their lives. This expansion contains roughly the same amount of missions as TLAD but once you complete the main story, you can choose to replay any mission from your phone and depending on factors such as time taken, damage taken among other objectives, you will get a ranking. Like TLAD, you can call on friends to sell you discounted weapons or to provide you with vehicles (and more are added as you progress in the story but you cannot call on them for backup) New vehicles include a NOOSE tank and a small attack helicopter known as the buzzard. New side jobs in TBOGT include drug wars, base jumping (which introduces parachutes back into the series) taking on triathlon races, working on club management, teeing it up at the golf range and entering an underground fight tournament (did someone say Flight Club?)
In the clubs you can dance, take shots (get completely wasted and you will wake up somewhere random if you drink enough) and partake in champagne drinking contests. New weapons at your disposal include: advance smg, the gold smg, the advanced mg, the 44. pistol, the advanced sniper rifle and sticky bombs. The grenade launcher and assault shotgun from the previous episode also return but this time you have the option of equipping explosive rounds which up the havoc and are a lot of fun. The story is a blast to play and without spoiling anything not only connects together at a certain point like TLAD and the base game but also answers some previously unanswered questions which I found to be very satisfying. In TBOGT there is much more of a glitz and glamour feel not found previously.
Closing comments
I found both episodes highly enjoyable to play (although I will say I preferred TBOGT just a bit more) If you're looking for more GTA IV adventures you simply cannot go wrong with this and it concludes the GTA IV saga. While the story in both episodes may not take too long to complete depending on how much you focus on it, there are many other activities to participate in for both episodes. If you're not bothered about achievement hunting however, the main missions will be more than satisfying. In terms of the content included I can't fault Rockstar for anything in these two episodes. It caps off the magnficence of Liberty in GTA IV.

The counterintuitive controls however, made it so that I could only to watch my units die one by one as the dumb AI targets enemies that I tell them not to and get overwhelmed on their way to the complete opposite end of the battlefield.
Even switching to manual control of the ships didn't help much as the targeting system would insist on targeting everyone besides the enemy in front of me that I happen to already be shooting at. Even going to turret mode for a better view only successfully gave me a better view of the hull of my ship before it gets blown up half of the time.
The loading times going in and out of tactical mode killed me. I don't want the ship I’m in; I want to see the map so I can choose something else that’s you know, TACTICAL! But nope! I need to wait until the game allows me to do anything that I want to do. All the while I get to listen to the groaning of the game telling me that I can't do what I want.
Maybe this game would be better with a sound track, who knows? I only heard 1 song, and when it ended, I did one final assault, lost everything, and rage quit. I hate to leave things half finished, and I paid good money for this game, but nothing is worth this much of a headache. Too bad it was a complete waste of my time and money.

Star Wars Republic Commando is a first person shooter featuring a band of 4 Special Ops Clone Troopers in the Clone Wars era. This game chronicles 3 different missions that they fought through. This game is very strange, as it doesn't feel a lot like Star Wars somehow. It still has that imagery that all Star Wars fans come to know, but some of the music tracks are wildly different from your normal John Williams score, and the credits theme sounds a song that was featured on the radio in 2003. It's really interesting, because it shows the divide between the grand battles that the Jedi get to fight in, compared to the more small scale attacks that these Clones deliver.
Now I mentioned that the game has 3 missions. Don't let that daunt you. This game isn't exactly THAT short. Each mission can last you quite a while. The shortest amount of time I spent on a mission was 4 hours. Each mission kind of has several different segments that can somewhat count as levels. Each missions has really good variety, so that it doesn't feel like you're doing the same stuff over and over again in similar environments.
This game's real length comes through it's difficulty. This game is HARD. You can hurt your squad mates, enemies come in many varieties, checkpoints are placed pretty far from each other, and your health isn't something that you'd expect to walk from a missile with. This game is challenging as hell, and that's where the team dynamic comes in.
You really have to constantly strategize and update on your squad mates, as they're just as fragile as you. It leads to many many many many moments in the game in which you have to prioritize who will be on a turret, and who will be sniping. This leads to a lot of creative ways to dispatch your enemies.
Every time a squad mate falls, you can revive them. The only real problem I have with this game is that when you yourself fall in combat, the other squad mates would rather try and kill off the rest of the enemies rather than revive you. And that could either lead to an inevitable game over, or a long 5 minutes on the ground with an eventual heal. You're better off just reloading a save file rather than sitting with the screen red and panicked.
Other than that, this game is solid. It really has a good amount of challenge and replayability to have you coming back. I highly recommend to Star Wars fans, especially Clone Wars fans. Sadly, this is no longer canon towards to the current Star Wars storyline, but hopefully we see something like this play on the big screen. Maybe "Republic Commando: A Star Wars Story".

I first got Star Wars: Republic Commando several years back, as part of a bundle my mom bought me in a Target. Unfortunately, the other two items in that bundle were the original Battlefront games, which were much more interesting to an 11- or 12-year-old. I only got a couple minutes into Republic Commando as a result, although I kept the disc (I don't know where it is now, otherwise I would've used its CD key to get it on Steam instead of paying money). However, I've played it now, and here are my thoughts.
On the surface, it's a perfectly agreeable mid-2000s console FPS—you run down a series of linear levels and shoot things and press F to use a lot and give basic commands to your three NPC friends. However, there's a lot of good design at play: the game never takes control of the camera away from you, it's full of scripted sequences that give information and tell little stories in the Half-Life style, the command controls are simple yet useful, the game gives you a lot of tools in any given situation and lets you decide which ones to use, and actions that take time don't reset if you walk away in the middle of doing them. Additionally, it's made very clear through gameplay how much more useful you are as part of a team. Alone, you can kill stuff and progress through levels well enough, but in a team, you're all helping out and taking care of different, interlocking tasks and quadrupling your individual firepower. You feel more complete with your NPC friends, which is a hard thing to pull off.
The writing's also pretty good. Each member of your squad has an individual personality that makes sense and is reflected in suble nuances in dialogue, and they make jokes that occasionally made me chuckle. Sometimes there're also examples of the sort of incredibly obvious logic that I always enjoy; I especially liked one moment where a room we were in started filling with poison gas, and the solution was to continue wearing our vacuum-sealed armor.
The game does have some flaws, however. The enemies can sometimes be really goddamn annoying, flying all over the place and firing beams that melt your health bar away or having tons and tons of health. Sometimes the game just spawns them infinitely until you accomplish an objective (usually destroying the thing that's spawning them), which is terrible.
Melee is often a ridiculously effective option. It'll kill most footsoldier enemies in one hit, and it has almost no cooldown whatsoever. You can just speed-melee your way through an entire squad without too much trouble, which is fun but kinda unbalanced.
I quite like the aesthetic. For some reason, I've always enjoyed kinda basic 3D; not the really early stuff, 'cause that just looks atrocious, but more like 3D from about 1999-2005, where polygons were still at a premium so everything looked really blocky and distinct, but there was enough detail to have it not look like a child's drawing. This game makes the most of that, having everything, especially the clone troopers, look colorful and chunky. Some may find it to have aged poorly, graphics-wise, but I appreciate it.
In conclusion, Star Wars: Republic Commando is quite good. It plays well, it looks nice, it has personality, and it's organic and fun. The enemies are sometimes damaging or tanky enough to bring the pace to a standstill, but usually it's a fun jaunt through some Star Wars stuff with NPC support that's actually pleasant to be around. I recommend it.

Let's be clear here: This game only costs 2 bucks. When it's not on sale. You can hardly ♥♥♥♥ up so hard that it won't be worth those 2 bucks. For me, it was worth about 7 hours of puzzling.
The game consists of 5 "worlds" with 25 levels each. Every world introduces new and different gimmicks, from speeding trains to waterfalls to machine guns to self driving lorry carts, elevators, etc. etc. Your goal each time is to blow up the big green safe and optionally the three piggie banks (and if you can and want the hidden object). Unfortunately, this being a mobile port, you need to destroy quite a few of those piggie banks to unlock later worlds, which is funny, because within each world every level is immediately available. To do so you have to generally blow up barrels and connect them with blackpowder lines. This is all pretty fun and stuff, IF NOT for the infuriating design decision to include timed "drag" levels. What I mean by that is that there are quite a few levels in the game in which you have to blow up an obstacle, ignite a fuse and "drag" it around the screen until the obstacle is gone and you can continue to the next obstacle. If you expect just a slow and peaceful puzzler, let this one go, as things can get quite hectic, especially later on, when you also have to manipulate the machinery and more in the levels. For example: In later levels it is crucial to change the direction of train tracks many different times while there is an on fire mine cart on its way. This can get very stressful.
If you can deal with that, however, you have yourself a nifty little "action puzzler" with ok graphics, ok music, incredibly annoying sound effects and the inclusion of a "story" for whatever reason. The 10 comic book style panels are just kind of unnecessary and don't even convey any meaningful information.
After you've destroyed enough piggie banks you can also unlock the "hidden levels", which is just another chapter of 25 that were supposedly scrapped from the game at some point? Dunno. The game teases you with "more levels soon" after that, but seeing as the last update on Steam was in 2015 I highly doubt that.

A charming cluster♥♥♥♥ of a trainwreck Visual Novel game.
Frustrating dialogue.
A UI that has aged poorly since its PSX days.
Gameplay segments with no gameplay and zero choice that trick you into thinking you have agency and serve no purpose.
A nonsense story that seems to be missing a few chapters with characters that don't seem to operate on human logic.
A NON-ENDING.
And I loved it.  I loved every bit of this lovingly crafted mess, because it oozes love and quality from the staff that created it, and I am a huge fan of massive, poorly crafted, ambiguous stories that make you fill in the blanks.
This is a gem of the PSX era of VNs and is a testament to the fact that you don't need to make a good game, or even a good STORY to make something that's utterly enjoyable, because presentation and love trumps all.
People who weren't teens or young adults during the PSX era might not really get it.  But I sure as hell do.

Indie games often get judged poorly and Astral Terra seems to be one of those titles that are getting unfair negative reactions.
Personally, I found this open world game charming: the soundtrack has the most soothing songs I've heard in a game in quite a while; the dynamics are unique by mixing RPG aspects with voxelated building tools. Also, the world is huge and beautiful.
Of course, the graphics don't have the quality of an AAA title, but indie devs don't have high budgets so it makes no sense to make this type of comparisons. Even though, you can see this small team has put a lot of effort on making a functional and aesthetically pleasing customizable land for players to enjoy and expand by using their own imagination. There are things that could be improved, such as adding more races and outfits, but I'm sure they'll add those elements in future updates. Overall, this game was a pleasant surprise for me and I find it pretty underrated.

Astral Terra feels like Minecraft and World of Warcraft got married and had a child.
Since the game is on Alpha, there are some bugs and glitches here and there, but it is a very promising game. For people who like to just explore and level up, it's there. For those who like to create things, it's there as well. The graphics looks very good and the artwork as well.
It looks like that the team responsible for the game is updating it on a regularly basis, showing the players what they have on schedule to improve it, that's why I highly recommend this game. They have a very good relationship with the public, they hear what's need to improve and they do it, so, the game will probably be fully released very soon, I will stay tuned for that!

This game is extremely good. I wholeheartedly recommend it. It's like the developers took X-Com's combat system and made it 2D.
Pros:
-The Combat System
SteamWorld Heist was able to take everything good about X-com's combat system and make it 2D. It also made some tweaks that I like more than X-com. One example is that shots are not based off of dice rolls. What that means is that when I line up a shot, it will hit whatever I'm aiming at. If you line up the shot correctly, you can shoot enemies that are behind cover.
-The Art Design
The game looks amazing. The robots are detailed and cool looking. Space looks awesome and colorful. My favorite part has to be that you can collect a bunch of different hats for your characters to wear.
-The Soundtrack
The music is really good. It's well composed and it fits the space western theme that the game is going for. I really wish that it was available to purchase.
-Boss Fights
I was honestly surprised when I came across the first boss. The games that I have played similar to SteamWorld Heist did not have what I would call bosses. The bosses that I have fought each have had special abilities and multiple phases.
Cons:
-The Story
Let's get this out of the way first, I'm NOT saying that the story is bad. What I'm saying is that the story is the weakest part of the game. The beginning, middle, and end of the game felt really disconnected to me. I can't go into more detail without spoiling the plot, but know going in that it's not the best.
-Lack of Mission Variety
My biggest problem with the game is that a lot of the missions feel the same. Most of the time it's go in, kill bad guys, collect loot, escape. The game adds things like doors that won't open until you destroy a generator, but it never feels any different. I can't tell you which mission would be my favorite (excluding boss fights) because they all feel so similar. This is somewhat solved with The Outsider DLC, but that felt more like a bandage instead of a fix.
There you have it. Like I said earlier, I recommend SteamWorld Heist. The Cons section is a bit nitpicky because there is honestly not a lot wrong with the game.
I hope this review was helpful to you,

You stand in a very blocky biker bar, surrounded by voxel strangers minding their own business, when you wander up to a random patron and suddenly slam them across the face with your blocky fist, instantly causing every patron in the bar to rise and begin fighting viciously. Anything not nailed down is a potential melee weapon, from chairs, plates, steaks, and pool cues, to knives, broken bottles and electric guitars. Your one goal after initiating the chaos is to be the last man standing, killing anyone who stands in your way in a particularly bloody and gory fashion. If that isn't exciting enough, as your enemies grow fewer, your special attacks charge, allowing you to either send out a concussive shockwave to stun your opponents, go into a insta-kill beserk mode, or remotely smite your enemies from across the room with a bolt of energy from above. On top of all this, there are many modifiers to either make gameplay easier or more challenging, as well as many steam workshop custom maps that can add a whole new experience to am already epic game.

Manor of the Damned! is an interesting RPG game. Retro style and graphics, a throwback to console style of RPGs.
It does have an engaging story that looks very interesting and is rather well detailed. Books explaining lore, NPCs who have either flavor or something to tell you about your quest.
Gameplay:
The game plays in an action RPG fashion and although it looks like a japanese console RPG, combat is realtime and not turn-based. You start with absolutely nothing
and wander around until you find your first sword! Extra points for being non-linear. You will find locked doors which you can't open until you find the key later on etc etc.
The game doesn't use a mouse, it's keyboard or gamepad only. But you don't really need one.
Graphics:
Retro style graphics, says everything really. They're very well done.
Music/Sound Design:
The soundtrack is great and extra points for not being packed. Meaning you will find the tracks in the game's directory as .ogg files.
Sound effects are also fitting the style of the game.
Pros:
-Engaging story from the get go.
-Solid gameplay (I hate those snakes!)
-Great soundtrack!
-Non-linear enough.
Neutral:
-Retro style. Always a matter of player taste.
Cons:
-Could not really find any. I did not meet any bugs and the game is exactly what is advertised.
Conclusion:
Go for it if you like retro style RPGs.

As mentioned by others, this game reminds me of Ziltoid. It is a 4x space sim with a lot of personality. While I can't say I'm a regular patron of the 4x genres, I do have room for an occasional space sim (see: Master of Orion), and I've grown fond of the genre in later years. Let me emphasize this 4x is not like any other - this is not about managing bases on planets, or diplomacy: it is about pure and utter conflict. The gameplay is simplistic in a beer & pretzel sense, where it does not require lots of focus to achieve a mission. What I like most is it seems to streamline the formula down to its essential core. Some people may find games like Civilization appealing, with its millions of choices, but all of that snowballs down into the same end result in a few dozen hours. Space Tyrant is refined. And it is different: with its focus on combat and its fun--YES, I said fun--personality. I think it captures the essentials of what makes a 4x fun, and its wholly unique in its focus on invasion and conquest. If you like 4x, or 4x set in space, buy it. If you find the overwhelming complexity of a Civilization game overwhelming, buy it. If you like strategy, but find it wholly lacking in depth of personality, buy it. I'd award this game an easy 8.5/10.

I'm not a 4X genre kind of guy. I've tried.
In fact
was my final attempt at breaking into the genre. This was my final
attempt.
Now, I do like
quite a bit, but it does suffer from some of the same issues that other 4X games have. The saving grace is that it simplifies things and distills mechanics down to something more digestible.
I think a staple of the 4X genre is having a complicated and breathy system.
Anyways,
is fairly easy to learn and has some great humor. Yeah, the RNG is wily, but it's also wily in those other 4X games BUT the RNG is just hidden better. You know I'm right about that.
At some point this title was described as a coffee-break game, but I disagree. Yes, it is easily played with one hand, but matches are certainly more than about 20 minutes. They are shorter than competitor titles, but still. The other point of concern is the roguelike nature and permadeath. That part makes me nervous, but the jury is still out on that. The permadeath spans over an entire CAMPAIGN that will easily take you, oh, probably 5-10 hours to complete. One false step and it's back to the begining. I'm not sure it works here, but again, I still need to play more.
+You can't even tell this is Early Access.
+Controls are intuitive and there is a solid tutorial system to ease you in.
+It definitely has that one-more-round addiction going on.
+They nicely distilled what I would consider an overly complicated system that 4X games adhere to into a bite-size package.
-While the music is good, it is very repetitive. There isn't enough variation.
-RNG is fairly brutal, but more importantly - everything hinges on this idea of permadeath and I'm just not sure it makes it more 'fun'. I'm still thinking on this.
-Alot of the dialogue is quite humorous but I find myself skipping through to see the end result. Again, the RNG leaves something to be desired. Choices don't feel meaningful. It's like just pick a button and see what happens most of the time.
If the idea appeals to you, by all means go for it.

is a casual, two-dimensional puzzle game with a large amount of short levels, a 3-star system, and leaderboards. It is cut from the same cloth as games like
,
, and the many other mobile-era puzzle games out there. Nevertheless,
does have its own independent identity. The gameplay is a perfect mix of planning and playing that combines well with the theme of the game to create a unique and charming experience.
It is a very simplistic game, so if you are seeking something with depth or immersion: this isn’t it. But if you enjoy playing casual puzzle games of this style, then
is probably going to be a good bet for you.
As I alluded to, the mixture of planning and action/reaction that is inherent in the puzzle-solving creates some really enjoyable gameplay. It will make you think a bit, but manages to not get overly confusing. That synthesizes brilliantly with the jovial, lighthearted theme of the game to make the whole experience unequivocally pleasurable. It is the perfect game to put a smile on your face in those moments you are just looking to kick-back and relax.
There are a lot of levels (150+), but they are pretty short and easy to solve; although some of the later levels are decently challenging. For all levels, once you find the solution there isn’t much reason to try again for the average gamer, unless you are someone who relishes in the opportunity to compete on the leaderboards. I was satisfied with the amount of content, but you will have to make your own assessment on that front.
So, while I understand not everyone is a fan of this genre, I posit that anyone who is a fan should have an easy time enjoying
. There was a good job done by the developers in creating a unique identity for the game, and it is one of the more entertaining examples of the genre.

Casual puzzle game with aesthetics straight out of your favorite western cartoons. Evil Boss Grimshaw has taken more then his fair share of the towns folks money.  Playing the role Incendio you have one simple goal, draw a line of gunpowder through all the explosive barrels and while making you way toward the stolen loot. Perhaps claiming some fame and glory along the way.
Levels start off simple but quickly increased in difficulty requiring you to take down entire walls, chain reactions that split into multiple paths, launch cannons on to moving river rafts and just time more explosions in general. Best scores come from taking out all the extra piggy banks which were often in more obscure locations that require careful planning. Puzzle fans who are perfectionists should find a rather addictive game and with the inclusion of a global high score board it certainly keeps you hitting the replay level button to refine skills. If not bothered can progress the story just by clearing the end safe.
While it's past history as a mobile game is rather obvious, it's far from being a terrible port. Gamepad support isn't provided given the drawing nature of the game but I had no issues with mouse control or menu navigation. Overall enjoyed Gunpowder enough to complete it as I have the spare time. Cheers folks. :)

The conversations take place on a simulated AIM, where you can look at a small buddy list, check profiles, and even see some fabricated profiles for some of your Steam friends. Cute touch.
Without spoiling too much of the experience, my recommendations are as follows:
- Try to imagine yourself in the situation when you're deciding on your conversation choices. Don't think about where you believe the game will go with various choices, just do your best to immerse yourself.
- In 2006, resist the temptation to say goodbye right away. The second half of the 2006 conversation was, for me, the most "real" experience of the whole game.
I liked the game for what it was. Don't expect too much out of it (it is *free* after all), and I think most people who experienced the "AIM era" of the internet will find it hits home.

I didn't know what to expect when I downloaded this game. I knew it was a game based around a desktop computer, a chat room and multiple option storyline based game, basically, a
book, based around a chatroom. I also knew it was a free game, and that I have a decent amount of friends who play it, including one with 400+ hours of today.
I normally don't play story based games, I don't like be told what to do, and when I have a set narrative, it is hard for me to enjoy the game. I went into this Emily is Away, however, with an open mindset. I thought maybe I would have a change of mind and maybe I could actually enjoy a game like this. Needless to say, I have mixed opinions. I tried to force myself to enjoy the game, and I found it less enjoyable than I should have. However, I also found myself having fun, in a maybe unintended way.
Throughout the game, which I played till completion about 3 times, each ending roughly around the same point, I tried and make my character the most edgy I could possibly be, or the nicest and etc. I found this, for me at least, to be the most enjoyable part of the game.
What really stuck with me as I played, however, was the conversations. Don't get me wrong, they would never past the Turing test, but I could feel a sense of emotion, possibly because of conversations that I had personally been in with a similar theme. However, I did realize that the conversations were very, and I mean very forced. Instances where you want to say one thing and have a desired outcome were pretty common. Predicatability of Emily, and her responses left most of the responses pretty bland. Many of the conversations are pretty unnatural, but this can be expected, as it only gives you three options to choose from. Anymore than three options would most likely be overbearing, however, I feel as the options are generally two of the same, just phrased differently or with a different emotion. This, in most cases, leads to the same outcome, and it gives a false sense of control, which is beneficial in a game so bound to a narrative.
The game's so-called "adventure tree", or basically the flow chart that your response helps dictate where you go in the story, is very large, and often lead back very far. This also adds some serious points to the games over all appeal. However, like a
book, many choices lead to one final outcome.
For me, the biggest issue of the game was the amount of time that it takes to complete a chapter. I felt that, for what it was worth, a chapter was way to long. I know, granted, that a chapter was suppose to take up one full year, and that messages can't be sent instantly, but there was so much unneeded dialouge that just made me want to hit a fast forward button or something of that nature. I felt that it was a good idea to include the typing mechanic, but I felt that it got boring after a while.
I understand that writing an intriguing story line is hard, additionally, I also know that creating games is hard. What the creator did was something, that personally I didn't enjoy, or at least I didn't enjoy it the intended way. If you are a story based player, and you want a quick and easy way to just relax and play a story based game, I would recommend this to you. If you aren't I can't say its worth the disk space to download this game. Overall I would give it 6/10, mostly because of my own personal level of enjoyment, but also because of the lack of control over your own character and the predictability of responses.

SteamWorld Heist is a fantastic turn-based strategy game sporting vibrant and polished aesthetics. This steampunk space adventure focuses on skill rather than chance, and is jam-packed with bullet-bouncing, turret weaving, robot commanding fun.
Following the events of a shattered planet, Cowbots farm leftover land for moisture and water. These resources are a precious commodity used by all bots, excluding the diesel-driven Royalists. With a new danger lurking in the depths of space, gentlebots have so much to worry about. Not wanting undue attention from the Royal Space Force, Piper Faraday, notorious smuggler and occasional pirate, leads a crew of seemingly misfit mercenaries on a quest to drive the bad-for-business Scrappers gang away from her domain. Little does she know what the universe has in mind for her and her crew.
Piper’s journey begins upon selecting one of three available game slots, then choosing a preferred difficulty level. These difficulties are listed as: Casual < Regular < Experienced < Veteran < Elite. Each tier provides various changes to: enemy damage, enemy quantity, mission failure punishment and bonus XP earned. SteamWorld Heist’s gaming structure is comprised of missions (primary and side/challenge missions) that must be unlocked with a reputation requirement (stars). Losing or aborting a mission will result in a loss of water (currency) at any difficulty level above Casual.
Every mission rewards the player with reputation which is used to proceed further into the game and unlock additional characters/weapons. Most missions are scored on a 3-star rating system; however, there will be missions that score differently. On each mission, various opportunities are presented to obtain loot in the form of loot bags, epic loot (chests), or hats. Perfecting a mission requires completing the objectives (clear the ship, defeat X, destroy X, retrieve all loot etc.) without having any casualties and retrieving the epic loot(s). Before beginning any mission, a loadout screen is presented where the player will choose the participating characters and their equipment. Due to a crew limitation on missions, it is advised to change up which characters go on each mission regularly to keep levels relatively even; however, this is definitely not required.
Each mission environment is procedurally generated, providing a unique experience for every player. Heist never feels repetitive because of this, along with the fact that random missions will have a theme (turret factory, explosive carrier etc.). Boss fights also introduce eccentric characters with unique abilities. If that’s not enough, alarms that trigger infinitely spawning enemies/turrets or countdown timers with difficult consequences may be included.
Heist’s combat utilizes a turn-based strategy system with a unique mechanic where the weapons are manually aimed and shot by the player. This removes a chance or hit % mechanic that many other similar turn-based strategy games use, and promotes skill-shots or ricocheting around objects to reach the target(s). The entire crew will individually perform their turns before the enemy performs theirs. Each turn is comprised of a movement phase, and a sprint/action phase.
Positioning is crucial in successfully attaining reputation. Each mission is littered with destructible barrels and walls for partial cover; however utilizing complete cover will be necessary at times. Typically averaging about 6 move spaces per turn, characters can move further using a sprint mechanic. Although it is not split into discrete phases, transitioning from the movement phase into the sprint phase is marked with a differently colored marker or floor space. If the player moves a character into a space beyond the movement range and requires sprinting, no further action can be made by that character. Sprinting is useful for running to partial cover, hiding from turrets, or eluding spawning enemies.
If the player chooses to keep a character within their movement range, that character can perform an action. An action would either constitute firing that character’s weapon after aiming it, using a special utility item’s free action, or performing a melee attack if an enemy is adjacent to the prioritized character. There are many different weapon types in Heist, and some weapons have specific requirements for use, such as a particular sniper rifle’s “move or shoot – pick one” specification. A rarity and tiered weapon system also promotes loot-based progression. Rare weapons will generally have higher base damage/critical damage stats, or attachments equipped (laser sight).
Aiming provides the primary game mechanic that sets Heist apart from other turn-based strategy games. If the player chooses to fire a weapon, it must be manually aimed to deal efficient damage. Depending on the weapon attachment or gun type, the projectiles may travel in an arc, bounce multiple times with or without subsequent damage reduction per bounce, travel in a straight line, or scatter. The characters have the ability to shoot directly straight above or below, 90 degrees from the horizontal; however, each character breathes, adding another level of skill required to hit the target(s).
Each character utilized in a mission gains XP after successful completion of that mission. At each level up, a passive ability will be gained. Some characters have unique abilities, while others gain more stats. A couple unique abilities that are very crucial in deciding team composition include:
Even though Heist is a steampunk world, it is very colorful and glossy. The artwork is extremely well polished, providing a truly immersive role-play. As opposed to using the traditional rustic, dull or textured color palettes seen in many steampunk artwork, bright blues, pinks and greens are employed. The settings used for the ships can also vary from oil-crusted rigs to royal and elegant cruisers. The pit stops/bars/social hubs in Heist are very active, filled with neon signs and questionable characters.
SteamWorld Heist was just recently released on Steam (Dec. 10th 2015 for the PS4, 3DS, Vita, WiiU and Xbox One versions). The developers have shown active and continued interest in Heist, as can be seen in the Steam Discussions board. Star Wars: Republic Commando is a really unique game. It tells a story that few other Star Wars games have attempted to do, by putting us in the shoes of a Clone.
Not just any Clone, however, but a Clone (or Republic) Commando. These Commandos have recieved superior training compared to regular Clones, and are armed to the teeth with a modular weapon.
Rather than just have one of you super soldiers running around in any given area, you are given three squadmates, with you taking the place of squad leader. They are as follows:
Sev, RC-1207, the Sniper of the squad, and also the most violent.
Fixer, RC-1140, the hacking expert of the squad
And Scorch, RC-1262, the demolitions expert of the squad.
Each squadmate has a unique personality, and to a further extent, voice. These little touches help you become immersed in the Star Wars universe, as well as a unique HUD that makes you feel like you truly are in the helmet and armor of a Republic Commando.
In terms of preformance, the game runs very well for a game of its age. However, the game does show its age, meaning that some graphics options are rather limited. The game does not support 1920x1080 screens, but this can be fixed by downloading a mod, which includes some other more advanced graphics options, as well as some quality of life improvements. I highly recommend it.

I wrote a big blog post on the storytelling methods in the Silver Case. You can read it here because I had screenshots and everything so I can't copy-paste it:
but I will share the basics.
The Silver Case is a really bizarre game. I can't say if I think the storytelling holds up or not. I believe that while the plot may have been revolutionary in 1999, so many of its elements have been harvested by other Japanese story-heavy games that we may be desensitized. It may blow your mind though still. I hope it does.
The writing is incredible. The characters are incredible. And goddamn the art direction use in the storytelling is the most interesting thing I've seen in a long time. If you're a game designer or even a graphic designer, I bet you'll get a lot out of the visual feeds in this game. It is really, really something, and I'm honetly stunned that I haven't seen people use the Film Window format before. It's very unusual, but take your time when you play and think about how the location of the images is used to expressed different things. It shows a first-person gaze like an element in comic book panelling.
The game takes place in 1999 and the localization was carefully constructed to reflect that. At times, it sounds like a crappy anime translation from 1999. This is deliberate, and contributes to the expression of the zeitgeist.
I can go on and on. In the end what I'm trying to say is that if you're just into a game for crazy plot twists and gameplay features, you may not like it. If you're interested in seeing a different way to tell a story, please play The Silver Case.
It is. really something.

There're two blocks:
"Transmitter" is the main story in which you're playing as MC, ex-special forces trooper (I think?), who joined Heinous Crime Unit to investigate Kamui Case.
"Placebo" is a side story told by ex-reporter Tokio Morishima hired by his ex-boss to look into Kamui Case for a scoop.

Have you ever seen something with a narrative you can only describe as "Ballsy"?
The Silver Case is a game with balls, the kind of balls even today you'll be hard-pressed to find anywhere, videogames or otherwise.
In a world where Her Story is deemed groundbreaking for how it was so different by virtue of being a pure Investigation Drama, this originally-from-1999 game not only took all that, it evolved the concept to the point it even added surreal touches that don't make it any less grounded than it already is. Not only that, but the style of dialog and narration is one that more people should actually follow. This game did things 17 years ago that only recently we've started to think "maybe games could do that".
Not only that but it's a story full of gray tones if there ever was one it's also a story that never handholds you and leaves you to think your way through many subplots and never underestimates its players. All of this while keeping a clear sense of humor that's never jarring and surreal touches that only add to the overall feel.
Unorthodox? Yeah. Clunky at times? Maybe. Worth every penny and a must-have for anyone even remotely interested in games as a narrative medium? Most definitely.

I'll get the bad out of the way first. In some ways the remaster still lacks polish, some messy scenes, the controls are still weird and clunky, and the entire plot will probably give you a headache at first consideration. Some of the UI is messy and confusing after jumping from menu screen to menu screen.
All this said The Silver Case lives up to being a classic Suda51 game in every respect. The writing (once you wrap your mind around it) is brilliant. It jumps from ham fisted to ethereal and mysterious. The translation while kind of tacky sometimes captures in this the sort of translation you'd expect in 1999 making the whole game feel like a dive into a time capsule.
The Silver Case is a heady postmodern masterwork that has all the quirks and loveable motifs from any Grasshopper Manufacture game. It is a rare slice of history kept true to source in an era where games preservation is fighting uphill. If you like off kilter visual novels or adventure games this is worth the trip.

The Silver Case:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

Kamui Uehara, a cold-blooded serial killer escaped the mental institute where he was kept. Several people were killed, including members of the Special Forces. But somethings doesn’t add up! You are now part of the team researching this event . . . . What are you going to discover. . . This is part of the Silver Case!
The Silver Case is a visual novel game. In this game, you will follow the steps of an officer of the Heinous Crime unit (in my case, Froggy) on several cases.  You also get to play a freelancer reporter, Tokio Morishima.
As you start the story, Kusabi (the man who arrested Kamui the first time around) was on his way home when he felt suddenly unsettled. Who can blame him when he saw this individual staring at him in the middle of the road with a human head on one of his hands!  After shooting at Kusabi, the stranger ran into the cauliflower tower. From here, your character becomes part of the story.
Being a visual novel, there is plenty of reading in The Silver Case. As you progress through the game, you will gain a good understanding of the main characters and how they react to situations.
I like a good novel (book) and part of the experience is to imagine the scenes of what you are actually reading. Here, in the Silver Case, you will actually see the scenes; there are cut-scenes (animations or video footage) and in some parts of the game you will be able to explore the environment as you investigate or report cases. You will also interact with characters and objects.  As a newcomer to this genre of game, I really appreciated the combination of all the above - I truly felt that I was involved in the story.
In terms of the dialogues, overall they are good.  I must admit that on occasion some of the text was a bit awkward, but that is my take on the read. I really like the soundtrack; it fits the cases/scenes very well.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Entertaining cases and story
-	Great soundtrack
-	Reading, exploring and cut-scenes combination is well done
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
7/10
The Silver Case integrates reading, cut-scenes and exploration. Whether you are familiar with visual novels, or new to this genre of game, give The Silver Case a read!
Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

This game is potentially great.  In fact, for the first 10 or 20 hours, I thought it WAS great.  I found myself wishing there were more of this sort of simplified, lighthearted 4X game.
I'll leave the list of things it does right to all the other good reviews, and just talk about its problems.
First, the difficulty of missions is extremely uneven.  The devs seem to leave to much control over missions to the RNG that you could be immediately set upon by a legitimately impossible confluence of events, or encounter zero drama from turn 1.
There are several different mission types, and in my experience, only one (in which you must capture and hold 2 of 3 specific planets) is consistently tense.  The others are always effectively decided within the first few turns - either the game throws everything at you as quickly as possible, or it doesn't.  If it doesn't, the entire mission is dead easy.
It also has a problematic meta-strategy layer wth the senate control mechanic in the mission selector.  My first ragequit happened when I won the last of the initial 12 missions you have to win before taking on the senate.  Upon winning it, the senate promptly sent two ships to the same area that already had 2 ships in it.  4 ships in one area, even for a moment, and the campaign is over.
I WON the last mission, kept more than 2 senate ships from ever being in the same area at any time for the entire campaign until the literal moment I won the last mission, and was greeted with the "game over" screen.  I've rarely been so mad at a video game.
With a few tweaks to smooth out the difficulty and fix a few "we've decided you lose now" problem mechanics, it'll be great.  Even with its frustrations, I still can't bring myself to give it a thumbs down, though.  Thumbs up, but I'm done playing until it impoves some things.

With its store front claim of delivering a "fast-paced roguelike-lite 5X" experience, chunky UI, and colorful cartoonish graphics, Space Tyrant may at first glance seem like just another one of those hyper-casual mobile games that we're seeing more and more of on Steam these days; but beneath the veneer lies a brilliantly conceived game that, despite lacking the depth of many 4X games that fans of the genre celebrate, delivers an entertaining experience that can be just as satisfying.
I've always had a soft spot for games that let me be the bad guy. Space Tyrant endeavors to join the ranks of titles like Dungeon Keeper, Evil Genius, and Overlord by casting the player in the role of the ultimate... well... Space Tyrant. You'll find no diplomatic standing screen here. There will be no trade routes. You will not be tweaking your economy (unless brutally oppressing your hapless citizens to increase their productivity counts as "tweaking"). You will foster no alliances, shaky or otherwise. There will be no negotiation. The galaxy will either submit to your will, or you will destroy it with your lasers and missiles. Or maybe you'll be the one who gets destroyed by lasers and missiles. Actually, that's probably what will happen.
The premise was immediately enticing to me, but even though my curators were recommending it and all of the other internet buzz surrounding the game was positive, I held back. The reason was simple: "Fast-paced" and "4X" are mutually exclusive terms in my world. I like my 4X games with layers upon layers of depth. I enjoy being able to wrest control of the universe from my enemies using strength, wit, and guile (along with a healthy dose of economic min-maxing). My current all-time favorite of the genre is Distant Worlds, and I've long since decided that if a 4X game can't deliver that sort of deep experience, then I simply don't have time for it.
Thankfully, after having been practically browbeaten by my peers into buying the game, I discovered that Space Tyrant is far more than it seems on the surface. A campaign plays out almost like a series of board games, if board games could be randomly generated. I won't get into the mechanical specifics of the game, as so many other reviews have already covered that; suffice it to say that despite the seemingly simple premise of "just blow everything up to win," there are tons of strategic and tactical options available to the player over the course of a campaign. Will you prioritize conquering crystal worlds in order to utilize your most powerful cards? Or will you favor wealthy worlds in the early game to quickly bolster your fleets? Or perhaps you will focus on tech worlds, so that even your most meager fleet will be able to deal with hordes of ill-equipped enemies.
You will need to do all three to succeed, but how you choose to prioritize objectives based on enemy movement, playfield layout, and other RNG factors will make or break you. Yes, you can play this game quick and dirty; but if you're not paying attention, the Galactic Senate will end you. Or the RNG. Or the space sharks. Yeah, there are space sharks. With lasers on their heads. Because why wouldn't a space shark have a laser on its head?
So in closing, if you're like me and find yourself hesitant to try this game based on any sort of 4X bias, just stop it. Stop being a 4X elitist. You should be ashamed. I know I am.

It's a great mix between simplified X4 / roguelite that plays really fast compared to other X4 games.
Space Tyrant is an interesting mix of 4x strategy game and roguelite. Your aim is to conquer the galaxy: you move your ships through the universe to capture the planets, combat enemies and encounter all sorts of random events as you keep capturing new bases.
The game process is the following: right now, you get to choose a side, then you have the “universe” map shown: you can assault one of three galaxies, while the fourth one is being locked away. Then, you are moved towards the galaxy where you have to complete a specific objective: capturing planets, acquiring wealth, researching new technologies. You choose a commander which determines what kind of a special ability your ship is going to have. It also gives you some mini-objectives for the mission that can influence your play style: completing them makes you stronger, you can get a special powerful cards that can be used on the galaxy map. You direct your fleets through “paths” between planets, and if they encounter another fleet – the battle starts.
The battle itself is pretty simple: two fleets stay opposite to each other and exchange fire. The targets are chosen randomly. Each of your ships has a special ability that they can use on the click. . (each side has only 4 purchasable ships (+ a few bonus stronger ones), but those 4 get upgraded as you play, adding stats / improving their abilities). The chosen hero also has a special ability like meteor strike or thorn wall that influences the battle. In addition to that, you get an active special effect of your choice at the start of the battle (think of it as a random mutator, like small ships deal 2x damage, destroy all fighters, and so on). So yes, while this sounds simple, there’s plenty of space for decision making.
If you got confused by that – that’s totally cool. In fact, this is what makes the game interesting. The mix of different things that you can do. What makes it even more impressive is the fact how tutorials are made: those are the sequences of small videos that gradually introduce you into the game as you play. Instead of reading walls of text, you’ll be watching small videos that introduce you to the game.
Only a few things hurt my experience: At the moment of writing this review, there’s no difference between clicking with left / right button. So when you pick an ability (i.e. death ray) and want to cancel using it – right click will actually trigger it the same way as left click.
Another thing is lack of battle targeting: sure, you influence the way the abilities are being used, but it’s frustrating not to be able to pick targets. I’ve lost one game 6v2 when 2 enemies didn’t do much damage, but kept regenerating shields and my fighters picked targets in worst possible way: 3 were firing at one ship, 3 – at another. The shield regeneration outlived my fighters so I had nothing else to do but slowly watch their demise knowing full well that I could win this had I been given a chance to rearrange targeting.
Every mission playthrough takes from somewhere around half an hour for smaller maps to an hour and a half for bigger scenarios. Overall, this is one of those “I’ll play 5 more minutes” games that eats your time at tremendous rate because it’s so engaging. Plenty of unlockable content and events even in the current early access state, I can confidently recommend the game for its gameplay to those of you who want to experience cosmic strategies but don’t have days to waste on a single battle scenario.

This game starts out with some very fine graphics, though, that may be where all of the good things end.
The controls for this game, especially in reguards to creation/editing are very much a pain to mess with. It seems more like the creator of this game decided to let the players have a go at the actual game engine/creation mechanics, instead of actually finishing the game and all of it's mechanics.
The basic crafting seems to be difficult to get a handle on, to the point that there are no real tutorials in game or explination of how to do anything. It's basically trial and error.
The combat system is juvinile at best, with the favor being in the enemies hands it seems. I can recall old 80's nes games which had a more advanced and balanced combat system over this one's pick something and hope it fires/works/or even selects during combat.
Building buildings, I can't say much about this since I coudl only ever manage to get some corners made and even then it was increasingly difficult to place/stack them. The construction system of this game is. . .for lack of better words, crap.
The creation menu, well, if I wanted to build a game world from scratch and were using a game editor interface then this would be fine. But, I doubt anyone enters into a game/game world and expects to have to actually make roads, cities, etc all on their own because the creators didn't take the time to set anything up.
The conversation/store/npc system is. . .severely lacking. You can't tell friend from foe, and typically when trying to talk to an npc you simply just swing at them.
As for money, well, no idea how you come across that. So, buying the over priced things at the one or two npc's I managed to find were impossible. They would sell you things but would buy nothing, so, you can get the idea out of your head that there is any real economy with in this game.
Movement and navigation is choppy at best, controls aren't set up for any sort of easy navigation, and camera views are more of a pain to adjust than moving.

Andrew ‘Rage’ Garfield was an honest working employee at the ‘Factory’. He was known by fellow colleagues for having ‘Big Hands’, due his callous fingers. He was not ashamed of these hands, they were merits of dedication to his craftsmanship. Repairing monstrous metal beasts was no easy task, and he wished only to produce the best quality products for his employers, as he dreamt only of becoming employee of the month. A goal that had not yet achieved in his long history with the company.
But as time grew on, his efforts weren’t unnoticed. Other employees saw that he too was after the famed position. But, they were unmatched in his prowess. His strength was unmatched, and left those gazing upon him in shock and awe. This did not please his co-workers, as they plotted behind his back, waiting for the right time to strike like a pack of hungry wolves.
As Andrew held a giant industrial screw, a feat that no regular man or beast was capable of, he was ambushed by his colleagues. However, their pathetic attempts at harming him were only angering him. He went berserk with rage an unleashed a barrage of assaults back at his attackers. Embellishing his co-workers in a flurry of agonizing bruises, the blood rushed to his brain, swelling him into blind rage...
But Andrew was not always like this...
He was gentle giant, an innocent and pure soul. Whom carries the weight that no man wishes to have. A burden to most, but a blessing to him. He wished for nothing more than to fight over petty issues amongst his online friends. The burden was great for Andrew, as he got to play video games with his friends online and in a variety of different activities.
One of his chums, known simply as “Raz”, who would be known as a “pointer-guy”. Someone who would lead onwards into the fray of battle, and another... An amphibious loving son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ named “ToadMyster”, a Witcher of Rivia and a toad-like mechanical menace to the world. He sought to bring envy to his fellow scrubs and villians alike.
Together they would bring the ultimate experience that no other person should have the privilege of knowing. Playing against lowly bottom feeding scrubs, that would destroy the comfort zone of anyone in a game of Overwatch.
This cycle would go on for several years with the help of the enigmatic individual known only as... the “_K”. A being that had influenced Andrew, Raz and Toad into meme-spewing warlords. The _K does not know why they became so enthralled by stuttering comments. The duo Raz and Toad had made it their ritualistic pact, to continue the legacy of the _K. But the _K does not mind, as he sees it fit, for his _Kingdom. Andrew however was not interested in such things, and he never really thought of the _K memes, as it was just an inside joke amongst the four of them.

I played Chapter 1 like I knew Travis but all the dialogue options in Chapter 2 were as if I didn't know him ("He's the♥♥♥♥♥♥with the parties!"). I LOVED that the game took some names from my actual Steam Friends though. There are some I had back in the AIM/MSN days and it was a happy nostalgia to see them on the in-game instant messaging client. Too bad when text faces were used they weren't replaced by emoticons though. I see from other players' screenshots that "Emily Is Away" was more AIM looking even with the actual AOL walking guy, so it makes me sad I played a later version even if I understand why it would be changed.
I also was happy to see it could be played on Windows XP too, though not the sequel :-(
Overall "Emily Is Away" really captures the time in which it is set. I was in high-school during the time this is set and was on AIM, MSN, & Y!M frequently. The option to change your text colours was a nice touch too; though I always went with bold-italic. It's a really nice concept for a game! I would highly recommend playing it "blind" though, to get the most impact from the story.

This is Suda51 in his prime. Fresh off of his stint with Human Entertainment, at which he made the absolutely deranged Syndrome games, he decided to go his own way and start Grasshopper Entertainment. The result was The Silver Case. Made with a tiny staff and hamstrung by all kinds of restrictions both financial and otherwise, this lead to the creation of the Film Window system.
The SIlver Case's labyrinthine plot consists of pages upon pages of text, yes, but the FIlm Window system brings it to life through all sorts of mediums, including but not limited to: live action, animation, still art, emails, chats, you name it.
(Fun fact: a professional film editor cut the live action segments, but he wasn't told the clips were for a game.)
This isn't just a visual novel or a procedural crime drama. This is a Suda51 Trip, the very definition of the phrase, and the fact that it got localized is nothing short of a miracle.
The story that continues into Flower, Sun, and Rain and ends with the tale of the Killer7 begins here.
