Leo's Fortune places you in control of the most adorable fuzzy ball with a mustache ever.
This is a simple, casual but enjoyable physics based puzzle plat-former with gorgeous whimsical art styling that makes a turn to be rather menacing looking near the end. Almost like a proper Pixar movie.
Leo is an inflatable ball, that when inflated can slow his descent. Which brings me into the actual plat-forming bit; You are a ball, the action of jumping is caused by rapidly inflating. So the physics here are not always the most accurate. You might think of Sackboy with his soft mushy feel. Leo is also kind of sticky, with some momentum he'll pretty much stick to anything not perpendicular to the ground. Additionally for no particular reason he is also able to rapidly descend, which comes in handy for traversal and puzzle solving alike.
None of the levels are all that challenging; there aren't that many stages. I finished them all in about 2 hours. You can unlock bonus levels by getting higher scores (collecting things in the level or completing with low fatality rate.) But to be honest, they aren't that interesting. After completing the game you unlock 'hardcore' mode which does not allow retries.
All in all, an enjoyable very cutesy filler game/palate cleanser between more substantial titles.

A Warning - If in-depth character development, story-rich plot and wondrous attention to visual detail are aspects of a game you pine after, then this game is not for you. Equally, if human empathy and sympathy are character traits you possess in the bucket loads - this game is also not for you.
That said, fellow sickos, I can't reccomend this game enough. Does it deserve a Game of the Year award or a Golden Joystick Award? No. But that's not a bad thing. The very fact that this game does not deserve either is why it is so excellent.
The game is the epitome of mindless violence. The aim is simple. Murder everyone you see, using whatever weapons you find to hand (to use the label 'weapon' is perhaps a stretch of the imagination - think, instead: bottles, drinking glasses, plates, legs of ham, weights, afro-combs, snooker balls and a variety of fruit). The gore mechanics implemented by the twisted developers are nothing short of outrageously funny and pleasantly stomach-churning. The best combination. The player's character also has three special abilities once an appropriate amount of lives have been claimed, which make the game all the more fun, and outlandishly bloody.
Mix all this in with a handful of level designs: A Prison riot, a brawl in a Biker Bar, a battle at a Pirate hideaway and an all out bloodbath at a thumping 1970s Disco - and you have the capacity to have an amazing amount of fun. Alongside this, players can make and have made their own maps, many of which are equal to or finer in quality than the maps made by the developers. When choosing a level; the player can go for a basic setting, or mess around with a selection of variables to make the playthrough rock-solid in difficulty or a super-human murder-fest.
This is the perfect game if you have ten minutes to kill now and then, or if you're someone who gets their kicks from becoming obnoxiously skilled at a game and if you plan to spend hours upon hours pulverising faces and dicing limbs like soft fruit.
I can't stress how much sober and intoxicated fun I've had on this game; alone or with friends (the game makes a perfect addition to any sesh with similar-minded friends, 1-upping eachother on the level of carnage one can cause in the shortest time possible). I wholeheartedly suggest throwing your money at this game.
You will not regret it.. perhaps until you find yourself lying on the chaise longue in a dimly lit, stuffy office, explaining your cravings for pixelated blood and murderous mayhem to your counsellor. But until then; enjoy.

Having stopped flight simming for more than a decade, I finally had to scratch that itch. As such, there isnt many options on the market now. Either X-plane or FSX and its derivatives (P3D). I took a bite with Xplane and here is my humble review:
1. Graphics : 9/10. Basically best and prettiest out of all of them. Flying during daybreak and sunset is really awesome. At night there are building and runway lights. There is also a free addon to overlay Orthophotos to replace textures with satelite/aerial photography. FPS is still shoddy though, running below 30 if reflections on, on my GTX 1070.
2. Planes: 8/10. The basic planes are there, but there are not many choices. Granted there are addons, free and payware.
3. Flight Control 9/10. It's Xplane, when you're flying you can feel the wind and turbulence on your plane. Ground handling is another matter, but will probably be fixed in the future.
4. ATC : 5/10. Basically my only gripe with this Sim. It's functional but not smart at all. Follow it to the letter and you'll end up hitting a mountain or another plane.
Considering FSX is more than a decade old, if you want a modern sim, Xplane is probably your best bet. I bought this full price, and have not regretted it.

Wrack is a game I want to like, but can't find myself enjoying. The game shows so much potential with the idea of the "addivtive kill chain system" but the reality is that the gameplay just doesnt play towards the concept. Enemies are always in small groups so the killchain rarely gets too high and you never really feel like you get to use a the 'finishers' on anything or at any point that really matters. Couple this with the very limited amount of enemy types and the arguably too high HP which slows down the gameplay of most of the enemies, and you've got a pretty underwhelming game.
I enjoy the concept, not huge fan of the visual but I see where it has its merits. Overall though unless you're really looking for a game that attempts (but fails) to capture the greatness set by DOOM, Quake, Painkiller, Serious Sam, then it's not really worth your time or money.

Flesh Eaters feels early access and incomplete. It lacks quality of life and content. It is also no longer being updated by the dev. Overall, with the bare bones tutorial, I was able to fully complete story mode at around 3 hours. It was enjoyable albeit a bit tedious. I do not recommend paying any amount of cash for this game as it's not worth it.
Story Mode consists of 40 days of survival where you attempt to:
Escape the city (via a humvee).
Find a cure (to the zombie outbreak).
Find the cause (to the zombie outbreak).
You're given 3 random options each day where choosing one option consumes 1 day.
-These can be anything from looting a supply crate to searching a building (Shelter, Police Station, Hospital, Etc...).
-Looting a building launches you into an 'instance' where you move your characters around and... loot...
-Shelters provide an additional 3 days provided you check the map table.
Survival Mode Sandbox consists of unlimited resources with probably more than 3 waves but after a couple hours of testing I've come to the conclusion that the zombies have too much health and spawn too quickly to survive with too few resources. (Welcome to suggestions but I can't get further than 3 or 4 waves.)
Survival Mode Objective consists of a room where you have limited resources and... see above...

Very short, very easy, very confusing at times, Mysterious Castle makes a lot of promises but fails to deliver them, just like Bob Huggins in the NCAA tournament.
The premise is simple enough --you are in a "castle" which is a series rooms.  You have to solve all of the puzzles in one room in order to access the next.  In each room is a variety of furniture and decorations, though the contents of each room doesn't change much.
Like all point and click adventures, you have to manipulate your mouse precisely and accurately so that you click on the correct object.  Unlike most point and click adventures, this game does not tell you when you move the mouse over something significant.  This was the first sign to me that this was going to be a bad game -- you literally have to click all over the room to grab something that makes no sense to grab -- like in the first room, the stick leaning against the shelves.  Why?
Ultimately, the lack of the pointer highlighting an object (or however else the game would let you know you're looking at something significant) leads to a prolonged experience.  And that's important with this game because it is EXTREMELY short.
As other reviewers have pointed out, your "movement" between areas in each room is EXTREMELY slow.  This was another bad sign when I started playing -- slow movement making up for a lack of content.
Other criticisms -- there doesn't seem to be much rhyme or reason why you would perform some actions or why you would want to explore one part of the room but be completely unable to explore another.  The objects that you pick up are a little obscure in their identity as well -- in one room I picked up am object that looked to me to be like a piece of undeveloped or developed film.  This made no sense because the game obviously takes place in kind of medieval times.  Unlike most point and click adventures, this game doesn't tell you what the object is when you pick it up, doesn't tell you what it is when you rest the pointer over it, and you can't right click on an item to have a closer look.  It was only with a combination of random clicks that I realized the piece of film wasn't that -- it was a box of nails.  That's a pretty big problem when you can't figure out what something is unless you have a purely random experience.
Many areas of each room make no sense that you would want to explore -- in the tutorial room, the second piece of what you are looking for is behind one of the lanterns on the wall.  Of course it is!  What rational person wouldn't look behind a lantern mounted on a wall?!
In the end, this game was reduced to random, frustrating clicks.  There isn't a storyline that I can find, other than somehow you've gotten yourself trapped in a castle whose builder apparently had no sense of proportion, direction, function, or decor.  Fung Shui has no meaning in this game.  It's like a digitized version of the famous Winchester House, where the owner built stairways that didn't go anywhere and doors that opened to brick walls.  I realized this finally when I had to set the dials on a lock that opened a window -- and then the window opened to another room.  Made sense.
Truly, I'm writing this review so that, when you look back on your life when you are in your elder years -- you don't dread wasting two hours of it on one of the sh*ttiest games on Steam.

I like escape rooms but don't really like the quest genre. This game is a video game version of real life escape room (which is a real life quest game). I had a few issue with it based on the first 5 levels:
* Bad feedback, sometimes there are sounds and sometimes there are not.
* Sometimes combining clues make no sense (like in real quest rooms rather for the sake to have interaction) like in level 2 you can't put a book aside unless you lit a candle. What? Why? In the same level even if you put the correct code it won't move unless the combine the 2 pieces of paper together. It makes no sense in a video game or real life. Also you can pick up only one of the pieces and you need to move it to the other. Why?!?!?!
* It is very inconsistent. The same rehashed models for desks and drawers are used everywhere in levels 1 - 3. The locks on the drawers are only decorations. Except for the one time when one lock isn't.
* The fire pick could only be picked while in movement. That's so wrong.
* The same schticks are on every level: something under a pillow, something with candles, key behind picture, key opens a box, box has code for another lock that even if you know it unless you did all the steps it won't open and then there's another key to the door.
* Sometimes clicking on something with an object will make interaction and sometimes it won't. Why so many inconsistency?
* It moves so slow..! And sometimes doesn't respond immediately.
* Some places are hard to get, you need to press from a certain place only to get there (I'm looking at you missing stairs at level 5).
* Immersion is kinda ruined that a skilled thief can't break on his own a broken wooden floor or jump like 1.2 feet up where stairs are missing (with no danger of hurting himself).
* The story and tutorial and bearable at best. At least this game have these.
Key was given by publisher for beta testing. I will play a little more to see if it gets better but clearly this game is made by someone that loves escape rooms but have no idea about the basics of good game design. Too bad.
Also, I'm not an escape room expert but from my experience this doesn't beat the real thing (but it is a good try though).
Also couldn't beat level 5. I've clicked on everything with the little box (I have no idea what it is) and the planks. No idea if it's a bug or I've missed something. The game could have a hint system for situations like this.
But not everything is grim, this game has two good virtues:
1. It's cheaper than going to a real escape room.
2. It allows disabled people to have a glimpse of the experience (based on the rooms I've been to, a person in a wheelchair could not participate).

Leo’s Fortune is a puzzle platforming game developed by 1337 and Senri LLC. The Swedish made game was originally developed for iOS, Android, Windows Phone and the Amazon App store in early 2014. It got later ported to Steam and PS4 in September 2015.
Gameplay in Leo’s Fortune is sublime. I am not normally a fan of the puzzle platforming type but the slick movement and clever way the puzzles are put together, makes play absolutely wonderfully. Leo is a cute little ball of fluffiness – you are able to squelch yourself to a smaller size, or puff yourself up which also in turn makes you jump and float. A lot of the game play uses a lot of momentum type physics meaning some of the maps you can be doing at quite a quick pace. The puzzles in Leo’s Fortune aren’t so difficult that you aren’t able to figure them out within a few seconds; the game doesn’t present many obstacles which prevent you from completing the level; it’s the Star rating system which offers the most complexity in the game – you are rewarded with 1 star for completing a level, 2 stars for not dying on the level, and 3 stars for completing the level in under 4 minutes (usually). Each set of four levels require you to have 5 stars in total to move onto the next block. It works as a sort of gating system, meaning you may have to replay previous levels in order to move on.
Leo’s Fortune has some really gorgeous looking graphics; although the game is only 2D, the world in which you are playing in is so amazingly rendered it is hard to believe that this is actually a mobile game at its core. The animation of Leo is perfect, the way you are able to move him about in all sorts of different shapes and sizes is just a testament to how good the animation really is in this game.  Whilst the game doesn’t have that much audio, Leo does have an interesting voice actor, you’ll get odd snippets of dialogue from him at times, he sounds a bit like a Muppet, and it is hilarious. He doesn’t say much but you really learn a lot about the character just from the small bits.
The game has varying levels of difficulty like I said above with the star rating system; similar to h ow it’s done in games like Angry Birds. But the game also offers an extra level of difficulty in the regular “normal and hard” mode difficulty levels. Only the hard core platforming players should really play the hard mode, as I had plenty of issues progressing on the higher stages with higher star ratings on the normal mode.
Sadly Leo’s Fortune is a very short game; I completed all 5 stages in just over one hour; granted I only just scrapped by on the Star requirements to progress on the stages, but even then, one hour is very short for a game nowadays. You can get a little extra time out of the game if you replay previous levels for a higher star rating, or ramping up the overall difficulty; but personally you are just rehashing old content so one play through is really enough for me.
The game needs to be played with a 360 controller; I couldn’t get the game to work with a keyboard.  I also couldn’t get the game to work with the Steam controller too. Small note for people wanting to use Fraps video capturing – it doesn’t work on this game either sadly.
The only downside to Leo’s Fortune is the shortness of the game; the rest of the game is stellar. The price for this game on iOS is £3, 99; compared to the Steam price of £5, 59. If you are really into the puzzle platforming games, you probably should check this game out for the regular price as I can guarantee you will get plenty of enjoyment out of it and you will find yourself wanting to complete the levels with three stars each time. If you are wanting a more casual experience out of the game; then wait for it to go on sale. Personally I am going to only recommend it when it is on sale, purely because of the short play time.

This review is based off of my steam purchase of X-plane 11 with a Steam sale.  Most of the details I have included are for new users to X-plane.
SOME HIGHLIGHTS/POSITIVES ABOUT X-PLANE 11
User Interface (UI):
Pleasing to the eyes.  The UI in X-plane 11 has been given a complete and welcome overhaul from past versions of the sim. Old and new users will find the settings easier to navigate and understand. Whether configuring a joystick, flight yoke or tweaking the sim’s graphics, the simple sliders, added search function and visuals make configuring X-plane 11 to your liking fun and intelligent.
Lighting:
Impressive. The lighting in X-plane 11 is simply amazing and in my opinion, more realistic than ever.  Lighting is vastly brighter (and more realistic IMO) than previous versions of X-Plane ever were.  There is a noticeable haze which is somewhat adjustable under weather visual settings and for me it enhances this sim.
Sound:
Good. Aside from the ATC audio, general environment and aircraft sounds are quite realistic and pleasing.  Audio for default X-plane 11 aircraft is generally acceptable.  Aircraft audio will depend on the original quality of aircraft you download or pay for.  (Payware aircraft tend to be more realistic both visually and sound-wise)
Clouds:
Clouds appear to be softer and whiter in X-plane 11 but my FPS did take at least a 10 point frame rate drop when flying in heavier fog/cloud layers unless you use a FlyWithLua shadow/cloud plugin which can help to improve frame-rates.
Frame-rates (FPS):
I have been pleasantly surprised by the improvement in frame-rates in X-plane 11 over X-plane 10.  My system is quite old but even with my older processor (Phenom AMD Phenom II 945 Quad Core, 8 gbs Ram and the GTX 750 ti 4gb GPU ) I was able to hover around 30fps when flying in my hometown  (KEKA, KACV)*.   At these settings within the Seattle Demo Area I was able to get around 22-23 fps, clear day and even better FPS at night. )
Graphics/Autogen:
Overall the default textures for terrain, buildings, road-networks, airports etc. are fantastic in X-plane 11.  Days (and nights) are more realistic  than ever in X-plane 11 with the new haze (particle system?)  that has been added to the atmosphere.   HDR lighting makes street lights, runways, and aircraft lighting look real.   With a decent graphics card (the more memory the better)  visual settings and lights will look great in your sim.
Combat mode and Scenerios:

X-plane 11 includes a combat mode which allows your aircraft to engage in combat with other AI air traffic.  Pretty cool!  Various scenerios such as glider tow, mid-air refueling, carrier take-off/landing, and space shuttle re-entry and landing are included.
Addons, Plugins and Tweaking
If you like tweaking,  modding and using addons/plugins you will love X-plane 11 because adding custom content is a breeze in X-plane 11 and will enhance your sim.   (The FlyWithLua plugin is a good example)

SOME NOTE-WORTHY CONS ABOUT X-PLANE 11

User Interface (UI):
If your are coming from X-plane 10 or even 9 you may miss the additional options for rendering that were available in those versions of X-plane.  X-plane 11 has simplified the User Interface which is great but I do wish there was an Advanced Option built-in.
Sounds:
ATC in X-plane 11 make work more realistically than in it did in previous versions of X-plane but I wouldn’t know because I haven’t tried it yet.  I find the synthesized voice that is used completely unbearable to listen to.  Screeching tires sounds when braking still exist in the default Cessna 172.
Steering/ Controls:
It might be just me, but I find the steering/rudder controls of the default Cessna 172 and helicopter erratic and somewhat difficult to control on take-off.  New users especially users coming from FSX may have some difficulty at first.
Clouds:
While generally clouds and fog in X-plane 11 are good we know they could be improved visually in terms of their shape, definition and overall appearance.  Thunderheads and storm clouds should appear like tall menacing thunderheads (cumulus cloud) rather than layers of stratus.  Contrails could be improved and made longer and whiter.  I don't remember ever seeing a grey/black contrail.
*Note about X-plane's default airports (for new users):
Some default airports in X-plane 11 will not include buildings but updated airports which do include buildings, hangers and terminals are being added to X-plane via updates.
CONCLUSION
Try the X-plane 11 Demo first.  See how it runs on your computer system.
If you enjoy flight simulators such as FSX or PrePar3d, I highly recommend X-plane 11 especially if you can get it on a steam sale.

I had high hopes for this game and was left really disappointed.
It's very much like playing a table top wargame, which is definitely not what I wanted.

I gave this game the good ole college try, but it never took.  The biggest appeal for me was its subject matter which is one that is rarely seen in PC wargames.  The age of pike and shot warfare in the 15th-17th centuries is an interesting subject and this is really the only tactical PC game about it on the market.  Also, the quantity of the campaigns, scenarios, and player-made content certainly is impressive.  Finally, the AI is actually very good.
However, this is a 1970's/1980's era board wargame ported over to the PC.  It has ZOCs, phases, action points, and other hallmarks of that Golden Age of board wargames.  I'm an old board wargamer myself, but this "blast from the past" on PC struck me as very dull and dry to play.  It just seems lifeless with its archaic boardgame rules and very primitive and basic graphics and sounds especially in comparison to other tactical PC wargames such as the Take Command/Scourge of War and Combat Mission series.
Matrix Games obviously has found a niche by publishing games that appeal to old boardgamers who may find comfort in seeing old standard rules with the heavy numbers crunching handled by the PC and Pike & Shot: Campaigns is definitely an example of such a game.   Yet, despite its interesting subject matter, I found it too dry and old-fashioned to hold my interest.

Some of the negative comments about this game that I remember seeing are about one thing or another that seemed unrealistic or un-historical to the reviewer.  The reviewers may have had slightly too rigid notions of what might happen in a real war, but for the most part I do not disagree with their comments.  My defense of Pike & Shot regarding these objections is that the developers have done a fantastic job of balancing realism with playability and balance.  In fact, I feel that the game is incredibly good that way.  In my opinion, fixing small realism issues is not worth the risk of reducing the playability and balance.  The progression of the difficulty levels is good.  It has been a lot of work to get good at the game, but very rewarding.  Easy enough to get started, a lot of work to get better, but a ton of fun getting there.  And still a lot of fun to keep playing even though I have recently reached a plateau in my mastery.  And you can see how many hours it took me, although you should divide the number by 2 or 3 because I don't think that the hours played is sensitive to inactive periods.
The place that I have come to is to play Campaigns, at Lieutenant General difficulty (difficulty 4 out of 5).  After a recent campaign where I struggled to win in 17 game-years, I feel like I should be able to win at this level in 3-10 game-years on the first try with any new combination of opposing army lists.  There are 5 campaign turns per game-year.  I much prefer campaigns for two reasons.  Firstly, the typical multi-player opponent seems to be much better at it than I am.  Secondly, I like the opportunity to recover from mistakes and build on successes and develop the skill level of units.
Keep in mind that the "Campaign" element of a campaign in this game is very light.  It is mostly a string of battles, good old-fashioned board-game-like battles as some other reviewers have said.  No research, no management of the economy, no resource types, none of that.  But keep in mind that these facts probably made it feasible to develop a game with such good balance and playability and re-playability.
It may not be your cup of tea.  As a variation on this metaphor, you may like tea or you may like coffee, or you may like both.  I like both.   I love this game but I also look forward to trying some of the games with real depth to the strategic and economic aspects.  I own several but have not got to them yet.

tldr; Not really a "game" but more of a "tool", especially if you are working on your PPL in real life. I bought it for that reason and am not dissapointed in any regards. Set a budget for yoursel because YOU MOST CERTAINLY will be buying addons! Very system intensive so be prepared to have a high end PC if you expect to get graphical results like you see in user videos/screen shots.
This is written around the specific fact that I am mid-way through my PPL training. I bought X-Plane 11 as a "tool" to compliment my real life lessons at my local airport. It does not dissapoint in any regards. I fly GA aircraft, not jets; so you will not find anything in this review about 737's or A320's. Out of the box I was flying the stock Cessna C172 as it was the closest GA aircraft to what I fly in training (Piper Warrior II). Eventually I upgraded to the AeroSphere Piper Warrior II and finally to the vFlightAir Piper Cherokee PA140 Original. The latter being, in my opinion, and much more realistic "feeling" expierience to what I actually fly in training. I base that statement off that fact that I know how the Warrior II handles in different flight configurations and this PA140 addon mimics very true to feel.
Out of the box (and a quick read through of the manual) you will be up and running pretty quickly. Whether you will be up and flying is another matter entirely! Again, going back to the fact I'm in training, I found it very easy to perform a cold & dark start. This goes back to the fact that this simulation is very spot on to real world procedures. Configuration of my gamepad, yoke and rudder pedals was very straightforward. Unfortunately I fly with the gamepad more than the yoke due to my poor choice in a yoke. Point is, the setup of external controllers is very easy.
X-Plane 11 is very GPU intensive. Even on an overclocked i7-6950x w/ OC'd 980 Ti, I cannot run the simulation at the highest graphical settings. Close, but not all the way for sure. A 1080 Ti would solve that, but I'm not there yet. Expect X-Plane 11 to use your GPU to its fullest extent. The more video memory the better as it will use it. If you can squeeze some extra juice out of your CPU and GPU, do that too. Furthermore, once you start plopping addons in like XEnviro and custom sceneries (or ortho's) you will be taxing your gear even more. I'm happy with my setup and can easily stay within 40-60 FPS unless XEnviro is really working hard to display significant weather events.
The only real downfall here (and I'm sure this is to be said for other flight sims) is that true VFR flying is not 100% obtainable due to the fact that obvious landmarks you'd use for naviagation are probably not going to be present. For example, when flying patterns at my local airport in the sim I am using different features than what I'd be using in real life. Why? Because they are not there.
On the flipside of that, certain addon sceneries for other airports include tremendous amounts of detail for not only the airport proper, but also the surrounding areas. In some cases the designer(s) go as far as to populate the surrounding countryside with 3D buildings as they would be. This makes VFR much more realistic, especially in the general vacinity of the airport in question.

X-Plane 11 is a major improvement from previous versions. Where to begin? The graphics, the interface, the tutorials, all of them have produced a much more well-rounded product. While a simulation game such as this still faces challenges such as showing the user how to actually fly planes, it is much better than X-Plane 10 as it provides examples of what to do. The graphics are a huge improvement from before, and the game runs smoother. Moreover, the interface is much easier to navigate and understand. Additionally, the game is built better for third-party scenery or mod integration. While there are many positives, there are also some drawbacks. The game still crashes randomly and does require a long time to load a specific location in the game environment. Also, to get the best experience, having peripherals such as a throttle, rudder pedals, etc., and these come with significant cost and do not come with the game. What would be good to see in future versions is some form of total immersion of flight school, where the user is able to learn the fundamentals of flight instead of having to search YouTube for quality training materials. Additionally, more default scenery would be appreciated by the developer. All things considered, version 11 is worlds better than 10, and I have thoroughly enjoyed it and would highly recommend it!

Do you like the 90's shooter DOOM? Yes, well so does Wrack, but can the game stand up to the legend? In short no, but here are the reasons.
The good:
+Movement is super fast and it feels great.
+The levels feature little secrets in the form of jumping puzzles.
+The scoring/combo system is a nice way of pushing yourself to stay inside the thick of the action.
The bad:
-The story is way to wordy for this type of game.
-The soundtrack is boring and sounds like  a rehash of DOOM.
-The game lacks polish and here are some examples: Missiles clip through walls, sometimes the teleportation effect doesn't play on enemies, lava is an insta-kill obstacles rather than a DOT like in DOOM (like why would they not steal this from DOOM), the golem/robot enemies don't have any visual particle effect when they ground slam so you'll just take damage instantly if you don't jump in time and you can skip door opening cutscenes but not boss-fight intro cutscenes.
-The weapons need a good tweaking and here's what I think could improve them: The pistol is useless and should have had a slower firing rate but done way more damage, the plasma rifle should not have bullet drop, the sword should not have a 2.5 second wind up because it doesn't fit with the fast gameplay and finally all ammo caps should have been doubled. The only two weapons that don't suck are the shotgun and the rocket launcher.
-The game needed to double down on guns and get creative, because you'll only recieve 4 bland weapons throughout the entire ordeal.
-Some boss-fights limit your movement speed and of course the boss has huge AOE attacks. Other bosses feature big arenas but the boss doesn't attack, seriously in one boss-fight I was only attacked once.
-Enemies will sometimes get stuck on corners and other times they simply forget to attack because they are stuck in an animation loop.
So just to reiterate Wrack is not worth your time or your money. It's so close to be good, but as of right now it's just a game with too many rough edges to be truly appreciated.
Really fun old-school FPS. Nice soundtrack, clean graphics, and tight gameplay. Lots of different modes for replay. Solid buy!

A deliberate throwback to the 90s style of FPS, with fast player movement, no reloading, rocket jumping, loads of secret areas, numerical health and armor and fast-paced music, courtesy of Doom's own Bobby Prince, as well as a plot that's juuuust thin enough to hold everything together without getting in the way of the action. Wrack has only four weapons: a Pistol, Shotgun, Pulse Rifle and Rocket Launcher, but they are enough for the task at hand. The game makes use of a unique combo system that allows each to to fire a powerful "finisher" if you get 3 or more kills in quick succession. Wrack rewards the twitchy shooter in much the same way as its predecessors, and has an eye-catching color palette and cel-shading, setting it apart from say, Quake and Hard Reset. It is regrettably short, comprising only the first "episode" of what seems to be a planned series, ending on a glaring cliffhanger, but the game does feature a level editor and Steam Workshop support, which has resulted in such gems as the entire first episode of Doom recreated. There is no multiplayer mode however, an odd omission for a game of this subgenre.

This game is a excersize in frustration. To begin with it's early access and that means it's not "finished". As of today 31/12/2015 it is still in Early access and I'm very close to NOT recommending the game.
The problem comes in with the games level of precision needed in later levels. You have to be super accurate while the game itself is not 100% coded. This is where the frustrations come in.
As an example. Eirene's level at the end is a great example of how frustrating this game can be. At the end you need to navigate a small, laval filled hallway with the odd rocket that can kill you thrown into the mix. The rockets seek you out and the small blocks you can land on are way too small. I began by saying that it's probably just me getting frustrated at the game and I'm seeing things. But fact was that the collision detection is a bit wonkey. Take-off's from standstill sometimes work great. Other times you land and do a quick take off and you shoot to the left or right faster than you are used to. Hitting the edge of the blocks pinball you sometimes into the lava.
However the worst problem with the game is the "jitter".
The "jitter" is when the game seems to skip a frame. It's a very small problem and a miniscule problem starting out with the game, but in later levels that 1 frame skip is super deadly.
Ok ok... so all that sounds bad, but I'd still say give it a shot. The game is very fun in the beginning and if it stayed like that there would not be a challenge. But the end game does step over that line very quickly.
Ah yes... the topic of the "artwork". Look there are dime a dosen games like this. Take your character from point A to B through a difficult maze. Or if it's the trying over and over again thing you can play Darksouls. From a marketing standpoint this is a great idea. Skandily clad female anime characters are the next best thing to the obvious other that sells very well. However then this game would not make it to steam. Trust me, after about 5 levels the picture is the last thing you're thinking about or looking at. If the pictures are the reason you are not buying the game then don't be a prude.

Leo's Fortune tells the story of one
mans journey to find his stolen gold. Scrooge McDuck levels of gold. Traveling through 5 worlds and 20 odd levels Leo faces many obstacles along the way.
Core of the game is focused on physics based platforming and for the most part it works quite well, for those moments it doesn't the game employs a passive checkpoint system which cuts down on restarts and frustrating deaths. Relatively short lived but the 2.5d-like artwork and accompanying soundtrack is just magic. Completing the game unlocks hardcore mode(1-death run) and levels contained a small number of collectibles that gave access to bonus areas so there was some reason to return. Don't hesitate to grab this one on sale if full price looks too high.

update! I actually changed my rating! I now recommend this game.  If you don't expect too too much in terms of a logic puzzle or character development, it's kind of a fun thing to play on a short break. Not too addictive.
Original review:
I commend this creative team.   If you like racing against the clock this is probably your best bet.  for me, The game LOOKS just beautiful.  But I kinda wish I tried a free demo first, or that this amazing artistry would be made into a point and click and logic adventure. I am older now and play games for their creative beauty and also for the challenge - not by trying over and over to get higher scores (for repetition I'd rather learn a new instrument or new language), but to challenge and delight my reasoning and creative abilities.

Overall I had fun with Leo's Fortune. The controls work well and there are some interesting physics puzzles. The graphics are nice and the story is better than I was expecting.
The game has three problems though. The game is short at around only two hours long. The game is quite easy and you won't be that challenged by it. Finally the game doesn't really include many original mechanics.
If you like platformers I think you will enjoy Leo's Fortune. Just don't expect a highly original, long or difficult game.

No nostalgia, no rose tinted glasses, for me BFBC2 never was a really big pleasure neither in the past nor now. I´ve played BF since 1942, and also played all BF including, Desert Combat, BF2, Vietnam, 2142, 3, 4, HL, BF1, and Project Reality. While in BF1942 and 2 styled games actual firefights happened and you had a sense for frontlines, with BFBC2 things changed, pace was raised a lot and it became a game about flanking and twitch shooting. BF and COD are often seperated, but for me since BFBC until today both are extremely similar in their shooting mechanics: Exagerated movement speed promoting permanent flanking and movement, ADS shooting, minimal recoil. It was BFBC which started this run, gun, jump out of helos right into infantry firefights, tagging enemies, and Michael Bay all over the place. Perhaps with rising age my taste changed but it was when BF for me started completely to loose its realism and to become another COD-like shooter just on a greater scale with more oppurtunities and vehicles. BF3 was a technical revolution but even made these aspects worse for me and since then BF franchise even further progressed into the arcade direction.
I certainly understand that people love this - and that is perfectly fine. Funny stuff happens "only in Battlefield" but unfortunately not much realistic stuff which prevents me from having a deep satisfying experience with this franchise.
If you are with me on this, BFBC2 won´t bring you pleasure. If look for a realistic "Battlefield" experience I  recommend you to try out games like Project Reality, Red Orchestra 2/Rising Sun, Verdun, and soon Rising Sun 2: Vietnam.

Fortix is a strategic puzzle game in which you must capture the castles by making lines and rectangles. There are turrets and dragons ready to kill you all around and you have a set amount of lives per stages.
The game is really stressful, because if you die in a set of levels, you will start over at the first one. Also in the later difficulties, with how hard it is to make pixel perfect squares, you will die to random 1x1 pixel bumps you have made while capturing terrain. This game could have been pretty good, I like the idea. There's even more bad things about the game...
This is a "puzzle" kind of game, but the enemies and bonuses doesn't spawn at the same place if you retry or start over. That makes it so you can win many levels just by re-trying until you get a "Stop-time" bonus in a convenient spot and clear the level in 20 seconds.
The game can be completed in less than 30 minutes (even on Impossible difficulty), but at least it's cheap...
I do not think it is too bad, but I cannot recommend it, way too punishing, it's 1$ though... So if you want to try a new type of puzzle/strategy game, sure, try it. Personally, I found it too punishing and frustrating. I also felt like I had no real control over certain of my deaths.

I wanted to get this game for some time, but I was somehow pushed back by some comments that it wouldn't work on Windows 10. But I found some mods and fixes that help with that so I decided to give it a go. And, oh boy, I can pretty much say that this is one of the best Star Wars games, especially because I prefer Clone Wars era more than Empire/Rebellion era.
One of many things that surprised me in this game was its AI. Your squadmates are actually useful, who would've thought right? They will use different weapons on different enemies, depending on their weaknesses. They will automatically revive squadmates without your orders and so on.
Enemies are smart too, and they are pretty accurately made. Geonosians will fly around making you really hard to shoot them. B2 Super Battle Droids will give you nightmare if you run out of grenade launcher ammo or if you don't have grenades. Small scavenger droids are fast as hell, and when they attack in packs, it's hard to kill them. But the best thing about AI enemy is that they will not just stand and let you shoot them, they will try to surround you.

Armello is a board game with several win conditions that are unique to it's universe. It also utilizes a day/night cycle in which unique events will happen and the games difficulty progresses. This time day night cycle is also a timer in which the game runs.  No game will last more than 12 Dawn's.
First won condition is prestige: prestige is your clans standing with the King. If you lead in prestige at dawn you get to make a choice between one of two decrees that will be enacted.  These are random but include things like adding more guards, creating more obstacles, adding bounties to players, and so on.  I have dubbed this win the afk won because you can get an amulet that let's you have 2 prestige, turn 1, and never have less than 2 through the game.  I also see it as the easiest to generate as killing players as well as the enemis (Banes) grants prestige.
Second is rot. Rot is a mechanic that is supposed to be the opposite of prestige. As you roll dice to achieve outcomes the rot symbol is typically a miss but once a character passes 5 rot it becomes a 'crit.' (note that the game uses what is called exploding dice.  This means if you 'crit' on the die roll it acts as a success and is rerolled for additional outcomes.) Rot is obtained by dying to banes, equipping some.items and casting some spells. You won with rot by killing the King with a higher rot factor than his. Rot is definitely a combat centered mechanic as the person with the higher rot count gets the opposing players rot count in additional combat dice. It's real good...
Third, the comabt win. Kill the king. Done. Not the easiest task as the King got some dank equipment but not the worst.
Lastly, the stones. You can collect four stones and heal the King for this goody two shoes win condition.
Now, each character has a unique playstyle and they have all been thought out very well by this team. However, you only.gain player experience when you win a game.  Needless to say, as a statistically challenged gamer (unluckiest man alive), I'm still a pretty low level.
Either way, fun with four friends for a few games before it gets stale and we move on to something else. Worth it all in all.

Armello is a turn based strategy played on a hexagonal field.
4 players compete against each other to claim the royal seat.
Each player takes turns moving their hero and drawing cards from a deck pool.
They can use cards in their hand against other opponents at any time,
as long as it isn’t on the target opponent’s turn, and not in their home base.
Such as;
You could use cards to equip items and set traps out of your turn.
You could use cards against an opponent who is not making their turn.
You can not use cards against an opponent who is making a turn.
There’s no deck building. So unlike card games like Dominion, you can’t customize the deck pool for people to draw cards from.
A game match on average takes 60+ minutes to complete on default settings. With a default maximum of 18 turns and on average ends around turn 15.
There are 3 objectives you can win the crown by;
Defeat the King in a battle and survive.
Be the Presiege Leader after King dies.
Purge the King with the 4 spirit stones.
There are multiple ways to work towards your objective, but as you follow one path, the other paths to victory become increasingly difficult to accomplish.
There are quite a few unfriendly game designs to keep in mind.
No Sound Notifications - There's no audio cue for finding a 'full lobby' nor audio cue for your turn.
Hard to differentiate settlement ownership - Settlements captured display flags based on the animal type, rather than the individual hero. So your opponents can be using the same flag.
Obscuring Clouds - Zooming out to look at the entire game board actually makes it harder to see anything.
Multiple Stats Hidden Windows - The game tries to show the important need-to-know stats of the heroes, but buries most of it in multiple window tabs.
Undefined Game Terms - Some tooltips on the cards uses game terms that aren't defined to the player. Unless if the player already know the term, they can't look it up during the match.
Player Disadvantage - Players who are at the start and end of a day/night cycle are at a slight disadvantage as they need to quickly spend their cards. There's no grace period for the players, once the day/night cycle starts gold and magic points are handed out.
E.G. The player first to go has a card(s) drawn in their hands, but doesn't have enough gold/magic to spend it. They need to wait till the Day/Night phrase for a payout, but they are the first player to take their turn on a phase change.
If they don't use the card(s) in time before their turn starts, they draw less card(s) than they would otherwise.
Vice versa, the last player has less of a chance of winning the game by killing the King, since they are the last player to have a go at it.

Few games feature titles which would be able to summarize the plotline, gameplay and experience itself better than the one I’m writing about today. “Into the Dark: Ultimate Trash Edition” says it all and even then you won’t be properly prepared to play it. It’s Homegrown Games’ first original Steam project since their previous work on Painkiller: Resurrection, makes that title seem like a family friendly game when compared to Into the Dark.
I like writing about abstract games in general. They provide a challenge, they don’t follow rules or logic. They truly reject reality and substitute their own. Despite reviewing for only a year or so, I had my fair share of mind fracks in video game form. And along comes Into the Dark: Ultimate Trash Edition which literally sets the dumpster on fire. Even if I’d make a sustained effort to explain the story and its characters to you (something I rarely do, since I despise spoilers), I have to confess that I had a hard time understanding this game as well.
All in-game evidence seems to point out that the protagonist is an alter ego of the main developer, Ivan Ertlov. In all honesty, it will matter not what the plotline represents, but where it shall take you towards. The means of transportation shouldn’t deter you from enjoying the journey. Or so I’m told. Just move along, shoot anything that’s moving since it will only be hostile and try to find a meaning to the random succession of rooms which are littered with semifictional propaganda. Less is more in this case. The less you try to understand, the better.
Into the Dark is powered by the FPSC graphics engine. A weird choice but then again, what’s not weird about this game? I’m almost certain that the rough looks and visual glitches are presented so on purpose. It’s an “ancient” graphics engine and it was never that good looking in the first place, but it does its intended job, I guess. Into the Dark has so much film grain imbedded into it, that the only time the textures will look crisp and detailed enough, is after you ingest in-game alcohol and become inebriated. The developer is jokingly (I hope) suggesting that playing the game while sober, ain’t the right way to do it.
Of course it could have looked better but since it’s a 2014 release running on an engine that was nearly a decade old even on Into the Dark’s launch date, I’m willing to cut it some slack. Miracles were made just by ensuring some degree of stability. I only had a few crashes to desktop when loading a save game. No frame rate dips since 4K resolution was only a dream back when FPSC was conceived. So glorious 1080p it is then. Visual glitches create the maze illusion during some levels and heavy motion blur kicks in also after you’re severely injured, not just drunk. The effects aren’t that bad once you overlook the goofy amount of film grain as I mentioned already.
Voice acting is actually the strong part in this game’s audio department. Ivan Ertlov and a female voice, can be heard constantly bickering over this random fact or the next one. It plays along nicely with the private eye and his unqualified secretary trope. Ivan even shares some monologues from time to time. They may not be as funny as anything spewed by Serious Sam or Duke Nukem over the years, yet they are still mildly entertaining. By contrast, the sound effects and OST are subpar.
As you probably guessed it by now, the gameplay in Into the Dark: Ultimate Trash Edition’s case makes about as much sense as its plotline. That isn’t necessarily a bad thing. You get (simplistic) puzzle sections mixed in with all that action and shooting. Even some exploration, despite the linear level design. I really appreciated the inclusion of save games from nearly all of the game’s 11 stages. It really saved me the trouble of enduring it for prolonged periods of time. If you’re an Achievement hunter, you’d best arm yourself with a ton of patience since Into the Dark will really test you out.
What’s a shooting game without a large and diversified arsenal? A Steam indie game you say? Shame on you! There are more guns than needed in this title. Some are overpowered while others won’t get you far. I’m really sad I never got to use that chainsaw to its full potential. By the time you reach it, most enemies with be shooting at you with supernatural efficiency. You don’t bring a knife to a gunfight. 1968’s Night of the Living Dead can be watched in its entirety in-game and I’m certain that Romero fans shall rejoice. It sure adds some much needed value to Into the Dark. I suggest the dev team to try some Ed Wood “masterpieces” next time, to be more in tune with the game’s themes.
There are so many pictures and references to Cthulhu and Ronald Reagan, that I’m surprised neither one of them ends up as the final mandatory boss fight. Enemy types are creative, but still lacking in the kind of diversity enjoyed by the boomsticks (Army of Darkness reference). You have the obligatory demons and nazi zombies but I bet you didn’t expect zombie go-go dancers whose undead breasts may be enlarged from the game’s settings. Nudity, swearing and parodies to political correctness, all seem innocent at this point. Stay classy, Ivan!
So why on Earth would I still recommend anyone to play this? Well for one, it ain’t the lazy and abysmal “work” of an asset flipping thief. This ain’t no Slaughtering Grounds, folks. It may look like its inbred cousin from afar, but in truth they aren’t related. It’s just Ivan Ertlov’s middle finger raised to game development itself, not to his potential players and customers. Into the Dark has a few redeeming points and I’m not referring to the Cards or Achievements. It’s quite unique, if not through its gameplay then at least story-wise. You’ll have a hard time finding a bigger digital absurdity that somehow still manages to entertain. Purchase it when heavily discounted and I’m certain the regrets shall be next to none.

I play mostly offline, so don't be mistaken by the low hour count. I don't recommend this game, for two reasons.
The first reason is that the game leaves you very little choice in how to play it. That starts with force selection: The number of units of a specific type is strictly limited, with several already being pre-selected by the game. No, I don't want those horse dudes, I want more foot skirmishers to screen my Tercios. Well bad luck; the designer doesn't allow me to.
And he doesn't want me to set up and command the units as I wish. The setup zone is quite small, and the way units interact with one another once combat commences further limits your choices. Whether or not you can charge an enemy, for instance, is dependent on whether your unit type is allowed to charge the enemy unit type (many infantry units are not allowed to charge cavalry), and you can charge only if the targeted unit is your unit's "priority target" (i.e., the greatest possible threat). That in effect means the game prevents many choices you could make and tactics you could come up with. Not being allowed to charge those pesky Cuirassiers theatening my flank because my perfectly positioned infantry unit has only 40% pikes (still leaving me with more pikemen than there are Cuirassiers) really sucks.
Control you have over your units is further limited by close combat (which ends either by victory or rout, not by you choosing to disengage), by fleeing, which can spread panic among neighbouring units, and by pursuing, which you cannot interrupt. Thus, there will be battles in which you spend entire turns looking at your units doing stuff you didn't order them to do. All this greatly limits your choices and your freedom as a player. Furthermore, battles effectively end when one side realises it is about to lose. That means, again and again: You fight off the enemy onslaught, move your units into position to deliver the final blow and eagerly click "end turn". Now it's payback time, you think with an evil grin on your face. Well you think wrong. The game will end the battle because "the enemy lost heart", depriving you of all the joy of smashing him to tiny bits. No fun at all.
To be fair though, much of the criticism above is against design decisions that are comprehensible, and even laudable in their own way. I do have some knowledge of warfare in the 16th century, having read Wilhelm Rüstow's Geschichte der Infanterie, Delbrück's History of the Art of War and Oman's Art of War in the Sixteenth Century, among other books, and lots of stuff on the Military Revolution debate, and I acknowlege that the designer has done some very respectable research into the mechanics of pike & shot warfare and early modern army composition. Thus, if you won't find too many foot skirmishers in Western European armies prior to the French Wars of Religion, that's actually quite accurate; if you quickly lose control over your units during combat or find units refusing to charge, that is spot on, and if battles are won by panic spreading after a unit routs, not by slaughtering an unbreakable enemy to the last man, that is realistic. 16th-century armies are neither Borg nor Space Marines. And they didn't set up in the map corner to prevent flanking.
Thus, the game design has its purpose. And there are genuinely good aspects about Pike & Shot. One of these is the simulation of unit cohesion. Unit cohesion in the early modern period was arguably more important for battlefield effectivenes than individual weapon skills (which separates the Pike & Shot era from the Middle Ages, or European armies from Oriental ones). The game simulates that; units in the game can be "steady", which means they fight at full effectiveness, they can be "disrupted", which greatly reduces their effectivity, or "fragmented" which almost nullifies it. There were those cases in which a Tercio's arquebusiers sought protection under the pikes, involuntarily pushing them upwards, which then made the whole unit vulnerable to a cavalry charge. This is exactly what the "fragmented" state simulates: A unit which is ineffective not because of the number, training or equipment of its men, but because order and coolheadedness have been lost. An effective way to win battles is to concentrate fire on a single unit, causing fragmentation, and then charging in to cause a rout which might spread panic among the enemy.
Obviously, the way the game works is due to design decisions which value above all else historical accuracy (or rather, the way the designer interprets and simulates it), not so much player freedom. That is very respectable and will find its fans, but I'm not one of them. Furthermore, I don't quite see why in a skirmish mode battle I am not allowed to try an army composition I prefer.
The second reason for me not liking the game is the combat results it produces. And this is what kills the game for me. I constantly have the feeling that the computer cheats (which it doesn't; you and the AI are treated as equals by the game engine). A single light artillery units takes one shot to cause monstrous casualties and "disrupt" my huge 2000-man regular Tercio, two more salvoes by Dutch 500-man battalions (250 musketeers each) rout it; swapping forces, I never cause more casualties than 9 (prediction: 1-63) to a huge Tercio with my heavy (!) artillery at short (!) range  and can never even "disrupt" it, and my Dutch battalions are whipped from the field in two turns. In other battles, my noble Gendarmes charge an average quality Cuirassiers unit and lose the melee, Tartars wreak havoc among my troops with their bows, whilst my firearms cause neglibile damage, and so on.
Yes, fortune is fickle, especially in war. But the casualties a unit causes and takes seem excessively random to me, as is the chance of it getting "disrupted" or "fragmented". That is arguably an issue within the (boardgame-based) game engine. After my elite Spanish Tercio Viejo, charging on even ground an average quality Dutch late Tercio and outnumbering it almost 2:1, was unable to rout this enemy in several rounds of melee combat and took as many casualties at it caused, I quit playing.

I highly recommend this if you like turn-based tactical strategy games.
It's very easy to get into, but there's a lot of depth in knowing the different advantages and matchups between armies and units. Because the military tactics of this period are not familiar with most people, knowing how a cuirassier would match up against a tercio isn't straightforward. That said, the tutorial will get you on your feet and the manual is excellent.
Battles are won by thoughtful pre-planning and making calculated decisions in chaotic situations in order to break enemy morale and rout them from the battlefield. One key feature that makes this game unique from other games is that you lose direct control of your units once they engage in melee. It makes sense from a realistic standpoint; armies would often pursue routing armies after winning a melee skirmish.
This may sound like an annoyance, but it adds more weight to your decisions. It might seem like a good idea to engage in melee and rout the fractured enemy unit in front of you, but you could be easily flanked by enemy calvary sitting behind enemy lines. Taking this into consideration and executing a successful plan is really satisfying.
There's a TON of content in this game. There are hundreds of hours worth of singeplayer content in the game and many more in the form of player-made mods. Some of them look really cool, like Napoleonic or Victorian era skirmishes. The vanilla campaigns and skirmishes themselves are awesome and it's a really fun way to learn about a period of history that is rarely covered in games and other forms of media. The random battle generator is excellent. This game also runs really well on low-end hardware.
If you pick this up, I recommend you get the sound and music mods on the game's forum. The base SFX and music are really weak.
I really hope the developer continues to support this game in the future. I'd LOVE to see achievements and trading cards, and I think an ironman mode would be perfect.
tl;dr: Excellent turn-based tactics game, definitely worth a buy if you like strategy with even a small interest in this time period.

Excellent wargame. It's sometimes frustrating, with a lot of ecclectic rules for different army sets , but the AI is surprisingly active and the dice-rolls are a good way of simulating the chaos of battle, keeping things nail-biting the whole way through. If the campaign feels tacked on, it's because it is. There's a lot of pointless whack-a-mole between armies, but the option of designing your army and carrying through one battle to another adds a lot tactical choice and investment into the game.
There's a huge variety of army types as warfare rapidly evolved through the period. Other developers might have chosen to make the content into 100 different DLCs, so by today's standards it's an impressive level of fidelity to the customer. Definitely worth the price of admission.
It's even possible to hotseat multiplayer, but you have to launch a server game with yourself, so it's a bit clunky. Overall, the best praise I can give for this game is that even after many hours of play the game remains challenging and victory is never certain. Have a good time cursing at your computer!

Pros:

Cons:
-Airport scenery (I was talking about like the ground and stuff when you're in the air in the pros) is mediocre, and small airports are very Very generic with only a few generic hangars, and the wrong runway, while FSX completely modeled accurately my local tiny regional airfield
-Long loading screens (I honestly don't care)
-Jet engine sounds are absolutely AWFUL (at least on the 737) it is just a generic whooshing sound thats very robotic and ugly sounding (there is a free soundpack to give the 737 real CFM-56 engine sounds)

-Default traffic is only GA aircrafts (even at unrealistic places like Washington National)
Overall this is an amazing simulator, and even though there are a lot of cons, these are tiny nit-pickings that have bothered me, but don't worry these don't matter that much, and I'd rate this sim 8/10.

Armello adds the third dimension to the numeric board-game in a pretty fashion.
It's tempting to compare this game with another 2D board-game on Steam which I won't mention here (Gremlins, Inc.), as buying one will induce buying the other. Don't try comparisons, there is no need for it.
This game features RNG, hexagonal tiles, quests, animals, prestige and rot. Mash it all up, generate a new board each time you play it again, put four players and you have it all.
The background is really pleasant to discover, and although the narrative is often underestimated in the reviews, I find it pleasant to read at times. Still, the text is only an introduction to the formal thing : the struggle for the throne.
I was happy to see a good equilibrium between RNG and strategy. Overcoming a bad card pick in the beginning of a turn is possible, avoiding RNG-fulfilled situations when you want to play safely is possible, planning paths and plans to win is possible. You're not tied with the dice, no matter how pretty they look (and there are quite a lot to be unlocked). You can sometimes guess what your opponents are up to, and you can try to dismantle their plans. Sometimes it works, and sometimes not. Balanced.
The tutorial will teach you quite a lot of details in order not to be crushed too badly, but you will still need 1 or 2 games with each character to become more familiar with their abilities. It's still a pleasure to play it while you are mastering it, when you begin to understand how things work and how to act properly.
In the end, I think this game has quite a good replayability, one game lasts for longer than an hour but it stills tempts you to play a second one right after. Developers are friendly and keep updating the game at fair amount of times.
I still have some issues with it, which won't make me downvote him, but (I hope) will make think twice the potential buyer and reader of this review :
- The servers are often overloaded, which result in a lot of online games experiencing lots of lag. It can basically force you to disconnect, preventing you from finishing your game. The visuals are simple but timeless, the audio is is pleasant and unobtrusive, and the lootbox incentive to play against random strangers online avoids the worst aspects such systems can introduce by sticking to cosmetic dice/skins.
DLC is handled in a fair way; a private game between friends/AI allows one player to share their DLC characters with the rest of the players.
A real treat and more games of this breed are needed.

To start off with, i was gifted this game by a friend who insisted i play this.
Never have i ever been interested in tabletop games card games or anything of the sort as my go to games are usually shooters of some sort along the lines of arma or csgo. But after giving this game a chance i was immediately hooked and now play this game daily wether it be by myself or friends, (As of this review, it wouldve been 3 days since. And definently more to go.)
Firstly, starting off with the gameplay in general,
- For me, It was unbelievably easy to understand the game's core mechanics with a beautifully made tutorial that was lore rich and very in depth about how the game works. The tutorial itself lasts about an hour but the entire time you're playing it, it feels like youre making the decisions rather than a forced "You go here and do this, good job you learned it" kind of deal.
- The gameplay centers itself around a clockwise turn taking rotation of players, And like other turn taking games, this one is amusing to watch instead of annoying to wait until your turn again. During your waiting period you can still play cards even if it's not your turn to do so yet, and can make it a game changer just based on studying your opponents. This also includes teleportation, Buff's and defences if you forsee a threat coming to you, and evasions if you're fast enough.
- I've encountered absolutely no bugs or unfair advantages to characters in my time of playing as everything is balanced out by how you play each character.
- Many characters to choose from with each one having their own special talent and preferred way to win. Whilst some characters are DLC locked, the default characters are still amazing to play as. Seeing as the game has been released for 3 years now, it was a very good idea to release some new characters into the game and very well recieved as i enjoy playing the dlc characters just as much as i do the default, But again as i said before, they give absolutely no unfair advantages over another character.
- The map itself is ever changing but always has that very familiar sense to it. Being the giant circle and all. Reason i say this is there is only one map but the map itself random generates to give a new feel to the game each time you play changing the locations of swamps, mountains and forests to hide in. Yet balanced in terms of where the player's spawns are.
The lore and time to make this beautifu game has made a very good impression on me. And im looking forward to the 2.0 release (Currently playing in 1.9) And other future amazing updates.
Overall i would give this game a   9 / 10

Overall, Armello is founded on some decently strong core concepts. The idea of a game where heroes vye for the crown as a mad king draws closer to death is pretty neat, and the various win conditions have interesting dynamics in how they play off one another. However, the game really starts to fall apart when you start to get into some of the execution and how they handled other gameplay elements.
The tutorial feels very sparse and doesn't teach you the game particularly well, deciding to focus on its narrative over the gameplay. Some aspects of play are just not touched on at all such as how turn order is determined (I think it's random but there's no real way to tell) and how the game determines ties with its Prestige mechanic (Characters with high Prestige in a game can choose powerful board affecting cards but it's very unclear how it determines who has highest Prestige when it's tied).
Success also feels far too based on RNG, and I don't even mean in respect to the die rolls for combat or the percentage chances for tests, I mean in how the game determines quest locations. Every player during a game gets quests that they have to reach on the board in order to gain important equipment, stat-increases, and at the very end a free pass to have a chance at winning but how the game determines where they'll be placed on the map can make or break a game. I've had games where I've never been able to catch-up because my quest was clear on the other side of the board and I'd just get killed over and over and other games where I was able to win by the third day because all of my quests were on the same side of the map.
To get more nitpicky the game also lacks a lot of variance in terms of settings and just small quality of life stuff. The map is locked at the same size, there's no way to adjust most of the base game settings without it turning off Steam achievements (if you care about that), and no good way to adjust turn timers (which is an issue because games mostly drag on due to people taking forever on their turns). In terms of QoL stuff, there's no way to determine the turn order (without the first set of turns just passing and you just trying to remember how the order goes), they put the game glossary in the escape menu instead of just in the HUD for the game, and the active game log is finnicky as to what it's willing to tell you is happening and what it's not.
All in all, Armello could really be something to have fun with if it just fixed a lot of the smaller stuff. Adding a small turn roster in the in-game HUD would honestly be enough for me to be able to positively recommend it. But there's just too many little things that drag down what was a kinda good game.

As someone who loves table-top games but doesn't have a lot of IRL friends, this is a VERY fun game to get into. The art is amazing, the gameplay is smooth and filled with fantasy, and the general game setup feels fantastic.
RNG can be very unforgiving at times, sometimes making the gameplay feel unfair or unbalanced. You can go from having everything to having nothing very quickly. Considering combat is based on dice rolls, you can go in well prepared and come out on the bottom still. If you're ok with RNG like I am, then it's not really a game deterent.
Online play is fun but also rather trying at times. You run a high chance of being placed with players who play "together". While one player attacks specific players, their partner will rush to win the game as soon as possible. You run the risk of this kind of play when doing anything online though.  At the end of the game you can reward good players with credit to their name.
New DLC, upgrades, and characters are also often being added which makes playing it over and over more refreshing. DLC can be a BIT pricey for some, but considering new character models and assets are created for each new character I find it to be worth the purchase if you really want the character.
Games can get a tad long, pushing past 30minutes per game, depending on RNG and player style. So be prepared to not have a short game.
All in all, it's a solid game and a good purchase in my book. Even if I play it once a week (or heck, even once a month) I'd still consider it worth the money I paid.

Disclaimer: I had the main developer in my friend's list once but we were at best: acquaintances. I spent much of my time in the Steam Group Chat with him and some other users who, some, became my friends. I don't like him, I don't hate him, I'm quite neutral towards him.
Wrack is Maze-Based First Person Shooter, obviously, trying to hit that nostalgia weak spot of the Doom fanatics with a very clean and attractive cell-shaded look. I love first person shooters and if your game description included "Doom" in it, then it better be as good as "Brutal Doom"!
Lets get the story part done with quickly, you're Kain, who is... some guy that needs to stop Earth from being invaded by the Aliens. He does this by, surprisingly, shooting a lot of stuff and preventing them from stealing the great Hyperion Generator! He's preety much the only character that gets any characterization, but even then, it's minimal as hell. Starlyn, which seems to be his girlfriend, doesn't have much to do during the whole story, only a convenient romantic plot device. She even gets kidnapped and the game forgets about her. The there's Fabian who has luscious long hair brown hair and is also a funny ponce, so basically John Romero. Finally there is the main villain, Exo, who just comes by as your average quirky bad guy. So nothing much on the story side but 10 euros isn't gonna get you an epic greek odyssey.
So what would make this a Doom-Like FPS? Well, during the glorious decade of 1990's, FPS concentrated on offering a labyrinth of nasty monster that you had to shoot. This was before Halo and CoDs came in and astonishingly enough, made an already simple formula, even more basic. Back then you had to work for your survival, traverse through some complicated well-thought out level design and use a good variation of weaponry to blast away your enemies! So does Wrack achieve these objectives?
For me, the most important part of any shooter is the actual shooting! Level design is great and all, but if I'm not seeing limbs of corpses flying, weapons shouting god's fury, skill-dependent guns, screen shaking (not too much though), walls being painted with visceral red fluids and better gunplay feedback than early access fanboy reports, then you're gunplay has, as Jim Sterling would say: "all the impact of the limpest willy of America". Wrack comes about halfway with this portion. Cartoon gibs explode to the air like a leprechaun pub vomit and most weapons sound preety good. The sword is as good as Serious Sam 3's sledgehammer (quick and snappy kills, although it is a bit risky), the pistol is♥♥♥♥♥♥weak, shotgun is competent (kills nearly everything in one shot and the fire rate lets you decide which body falls next), plasma pulse rifle is ok (requires some good aiming since the shots fall off) and the rocket launcher has nothing wrong with it to be honest. Each rocket is a precise mini nuke that'll make a room full of enemies, a quick sludge of organs. Not an amazing list of weapons, so I'd say it's competent, but combined with the speed of your character, then it's near to an adrenal fueled experience like that of Shadow Warrior (2013).
Wrack's gimmick includes a combo meter that can power your weapons with powerful secondaries. I do think it's a nice little idea, however, it doesn't work perfectly. The secondary shots aren't all that imaginative. The shotgun and the rocket launcher just make a bigger bang, the pistol shoots thing railgun-like laser, the sword gives also a bigger bang firing three plasma shots and the pulse plasma rifle fires a slow gigantic projectile that eats everything on its way. The combo meter decreases quickly and most enemies require at least 2 shots to kill them, so you better keep up. And once you clear a room with a combo meter prepared then you'll have to hold down the secondary fire button for a good while until you find a suitable target. Honestly, I wish you could fire these special shots any time you wanted as long as you had the special ammo for it. This would probably work better in an FPS arena-based shooter.
As for the level design, it's alright, for moments you'll get some nice imaginative sections, but they're a handful. This issue comes along with the enemy variation. Now if the enemy variation was low but dynamic, then I wouldn't mind, unfortunately you'll only face robot spiders, kamikaze robot spiders, kid aliens, adult aliens that change shirts from time to time, flying turrets and a giant damage sponge robot. Most of them fire a small colourful projectile which aren't too hard to dodge. The real challenge is when the game combines a group of enemies and one closed room, this happens quite often ambushes. It's not bad, it's actually what these kind of games and I love it, but it can be sometimes quite cheap. The WORST enemy would be the railgun laser alien. He charges up his laser and no matter where you are, how fast you are, you're gonna get hit unless you hide behind a wall, preferably one of the size of a chest. They're specially annoying when they're placed real far away from you, behind a bunch of of enemies and you can't hear them charge their laser rifle!
Now I don't like boss fight, however, most of the ones in this game are tolerable. Except for three of them: the last one (annoying, but hard as expected), the penultimate and the second one. All because of black missiles! They're heat seeking missiles and they track you so well that not a even a speedhacks can save you!
Now, what I've been saying during the rest of the review might make Wrack seem like an average game, but I don't think I should demand immensely from a game with a 15 euro price tag. Even then, I would recommend other games like Brutal Doom for it's gore and Rise of the Triad (2013) for its expansive levels over this one. But you know what, a simple (by that I don't mean one that shoves you into a gritty and grey line), fast-paced, short (5 hours) and well constructed first person shooter in the middle of time where you don't get much Doom-like games like this one is more than welcome. So I recommend it!
